lessons.title: Flutter and Dart: the big picture
lessons.summaryHtml:
Flutter is Google’s open-source UI toolkit for building apps for Android, iOS, web, Windows, macOS and Linux from one codebase. You write the app in Dart, a typed language that compiles to fast native machine code for release builds and supports hot reload while you develop.

Flutter does not wrap the platform’s own buttons and lists. It draws every pixel itself with its own rendering engine, so your app looks the same everywhere. You describe the screen as a tree of widgets; when data changes, Flutter rebuilds the widgets and repaints only what changed.

In this track you learn Dart first, then Flutter layout, theming, navigation, state management (ending with BLoC), data, testing and publishing, building a small app in each module.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Flutter is a toolkit for building apps. You write your app once, in a language called Dart, and Flutter turns it into an Android app, an iPhone app, a website and a desktop program for Windows, macOS or Linux.

Think of Flutter as a painter who brings their own canvas and paint to every house. Other tools ask each house (Android, iOS, the browser) to lend them its furniture: its buttons, its lists, its text boxes. Flutter does not borrow. It paints every pixel itself. That is why a Flutter app looks the same on a cheap Android phone and on a new iPhone, unless you decide it should not.

You build the screen out of widgets. A widget is a small description of a piece of UI: “some text”, “a row of things”, “16 pixels of padding”, “a whole page with an app bar”. You nest widgets inside widgets, like boxes inside boxes, until you have a full screen.

Why it matters

Most companies need their app on Android and iOS, and often on the web too. Building each one separately means two or three teams, two or three codebases and bugs fixed two or three times. With Flutter, a small team ships one codebase to all of them. That is why agencies and start-ups like it: a single developer can deliver a client app for both stores.

For you as a developer, Flutter has three big benefits:

  • Speed of development. Hot reload shows your change in about a second without losing where you are in the app.
  • Full control of the design. Because Flutter paints everything, a custom design from a designer is not harder than a standard one.
  • Good performance. Release builds are compiled to native machine code, and the engine is built to draw smooth animations.

Flutter jobs usually ask for the same core skills this track teaches: Dart, layouts, state management (often BLoC or Provider), REST APIs, local storage, Firebase, testing and publishing to the stores.

How it works

To understand Flutter you need four ideas: its layers, the role of Dart, widgets as descriptions, and the trees Flutter keeps behind the scenes.

The layers

A Flutter app has three layers. You mostly work in the top one.

LayerWhat it doesWritten in
FrameworkWidgets, layout, Material Design components, animation, gestures. This is the code you import with package:flutter/material.dart.Dart
EngineDraws pixels (with the Impeller renderer on iOS and modern Android), lays out text, runs Dart, talks to the GPU.C++
EmbedderHosts the engine inside each platform: creates the window, passes touches and keyboard input, gives access to plugins.Kotlin/Java, Swift/Objective-C, C++ and others

Where Dart fits

Dart was designed for building user interfaces, and Flutter uses two of its tricks:

  • JIT (just-in-time) compilation in debug mode. The Dart VM can swap in changed code while the app runs. This is what powers hot reload.
  • AOT (ahead-of-time) compilation in release mode. Your code is compiled to native ARM or x64 machine code before it ships, so it starts fast and runs predictably. For the web, Dart compiles to JavaScript or WebAssembly.

Dart is also type-safe and null-safe, which catches many mistakes in the editor before you even run the app. Module 1 teaches Dart properly before you touch widgets.

Widgets and the declarative idea

In older UI toolkits you created a label, kept a reference to it, and later said “label, change your text”. Flutter is declarative: you write a build method that describes what the screen looks like for the current data. When the data changes, Flutter calls build again and compares the new description with the old one. It then updates only the parts of the screen that really changed.

A common way to say this is UI = f(state): the interface is a function of the state.

Here is a complete Flutter app. Read it from the top: main calls runApp with the root widget, MaterialApp sets up the theme, Scaffold gives a standard page with an app bar, and Center, Column, Icon and Text build the body.

Screen 1: Hello Flutter lib/main.dart

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

void main() {
  runApp(const HelloApp());
}

class HelloApp extends StatelessWidget {
  const HelloApp({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MaterialApp(
      theme: ThemeData(
        colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Colors.indigo),
      ),
      home: Scaffold(
        appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Hello Flutter')),
        body: const Center(
          child: Column(
            mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
            children: [
              Icon(Icons.flutter_dash, size: 64),
              SizedBox(height: 12),
              Text('Everything here is a widget'),
            ],
          ),
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

A complete app: MaterialApp gives the theme, Scaffold gives the page, and Center, Column, Icon and Text are all widgets nested in a tree.

Notice three things you will see in every Flutter file:

  • StatelessWidget with a build(BuildContext context) method that returns widgets.
  • const in front of widgets that never change, which lets Flutter skip rebuilding them.
  • ColorScheme.fromSeed: you give one colour and Material 3 generates a full, matching palette.

Three trees (a first look)

Widgets are cheap, short-lived descriptions. Behind them Flutter keeps an element tree (which widget is mounted where, and which state belongs to it) and a render tree (objects that know their size and position and paint themselves). You write widgets; Flutter manages the other two. Lesson 2.1 goes deep on this.

Example: a tour of the course apps

Each module ends with a small app you can show in a portfolio. The first ones are console programs, so you can focus on Dart without any UI.

ModuleAppWhat it teaches
1 Dart in depthGrade Book, Library Manager, Weather Fetcher (console)Types, null safety, classes, async code
2 Flutter fundamentalsBusiness Card, counter and tip calculatorMaterialApp, Scaffold, stateless and stateful widgets
3 LayoutRecipe BookRows, columns, constraints, lists and grids
4 Material and themingTravel ExplorerMaterial 3 components, dark mode, custom widgets
5 Navigation and formsShop Catalog, Event RegistrationNavigator, go_router, validated forms
6 State managementShopping Cart (Provider), Task Tracker (BLoC)App state, Cubit, Bloc, testing blocs
7 Data and backendNews Reader, Notes, ChatHTTP and JSON, local storage, Firebase
8 Polish and shipOnboardingAnimations, tests, performance, publishing

Below is a small version of the Task Tracker. Switch between the two frames: tapping a checkbox changes the data in _tasks, setState asks Flutter to rebuild, and the “tasks left” text updates by itself. You never write “change that label”.

Screen 2: Task Tracker preview lib/main.dart

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

void main() => runApp(const TaskApp());

class TaskApp extends StatelessWidget {
  const TaskApp({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MaterialApp(
      title: 'Task Tracker',
      theme: ThemeData(
        colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Colors.teal),
      ),
      home: const TaskScreen(),
    );
  }
}

class TaskScreen extends StatefulWidget {
  const TaskScreen({super.key});

  @override
  State<TaskScreen> createState() => _TaskScreenState();
}

class _TaskScreenState extends State<TaskScreen> {
  final _tasks = <String, bool>{
    'Buy groceries': true,
    'Finish Dart lesson': false,
    'Call the client': false,
  };

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final left = _tasks.values.where((done) => !done).length;
    final label = left == 1 ? '1 task left' : '$left tasks left';
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('My tasks')),
      body: ListView(
        children: [
          Padding(
            padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
            child: Text(label,
                style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleMedium),
          ),
          for (final entry in _tasks.entries)
            CheckboxListTile(
              title: Text(entry.key),
              value: entry.value,
              onChanged: (value) {
                setState(() {
                  _tasks[entry.key] = value ?? false;
                });
              },
            ),
        ],
      ),
      floatingActionButton: FloatingActionButton(
        onPressed: () {},
        child: const Icon(Icons.add),
      ),
    );
  }
}

A small finished app. Tapping a checkbox calls setState, Flutter rebuilds the list and the “tasks left” count updates. You will rebuild this app properly with BLoC in module 6. States: Start → After one tap.

You do not need to understand every line yet. By the end of module 2 you will be able to write this from memory, and in module 6 you will rebuild it with BLoC, the architecture many production teams use.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking Flutter is a web view. It is not. Flutter apps are compiled and draw with their own engine; they do not run HTML inside the app.
  • Skipping Dart. Many beginners jump straight into widgets and then struggle with null safety, async code and classes. Learn the language first; widgets become much easier.
  • Judging performance in debug mode. Debug builds use JIT and extra checks, so they can feel slow. Measure speed with a profile or release build (flutter run --profile or --release).
  • Expecting native look automatically. Material widgets look like Material on iOS too. If a client wants an iOS look, use the Cupertino widgets or adaptive constructors on purpose.
  • Treating widgets like objects you edit. You do not keep a reference to a Text and change it. You change the data and rebuild.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “How is Flutter different from React Native?” A good short answer: React Native renders the platform’s own native components and runs JavaScript; Flutter paints its own widgets with its own engine and compiles Dart to native code. Avoid claiming one is always faster; say it depends on the app.
  • “Why Dart?” Mention JIT for hot reload in development, AOT for fast release builds, sound null safety, and a single language for UI and logic.
  • “What is a widget?” An immutable description of part of the UI. The framework compares widgets between builds and updates the element and render trees.
  • In client work, Flutter shines for custom-branded apps that must ship on Android and iOS together. For apps that are mostly heavy native features (for example deep system integrations), you may still write some platform code through plugins or platform channels, covered in module 8.
Remember: in Flutter you describe the screen for the current data. Change the data, and the framework rebuilds the screen for you.

terms.definition: Google’s open-source UI toolkit that builds apps for mobile, web and desktop from one Dart codebase.
The client-optimised, typed language Flutter apps are written in. It compiles ahead of time for release and just in time for development.
An immutable description of part of the UI, such as a Text, a Row or a whole screen.
The part of Flutter that lays out and paints pixels on a canvas; Impeller is the default renderer on iOS and modern Android.
Injects changed code into the running app and rebuilds the UI in about a second while keeping the current state.
You describe what the UI should look like for the current state; the framework works out how to update the screen.

quiz.question: How does Flutter put a button on the screen?
options: It asks Android or iOS to create a native button
It draws the button itself with its own rendering engine
It embeds a web page in a WebView
It converts Dart code to Kotlin or Swift first
quiz.explanation: Flutter paints its own widgets on a canvas through its engine. That is why a Flutter button looks the same on every platform unless you choose otherwise.

quiz.question: Why can a Flutter release build start fast and run smoothly on a phone?
options: Dart is interpreted line by line
The app downloads code from a server
Dart is compiled ahead of time (AOT) to native machine code
Flutter uses the phone’s JavaScript engine
quiz.explanation: Release builds are compiled ahead of time to native ARM or x64 code. Debug builds use a JIT compiler, which is what makes hot reload possible.

quiz.question: What does “declarative UI” mean in Flutter?
options: You describe the UI for the current state and Flutter rebuilds when the state changes
You write XML layout files and connect them to code
You change each label and colour by hand when data changes
You design screens only in a visual editor
quiz.explanation: In Flutter the UI is a function of state. You change the state (for example with setState) and the framework rebuilds the widgets that depend on it.

quiz.question: Which statement about widgets is correct?
options: Only buttons and text are widgets
Widgets are mutable objects that you edit in place
Widgets are the pixels on screen
Layouts, padding, text and whole screens are all widgets, combined into a tree
quiz.explanation: Everything you compose in Flutter is a widget: Padding, Row, Text, Scaffold and your own screens. They are small, immutable descriptions arranged in a tree.

lessons.title: Set up your machine
lessons.summaryHtml:
To build Flutter apps you need the Flutter SDK (which includes Dart), an editor such as VS Code with the Flutter extension or Android Studio with the Flutter plugin, and at least one place to run the app: an Android emulator, a real phone, Chrome or your desktop. iOS and macOS builds need a Mac with Xcode.

flutter doctor checks your setup and tells you exactly what is missing. flutter create makes a new project, and flutter run starts it with hot reload. DartPad runs Dart and Flutter in the browser with nothing to install, which is perfect for the small examples in this course.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Before you can build Flutter apps, your computer needs a small workshop: the Flutter SDK (the tools and the framework, with Dart included), an editor to write code, and somewhere to run the app, such as an Android emulator, your own phone, Chrome or your desktop.

Setting up is like preparing a kitchen before cooking. It takes an hour or two the first time, and then you rarely think about it again. Flutter even includes an inspector for your kitchen: flutter doctor checks every tool and tells you what is missing.

If you want to start right now, DartPad (dartpad.dev) runs Dart and Flutter code in the browser. Most small examples in this course work there. It cannot run plugins such as Firebase or sqflite, so for those lessons you need the full setup.

Why it matters

A broken setup wastes more beginner hours than any language feature. Common problems are a missing Android licence, an emulator that will not start, or two different Flutter versions on the same machine. A clean, checked setup means that when something fails, it is your code and not your tools.

In a job, you will also set up machines for new projects, CI servers and teammates. Knowing what each piece does (SDK, toolchain, device, editor) makes you the person who can fix “it works on my machine” problems.

How it works

The setup has five parts. Install them in this order, and run flutter doctor after each one.

1. Install the Flutter SDK

Follow the install guide for your operating system on docs.flutter.dev. You can either let the VS Code Flutter extension download the SDK for you, or download it yourself and add its bin folder to your PATH. The SDK contains the flutter command, the framework source, the engine and a matching Dart SDK, so you do not install Dart separately.

Check it works in a new terminal:

flutter --version
flutter doctor

Stay on the stable channel for course work and client projects. Update later with flutter upgrade.

2. Choose an editor

EditorAddGood for
VS CodeThe Flutter extension (it installs the Dart extension too)Light and fast; the most common choice
Android StudioThe Flutter plugin (it adds the Dart plugin)Includes the Android SDK and emulator manager in one place

Both give you code completion, quick fixes, a debugger, hot reload on save and access to Flutter DevTools.

3. Set up a target platform

  • Android: install Android Studio (even if you code in VS Code) to get the Android SDK, command-line tools and an emulator. Then accept the licences with flutter doctor --android-licenses. Create a virtual device in the Device Manager, or connect a real phone with USB debugging turned on in Developer options.
  • iOS and macOS: need a Mac with Xcode. Open the iOS Simulator from Xcode, or connect an iPhone.
  • Web: Chrome is enough.
  • Desktop: each desktop platform builds on its own OS. Windows desktop apps need Visual Studio (not VS Code) with the “Desktop development with C++” workload.

List what Flutter can see:

flutter devices
flutter emulators
flutter emulators --launch <emulator_id>

4. Create and run a project

flutter create hello_flutter
cd hello_flutter
flutter run

Use lowercase with underscores for project names. In real projects add your organisation’s reverse domain, which becomes the Android package and iOS bundle ID: flutter create --org com.ralfiz hello_flutter. Changing it later is tedious, so choose it at the start.

While flutter run is active in a terminal, press r for hot reload, R for hot restart and q to quit. In VS Code, saving a file triggers hot reload.

Hot reloadHot restartFull restart
Keeps app stateYesNoNo
SpeedAbout a secondA few secondsFull build
Use afterChanging build methods and most codeChanging main(), global or static initialisers, or when the screen looks staleAdding a plugin, changing native files or pubspec assets

5. Know the project structure

PathWhat it holds
lib/main.dartYour Dart code starts here. Nearly all your work lives in lib/.
pubspec.yamlApp name, version, Dart SDK constraint, dependencies, assets and fonts.
pubspec.lockThe exact package versions resolved. Commit it for apps.
test/Tests; the template includes widget_test.dart.
analysis_options.yamlLint rules, starting with the recommended flutter_lints set.
android/, ios/, web/, windows/, macos/, linux/Platform host projects: icons, permissions, signing, native settings.
build/, .dart_tool/Generated files. Never edit or commit them.

Packages are added with flutter pub add, which updates pubspec.yaml and downloads the package:

flutter pub add http
flutter pub get

Example: your first run of the counter app

Every new project starts with the counter app. It is worth reading slowly, because it already contains the core of Flutter: a stateless root widget, a stateful page, setState and a theme built from a seed colour.

  1. Run flutter create --org com.example hello_flutter, open the folder in your editor, and choose a device in the status bar (VS Code) or the device menu (Android Studio).
  2. Start the app with flutter run or the Run button. The first Android build takes a few minutes while Gradle downloads its tools; later builds are much faster.
  3. Tap the + button three times. The number goes from 0 to 3.
  4. Change the text 'You have pushed the button this many times:' to 'Taps so far:' and save. Hot reload shows the new text and the counter still says 3.
  5. Now press R for hot restart. The counter goes back to 0, because the whole app, and its state, was restarted.

Screen 1: The starter counter app lib/main.dart

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

void main() {
  runApp(const MyApp());
}

class MyApp extends StatelessWidget {
  const MyApp({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MaterialApp(
      title: 'Flutter Demo',
      theme: ThemeData(
        colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Colors.deepPurple),
      ),
      home: const MyHomePage(title: 'Flutter Demo Home Page'),
    );
  }
}

class MyHomePage extends StatefulWidget {
  const MyHomePage({super.key, required this.title});

  final String title;

  @override
  State<MyHomePage> createState() => _MyHomePageState();
}

class _MyHomePageState extends State<MyHomePage> {
  int _counter = 0;

  void _incrementCounter() {
    setState(() {
      _counter++;
    });
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(
        backgroundColor: Theme.of(context).colorScheme.inversePrimary,
        title: Text(widget.title),
      ),
      body: Center(
        child: Column(
          mainAxisAlignment: MainAxisAlignment.center,
          children: [
            const Text('You have pushed the button this many times:'),
            Text(
              '$_counter',
              style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.headlineMedium,
            ),
          ],
        ),
      ),
      floatingActionButton: FloatingActionButton(
        onPressed: _incrementCounter,
        tooltip: 'Increment',
        child: const Icon(Icons.add),
      ),
    );
  }
}

A trimmed copy of what flutter create generates. Each tap on + calls setState, which rebuilds the widget and shows the new count. The app bar uses the colour scheme’s inversePrimary role. States: First run → After 3 taps.

This is a trimmed copy of the generated code (the template also has comments explaining each part). You will write your own version in the lab.

Common mistakes

  • Ignoring flutter doctor. Read every line with a cross or an exclamation mark. It usually names the fix, for example running flutter doctor --android-licenses.
  • Installing the SDK in a protected folder such as C:\Program Files, or a path with spaces or special characters. Use something like C:\dev\flutter or ~/development/flutter.
  • Two Flutter SDKs on one machine. Your terminal and your editor may use different ones. Check with which flutter (macOS/Linux) or where flutter (Windows), and point the editor at the same SDK.
  • Expecting hot reload to pick up everything. Changes to main(), static fields, native code, plugins and assets need a hot restart or a full rebuild.
  • Editing files in build/ or committing them. They are regenerated on every build. Keep them out of version control.
  • Using CamelCase or hyphens in project names. Dart package names must be lowercase with underscores.

Interview and real-world notes

  • You may be asked “What is the difference between hot reload and hot restart?” Answer with state: reload keeps it, restart resets it, and explain when reload is not enough.
  • On a team, everyone should use the same Flutter version. Many teams record it in the README or use a version manager such as FVM, and CI pins the same version.
  • Start every project with the --org you will publish under. The package name appears in the Play Store URL and cannot change after publishing.
  • Keep flutter analyze clean from day one. Reviewers notice warnings.
Watch out: DartPad is great for learning widgets, but it cannot run packages that need native code (Firebase, sqflite, image_picker). Set up an emulator or phone before module 7.

lessons.title: Dart basics: variables, types and operators
lessons.summaryHtml:
Every Dart value has a type: int, double, String, bool and many more. You declare variables with var (type inferred, can be reassigned), final (set once) or const (fixed at compile time), and Dart checks types before the program runs.

Operators combine values: / always gives a double, ~/ gives a whole-number result, and % gives the remainder. Strings use $name interpolation, and you convert between types with int.parse, toString and toStringAsFixed. You start the Grade Book console app, which grows through module 1.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A program works with values: a student’s name, a mark, whether they passed. A variable is a labelled box that holds a value. A type says what kind of value may go in the box: whole numbers, decimals, text, true/false.

Dart is statically typed. The type of every variable is known before the program runs, so the editor can warn you when you try to put text into a number box. You do not always have to write the type; Dart can infer it from the first value you store.

Operators are the verbs: + adds, / divides, == compares, && means “and”. Together, variables, types and operators are enough to build the first version of our Grade Book.

Why it matters

Every Flutter screen is built from these basics. A price label divides and formats numbers. A login button checks two conditions with &&. A counter changes a variable. Mistakes here, such as dividing two ints and expecting an int back, or comparing decimals with ==, cause real bugs in real apps: wrong totals on an invoice, a progress bar stuck at 0.

Choosing final and const well also matters in Flutter specifically: const widgets are created once and reused, which saves work on every rebuild.

How it works

Run any snippet below in DartPad or with dart run. Each is a complete program or a part of main().

Declaring variables

void main() {
  var city = 'Kochi';          // inferred as String, can change
  city = 'Calicut';            // OK: same type
  // city = 42;                // error: an int is not a String

  final joined = DateTime.now(); // set once, value known at run time
  const maxMarks = 100;          // compile-time constant

  String course = 'Flutter';   // explicit type
  int? rank;                   // nullable: may hold null (lesson 1.2)

  print('$city $joined $maxMarks $course $rank');
}
KeywordCan reassign?When is the value fixed?Use for
varYesNeverValues that change, such as a running total
finalNoAt run time, when first assignedMost local variables; values read from input or computed
constNoAt compile timeLiteral settings such as pass marks, padding sizes, const widgets

A final list can still have items added; only the variable cannot point to a different list. A const list is deeply immutable. You will use that difference in lesson 1.5.

The core types

TypeExampleNotes
int42, -7, 0xFFWhole numbers. On the web they follow JavaScript number rules.
double3.5, 1e364-bit floating point decimals.
numeitherSupertype of int and double.
String'Asha', "Asha"UTF-16 text. Single quotes are the Dart style.
booltrue, falseOnly real booleans work in if; if (1) is an error.
Object? / dynamicanythingObject? keeps type checks; dynamic switches them off.

Arithmetic and assignment

void main() {
  const total = 256;
  print(total / 3);    // 85.33333333333333  (/ always gives a double)
  print(total ~/ 3);   // 85                 (~/ truncates to an int)
  print(total % 3);    // 1                  (remainder)

  var score = 10;
  score += 5;          // 15, same as score = score + 5
  score++;             // 16
  score ~/= 3;         // 5
  print(score);
}

Mixing types works where it is safe: 2 + 1.5 is 3.5. But you cannot store a double into an int variable: int avg = total / 3; is a compile error. Choose ~/, round(), floor() or toInt() on purpose.

Comparison, logic and the conditional operator

void main() {
  const mark = 72;
  const attendance = 0.81;
  final passed = mark >= 40 && attendance >= 0.75;
  final needsHelp = mark < 50 || attendance < 0.6;
  final label = passed ? 'Pass' : 'Fail';
  print('$passed $needsHelp $label'); // true false Pass
  print(mark is int);                 // true
}

&& and || short-circuit: if the left side already decides the result, the right side is not evaluated. is tests a type, and as casts (it throws if the cast is wrong, so prefer is).

Strings

void main() {
  const name = 'Asha';
  const marks = 92;
  print('$name scored $marks');          // interpolation
  print('Name length: ' + name.length.toString());
  final len = name.length;
  print('Name length: $len');            // same result, cleaner
  print('It\'s done');                   // escape a quote
  print(r'Raw: $name \n stays as typed'); // raw string
  print('''Line one
Line two''');                            // multi-line string
  print('ab' * 3);                       // ababab
}

$name inserts a variable. It only takes a simple identifier, so '$name.length' prints Asha.length. For anything more than a name, compute a local variable first (as with len above) or use concatenation.

Converting between types

void main() {
  final age = int.parse('21');           // String to int
  final price = double.parse('49.5');    // String to double
  final maybe = int.tryParse('abc');     // null instead of an exception
  final text = age.toString();           // int to String
  final avg = 256 / 3;
  print(avg.toStringAsFixed(1));         // 85.3
  print(avg.round());                    // 85
  print('$age $price $maybe $text');
}

Use tryParse for anything a user typed. parse throws a FormatException on bad input.

Everything is an object

In Dart every value is an object, even numbers, booleans and null. That means values have methods and properties you can call directly:

void main() {
  print(7.isOdd);              // true
  print(3.7.floor());          // 3
  print((-12).abs());          // 12
  print('flutter'.toUpperCase()); // FLUTTER
  print(' Asha '.trim().length);  // 4
  print(42.runtimeType);       // int
}

Your editor’s code completion is the fastest way to explore these: type a value, a dot, and read the list. Because the types are known before the program runs, completion only offers methods that really exist on that type, which is one of the everyday benefits of static typing.

One platform detail is worth knowing early. On phones and desktops, an int is a 64-bit integer. When Dart is compiled to JavaScript for the web, numbers follow JavaScript rules, so very large integers lose precision and a whole-number double such as 3.0 prints as 3. For normal app values this never matters, but it explains small differences you may see in DartPad.

Example: Grade Book v1

The Grade Book is our module 1 console app. Version 1 stores one student’s marks in variables and prints a report card. Later lessons add null safety, loops, functions, classes and async loading.

void main() {
  const courseName = 'Flutter Foundations';
  const passMark = 40;
  final studentName = 'Asha Menon';
  final math = 88;
  final science = 76;
  final english = 92;

  final total = math + science + english;
  final average = total / 3;
  final avgText = average.toStringAsFixed(1);
  final passed = math >= passMark && science >= passMark && english >= passMark;
  final result = passed ? 'PASS' : 'FAIL';

  print('$courseName report');
  print('Student: $studentName');
  print('Total: $total / 300');
  print('Average: $avgText');
  print('Result: $result');
}

Output:

Flutter Foundations report
Student: Asha Menon
Total: 256 / 300
Average: 85.3
Result: PASS

Notice the choices: const for values fixed in the source, final for everything computed once, and a local avgText so the print line uses plain $avgText interpolation.

Common mistakes

  • Expecting / to give an int. 7 / 2 is 3.5. Use ~/ for whole-number division.
  • Comparing doubles with ==. 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false. Compare with a small tolerance, or store money as integer paise or cents.
  • Writing '$user.name' and getting the object followed by “.name”. Only a plain identifier follows $.
  • Using var everywhere. It hides intent. If a value never changes, final tells readers and the compiler so.
  • Using dynamic to “make errors go away”. The errors come back at run time, often in front of a user.
  • Using int.parse on user input. One stray space or letter throws. Use int.tryParse and handle null.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “final vs const?” Both are single assignment. const must be known at compile time and creates canonical, deeply immutable values; final can be computed at run time. In Flutter, const widget constructors let the framework reuse instances.
  • “dynamic vs Object?” Both can hold anything. Object? still requires a check or cast before calling specific methods; dynamic allows any call and fails at run time.
  • For money in real apps, avoid doubles for stored amounts. Keep the smallest unit as an int and format only for display (the intl package helps with currency formats later).
  • Code style matters in reviews: lowerCamelCase for variables, single quotes for strings, and a clean dart analyze.
Remember: default to final, use const for compile-time values, and var only for values that really change.

Answers

  1. C. / always returns a double (3.5). ~/ divides and truncates towards zero, so 7 ~/ 2 is 3 and -7 ~/ 2 is -3, not -4. % gives the remainder 1.
  2. B. $name only takes the identifier name, so .length is printed as plain text. The addition in brackets runs first (100), then toString() turns it into text.
  3. A. Doubles are binary floating point, so 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 and not equal to 0.3. toStringAsFixed(2) rounds to 0.30. An int and a double with the same numeric value compare equal.
  4. D. c is a copy of the value in b, so changing c does not change b. Every value here is an int, so is int is true and runtimeType prints int.

lessons.examTip: Default to final for local variables. Reach for var only when the value really changes, and const for values fixed at compile time. Reviewers and the linter will ask for this.

quiz.question: You write final total = 90; and later total = 95;. What happens?
options: It compiles and total becomes 95
It is a compile-time error because a final variable can be assigned only once
It throws an exception when the line runs
total becomes a double
quiz.explanation: final means single assignment. The analyzer reports the second assignment as an error before the program runs.

quiz.question: Which declaration is NOT allowed?
options: final now = DateTime.now();
var count = 0;
const now = DateTime.now();
const pi = 3.14159;
quiz.explanation: const needs a value known at compile time. DateTime.now() is only known when the program runs, so it can be final but not const.

quiz.question: marks is an int holding 256. Which expression gives the average of 3 subjects as a double?
options: marks / 3
marks ~/ 3
marks % 3
int.parse(marks) / 3
quiz.explanation: The / operator always returns a double. ~/ truncates to an int, and % returns the remainder.

quiz.question: Why should you usually avoid declaring variables as dynamic?
options: dynamic variables use more memory
dynamic cannot hold strings
dynamic is deprecated in Dart 3
It turns off static type checking, so mistakes show up only at run time
quiz.explanation: With dynamic, the analyzer lets any method call through. Typos and wrong types become run-time crashes instead of editor errors. Prefer a real type or Object?.

lessons.title: Null safety in depth
lessons.summaryHtml:
Dart has sound null safety: a variable of type String can never be null. If a value may be missing, you say so with String?, and the compiler makes you handle the null case before you use it.

You handle nulls with ?? (default value), ??= (assign if null), ?. (call only if not null), an if (x != null) check that promotes the type, or, as a last resort, ! (“I promise it is not null”). late delays initialisation, and required marks named parameters that callers must pass. Grade Book v2 handles absent students and missing marks safely.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

null means “no value”: a student with no nickname, a mark for an exam they missed, a user who has not logged in yet. In many languages any variable can secretly be null, and the program crashes the moment you use it. Tony Hoare, who introduced null references, later called them his “billion-dollar mistake”.

Dart fixes this with sound null safety. Types are non-nullable by default: a String is always a real string. If a value might be missing, you must say so by adding a question mark, String?. The compiler then refuses to let you use it as a plain String until you have dealt with the null case.

It is like a form with required and optional fields. Required fields are always filled in. Optional fields are clearly marked, and you must check them before relying on them.

Why it matters

Null errors were once the most common crash in mobile apps. In Flutter, data comes from many uncertain places: JSON from an API with missing fields, a search that finds nothing, a text field the user left empty, a logged-out user. Null safety moves those problems from run time (a crash on the user’s phone) to compile time (a red line in your editor).

Because Dart’s null safety is sound, the compiler can trust it completely: if the type says non-nullable, it can never be null at run time. That also lets the compiler generate faster code.

How it works

Nullable and non-nullable types

void main() {
  String name = 'Asha';
  // name = null;            // error: String cannot hold null
  String? nickname;          // nullable, starts as null
  int? absentMark = null;    // explicit null is fine too
  print('$name $nickname $absentMark'); // Asha null null
}

Non-nullable local variables do not need a value right away, but they must be definitely assigned before they are read. Dart’s flow analysis checks every path.

The null-aware operators

OperatorMeaningExampleResult when x is null
??Use a fallbackx ?? 'Guest''Guest'
??=Assign only if nullx ??= 'Guest';x becomes 'Guest'
?.Call only if not nullx?.lengthnull
?[]Index only if not nulllist?[0]null
...?Spread only if not null[...?extras]Adds nothing
!Assert not nullx!.lengthThrows a TypeError
 
void main() {
  final marks = {'Math': 88, 'Science': 76};
  final history = marks['History'];        // int? because the key may be missing
  print(history ?? 0);                      // 0
  final label = history?.toString() ?? 'not taken';
  print('History: ' + label);               // History: not taken
}

Chains of ?. short-circuit: in user?.address.city, if user is null the whole expression is null and .city is never called.

Type promotion with flow analysis

Once you check a local variable for null, Dart promotes it to the non-nullable type inside the safe region:

String describe(int? mark) {
  if (mark == null) {
    return 'absent';
  }
  // From here on, mark is promoted to int.
  final grade = mark >= 40 ? 'pass' : 'fail';
  return '$mark ($grade)';
}

void main() {
  print(describe(null)); // absent
  print(describe(72));   // 72 (pass)
}

Promotion also works with if (mark != null) { ... }, early return, throw, is checks and &&. It works on local variables and parameters. Since Dart 3.2, private final fields can be promoted as well. Public fields and non-final fields are not promoted, because another piece of code (or a subclass getter) could return a different value on the second read. The fix is to copy the field into a local variable:

class Student {
  Student(this.name, {this.nickname});
  final String name;
  String? nickname; // public and mutable: will not promote

  String get displayName {
    final nick = nickname;          // copy to a local
    if (nick != null && nick.isNotEmpty) return nick;
    return name;
  }
}

void main() {
  print(Student('Asha Menon', nickname: 'Ash').displayName); // Ash
  print(Student('Ravi Kumar').displayName);                 // Ravi Kumar
}

The ! operator: use sparingly

value! tells the compiler “trust me, this is not null”. If you are wrong, the app throws at run time with “Null check operator used on a null value”, one of the most common Flutter crash messages. Use ! only when a null truly means a bug, such as reading a map key you just inserted. Otherwise prefer a check, ?? or ?..

late: initialise later

late final String reportTitle;   // assigned once, later

String loadConfig() {
  print('Reading config...');
  return 'dark';
}

void main() {
  reportTitle = 'Term 1';
  late final theme = loadConfig(); // lazy: runs on first read
  print(reportTitle);
  print(theme);                    // prints Reading config... then dark
}

late moves the “is it assigned?” check from compile time to run time. Reading it too early throws LateInitializationError. In Flutter, you will see late for things created in initState, such as an AnimationController. A late variable with an initialiser is lazy: the expression runs only when first read.

required named parameters

String formatLine({required String subject, int? mark}) {
  if (mark == null) return '$subject: absent';
  return '$subject: $mark';
}

void main() {
  print(formatLine(subject: 'Math', mark: 88)); // Math: 88
  print(formatLine(subject: 'Science'));        // Science: absent
  // formatLine(mark: 50);                      // error: subject is required
}

Named parameters are optional unless marked required. An optional one must be nullable or have a default. This is exactly how Flutter widgets declare parameters, for example Text(data, style: ...) and MyHomePage({super.key, required this.title}).

Choosing between nullable, late and a default

When a variable has no value yet, you have three honest options. Pick by asking what “no value” means in your app:

SituationChooseExample
The value may genuinely be missing, and the UI should show thatNullable typeString? nickname, int? mark for an absent student
There is a sensible neutral valueNon-nullable with a defaultint attempts = 0, List<String> tags = const []
The value always exists before use but cannot be created at declarationlateA controller created in initState

Most nulls enter your app at the edges: user input, JSON, databases, platform APIs. Resolve them there, once, and pass clean non-nullable values inward:

int readMark(String typed) {
  final parsed = int.tryParse(typed.trim()); // int?
  return parsed ?? 0;                        // int from here on
}

void main() {
  print(readMark(' 72 ')); // 72
  print(readMark('abc'));  // 0
}

Example: Grade Book v2

Real grade data has holes: a student missed an exam, some have nicknames, a subject may not exist. Version 2 models these with nullable types and handles every case without a single !.

String? nicknameFor(String name) {
  const nicknames = {'Asha Menon': 'Ash'};
  return nicknames[name];
}

void main() {
  final Map<String, int?> marks = {'Math': 88, 'Science': null, 'English': 92};
  final display = nicknameFor('Asha Menon') ?? 'Asha Menon';
  print('Student: $display');

  var total = 0;
  var attempted = 0;
  for (final subject in marks.keys) {
    final mark = marks[subject];          // int?
    if (mark != null) {
      total += mark;                      // promoted to int
      attempted++;
    }
    print(mark == null ? '$subject: absent' : '$subject: $mark');
  }

  final double? average = attempted == 0 ? null : total / attempted;
  final avgText = average?.toStringAsFixed(1) ?? 'n/a';
  print('Attempted: $attempted, average: $avgText');
}

Output: Student: Ash, then Math: 88, Science: absent, English: 92, and Attempted: 2, average: 90.0. The lab adds a late title, a required parameter and a missing-subject lookup.

Common mistakes

  • Adding ! whenever the compiler complains. It silences the error by turning it into a possible crash. Ask “what should happen if this is null?” and write that.
  • Making everything nullable. String? everywhere spreads null checks through the whole app. Keep values non-nullable and resolve nulls at the edges (parsing JSON, reading input).
  • Expecting fields to promote. Copy a public or mutable field to a local variable, then check it.
  • Using late to avoid thinking. If the value might genuinely be absent, it should be nullable, not late.
  • Forgetting that map lookups are nullable. map[key] returns V? because the key may not exist.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “What does sound null safety mean?” Non-nullable types can never contain null at run time; the guarantee holds across the whole program, so the compiler can rely on it.
  • “When would you use late?” For values that cannot be created in the constructor but will definitely exist before use, such as controllers set up in initState, or for expensive values you want computed lazily.
  • “Why does my field not promote?” Explain that only locals, parameters and private final fields promote, and show the local-copy fix.
  • In API models, decide per field: required fields are non-nullable and fail fast when missing; optional fields are nullable with a clear default in the UI.
Watch out: “Null check operator used on a null value” in a Flutter error log always points to a !. Search your code for it first.

Answers

  1. B. ?. returns null when the receiver is null instead of calling length. ?? falls back to Guest, which has 5 characters.
  2. A. Asha and Anu start with A and get 2 each; Ravi gets null, which ?? turns into 0. 80 + 2 + 0 + 2 = 84.
  3. C. Reading a late variable before it is assigned throws LateInitializationError, which the catch block handles. After the assignment it reads normally.
  4. D. A late variable with an initialiser is lazy: load() runs on the first read, after before is printed, and only once because the result is stored.
  5. A. A map lookup returns a nullable value. Asha exists, so ! is safe and a is 91. Charu is not a key, so c is null and prints as null.

terms.definition: A type with ? such as int? that allows null as well as normal values.
Flow analysis treating a nullable local variable as non-nullable after a null check proves it is not null.
Casts away nullability; throws a TypeError at run time if the value is actually null.
Marks a non-nullable variable that is initialised later, or lazily on first read if it has an initialiser.
Keyword that makes a named parameter mandatory, so callers must pass it.
The guarantee that a non-nullable expression can never evaluate to null at run time.

lessons.examTip: Count the ! operators in a code review. Each one is a possible crash; most can be replaced by a local variable plus a null check, ?? or ?..

quiz.question: What is the difference between String and String? in Dart 3?
options: String? is a slower String
There is no difference at run time or compile time
String can never hold null; String? can hold a string or null
String? is only for text read from files
quiz.explanation: With sound null safety, non-nullable types exclude null. Adding ? creates a nullable type, and the compiler forces you to handle the null case.

quiz.question: user.nickname is a public, non-final field of type String?. After if (user.nickname != null), you still cannot call user.nickname.length. Why?
options: Null checks never promote in Dart
A public non-final field could change between the check and the use, so it is not promoted; copy it to a local variable first
You must use late for fields
length does not exist on String
quiz.explanation: Promotion works on local variables (and, since Dart 3.2, private final fields). A public mutable field could be changed by a getter override or another piece of code, so Dart does not trust the check.

quiz.question: You declare late String token; and read it before assigning it. What happens?
options: A LateInitializationError is thrown at run time
token is an empty string
token is null
The code does not compile
quiz.explanation: late moves the check to run time. Reading a late variable before it has a value throws LateInitializationError.

quiz.question: Which is usually the best way to show “Guest” when name (String?) is null?
options: name!
name as String
late name
name ?? 'Guest'
quiz.explanation: ?? returns the left side if it is not null, otherwise the right side. It never crashes, unlike ! or as.

lessons.title: Control flow and pattern matching
lessons.summaryHtml:
Control flow decides which code runs and how often: if/else, for, for-in, while, do-while, break and continue. Dart 3 adds powerful patterns, so switch can match values, ranges, types, lists and maps and pull values out of them at the same time.

A switch expression returns a value and must cover every case (it is exhaustive). Cases can add a guard with when, and if-case tests one pattern. Switch statements no longer need break. Grade Book v3 uses loops and patterns to validate rows and assign grades.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

So far our programs run from top to bottom, one line after another. Real programs make decisions (“if the mark is below 40, show a warning”) and repeat work (“for every student, print a line”). That is control flow.

Dart 3 added something more powerful on top: pattern matching. A pattern describes the shape of a value, such as “a number of at least 90”, “a list with exactly one item” or “a map with a String name and an int score”. Dart checks whether the value fits the shape and, if it does, pulls out the parts you need into variables, all in one step.

Think of a sorting office. Control flow is the conveyor belt and the switches that send parcels left or right. Patterns are the labels the switches read: size, destination, “fragile”.

Why it matters

Flutter UIs are full of decisions: show a spinner while loading, a list when data arrives, an error message when it fails. Loops build lists of widgets. Parsing JSON from an API means checking that each field exists and has the right type. Patterns make all of this shorter and safer, and exhaustiveness checking means the compiler tells you when you forgot a case, for example a new order status that no screen handles yet.

How it works

if and else

void main() {
  const mark = 67;
  if (mark >= 75) {
    print('Distinction');
  } else if (mark >= 40) {
    print('Pass');       // printed
  } else {
    print('Fail');
  }
}

The condition must be a real bool. Always use braces for multi-line bodies; the Dart style guide allows a braceless if only when the whole statement fits on one line.

Loops

void main() {
  final marks = [88, 76, 92];

  for (var i = 0; i < marks.length; i++) {   // classic for: you need the index
    print('Subject $i: ' + marks[i].toString());
  }
  for (final m in marks) {                    // for-in: you only need the items
    print(m);
  }

  var attempts = 0;
  while (attempts < 3) {                      // checks first
    attempts++;
  }
  do {                                        // runs at least once
    attempts--;
  } while (attempts > 5);
  print(attempts);                            // 2
}

break leaves the loop immediately; continue skips to the next iteration. Prefer for-in when you do not need the index: there is no off-by-one risk.

switch statements

void main() {
  const command = 'add';
  switch (command) {
    case 'add' || 'new':          // logical-or pattern
      print('Adding a student');
    case 'list':
      print('Listing students');
    case 'quit':
    case 'exit':                  // empty case shares the next body
      print('Bye');
    default:
      print('Unknown command');
  }
}

In Dart 3 a non-empty case never falls through, so break is optional. Empty cases share the body of the next case.

switch expressions

A switch expression produces a value. Arms use =>, are separated by commas, and are tried from top to bottom. The first match wins.

String gradeFor(double average) => switch (average) {
      >= 90 => 'A',
      >= 75 => 'B',
      >= 60 => 'C',
      >= 40 => 'D',
      _ => 'F',
    };

void main() {
  print(gradeFor(85.3)); // B
}

>= 90 is a relational pattern; _ is the wildcard that matches anything. A switch expression must be exhaustive: without the _ arm, this one would not compile, because doubles below 40 would have no result.

The main kinds of pattern

PatternExampleMatches
Constant'quit', 0An equal value
Relational>= 90, < 0A comparison that is true
Logical or / and'a' || 'b', >= 0 && <= 100Either / both sub-patterns
Variable and type testint n, final xA value of that type, bound to a name
List[], [final first, ...]A list of the right length and contents; ... is the rest
Map{'name': String name}A map that has these keys with matching values
Wildcard_Anything

Records and object patterns ((x, y), Circle(radius: r)) come in lesson 1.8, together with sealed classes, where exhaustiveness really shines.

Guards

A guard adds a condition with when. The case matches only if the pattern fits and the guard is true:

String check(int mark) => switch (mark) {
      < 0 || > 100 => 'invalid',
      final m when m.isOdd => 'odd mark $m',
      _ => 'ok',
    };

void main() {
  print(check(120)); // invalid
  print(check(77));  // odd mark 77
  print(check(80));  // ok
}

if-case: test one pattern

When you only care about one shape, if-case is shorter than a switch. Variables bound by the pattern exist only inside the if block, already typed:

void main() {
  final Map<String, Object?> json = {'name': 'Asha', 'marks': [88, 76, 92]};
  if (json case {'name': String name, 'marks': List<int> marks}) {
    print('$name has ' + marks.length.toString() + ' marks');
  } else {
    print('Invalid student data');
  }
}

This replaces several lines of containsKey checks and as casts, and it can never throw a cast error.

Choosing the right tool

You need to...Use
Run one of two blocks of codeif / else
Pick a value from two optionsThe conditional operator a ? b : c
Pick a value from several options or rangesA switch expression
Run different statements for several casesA switch statement
Check one shape and pull values out of itif-case
Visit every item of a collectionfor-in
Repeat until a condition changes (unknown count)while or do-while

When loops are nested, break and continue affect only the innermost loop. To leave an outer loop, put a label before it and name it: outer: for (...) { for (...) { if (found) break outer; } }. Labels are rare in app code; often a small function with an early return reads better.

Example: Grade Book v3

Version 3 reads a list of rows that might be messy, as data from a file or an API often is. It validates each row with a map pattern, fails any student who scored below the pass mark in a subject, and grades the rest with a switch expression and a guard.

void main() {
  const passMark = 40;
  final List<Map<String, Object>> rows = [
    {'name': 'Asha', 'marks': [88, 76, 92]},
    {'name': 'Ravi', 'marks': [45, 38, 60]},
    {'name': 'Joel'},
  ];

  for (final row in rows) {
    if (row case {'name': String name, 'marks': List<int> marks}) {
      var total = 0;
      var failedOne = false;
      for (final m in marks) {
        total += m;
        if (m < passMark) failedOne = true;
      }
      final avg = total / marks.length;
      final grade = switch (avg) {
        _ when failedOne => 'F (failed a subject)',
        >= 75 => 'B or better',
        _ => 'C or below',
      };
      final avgText = avg.toStringAsFixed(1);
      print('$name: $avgText, $grade');
    } else {
      print('Skipping bad row: $row');
    }
  }
}

Output: Asha: 85.3, B or better, Ravi: 47.7, F (failed a subject) and Skipping bad row: {name: Joel}. The lab version adds full grades, an empty-marks case and a class summary.

Common mistakes

  • Wrong order of arms. Arms are tried top to bottom. If >= 40 comes before >= 90, nobody ever gets an A.
  • Writing break out of habit and expecting it to leave the loop. Inside a switch that sits in a loop, break ends the switch statement, not the loop. Use a return, a flag or a labelled break.
  • Off-by-one loops such as i <= list.length, which reads one past the end and throws a RangeError. Prefer for-in.
  • Casting JSON with as (row['score'] as int) and crashing on bad data. Use if-case or a switch with map patterns.
  • Adding _ => to a switch over an enum or sealed type “just in case”. It turns off the exhaustiveness check that would warn you about new values.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Know the difference between a switch statement (runs code) and a switch expression (produces a value, must be exhaustive).
  • In Flutter you will often write return switch (state) { Loading() => ..., Loaded(:final items) => ..., Failed(:final message) => ... }; inside build. That style arrives with sealed classes in lesson 1.8 and BLoC in module 6.
  • Collection if and for inside list literals ([if (isAdmin) adminTile, for (final s in students) Text(s)]) are covered in lesson 1.5; they are the loop and branch tools you use most inside widget trees.
  • Reviewers like guards and patterns that replace deeply nested if blocks. Flat code is easier to test.
Remember: a switch expression must cover every case. Let the compiler find the cases you forgot.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

  • C [A, B, C, F]

    switch (day) {

  var sum = 0;

  switch (xs) {

    case [final first, ..., final last]:

Answers

  1. C. Arms are tried from top to bottom and the first match wins: 75 matches >= 75 (B) and 74 falls to >= 50 (C). toList() prints with square brackets.
  2. B. The empty Sat case shares the Sun body. Non-empty cases do not fall through in Dart 3, so each day prints exactly one line.
  3. A. continue skips even numbers. The odd numbers 1, 3, 5 and 7 are added (16). At i = 9 the break ends the loop.
  4. D. List patterns match by length. [-2, 5] matches the guarded case first because -2 < 0. The rest element ... skips the middle, so [3, 8, 1] binds first 3 and last 1.
  5. B. Ravi has no score key, so the map pattern fails. Anu’s score is the String '90', not an int, so the type test fails too.

terms.definition: A switch that produces a value, written with => arms and no case keyword; it must be exhaustive.
A shape a value is tested against, such as a constant, a range (>= 90), a type (int n), a list or a map; it can also bind variables.
An extra boolean condition on a case; the case matches only if the pattern matches and the guard is true.
The compiler check that a switch handles every possible value of the matched type.
An if statement that matches one pattern and binds its variables only inside the if block.
A pattern that matches anything without binding a name; used as the default arm.

lessons.examTip: When a chain of if/else if picks one value from several options, rewrite it as a switch expression. It is shorter and the compiler checks you covered every case.

quiz.question: In a Dart 3 switch statement, what happens at the end of a non-empty case?
options: Execution falls through to the next case
It is a compile error unless you write break
The whole program stops

quiz.question: Why does a switch expression over an enum not need a default arm when every value is listed?

Because enums cannot be switched on
Because Dart adds a hidden default that returns null
Because switch expressions ignore missing cases
quiz.explanation: Exhaustiveness checking knows all enum values. If you add a new value later, every switch that misses it becomes a compile error, which is exactly what you want.

quiz.question: Which loop always runs its body at least once?

for-in
do-while
while
quiz.explanation: do-while checks its condition after the body, so the body runs once even if the condition starts out false.

lessons.title: Functions and closures
lessons.summaryHtml:
Functions are the building blocks of every Dart and Flutter program. A function can take positional, optional positional ([ ]) and named ({ }) parameters, with defaults and required. Short functions use the arrow syntax => expression.

Functions are first-class values: you can store them in variables, pass them to other functions (as Flutter’s onPressed does) and return them. A closure is a function that remembers the variables around it. typedef gives a function type a readable name. Grade Book v4 is refactored into small, reusable functions.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A function is a named, reusable piece of code. You give it inputs (parameters), it does some work, and it can give back a result. Instead of copying the “calculate the average” lines everywhere, you write average(marks).

In Dart, functions are also values, just like numbers and strings. You can put a function in a variable, hand it to another function, or get one back. When you write onPressed: () => save() on a Flutter button, you are handing the button a small function to call later.

A closure is a function that remembers the variables around it, like a note-taker who keeps a notebook from the meeting where they were created and can keep writing in it afterwards.

Why it matters

Good functions make code readable, testable and easy to change. In Flutter, callbacks are everywhere: onPressed, onChanged, validator, itemBuilder, builder. Widget constructors use named parameters for all their options. Understanding parameters, function types and closures is what turns Flutter code from confusing to obvious.

Functions are also the unit of reuse and testing. A calculation hidden inside a button handler can only be checked by tapping the button. The same calculation in a small, named function can be called from a test with a dozen inputs in milliseconds. Teams that keep business rules in plain functions (and later in Cubits and repositories) change their apps with far less fear.

How it works

We start with declarations and parameters, then treat functions as values, and finish with closures and typedefs.

Declaring functions

int add(int a, int b) {
  return a + b;
}

int multiply(int a, int b) => a * b;   // arrow: body is one expression

void sayHi() => print('Hi');           // void: returns nothing useful

void main() {
  print(add(2, 3));      // 5
  print(multiply(4, 5)); // 20
  sayHi();
}

Always write the return type and parameter types on public functions. => expr is short for { return expr; } and only works for a single expression, not statements such as if blocks.

Parameters: positional, optional and named

KindSyntaxCallNotes
Required positionalf(int a)f(1)Order matters
Optional positionalf(int a, [int b = 0])f(1) or f(1, 2)Needs a default or a nullable type
Namedf({int b = 0})f(b: 2)Optional unless required; any order
Required namedf({required int b})f(b: 2)Clear call sites; Flutter’s favourite
 
String describe(String name, [int? age]) =>
    age == null ? name : '$name ($age)';

String report({required String name, double average = 0, bool detailed = false}) {
  final avg = average.toStringAsFixed(1);
  return detailed ? '$name has an average of $avg' : '$name: $avg';
}

void main() {
  print(describe('Asha'));                                   // Asha
  print(describe('Ravi', 20));                               // Ravi (20)
  print(report(name: 'Asha', average: 85.33));               // Asha: 85.3
  print(report(detailed: true, name: 'Ravi', average: 47.7)); // Ravi has an average of 47.7
}

A function cannot mix optional positional and named parameters. When a function has more than two or three parameters, or any bool flag, prefer named ones: report(name: 'Asha', detailed: true) says what true means.

Functions as values

int square(int n) => n * n;

int applyTo(int value, int Function(int) operation) => operation(value);

void main() {
  final int Function(int) op = square;    // a tear-off: the function itself
  print(op(4));                           // 16
  print(applyTo(5, square));              // 25
  print(applyTo(5, (n) => n + 1));        // 6, with an anonymous function
  [1, 2, 3].forEach(print);               // passes print itself
}

The type of a function is written ReturnType Function(ParameterTypes). Writing square without brackets is a tear-off: the function object. Writing square(4) calls it. This is the difference between onPressed: _save (correct) and onPressed: _save() (calls it during build).

Closures

int Function(int) makeCurve(int bonus) {
  return (int mark) {
    final curved = mark + bonus;   // bonus is captured from makeCurve
    return curved > 100 ? 100 : curved;
  };
}

void main() {
  final easyCurve = makeCurve(5);
  final bigCurve = makeCurve(15);
  print(easyCurve(90)); // 95
  print(bigCurve(90));  // 100
}

Each call to makeCurve creates a new closure with its own bonus. Closures capture variables, not just values: if the captured variable changes later, the closure sees the change. That is how a counter closure can keep counting. Inside a for loop, Dart creates a fresh loop variable for every iteration, so closures made in the loop each capture their own value.

typedef: naming function types

typedef MarkRule = String? Function(int mark);

String? notNegative(int m) => m < 0 ? 'Mark cannot be negative' : null;
String? atMost100(int m) => m > 100 ? 'Mark cannot exceed 100' : null;

List<String> validate(int mark, List<MarkRule> rules) {
  final errors = <String>[];
  for (final rule in rules) {
    final error = rule(mark);
    if (error != null) errors.add(error);
  }
  return errors;
}

void main() {
  print(validate(120, [notNegative, atMost100])); // [Mark cannot exceed 100]
}

This is the same shape as Flutter’s form validators, which return an error string or null when the input is valid. You will write them in lesson 5.3.

Lexical scope

Dart is lexically scoped: a function can see variables declared in the blocks around it, determined by where the code is written. Inner functions (like square declared inside main) are fine and useful for small helpers that no one else needs.

Anonymous functions in practice

Many APIs ask you for a small function that is used only once. Writing it inline, without a name, keeps the logic next to where it is used:

void main() {
  final names = ['Meera', 'Asha', 'Ravi', 'Joel'];
  names.sort((a, b) => a.compareTo(b));           // alphabetical
  print(names);                                    // [Asha, Joel, Meera, Ravi]

  final marks = {'Asha': 85, 'Ravi': 48, 'Meera': 95};
  marks.forEach((name, mark) {
    final label = mark >= 50 ? 'pass' : 'needs help';
    print('$name: $label');
  });
}

The comparator given to sort returns a negative number, zero or a positive number to say which item comes first. The Flutter version of this idea is everywhere: ListView.builder(itemBuilder: (context, index) { ... }) is an anonymous function the list calls for each visible row. For simple loops over a list, prefer a for-in loop to forEach with a closure: it is easier to read and supports break, continue and await.

Example: Grade Book v4

Version 4 splits the program into small functions, each doing one job: validating marks, computing the average, grading and formatting. main becomes a short story you can read at a glance.

typedef Grader = String Function(double average);

double average(List<int> marks) {
  if (marks.isEmpty) return 0;
  var total = 0;
  for (final m in marks) {
    total += m;
  }
  return total / marks.length;
}

String standardGrade(double avg) => switch (avg) {
      >= 90 => 'A',
      >= 75 => 'B',
      >= 60 => 'C',
      >= 40 => 'D',
      _ => 'F',
    };

String passFail(double avg) => avg >= 40 ? 'Pass' : 'Fail';

String formatRow(String name, List<int> marks, {required Grader grader}) {
  final avg = average(marks);
  final avgText = avg.toStringAsFixed(1);
  final grade = grader(avg);
  return '$name: $avgText ($grade)';
}

void main() {
  print(formatRow('Asha', [88, 76, 92], grader: standardGrade)); // Asha: 85.3 (B)
  print(formatRow('Ravi', [45, 38, 60], grader: passFail));      // Ravi: 47.7 (Pass)
}

Because the grading rule is a parameter, the same formatRow works for letter grades, pass/fail or any future scheme. That is the strategy pattern, done with a single function type.

Common mistakes

  • Calling instead of passing: onPressed: submit() runs submit during build. Pass submit, or () => submit(form) if you need arguments.
  • Long lists of positional bool parameters like printReport(true, false, true). Nobody can read that. Use named parameters.
  • Forgetting return in a block body. int twice(int n) { n * 2; } is an error; write return n * 2; or use =>.
  • Mixing arrow and braces: () => { print('x') } is not a block. It is an arrow function that returns a Set literal, and with a semicolon inside it does not compile at all. Use () { print('x'); } for statements.
  • Giant functions. If a function needs a comment for each section, split it. Small functions are easier to test with package:test (lesson 1.14).

Interview and real-world notes

  • “What is a closure? Give an example.” Use the counter or curve example above, and mention that Flutter callbacks such as () => setState(...) capture this and local variables.
  • “Named vs positional parameters?” Named parameters are self-documenting and order-independent; required keeps them mandatory. Flutter widgets use them for almost everything except the main child or data.
  • Pure functions (same input, same output, no side effects) are the easiest to test. BLoC and Cubit logic in module 6 benefits greatly from keeping calculations pure.
  • Useful Flutter function types to recognise: VoidCallback (void Function()), ValueChanged<T> (void Function(T value)) and FormFieldValidator<String>.
Remember: a function name without brackets is the function itself; with brackets it is a call. Pass the function when something else should decide when to run it.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What does this print?

String greet(String name, {String greeting = 'Hello', bool shout = false}) {
  final text = '$greeting, $name!';
  return shout ? text.toUpperCase() : text;
}

void main() {
  print(greet('Asha'));
  print(greet('Ravi', shout: true, greeting: 'Hi'));
}

typedef Rule = String? Function(int mark);

String? notNegative(int m) => m < 0 ? 'negative' : null;
String? max100(int m) => m > 100 ? 'too high' : null;

void main() {
  final List<Rule> rules = [notNegative, max100];
  for (final mark in [50, -3, 120]) {
    final errors = rules.map((rule) => rule(mark)).whereType<String>().toList();
    print('$mark $errors');

Answers

  1. B. Named arguments can be passed in any order. The first call uses the defaults; the second uses Hi and shouts the whole text.
  2. C. Each call to makeCounter creates a new count variable, and its closure keeps it alive. a has been called three times; b once, with its own count.
  3. A. Dart gives each iteration of a for loop a fresh i, so each closure captures its own value. (JavaScript with var would print 3 three times.)
  4. C. applyTwice calls the function on its own result: 1 + 10 + 10 = 21 and (3 × 3)² = 81. map returns a lazy Iterable, which prints with round brackets.
  5. D. Each rule returns an error or null. whereType<String>() keeps only the non-null strings, and toList() prints with square brackets.
