lessons.title: Collections in depth
lessons.summaryHtml: Dart has three core collections: List (ordered, indexed), Set (unique items) and Map (key to value). All of them share the Iterable toolbox: map, where, fold, expand, any, every and more. Most of these methods are lazy: they describe work and only run when you loop or call toList(). Collection if, collection for and the spread operator ... let you build lists, sets and maps in one readable literal, which is exactly how Flutter builds lists of widgets. Finally you learn the difference between a final variable, a const collection and an unmodifiable view.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A collection is a container for many values. Dart gives you three that you will use every day.

  • List: an ordered row of items you reach by index, like seats in a cinema row. ['Asha', 'Ben']
  • Set: a bag of unique items, like the tags on a post. Adding a duplicate does nothing. {'dart', 'flutter'}
  • Map: a lookup table from keys to values, like a phone book. {'Asha': 82, 'Ben': 67}

On top of these sits the Iterable toolbox: methods that filter, transform and combine items without writing loops by hand.

Why it matters

Almost every screen in a Flutter app is a collection turned into widgets: a list of products becomes a list of cards, a map of settings becomes a list of switches. The children of a Column is a List<Widget>. If you know map, where, collection for and collection if, your build methods become short and declarative. If you don’t, you end up with temporary lists, index counters and bugs where one screen mutates data another screen is still showing.

How it works

We look at the three collection types, then the methods they share, then the literal syntax Flutter code relies on, and finally how to stop a collection from changing.

Lists, sets and maps

final names = <String>['Asha', 'Ben'];      // List<String>, growable
names.add('Chen');
print(names[0]);                             // Asha
print(names.indexOf('Ben'));                 // 1

final tags = <String>{'dart', 'flutter'};    // Set<String>
print(tags.add('dart'));                     // false: already there
print(tags.contains('flutter'));             // true, and fast

final scores = <String, int>{'Asha': 82};    // Map<String, int>
scores['Ben'] = 67;                          // add or replace
final int? eve = scores['Eve'];              // null: missing key
scores.update('Asha', (s) => s + 5, ifAbsent: () => 0);
scores.putIfAbsent('Chen', () => 91);

Two details trip beginners. First, map[key] returns a nullable type (int?), because the key might be missing. Handle it with ?? 0 or a null check, not with !. Second, an empty {} is a Map, not a Set. Write <String>{} for an empty set.

The default Set and Map keep insertion order (they are linked hash collections). Lookup with contains or containsKey is fast; on a List, contains checks every element one by one.

The Iterable toolbox

MethodReturnsUse it to
map(f)lazy Iterabletransform each item (score to letter, model to widget)
where(test)lazy Iterablekeep only matching items
expand(f)lazy Iterableturn each item into zero or more items, for example flatten a list of lists
fold(init, f)one valuesum, count or build a result from a starting value
reduce(f)one valuecombine items when the collection cannot be empty
any / everyboolask “is at least one / is every item …?”
firstWhere, firstOrNullone itemfind an item; firstOrNull returns null when empty
take, skiplazy Iterablepaging: the first 10, everything after 10
toList(), toSet()new collectionrun the lazy work once and keep the result

Lazy means map and where do not produce results straight away. They return an object that remembers the work. The work runs when you loop, print or call toList(), and it runs again every time you iterate. That is efficient for one pass, but wasteful if you iterate the same lazy result many times.

final prices = [120.0, 80.0, 45.5];
final total = prices.fold<double>(0, (sum, p) => sum + p);   // 245.5
final cheap = prices.where((p) => p < 100).toList();         // [80.0, 45.5]
final labels = prices.map((p) => 'Rs ' + p.toStringAsFixed(0)).toList();
final anyFree = prices.any((p) => p == 0);                   // false

Give fold an explicit type (fold<double>) when the start value alone would infer the wrong one. reduce throws a StateError on an empty collection, so prefer fold when emptiness is possible. Dart 3 also added handy extensions to dart:core: firstOrNull, lastOrNull, indexed (pairs of index and item as records) and nonNulls (drops the nulls from an iterable).

Collection if, collection for and spread

Inside any list, set or map literal you can write if, for and .... They decide which elements the literal contains.

List<String> menu(bool isAdmin, List<String> extras, List<String>? recent) => [
      'Home',
      for (final e in extras) e.toUpperCase(),   // collection for
      if (isAdmin) 'Admin' else 'Help',          // collection if / else
      ...?recent,                                // null-aware spread
    ];

final squares = {for (var i = 1; i <= 3; i++) i: i * i};   // {1: 1, 2: 4, 3: 9}

This is the pattern you will use in Flutter: children: [header, for (final p in products) ProductCard(p), if (loading) const CircularProgressIndicator()]. There are no braces around the element, and no statements: each if or for produces elements, not side effects.

final, const and unmodifiable

CodeReassign variable?Change contents?
var list = [1, 2];yesyes
final list = [1, 2];noyes
const list = [1, 2];nono (compile-time constant, deeply immutable)
final list = List.unmodifiable(other);nono (runtime copy that cannot change)

Collections are objects passed by reference. final b = a; does not copy: both names point at the same list. Copy with List.of(a), [...a], Set.of or Map.of. In state management (Provider, BLoC) you will create a new list on every change, such as [...todos, newTodo], instead of mutating the old one, so that the framework can tell that something changed.

Example: Grade Book report

The Grade Book stores three test scores per student. We turn it into averages, a ranked pass list, an honours list and the set of letter grades used.

const Map<String, List<int>> gradeBook = {
  'Asha': [82, 91, 77],
  'Ben': [67, 58, 72],
  'Chen': [95, 88, 92],
  'Divya': [45, 61, 50],
};

double average(List<int> s) => s.fold<int>(0, (sum, x) => sum + x) / s.length;

void main() {
  final averages = <String, double>{
    for (final e in gradeBook.entries) e.key: average(e.value),
  };
  final passing = averages.entries.where((e) => e.value >= 60).toList()
    ..sort((a, b) => b.value.compareTo(a.value));
  final names = passing.map((e) => e.key).toList();
  final allScores = gradeBook.values.expand((s) => s).toList();
  final best = allScores.reduce((a, b) => a > b ? a : b);
  final honours = [
    for (final e in averages.entries) if (e.value >= 90) e.key,
  ];
  print('Passing: $names');     // Passing: [Chen, Asha, Ben]
  print('Best: $best');         // Best: 95
  print('Honours: $honours');   // Honours: [Chen]
}

Notice the cascade ..sort(...). sort changes the list in place and returns void, so the cascade lets us sort and still keep the list in passing. The lab adds the class average and a Set of letter grades.

Common mistakes

  • Treating map() as a List. items.map(f)[0] does not compile, and printing it shows round brackets. Add toList().
  • Assigning the result of sort. final sorted = list.sort(); gives you void. Sort in place, use a cascade, or sort a copy: [...list]..sort().
  • Using reduce on data that can be empty. It throws Bad state: No element. Use fold with a start value.
  • Forcing map lookups with !. scores[name]! crashes on a missing key. Use ?? 0 or containsKey.
  • Expecting final to freeze a list. It freezes the variable, not the contents. Mutating a list that another widget still holds causes stale screens.
  • Writing {} for an empty set. That is an empty map. Use <String>{}.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Be ready to explain lazy iterables and why toList() matters. A classic follow-up: “Why does my print inside map never run?” Because nothing iterated the result.
  • Know the difference between List.of, List.from and List.unmodifiable. List.of keeps the element type; List.from accepts any iterable and checks types at runtime.
  • Immutable updates ([...old, item], {...map, key: value}) are the daily routine in Provider and BLoC code, and equatable compares lists by content for you.
  • For extra helpers such as groupBy, firstWhereOrNull and deep equality, teams use the official collection package. Know that it exists, but master the core methods first.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What does this print?

void main() {
  final nums = [1, 2, 3, 4];
  final result = nums.where((n) => n.isEven).map((n) => n * 10);
  print(result);
}
  • A [20, 40]
  • B (20, 40)
  • C Instance of 'MappedIterable<int, int>'
  • D [2, 4]

Snippet 2. What does this print?

void main() {
  final isAdmin = false;
  final base = [1, 2];
  final menu = [0, ...base, if (isAdmin) 99, for (final n in base) n * 3];
  print(menu);
}
  • A [0, 1, 2, 99, 3, 6]
  • B [0, [1, 2], 3, 6]
  • C [0, 1, 2, 3, 6]
  • D [0, 1, 2, 1, 2]

Snippet 3. What does this print?

void main() {
  final tags = <String>{};
  tags.addAll(['dart', 'flutter', 'dart']);
  tags.add('bloc');
  print(tags.length);
  print(tags);
}
  • A 
    4
{dart, flutter, dart, bloc}
  • B 
    3
{bloc, dart, flutter}
  • C 
    3
[dart, flutter, bloc]
  • D 
    3
{dart, flutter, bloc}

Snippet 4. What does this print?

void main() {
  final scores = {'Asha': 82, 'Ben': 67, 'Chen': 91};
  final total = scores.values.fold(0, (sum, s) => sum + s);
  final top = scores.entries
      .where((e) => e.value >= 80)
      .map((e) => e.key)
      .toList();
  print('$total $top');
}
  • A 240 [Asha, Chen]
  • B 240 (Asha, Chen)
  • C 240.0 [Asha, Chen]
  • D 240 [MapEntry(Asha: 82), MapEntry(Chen: 91)]

Snippet 5. What does this print?

void main() {
  final a = [1, 2, 3];
  final b = a;
  final c = List.of(a);
  b.add(4);
  print([a.length, c.length]);
}
  • A [3, 3]
  • B [4, 4]
  • C [4, 3]
  • D A compile error, because a is final

Answers

  1. B. where and map return a lazy Iterable, not a List. Printing an Iterable shows its elements in round brackets. Add .toList() to get [20, 40].
  2. C. The spread inserts 1 and 2, the collection if adds nothing because isAdmin is false, and the collection for adds 1 * 3 and 2 * 3.
  3. D. A Set ignores the second dart. The default Set is a LinkedHashSet, so it keeps insertion order, and sets print with curly braces.
  4. A. 82 + 67 + 91 is 240, an int because the initial value is 0. toList() turns the lazy result into a List, which prints with square brackets.
  5. C. b points to the same list object as a, so adding through b changes a. List.of made c an independent copy. final stops reassignment, not mutation.

terms.definition: Anything you can loop over with for-in. List and Set are Iterables; a Map exposes keys, values and entries as Iterables.
The result of map, where or expand. It stores the recipe, not the results, and runs each time you iterate it.
Combines all elements into one value, starting from an initial value you give. Works on empty collections, unlike reduce.
Loops and conditions written inside a list, set or map literal to decide which elements it contains.
... inserts every element of another collection into a literal; ...? skips a null collection.
A collection that throws UnsupportedError when you add, remove or replace elements, such as a const literal or List.unmodifiable.

lessons.examTip: Interviewers love “what does .map() return?”. Answer: a lazy Iterable, not a List. Call toList() when you need a List, and never put side effects inside map.

lessons.title: Classes, objects and constructors
lessons.summaryHtml: A class is a blueprint; an object is one thing built from it. Classes bundle fields (data) with methods (behaviour), and getters and setters let you expose computed or guarded values that read like fields. Dart has several constructor kinds: generative with this.field shorthand, named, redirecting, const and factory, plus initializer lists that run before the body. Names that start with _ are private to their file. Every Flutter widget is a class with a const constructor, so this lesson is the foundation for everything that follows. You start the Library Manager console app.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A class is a blueprint, like the plan for a library card. An object (an instance) is one real card made from that plan, with its own name and number printed on it. The class says what every card has (fields) and what every card can do (methods). You can make as many objects from one class as you like.

A constructor is the machine that makes objects. Dart gives you several kinds of machine, each for a different job: the normal one, named ones, ones that forward to another, ones that make constant objects, and factories that can decide what to hand back.

Why it matters

Everything in a Flutter app is an object. Your data models (Book, User, Order) are classes. Every widget is a class, and almost every widget you write will have a const constructor with named parameters like const ProfileCard({super.key, required this.name}). JSON parsing uses factory constructors named fromJson. If you understand constructors, you can read any Flutter codebase; if you don’t, the syntax looks like magic.

How it works

First the parts of a class, then the five constructor kinds, then the two that need the most care: initializer lists and const or factory constructors.

Fields, methods, getters and setters

class BankAccount {
  BankAccount(this.owner);        // generative constructor

  final String owner;             // set once, never changes
  double _balance = 0;            // private: starts with _
  static int accountsOpened = 0;  // shared by the class

  String _nickname = '';

  double get balance => _balance;          // read-only from outside
  bool get isEmpty => _balance == 0;       // computed getter

  String get nickname => _nickname;
  set nickname(String value) {             // setter with a guard
    if (value.length > 20) throw ArgumentError('nickname too long');
    _nickname = value;
  }

  void deposit(double amount) {            // method
    if (amount <= 0) throw ArgumentError('amount must be positive');
    _balance += amount;
  }
}

A getter looks like a field to the caller (account.balance) but runs code. Use getters for derived values so they can never go out of sync. A setter runs when you assign (account.nickname = 'Travel';), so it can reject bad values. Dart privacy is per library (in practice, per file): any code in the same file can read _balance, but code in other files cannot. There is no public or private keyword. Inside a class, this is optional unless a parameter has the same name as a field.

Constructor kinds

KindSyntaxUse it when
GenerativeBook(this.title, {required this.year});you create a new object from values; this.x assigns a field directly
NamedBook.draft()you need a second way to build the object (Dart has no overloading)
RedirectingBook.draft() : this('Untitled', year: 0);one constructor is a special case of another
constconst Tag(this.name);all fields are final and objects are value-like, such as widgets and colours
Factoryfactory Book.fromJson(Map json) {...}you validate or parse first, return a cached object, or return a subtype

Initializer lists

A final field must have its value before the constructor body runs. When the value needs a calculation, you set it in the initializer list, after a colon. The list can also hold assert checks, which run only in debug mode (Flutter debug builds, or dart run --enable-asserts).

class Rectangle {
  Rectangle(this.width, this.height)
      : assert(width >= 0 && height >= 0),
        area = width * height;

  Rectangle.square(double side) : this(side, side);   // redirecting

  final double width;
  final double height;
  final double area;
}

const and factory constructors

A const constructor has no body and every field is final. When you call it with const and constant arguments, Dart builds the object at compile time and reuses one instance for equal values. That is why const Text('Hi') in Flutter is cheap: the framework sees the same instance and can skip work. Calling the same constructor without const still creates a new object.

A factory constructor is like a static method that must return an instance of the class. It cannot use this or initializer lists. It is the natural home for fromJson, for caches and for validation that throws before any object exists.

class User {
  const User({required this.id, required this.name});

  final int id;
  final String name;

  factory User.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) {
    return User(id: json['id'] as int, name: json['name'] as String);
  }

  @override
  String toString() => 'User($id, $name)';
}

Named parameters in braces are optional unless marked required, and they make call sites readable: User(id: 1, name: 'Asha'). Flutter uses them everywhere. The cascade operator .. lets you call several methods on the same object: StringBuffer()..write('a')..write('b').

Example: Library Manager

The Book class uses almost every constructor kind. A static counter hands out ids in the initializer list, a redirecting constructor fills in a default author and a factory validates raw data.

class Book {
  static int _nextId = 1;

  final int id;
  final String title;
  final String author;
  final int year;
  bool _onLoan = false;

  Book({required this.title, required this.author, required this.year})
      : assert(title.isNotEmpty, 'title must not be empty'),
        id = _nextId++;

  Book.unknownAuthor({required String title, required int year})
      : this(title: title, author: 'Unknown', year: year);

  factory Book.fromMap(Map<String, Object?> map) {
    final title = map['title'];
    final author = map['author'];
    final year = map['year'];
    if (title is! String || author is! String || year is! int) {
      throw FormatException('Invalid book data: $map');
    }
    return Book(title: title, author: author, year: year);
  }

  bool get isAvailable => !_onLoan;

  bool checkOut() {
    if (_onLoan) return false;
    _onLoan = true;
    return true;
  }

  @override
  String toString() {
    final status = _onLoan ? 'on loan' : 'available';
    return '#$id $title by $author ($year) - $status';
  }
}

In fromMap, the is! checks followed by throw let flow analysis promote title, author and year to their real types, so the final return compiles without casts. A Library class then keeps a private List<Book> and exposes availableCount as a getter. The lab builds it.

Common mistakes

  • Setting a final field in the body. Book(String t) { title = t; } fails for a final field. Use this.title or the initializer list.
  • Forgetting to override toString. Logs full of Instance of 'Book' make debugging slow.
  • Thinking _ means class-private. It means file-private. Two classes in one file can see each other’s private members.
  • Expecting const without the keyword. A const constructor only canonicalises when you call it with const (or inside a const context).
  • Public mutable fields everywhere. Prefer final fields plus methods that enforce rules, so objects cannot get into invalid states.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “What is the difference between a factory and a generative constructor?” A generative constructor always creates a new instance of exactly that class; a factory can return a cached instance or a subtype, and cannot use initializer lists or this.
  • “Why does Flutter lint ask for const?” The prefer_const_constructors lint helps Flutter reuse widget instances and skip rebuild work.
  • In real apps, model classes are usually immutable: all fields final, a const constructor, fromJson/toJson and a copyWith method that returns a changed copy. Packages such as freezed or json_serializable can generate this code, but you should be able to write it by hand first.
  • late final fields are set once, later than construction. Use them sparingly; a missing assignment is only caught at runtime.

lessons.title: Inheritance, interfaces, mixins and extensions
lessons.summaryHtml: Dart gives you four ways to share behaviour. extends creates a subclass that inherits code and can override it. implements promises to fulfil another class’s interface without inheriting any code; every class is also an implicit interface. Mixins (with) plug reusable code into many unrelated classes, and extension methods add new methods to types you do not own, such as String or DateTime. You also learn operator overloading and how to override == and hashCode together, so value objects work in sets and maps. Flutter itself uses all of these: extends StatelessWidget, with SingleTickerProviderStateMixin and context.read (an extension).
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Imagine a library. Books, DVDs and magazines are all library items: each has an id and a title. That shared “is a” relationship is inheritance (extends). Some items can be borrowed, some cannot. “Can be borrowed” is a contract, a promise to provide certain methods: that is an interface (implements). The actual loan logic is the same for books and DVDs, so you write it once and plug it in: that is a mixin (with). Finally, you want a ymd method on DateTime, a class you do not own: that is an extension.

Why it matters

Flutter is built on these ideas. Every widget you write extends StatelessWidget or StatefulWidget and overrides build. Animation states add with SingleTickerProviderStateMixin. Provider and BLoC give you context.read and context.watch, which are extension methods on BuildContext. Repositories in clean architecture are abstract classes that real and fake data sources implement, which is what makes code testable. Getting == and hashCode right is what lets BLoC decide whether a state really changed.

How it works

Each tool answers a different question. extends: what is it? implements: what does it promise? with: what extra abilities does it carry? extension: what would I like to call on a type I cannot edit?

extends and override

A class can extend exactly one superclass. It inherits every member and may override methods, getters and operators. Mark overrides with @override so the analyzer catches typos. Call the parent version with super.method(). Constructors are not inherited; super parameters pass values up with little code.

abstract class Shape {
  const Shape(this.name);
  final String name;
  double get area;                              // abstract: no body
  @override
  String toString() => name + ' with area ' + area.toStringAsFixed(1);
}

class Circle extends Shape {
  const Circle(this.radius) : super('Circle');
  final double radius;
  @override
  double get area => 3.14159 * radius * radius;
}

class Square extends Shape {
  const Square(this.side, {String name = 'Square'}) : super(name);
  final double side;
  @override
  double get area => side * side;
}

An abstract class cannot be created with Shape(...). It exists to be extended or implemented, and it can mix finished methods (toString) with abstract ones (area). Calls are dispatched on the runtime type: a variable typed Shape that holds a Circle runs the circle’s area. This is polymorphism.

implements: interfaces

Dart has no separate interface keyword for plain contracts: every class is an implicit interface. When you write class FakeApi implements Api, you get the type but none of the code, so you must implement every member yourself. A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class. This is the backbone of testing: production code depends on abstract class WeatherRepository, the app uses HttpWeatherRepository implements WeatherRepository, and tests use FakeWeatherRepository implements WeatherRepository. (Dart 3 adds interface class and other modifiers to control this; lesson 1.8 covers them.)

Mixins

mixin Rateable {
  final List<int> _ratings = [];
  void rate(int stars) => _ratings.add(stars);
  double get averageRating =>
      _ratings.isEmpty ? 0.0 : _ratings.reduce((a, b) => a + b) / _ratings.length;
}

mixin Lending on LibraryItem implements Borrowable {
  String? _borrower;
  @override
  void borrow(String member) {
    if (_borrower != null) throw StateError('$title is already on loan');
    _borrower = member;
  }
  // ...
}

class Book extends LibraryItem with Lending, Rateable { /* ... */ }

A mixin is a reusable slice of a class. It can have fields, getters and methods, but no generative constructors. on LibraryItem restricts the mixin to subclasses of LibraryItem, which lets it use title and super. Several mixins are applied left to right: in with A, B, B’s methods win, and B’s super calls go to A. Use a mixin for “can do” behaviour shared across unrelated classes; use extends for a true “is a” relationship.

Extension methods

extension StringX on String {
  String get initials =>
      split(' ').where((w) => w.isNotEmpty).map((w) => w[0].toUpperCase()).join();
  bool get isEmail => contains('@') && contains('.');
}

void main() {
  print('asha rao'.initials);            // AR
  print('asha@ralfiz.dev'.isEmail);      // true
}

Extensions are resolved at compile time from the static type. They do not change the class, cannot add fields, and do not work on values typed dynamic. If two extensions add the same name, you get an ambiguity error and must pick one explicitly, as in StringX('x').initials.

Operators, == and hashCode

You can overload operators such as +, -, <, [] and == by writing operator methods. The default == checks identity (same object). For value objects such as money, ISBNs or states, compare fields instead, and keep hashCode consistent, because sets and maps use it first.

class Isbn {
  Isbn(String raw) : digits = raw.replaceAll('-', '');
  final String digits;

  @override
  bool operator ==(Object other) => other is Isbn && other.digits == digits;

  @override
  int get hashCode => digits.hashCode;   // several fields: Object.hash(a, b)
}

Example: Library Manager, part 2

The lab turns lesson 1.6’s single Book class into a small hierarchy:

  • abstract class LibraryItem holds id, title, an abstract kind getter and a shared toString.
  • Book extends LibraryItem with Lending, Rateable, Dvd extends LibraryItem with Lending and Magazine extends LibraryItem, whose toString adds “(reading room only)” after super.toString().
  • Borrowable is the contract. A single function void lend(Borrowable item, String member, DateTime today) works for books and DVDs, and for any future type.
  • extension LoanDates on DateTime adds plusDays and ymd, so the due date prints as 2026-09-22.
  • Isbn overrides == and hashCode, so two ISBNs written with and without dashes are equal and a Set keeps one.
void lend(Borrowable item, String member, DateTime today) {
  item.borrow(member);                       // may throw StateError
  final title = item.title;
  final due = today.plusDays(item.loanDays).ymd;
  print('$member borrows $title, due $due');
}

Common mistakes

  • Using extends to reuse a few methods. If it is not a true “is a” relationship, prefer a mixin or composition (a field holding a helper object).
  • Expecting implements to inherit code. It never does. The compiler lists every member you still have to write.
  • Overriding == without hashCode. Sets keep duplicates and map lookups fail. Many teams use equatable to generate both.
  • Forgetting @override. A typo such as String tostring() silently adds a new method instead of overriding.
  • Calling extensions on dynamic. Give the value a static type first, for example from jsonDecode via a cast.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “extends vs implements vs with” is a standard question. Answer with code reuse (extends, with) versus contract only (implements), and single versus multiple.
  • Know mixin linearization: the last mixin wins and super chains backwards through the list.
  • Prefer composition over deep inheritance trees. Flutter itself composes small widgets rather than subclassing big ones.
  • Extension methods are how packages add friendly APIs, such as context.read<T>() from provider and context.go('/path') from go_router.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

  String speak() => '...';
  String describe() => 'I say ' + speak();

class Dog extends Animal {
  @override
  String speak() => 'Woof';
}

void main() {
  Animal a = Dog();
  print(a.describe());
}

mixin A on Base {
  @override
  String hello() => 'A>' + super.hello();
}

mixin B on Base {

  String hello() => 'B>' + super.hello();

class C extends Base with A, B {}

void main() {
  print(C().hello());

extension on int {
  int get doubled => this * 2;
}

extension Shout on String {

void main() {
  print(5.doubled);

Snippet 5. What does this print?

class Money {
  final int cents;
  const Money(this.cents);

  Money operator +(Money other) => Money(cents + other.cents);

  @override
  String toString() => 'Money($cents)';
}

void main() {
  var total = const Money(150);
  total += const Money(275);
  print(total);
}

  • B Money(150)
  • C Money(425)
  • D Instance of 'Money'

Answers

  1. B. Method calls are dispatched on the runtime object. describe() comes from Animal, but the speak() it calls is the Dog override.
  2. C. Mixins are applied left to right, so B sits on top of A, which sits on top of Base. C().hello() runs B first, whose super is A, whose super is Base.
  3. D. Without an override, == checks identity. a and b are two separate objects (no const keyword at the call), so they are not equal and the set keeps both.
  4. A. Extensions add members to existing types. Inside an extension, this is the value the method is called on, and other members such as toUpperCase can be called without this.
  5. C. total += x means total = total + x, which calls the overloaded + operator and returns a new Money of 425 cents.

A method added to an existing type from the outside, resolved at compile time from the static type.
An int used by sets and maps to find objects quickly; equal objects must have equal hash codes.

lessons.title: Dart 3: records, sealed classes and enums
lessons.summaryHtml: Dart 3 added tools for modelling data precisely. Records such as (int, String) or ({String name, int age}) group values without writing a class, and you destructure them with patterns. Sealed classes declare a closed family of subtypes, so a switch over them is checked for exhaustiveness: forget a case and the code does not compile. Enhanced enums carry fields, constructors and methods. Class modifiers (base, interface, final, sealed, mixin class) control who may extend or implement your types. Together they are how modern Flutter code models UI states such as loading, loaded and error.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Dart 3 gave the language three tools for describing data exactly.

  • A record is a quick, typed bundle of values, like a paper clip holding a few notes together. You do not need a class to return two things from a function.
  • A sealed class is a closed menu. A traffic light is red, amber or green, never anything else. Because the menu is closed, the compiler can check that you handled every item.
  • An enhanced enum is a fixed list of named values that can carry data, such as membership levels that each know their loan limit.

Why it matters

Most bugs in apps are “impossible” states that turn out to be possible: a screen that shows a spinner and an error at once, or a new status nobody handled. Sealed classes plus switch expressions make those states unrepresentable and turn a forgotten case into a compile error. That is exactly how BLoC states are modelled in modern Flutter code. Records remove the boilerplate of tiny result classes, and enhanced enums replace scattered if (level == 'premium') string checks with typed values that carry their own rules.

How it works

We start with records and destructuring, then sealed classes and exhaustive switches, then enhanced enums, and end with the class modifiers.

Records

(double, double) coordinates() => (11.25, 75.78);        // positional
({String name, int age}) user() => (name: 'Asha', age: 21); // named

void main() {
  final pos = coordinates();
  print(pos.$1);                  // 11.25: positional fields are $1, $2...
  final (lat, lng) = coordinates(); // destructure
  final (:name, :age) = user();     // :name means "a variable called name"
  print('$name is $age');
}

Records are immutable and have value equality: two records with the same shape and equal fields are ==. Their type is structural, so you never declare them; a typedef gives a long record type a readable name: typedef Member = ({String name, Membership tier});. Use records for small, local groupings such as a function’s multiple return values. When the data has behaviour, validation or is used across many files, write a class.

Sealed classes and exhaustive switches

sealed class LoanStatus {
  const LoanStatus();
}
final class Available extends LoanStatus { const Available(); }
final class OnLoan extends LoanStatus {
  const OnLoan({required this.member, required this.daysLeft});
  final String member;
  final int daysLeft;
}
final class Overdue extends LoanStatus {
  const Overdue({required this.member, required this.daysLate});
  final String member;
  final int daysLate;
}

String describe(LoanStatus status) => switch (status) {
      Available() => 'on the shelf',
      OnLoan(:final member, daysLeft: 0) => 'due today from $member',
      OnLoan(:final member, :final daysLeft) => 'with $member, $daysLeft days left',
      Overdue(:final member, :final daysLate) => '$daysLate days late ($member)',
    };

sealed makes the class abstract and requires every direct subtype to be in the same library (file). The compiler therefore knows the complete list, and the switch expression needs no default or _ arm. Each arm is an object pattern: OnLoan(:final member) checks the type and extracts the field in one step, and daysLeft: 0 matches only that constant. Arms are tried top to bottom, so the specific case goes first. You can add a guard with when and combine patterns with ||, as in Available() || OnLoan() => 0.

Remember: avoid a wildcard arm on a sealed type unless you truly mean “everything else”. The wildcard silences the compiler, so a newly added subtype is handled by accident.

Enhanced enums

enum Membership {
  basic(maxLoans: 2, finePerDay: 10),
  premium(maxLoans: 5, finePerDay: 5);

  const Membership({required this.maxLoans, required this.finePerDay});
  final int maxLoans;
  final int finePerDay;

  bool canBorrow(int current) => current < maxLoans;
}

Values come first, then a semicolon, then a const constructor, final fields and any methods or getters. Every enum has values (a list of all values), name ('basic') and index. Enums are always exhaustive in a switch too. Use Membership.values.byName('premium') to parse a stored string back to a value.

Class modifiers

DeclarationCreate objects?Extend outside its library?Implement outside its library?
classyesyesyes
base classyesyesno
interface classyesnoyes
final classyesnono
sealed classnonono
abstract interface classnonoyes (a pure contract)
mixin classyesyesyes, and usable with with

The restrictions apply to code in other libraries; inside the same file you can still do anything. For app code, the most useful ones are sealed for state families, final for their subclasses and abstract interface class for repository contracts.

Example: the Loan Desk

The lab combines all three tools. Titles map to a LoanStatus, members are records, and a summary returns three counts at once:

(int, int, int) summarise(Iterable<LoanStatus> all) {
  var shelf = 0, out = 0, overdue = 0;
  for (final status in all) {
    switch (status) {
      case Available():
        shelf++;
      case OnLoan():
        out++;
      case Overdue():
        overdue++;
    }
  }
  return (shelf, out, overdue);
}

void main() {
  const Member asha = (name: 'Asha', tier: Membership.basic);
  final catalogue = <String, LoanStatus>{
    'Clean Code': const Available(),
    'Inception': Overdue(member: asha.name, daysLate: 3),
  };
  for (final MapEntry(key: title, value: status) in catalogue.entries) {
    final text = describe(status);
    print('$title: $text');
  }
  final (shelf, out, overdue) = summarise(catalogue.values);
  print('Shelf $shelf, out $out, overdue $overdue');
}

Dart 3 switch statements do not fall through, so no break is needed. The full lab also calculates fines from the member’s enum level: 3 days late at Rs 10 a day is Rs 30.

Common mistakes

  • Using a Map or List to return several values. You lose types and names. Return a record.
  • Adding a default arm to a sealed switch. It hides future cases. Let the compiler do its job.
  • Putting the general case first. OnLoan() above OnLoan(daysLeft: 0) means the specific arm never runs; the analyzer warns that it is unreachable.
  • Declaring subclasses of a sealed class in another file. Not allowed (unless you use part files). Keep the family together.
  • Using a record where a class belongs. Records cannot have methods or validation. Once a record travels across many files, promote it to a class.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Expect “How do you model loading, success and error states?” Answer: a sealed class with one subclass per state, rendered with a switch expression in the widget, often in a BLoC.
  • Be able to explain exhaustiveness checking and why it beats if/else chains with is checks.
  • freezed was popular for union types before Dart 3; many teams now write sealed classes by hand.
  • Records work well for returning pairs from helpers and for grouping values in Future.wait style code, which you meet in lesson 1.11.

Predict the output

  1. A. Records print their positional fields, then the named ones with their names. Records have value equality: same shape and equal fields means ==.
  2. C. minMax returns (1, 9). The pattern assignment (a, b) = (b, a) builds the right-hand record first, then assigns, so the values swap to 9 and 1.

lessons.title: Generics
lessons.summaryHtml: Generics let you write one class or function that works with many types while keeping full type safety. List<String>, Future<User> and Map<String, int> are generic types you already use. You learn to write your own generic classes (Box<T>), generic methods (T firstOr<T>(...)), and bounds (T extends Entity) that let generic code call members safely. Dart generics are reified: the type argument exists at runtime, so is List<int> works. You finish by building a Result<T> type and a typed repository, patterns that appear in almost every production Flutter codebase.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A generic type is a container with a label on it. A box labelled “books only” is still the same kind of box as one labelled “DVDs only”, but once it is labelled, you can only put books in, and everything you take out is known to be a book. In Dart the label is the type argument: List<Book>, Future<User>. You write the box once, with a placeholder such as T, and users choose the label.

Why it matters

Without generics you have two bad choices: write a BookRepository, a MemberRepository and an OrderRepository that are 95% identical, or write one repository of Object and cast everything that comes out (and crash when a cast is wrong). Generics give you one implementation with compile-time checks. Flutter and its packages are full of them: State<CounterPage>, ValueNotifier<int>, FutureBuilder<List<Post>>, BlocBuilder<CartCubit, CartState>, context.read<AuthRepository>(). Reading those types fluently is a core junior-developer skill.

How it works

We cover generic classes, generic functions, bounds and a few runtime rules, then combine them in a Result type.

Generic classes

class Box<T> {
  Box(this.value);
  T value;

  Box<R> map<R>(R Function(T value) f) => Box(f(value));

  @override
  String toString() => 'Box($value)';
}

void main() {
  final name = Box('asha');                   // Box<String>, inferred
  final length = name.map((s) => s.length);   // Box<int>
  print(length.value + 1);                    // 5: value is an int
  // name.value = 42;                         // compile error: not a String
}

By convention type parameters are single capital letters: T for a type, E for elements, K and V for keys and values, R for a return type. Usually you do not write the type argument yourself: type inference reads it from the constructor arguments or from the variable type. Write it explicitly for empty literals (<String>[]) and when inference would pick something too wide.

Generic functions and methods

T firstOr<T>(List<T> items, T fallback) => items.isEmpty ? fallback : items.first;

Map<K, int> countBy<T, K>(Iterable<T> items, K Function(T item) keyOf) {
  final counts = <K, int>{};
  for (final item in items) {
    final key = keyOf(item);
    counts[key] = (counts[key] ?? 0) + 1;
  }
  return counts;
}

The type parameters go after the function name. Each call gets its own type arguments: countBy(books, (b) => b.author) infers T as Book and K as String, so the result is a Map<String, int>. Dart infers the closure parameter b from the earlier argument, so you rarely need to annotate it.

Bounds

Inside class Repository<T>, the compiler knows nothing about T, so item.id is an error. A bound fixes that:

abstract interface class Entity {
  String get id;
}

class InMemoryRepository<T extends Entity> {
  final Map<String, T> _items = {};

  void save(T item) => _items[item.id] = item;   // id is known: T is an Entity
  T? findById(String id) => _items[id];
  List<T> get all => _items.values.toList();
}

Now InMemoryRepository<Book>() works if Book implements Entity, and InMemoryRepository<int>() is a compile error. Bounds on generic functions work the same way: T largest<T extends Comparable<T>>(List<T> xs) can call compareTo.

Generic type aliases

Long generic types get hard to read. A typedef gives them a name, and the alias itself can be generic:

typedef Json = Map<String, dynamic>;
typedef FromJson<T> = T Function(Json json);

List<T> parseList<T>(List<dynamic> raw, FromJson<T> fromJson) =>
    raw.map((item) => fromJson(item as Json)).toList();

// Later, with a User model:
// final users = parseList(decoded, User.fromJson);   // List<User>

You will write exactly this kind of helper in the networking lessons, where every model has a fromJson factory and one generic function turns a decoded JSON list into typed objects.

Reified and covariant

Unlike Java, Dart keeps type arguments at runtime (reified generics), so value is List<int> is an exact check. Dart generics are also covariant: a List<int> can be assigned to a List<num> variable. That is convenient, but writing a double into it through the List<num> view throws a runtime type error, because the list is still a List<int>.

Example: a Result type and a typed repository

Many apps return Result<T> from repositories instead of throwing, so every caller must handle failure. It combines a sealed class (lesson 1.8) with generics:

sealed class Result<T> {
  const Result();
}
final class Success<T> extends Result<T> {
  const Success(this.value);
  final T value;
}
final class Failure<T> extends Result<T> {
  const Failure(this.error);
  final String error;
}

extension ResultX<T> on Result<T> {
  R when<R>({
    required R Function(T value) success,
    required R Function(String error) failure,
  }) =>
      switch (this) {
        Success(:final value) => success(value),
        Failure(:final error) => failure(error),
      };
}

// In InMemoryRepository<T extends Entity>:
Result<T> findById(String id) {
  final item = _items[id];
  return item == null ? Failure('No item with id $id') : Success(item);
}

The caller writes books.findById('b2').when(success: (book) => book.title, failure: (e) => e). Inside success, book is typed Book, with no cast. The lab stores books and members in two repositories built from the same class and prints each result.

Common mistakes

  • Falling back to dynamic. List without a type argument, or Map<String, dynamic> passed deep into your app, switches off the checks generics give you. Convert JSON maps to typed models at the edge.
  • Casting instead of bounding. (item as Entity).id inside a generic class moves an error from compile time to runtime. Add T extends Entity.
  • Empty literals without a type. final items = []; is a List<dynamic>. Write <Book>[] or declare the variable type.
  • The int and Comparable surprise. int implements Comparable<num>, not Comparable<int>, so largest<T extends Comparable<T>> rejects a List<int>. A looser bound such as T extends Comparable<Object> accepts it.
  • Relying on covariance for writes. Passing a List<int> where a List<num> is expected is fine for reading, but adding a double throws.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Be ready to write a small generic class or function on a whiteboard, such as a Stack<E> with push, pop and peek.
  • Explain the difference between Object, dynamic and T: Object is safe but needs casts; dynamic turns off checks; T keeps the exact type.
  • Result types appear in clean-architecture codebases, sometimes from packages (such as Either in functional libraries) and often hand-written like ours. A sealed class is enough.
  • In BLoC, Bloc<Event, State> has two type parameters, and widgets like BlocBuilder<B, S> use bounds (B extends StateStreamable<S>). You will read these signatures in lesson 6.3.

  Ok(this.value);

}

  Err(this.message);
  final String message;

Result<int> parse(String s) {
  final n = int.tryParse(s);
  return n == null ? Err('not a number: $s') : Ok(n);
}

void main() {
  for (final input in ['42', 'x']) {
    final text = switch (parse(input)) {
      Ok(:final value) => 'ok ' + (value * 2).toString(),
      Err(:final message) => 'error ' + message,
    };
    print(text);

Snippet 5. What does this print?

void main() {
  List<num> nums = <int>[1, 2];

  print(nums);
  try {
    nums.add(1.5);

Answers

  1. A. Inference makes a a List<int> and b a List<num> (int and double have num in common). Dart keeps type arguments at runtime, so the is checks are exact.
  2. C. T is inferred as String, then int. The second call returns 3 with static type int, so + 1 compiles and prints 4.
  3. D. The bound lets the code call compareTo. Strings compare alphabetically, so pear is largest. The later date is in 2026, and the result is typed DateTime, so .year compiles.
  4. B. 42 parses, so Ok(42) matches and value * 2 is 84. x fails, so Err is returned and its message is printed. The switch is exhaustive because Result is sealed.
  5. C. Generics are covariant, so a List<int> may sit in a List<num> variable. The object is still a List<int>, so adding a double fails the runtime type check and throws.

terms.definition: A placeholder type such as T in class Box<T>, filled in when the class or function is used.
The real type supplied for a type parameter, such as String in Box<String>.
A limit on a type parameter, written T extends Entity, so code can safely use Entity members on T.
A function or method with its own type parameters, such as T firstOr<T>(List<T> items, T fallback).
Type arguments are kept at runtime in Dart, so checks such as x is List<int> are accurate.
A generic sealed type that holds either a success value of type T or an error, making failures explicit in the return type.

lessons.title: Errors and exceptions
lessons.summaryHtml: Dart separates two kinds of problems. An Exception is an expected failure the program should handle, such as bad user input, a missing file or a network timeout. An Error is a programming bug, such as an index out of range or calling a method in the wrong state, and it should be fixed rather than caught. You handle failures with try, on (by type), catch (to get the object and stack trace), finally (cleanup that always runs) and rethrow. You design custom exceptions for your domain, and you use assert to document assumptions that are checked in debug builds only.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Things go wrong in every program. Dart asks you to sort them into two boxes.

  • Exceptions are problems you expect and can recover from: the user typed letters into a number field, the Wi-Fi dropped, the server said “not found”. You catch them and show a helpful message.
  • Errors are bugs in your code: reading item 10 of a 3-item list, calling reduce on an empty list, a failed cast. You don’t catch them; you fix the code.

Think of a restaurant. A customer ordering a dish that is sold out is an exception: the waiter apologises and suggests something else. A cook who forgets to switch on the stove is an error: you fix the kitchen process.

Why it matters

Users forgive a clear “Could not connect. Try again.” They do not forgive a red error screen or an app that closes. Good error handling decides which failures become friendly messages, which are retried, and which are logged as bugs for the team. In Flutter you will wrap network calls in try/catch, turn failures into error states for the UI, and send unexpected errors to a crash reporter. All of that starts with the language basics in this lesson.

How it works

First the two families, then the syntax for catching, then throwing your own exceptions, then asserts.

Exception and Error types

TypeFamilyTypical causeWhat to do
FormatExceptionExceptionint.parse('12a'), invalid JSONcatch it, or use tryParse
TimeoutExceptionExceptiona Future took too long (dart:async)catch it, offer retry
Your own ...ExceptionExceptionbusiness rules: not found, limit reachedcatch it, show a message
RangeErrorErrorbad index, value out of rangefix the code
StateErrorErrorfirst on an empty list, wrong object statefix the code
ArgumentErrorErrora caller passed an invalid argumentfix the caller
TypeErrorErrora failed as castfix the types

Anything can technically be thrown, even a string (throw 'oops'), but don’t: always throw objects that implement Exception or extend Error, so callers can catch by type.

try, on, catch, finally

Future<void> refresh() async {
  try {
    final data = await api.fetchPosts();         // may throw
    render(data);
  } on TimeoutException {
    showMessage('The server is slow. Try again.');
  } on FormatException catch (e) {
    showMessage('Unexpected data: ' + e.message);
  } catch (e, stackTrace) {
    log('Unexpected: $e', stackTrace);            // a bug: record it
    rethrow;                                      // and let it surface
  } finally {
    hideSpinner();                                // always runs
  }
}
  • on Type catches only that type (and subtypes). Add catch (e) to get the object, and catch (e, stackTrace) to get the StackTrace as well.
  • Clauses are tested top to bottom, and the first match wins. Put specific types before general ones.
  • finally runs whether the try succeeded, a clause handled the problem, or the problem is still travelling up. Use it for cleanup such as hiding a spinner or closing a file.
  • rethrow passes the same object on with its original stack trace. throw e would start a new trace at the catch block and hide where the bug happened.
  • With async/await, a failed Future throws at the await, so the same try/catch works. Lesson 1.11 covers this in depth.

Custom exceptions

sealed class LibraryException implements Exception {
  const LibraryException(this.message);
  final String message;

  @override
  String toString() => message;
}

final class BookNotFoundException extends LibraryException {
  BookNotFoundException(String id) : super('No book with id $id');
}

final class LoanLimitException extends LibraryException {
  LoanLimitException(String member, int limit)
      : super('$member has reached the limit of $limit loans');
}

Implement Exception (it is an interface) and override toString. A sealed base class gives you both options at the call site: on LibraryException catches the whole family, or on LoanLimitException handles one case differently. Name them after the problem in your domain, not after the technical cause.

assert

assert(condition, 'message') throws an AssertionError when the condition is false, but only when asserts are enabled: in Flutter debug builds, in tests, and with dart run --enable-asserts. Release builds strip them out. Use asserts to document assumptions inside your own code, for example in constructor initializer lists. Never use them to validate user input or API data, because in production they do nothing.

Example: the Library Command Desk

The lab processes ten text commands in a loop. Each command is parsed with a switch on list patterns, rule violations throw custom exceptions, and the loop keeps going whatever happens:

for (final line in commands) {
  try {
    final result = desk.run(line);
    print('OK    $result');
    ok++;
  } on LibraryException catch (e) {
    print('DENY  $e');                 // expected rule: explain it
    failed++;
  } on FormatException catch (e) {
    final message = e.message;
    print('BAD   $message');           // bad input: explain it
    failed++;
  } catch (e, stackTrace) {
    print('BUG   $e');                 // unexpected: log and rethrow
    print(stackTrace);
    rethrow;
  } finally {
    processed++;                       // counted every time
  }
}

“borrow b9 asha” prints DENY No book with id b9, “fine asha -5” prints BAD Fine must be a positive whole number: -5, and the summary line reads Processed 10 commands: 4 ok, 6 failed.

Common mistakes

  • Swallowing everything. catch (e) {} hides bugs and leaves the app in a broken state with no clue why. Catch specific types; log and rethrow the rest.
  • Catching Errors to hide bugs. Catching RangeError to avoid a crash treats the symptom. Check lengths, use firstOrNull, fix the logic.
  • Using exceptions for normal flow. If “not found” is common, tryParse, a nullable return or a Result type is clearer and cheaper than throwing.
  • Forgetting toString on custom exceptions. Logs then show Instance of 'LoanLimitException' with no details.
  • Relying on assert for validation. It disappears in release builds.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “What is the difference between Exception and Error in Dart?” is a favourite. Answer: recoverable condition versus programming bug, and give one example of each.
  • Explain on versus catch, and why rethrow is better than throw e.
  • In Flutter, unhandled errors reach FlutterError.onError (framework errors) and PlatformDispatcher.instance.onError (other uncaught errors). Crash reporting tools hook into these; you will meet them again later in the course.
  • Repositories usually catch low-level exceptions (network, parsing) and convert them into domain failures such as Failure('No internet connection'), so the UI never needs to know about HTTP details.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

  4. C. Exception and StateError have their own toString. A custom class only prints Instance of ... until you override toString, which is why custom exceptions should always do so.

lessons.title: Asynchronous Dart: Futures and async/await
lessons.summaryHtml: Dart runs your code on one thread with an event loop. Slow jobs such as network calls return a Future straight away, and the future completes later with a value or an error. async and await let you write that waiting code top to bottom without blocking the app, and try/catch handles async errors like normal ones. The event loop drains the microtask queue before each event, which explains the order things print. You build a Weather Fetcher console app that compares sequential waiting with Future.wait and adds a timeout.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Some work takes time: downloading data, reading a file, waiting for a server. If your program stood still until each job finished, your app would freeze. Dart solves this with asynchronous code. You start a slow job, get a Future back straight away, and carry on. When the job is done, the future completes with a value or an error.

Think of ordering food at a busy café. You pay, get a receipt with a number, and sit down. The receipt is the future. You can chat, read or order a drink while you wait. When your number is called, the future has completed and you collect your meal. If the kitchen runs out of your dish, the future completes with an error instead.

async and await let you write this waiting code so it reads top to bottom, like normal code, without blocking anything.

Why it matters

Almost every real Flutter app talks to something slow: a REST API, a database, Firebase, the camera, secure storage. Every one of these returns a Future or a Stream. If you do not understand futures, you will write screens that show stale data, crash on errors nobody caught, or freeze while waiting.

Flutter draws the screen on the same thread that runs your Dart code. That thread must stay free to paint frames. Async code keeps it free while the network or the disk does the waiting. Later in the course, FutureBuilder, the http package, sqflite and every BLoC that loads data are built on what you learn here.

How it works

One thread and an event loop

Your Dart code runs in an isolate: one thread with its own memory. Inside it, an event loop picks up work one piece at a time. There are two queues:

  • The microtask queue: tiny follow-up jobs, such as "run the next part of this completed future". It is always emptied first.
  • The event queue: outside events such as timers, finished I/O, taps and messages.

The loop works like this: run the current synchronous code to the end, then drain every microtask, then take one event, then drain microtasks again, and so on. Nothing interrupts code that is running. That is why a long for loop freezes the app: the loop never gets a turn.

void main() {
  print('A');
  Future(() => print('B'));            // event queue
  Future.microtask(() => print('C'));  // microtask queue
  print('D');
}
// A, D, C, B

A and D are synchronous. Then the microtask C runs, and only then the event B. In daily work you rarely schedule microtasks yourself, but this order explains many "why did that print first?" puzzles.

Creating and using futures

Constructor or methodWhat it does
Future.value(x)A future that is already complete with x.
Future.error(e)A future that completes with an error.
Future.delayed(d, () => x)Completes with x after duration d. Great for simulating a slow server.
.then(f) / .catchError(f)Register callbacks. Works, but chains get hard to read.
.timeout(d)Fails with TimeoutException if the future takes longer than d.
Future.wait([...])Waits for several futures running at the same time and gives a list of results in the same order.

async and await

Mark a function async and it always returns a Future. Inside it, await pauses this function only until the future completes, then gives you its value. The rest of the program keeps running.

Future<String> fetchName() async {
  await Future.delayed(const Duration(seconds: 1));
  return 'Asha';
}

Future<void> main() async {
  print('Loading...');
  final name = await fetchName();
  print('Hello, $name');
}

One detail surprises people: an async function runs synchronously until its first await. Only then does it hand control back to the caller.

Errors in async code

With await, errors behave like normal exceptions, so you use try, on, catch and finally. An error thrown inside an async function does not escape immediately. It is stored in the returned future and re-thrown where someone awaits it.

Future<void> main() async {
  try {
    final data = await loadProfile().timeout(const Duration(seconds: 5));
    print(data);
  } on TimeoutException {
    print('The server is slow. Try again.');
  } on FormatException catch (e) {
    print('Bad data: ' + e.message);
  } finally {
    print('Hide the spinner');
  }
}

TimeoutException lives in dart:async, so import it.

Sequential or parallel?

Awaiting one future after another runs them one after the other. If they do not depend on each other, start them all first and wait once:

// Sequential: about 1 s + 1 s
final a = await fetchWeather('Kochi');
final b = await fetchWeather('Dubai');

// Parallel: about 1 s in total
final results = await Future.wait([
  fetchWeather('Kochi'),
  fetchWeather('Dubai'),
]);

// Dart 3: a record of futures, with typed results
// (.wait on records needs import 'dart:async';)
final (kochi, dubai) = await (fetchWeather('Kochi'), fetchWeather('Dubai')).wait;

Future.wait keeps the results in the order you passed the futures, not the order they finished. If any future fails, the combined future fails too. The record form with .wait keeps each result's own type, which is handy when the futures return different types.

Example: Weather Fetcher console app

We build a small console app that pretends to call a weather service. Each city has a fake delay, so we can see sequential and parallel timing, errors and timeouts without any real network.

import 'dart:async';

class CityNotFoundException implements Exception {
  CityNotFoundException(this.city);
  final String city;
  @override
  String toString() => 'No weather data for $city';
}

typedef Weather = ({String city, double tempC, String sky});

const _data = {'Kochi': (29.5, 'Humid'), 'Dubai': (38.0, 'Sunny')};

Future<Weather> fetchWeather(String city) async {
  await Future.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 800));
  final entry = _data[city];
  if (entry == null) throw CityNotFoundException(city);
  final (temp, sky) = entry;
  return (city: city, tempC: temp, sky: sky);
}

Future<void> main() async {
  final watch = Stopwatch()..start();
  final list = await Future.wait([fetchWeather('Kochi'), fetchWeather('Dubai')]);
  for (final (:city, :tempC, :sky) in list) {
    print('$city: $tempC C, $sky');
  }
  final ms = watch.elapsedMilliseconds;
  print('Both cities in $ms ms');

  try {
    await fetchWeather('Atlantis');
  } on CityNotFoundException catch (e) {
    print('Error: $e');
  }
}
  1. The Weather record typedef gives us a light data type with named fields.
  2. fetchWeather waits 800 ms, then either throws a custom exception or returns a record.
  3. Future.wait starts both requests together, so the total is about 800 ms, not 1,600 ms.
  4. The for loop destructures each record with a pattern: (:city, :tempC, :sky).
  5. The unknown city shows that an error thrown after an await is caught by the caller's try.

In the lab you extend this app with a slow city and a timeout.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting await. final w = fetchWeather('Kochi'); gives you a Future<Weather>, not a Weather. Printing it shows Instance of 'Future<...>'. Turn on the unawaited_futures or discarded_futures lint to catch this.
  • Awaiting in a loop when order does not matter. Ten independent requests awaited one by one take ten times as long. Use Future.wait.
  • Catching errors in the wrong place. A try around a call without await does not catch the async error, because the error arrives later.
  • Thinking async means "another thread". Async code still runs on the same thread. It helps with waiting, not with heavy computing. For heavy work you need isolates (lesson 1.13).
  • Using .then chains and await mixed together. Pick async/await for readability; mixing both makes error flow hard to follow.
Remember: await pauses the current function, not the app. Other events, taps and frames keep running.

Interview and real-world notes

  • "Explain the event loop" is a classic Flutter interview question. Mention the single thread, the microtask queue drained before each event, and why a long synchronous loop causes jank.
  • Know the difference between Future.wait (parallel waiting) and awaiting in sequence, and say that results keep the input order.
  • Be ready to say what happens to an uncaught error in a future: it is reported as an unhandled error, and in Flutter it shows up in the console and error reporting, not as a friendly message to the user.
  • In real apps, wrap network calls with a timeout and turn low-level exceptions into your own error types. Your UI and BLoCs then deal with a few clear cases instead of every possible exception.
  • .timeout does not cancel the original work. It only stops you waiting for it.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. In what order are the letters printed?

void main() {
  print('A');
  Future(() => print('B'));
  Future.microtask(() => print('C'));
  print('D');
}
  • A A, B, C, D
  • B A, D, B, C
  • C A, D, C, B
  • D A, C, B, D

Snippet 2. What does this print?

Future<void> greet() async {
  print('1');
  await Future.delayed(Duration.zero);
  print('3');
}

void main() {
  greet();
  print('2');
}
  • A 1, 2, 3
  • B 1, 3, 2
  • C 2, 1, 3
  • D 2, 3, 1

Snippet 3. What does this print?

Future<int> load() async {
  throw FormatException('bad');
}

Future<void> main() async {
  try {
    final v = await load();
    print('Value $v');
  } on FormatException catch (e) {
    print('Caught ' + e.message);
  } finally {
    print('Done');
  }
}
  • A Value 0, Done
  • B Done, Caught bad
  • C Caught FormatException: bad, Done
  • D Caught bad, Done

Snippet 4. What does this print?

Future<int> slow(int value, int ms) =>
    Future.delayed(Duration(milliseconds: ms), () => value);

Future<void> main() async {
  final results = await Future.wait([
    slow(1, 300),
    slow(2, 100),
    slow(3, 200),
  ]);
  print(results);
}
  • A [2, 3, 1]
  • B [1, 2, 3]
  • C [3, 2, 1]
  • D 6

Snippet 5. What does this print?

Future<int> answer() async => 42;

void main() {
  final a = answer();
  print(a is Future<int>);
}
  • A 42
  • B false
  • C true
  • D Instance of 'int'

Answers

  1. C. A and D are synchronous. Then the microtask queue is drained (C), and only then the event queue runs the Future callback (B).
  2. A. greet runs synchronously until its first await, so 1 prints first. Then control returns to main, which prints 2. After the delay, greet resumes and prints 3.
  3. D. The error is stored in the Future returned by load and re-thrown at await. The on FormatException block prints the message only (bad), then finally prints Done.
  4. B. Future.wait returns results in the order the futures were passed, not the order they finished.
  5. C. Without await, a is the Future itself, not the int inside it. This is the classic forgotten-await bug.

terms.definition: An object that will complete later with a value of a given type, or with an error.
async makes a function return a Future; await pauses that function until a future completes, without blocking the thread.
The loop that runs one task at a time: synchronous code first, then all microtasks, then the next event.
A high-priority queue of small follow-up jobs, always emptied before the next event such as a timer or I/O result.
Waits for several futures that run at the same time and returns their results in the order they were passed.
Thrown by future.timeout(duration) when the future takes too long. It lives in dart:async.

quiz.question: Which statement about the event loop is correct?
options: All pending microtasks run before the next event from the event queue

quiz.question: You wrap loadData() in try/catch but forget to write await. loadData throws after one second. What happens?
options: The catch block runs after one second

quiz.explanation: Without await, the try block finishes before the error happens. The error is stored in the Future and reported as unhandled if nobody awaits it.

lessons.title: Streams
lessons.summaryHtml: A Stream delivers many values over time, plus errors and a final done event. You consume it with await for or listen, which returns a StreamSubscription you can pause and cancel. async* generators with yield create lazy streams, and a StreamController lets you push values yourself. Single-subscription streams allow one listener; broadcast streams allow many but late listeners miss earlier events. You build a Weather Station that transforms sensor readings and sends alerts to two listeners.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A Future gives you one value, later. A Stream gives you many values over time, one after another, and then maybe says "done". Taps on a button, messages in a chat, GPS positions, download progress and live prices are all streams.

Think of a Future as a parcel you are waiting for, and a Stream as a newspaper subscription. The parcel arrives once. The newspaper keeps arriving every morning until you cancel or the paper stops printing. You listen to a stream, react to each value, and cancel when you no longer care.

Why it matters

Streams are everywhere in Flutter work:

  • Firebase Auth gives you authStateChanges(), a stream of the signed-in user.
  • Cloud Firestore gives you snapshots(), a stream of live query results.
  • A BLoC exposes its states as a stream, and BlocBuilder rebuilds the UI when a new state arrives.
  • StreamBuilder turns any stream into widgets.

If you know how streams start, deliver, fail, finish and get cancelled, you can reason about all of these with one mental model. If you do not, you get memory leaks from subscriptions nobody cancelled and "Stream has already been listened to" errors.

How it works

Events a stream can send

A stream delivers three kinds of events: data events (the values), error events, and one done event at the end. An error does not end a stream by default; more data may follow. The done event is always last.

Listening: await for and listen

There are two ways to consume a stream.

Stream<int> countdown(int from) async* {
  for (var i = from; i > 0; i--) {
    await Future.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 500));
    yield i;
  }
}

Future<void> main() async {
  // 1. await for: reads like a loop, waits for done
  await for (final n in countdown(3)) {
    print('T minus $n');
  }
  print('Lift off!');

  // 2. listen: callback style, returns a subscription
  final sub = countdown(5).listen(
    (n) => print('tick $n'),
    onError: (Object e) => print('error: $e'),
    onDone: () => print('done'),
  );
  await Future.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 1200));
  await sub.cancel(); // stop early, no more ticks, no 'done'
}

await for is best when you want to process every value and then continue. listen is best when you want to keep going and react in the background, and when you might need to pause, resume or cancel. Cancelling does not fire onDone.

Creating streams with async* and yield

A function marked async* is a generator. It returns a Stream, and each yield sends one value. yield* forwards every value from another stream. The body only starts running when someone listens, and it stops at the next yield if the listener cancels. That laziness makes generators cheap and safe.

Other handy constructors: Stream.fromIterable([1, 2, 3]), Stream.value(x), and Stream.periodic(duration, (i) => i) for a tick every period.

Single-subscription and broadcast streams

Single-subscriptionBroadcast
ListenersOne at a time. A second listen throws a StateError.Any number.
Missed valuesBuffers events until someone listens, so nothing is lost.A listener only gets events sent after it subscribed.
Typical useA file being read, an HTTP response body, a generator.Button clicks, app-wide notifications, sensor events many widgets watch.
How to get oneDefault for most streams, StreamController().StreamController.broadcast() or stream.asBroadcastStream().

Check with stream.isBroadcast. Some library streams are special: Stream.fromIterable can be listened to more than once, and each listener iterates the list from the start.

StreamController: push values yourself

When values come from your own code (a timer, a callback, a user action), use a StreamController. You add data, addError errors, and close when finished. Expose only the stream to the outside so other code cannot add values.

import 'dart:async';

class ChatRoom {
  final _controller = StreamController<String>.broadcast();

  Stream<String> get messages => _controller.stream;

  void send(String text) {
    if (text.trim().isEmpty) {
      _controller.addError(ArgumentError('Empty message'));
      return;
    }
    _controller.add(text);
  }

  Future<void> dispose() => _controller.close();
}

Transforming streams

Streams have many of the same methods as lists, but they work on values as they arrive and return new streams: map, where, take, skip, distinct, asyncMap (for an async step per value), expand and handleError. Methods such as first, toList, fold and length return a Future, because they need the stream to finish (or at least produce a value).

final evensSquared = Stream.fromIterable([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
    .where((n) => n.isEven)
    .map((n) => n * n);
print(await evensSquared.toList()); // [4, 16, 36]

For reusable logic you can write a StreamTransformer, but a simple async* function that takes a stream and yields new values is usually easier to read.

Example: Weather Station ticker

We extend the Weather Fetcher idea. A fake sensor streams temperatures. We convert them, keep the first five, and send alerts to a broadcast controller that two listeners watch.

import 'dart:async';

Stream<double> sensor() async* {
  const readings = [28.0, 29.5, 33.2, 31.0, 35.8, 30.1, 36.4];
  for (final c in readings) {
    await Future.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 300));
    yield c;
  }
}

Future<void> main() async {
  final alerts = StreamController<String>.broadcast();
  alerts.stream.listen((a) => print('Phone: $a'));
  alerts.stream.listen((a) => print('Watch: $a'));

  await for (final c in sensor().take(5)) {
    final f = (c * 9 / 5 + 32).toStringAsFixed(1);
    print('Reading $c C = $f F');
    if (c > 33) alerts.add('Hot! $c C');
  }
  await alerts.close();
  print('Station closed');
}
  1. sensor() is a generator. Nothing happens until await for listens.
  2. take(5) cancels the generator after five values, so readings six and seven are never produced.
  3. The alerts controller is broadcast, so the phone and the watch both receive Hot! 33.2 C and Hot! 35.8 C.
  4. Closing the controller sends a done event to both listeners. Always close controllers you create.

Common mistakes

  • Never cancelling a subscription. In a StatefulWidget, store the StreamSubscription and call cancel() in dispose(). Otherwise the callback keeps running after the screen is gone.
  • Never closing a controller. Listeners waiting for done wait forever, and await for never finishes.
  • Listening twice to a single-subscription stream. This throws "Bad state: Stream has already been listened to". Use a broadcast stream, or create a new stream for each listener.
  • Expecting a broadcast listener to see old values. A late listener misses everything sent before it subscribed. If you need "latest value on subscribe", keep the last value yourself (BLoC does this for its state).
  • Putting await for on an endless stream in main and expecting code after it to run. The loop only ends when the stream is done.
Watch out: an error event inside await for is thrown as an exception and ends the loop. Wrap the loop in try/catch, or use handleError before it, if the stream may fail.

Interview and real-world notes

  • "Future vs Stream" and "single-subscription vs broadcast" are very common interview questions. Answer with an example of each.
  • Know that async* plus yield creates a lazy stream, and that yield* delegates to another stream.
  • In Flutter you will mostly consume streams (Firebase, BLoC) with StreamBuilder or BlocBuilder. You create your own with StreamController mainly inside repositories and services.
  • Name the leak: a subscription not cancelled in dispose(). Reviewers look for this in pull requests.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What does this print?

Stream<int> countTo(int n) async* {
  for (var i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
    yield i;
  }
}

Future<void> main() async {
  await for (final v in countTo(3)) {
    print(v * 10);
  }
  print('end');
}
  • A 10, 20, 30, end
  • B end, 10, 20, 30
  • C 1, 2, 3, end
  • D 10, 20, 30

Snippet 2. What does this print?

Future<void> main() async {
  final s = Stream.fromIterable([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);
  final list = await s.where((n) => n.isOdd).map((n) => n * n).toList();
  print(list);
}
  • A [1, 3, 5]
  • B [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]
  • C [1, 9, 25]
  • D Instance of 'Future<List<int>>'

Snippet 3. What does this print?

import 'dart:async';

void main() {
  final controller = StreamController<int>();
  controller.stream.listen((v) => print('A got $v'));
  try {
    controller.stream.listen((v) => print('B got $v'));
  } on StateError {
    print('Second listen failed');
  }
  controller.add(1);
  controller.close();
}
  • A A got 1, B got 1
  • B A got 1, Second listen failed
  • C Second listen failed, A got 1
  • D Second listen failed

Snippet 4. What does this print?

import 'dart:async';

Future<void> main() async {
  final c = StreamController<String>.broadcast();
  c.stream.listen((m) => print('first: $m'));
  c.add('hi');
  await Future.delayed(Duration.zero);
  c.stream.listen((m) => print('second: $m'));
  c.add('yo');
  await c.close();
}
  • A first: hi, second: hi, first: yo, second: yo
  • B first: hi, first: yo, second: yo
  • C second: yo, first: hi, first: yo
  • D first: hi, first: yo

Answers

  1. A. await for processes each yielded value in order and only continues after the stream is done, so end prints last.
  2. C. where keeps 1, 3 and 5, map squares them, and toList collects the results. The await unwraps the Future.
  3. C. A plain StreamController is single-subscription, so the second listen throws a StateError straight away. The added value is delivered asynchronously, after main finishes, so A got 1 prints last.
  4. B. A broadcast listener only receives events sent after it subscribed, so second never sees hi. Both listeners get yo, in the order they subscribed.

terms.definition: A sequence of asynchronous events: data, errors and one final done event.
The object returned by listen. Use it to pause, resume or cancel listening.
An async* function returns a Stream; each yield sends one value. The body runs only while someone listens.
An object you add values, errors and a close to; its stream property is what listeners use.
A stream that allows many listeners at once. A listener only gets events sent after it subscribed.
The default kind: exactly one listener, and events are buffered until it starts listening.

lessons.examTip: Every listen in a widget needs a matching cancel in dispose(). Reviewers look for this leak, and interviewers ask about it.
