quiz.question: A settings service must notify three different screens whenever the theme changes. What should it expose?
options: A Future that completes on each change
A broadcast stream from a StreamController.broadcast()
A single-subscription stream that each screen listens to
A List that the screens check every second
quiz.explanation: Many listeners need the same events, so a broadcast stream fits. A single-subscription stream would throw on the second listen.

quiz.question: What happens when you cancel a StreamSubscription?
options: The listener receives the done event
The stream restarts from the beginning
Remaining events are delivered first, then it stops
No more events reach that listener and onDone is not called
quiz.explanation: Cancelling stops delivery immediately and does not call onDone. For an async* generator it also stops the generator at its next yield.

quiz.question: Which method returns a Future rather than a Stream?
options: toList()
where()
map()
take()
quiz.explanation: toList needs the stream to finish before it can return all values, so it returns Future<List<T>>. where, map and take return new streams.

quiz.question: An await for loop is reading a stream and the stream sends an error event. What happens by default?
options: The error is skipped and the loop continues
The loop pauses until you call resume
The error is thrown as an exception and the loop ends
The error is converted to a null value
quiz.explanation: Inside await for, an error event is thrown at the loop. Use try/catch around the loop, or handleError before it, to deal with it.

lessons.title: Isolates and concurrency
lessons.summaryHtml: Async code helps you wait; it does not make heavy computing faster, because it still runs on one thread. An isolate is a separate worker with its own memory and event loop that can run on another CPU core. Isolates share no mutable memory and talk only by messages. Use Isolate.run for one-off heavy jobs, Flutter's compute when you also target the web, and Isolate.spawn with ports for long-lived workers. You build a Prime Counter that shows a heartbeat timer freezing on the main isolate but not with Isolate.run.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

In the last two lessons you learned that async code helps you wait without freezing. But what if the work itself is heavy, such as parsing a huge JSON file, resizing a photo or crunching numbers? Waiting is not the problem then; computing is. Async does not help, because the computing still happens on your one thread.

Dart's answer is the isolate. An isolate is like a separate worker with its own desk, its own memory and its own event loop. You hand it a job, it works in parallel on another CPU core, and it sends back the result. Workers never share a desk: they only pass notes (messages) to each other.

Why it matters

Flutter aims to draw a new frame many times per second. At 60 frames per second, each frame has about 16 milliseconds. Your build methods, animations and gesture handling all run in the main isolate, also called the UI isolate. If one function keeps that isolate busy for 300 ms, the app drops many frames in a row. Users see a stutter, called jank, or a spinner that stops spinning.

Moving heavy work to another isolate keeps the UI smooth. It is also a common interview topic because it shows you understand how Dart runs code.

How it works

Isolates do not share memory

Many languages use threads that share memory and need locks to avoid data races. Dart isolates do not share mutable memory at all. Each isolate has its own copy of global variables and its own heap. They communicate only by sending messages through ports. This design removes a whole class of bugs: two isolates can never change the same object at the same time.

The cost is that data you send is usually copied, so sending a very large object back and forth is not free. Send what the worker needs, and return a compact result.

Isolate.run: the easy way

For a one-off job, Isolate.run (from dart:isolate) does everything for you: it starts an isolate, runs your function there, returns the result as a Future, and shuts the isolate down.

import 'dart:isolate';

int countPrimes(int limit) {
  var count = 0;
  for (var n = 2; n < limit; n++) {
    var isPrime = true;
    for (var d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
      if (n % d == 0) {
        isPrime = false;
        break;
      }
    }
    if (isPrime) count++;
  }
  return count;
}

Future<void> main() async {
  final count = await Isolate.run(() => countPrimes(2000000));
  print('Primes below 2,000,000: $count');
}

If the function throws, Isolate.run throws the same error in the calling isolate, so a normal try/catch around the await works.

The official docs warn that a closure can accidentally capture extra state from around it and send it along. Keep the closure tiny, like () => countPrimes(limit), and put the real work in a top-level or static function that receives everything it needs as arguments.

compute in Flutter

Flutter's package:flutter/foundation.dart offers compute(function, message). It takes a function with one argument and the argument to pass. On mobile and desktop it runs the function in a new isolate. On the web, where Dart isolates are not available in the same way, it runs the function on the main thread, so your code still works. Use Isolate.run in pure Dart and either one in Flutter apps; compute is handy when you also target the web.

import 'dart:convert';
import 'package:flutter/foundation.dart';

List<Map<String, dynamic>> parsePosts(String body) {
  final list = jsonDecode(body) as List<dynamic>;
  return [for (final item in list) item as Map<String, dynamic>];
}

Future<List<Map<String, dynamic>>> loadPosts(String body) {
  return compute(parsePosts, body);
}

Long-lived workers with Isolate.spawn and ports

If you need a worker that stays alive and handles many requests, use Isolate.spawn with a ReceivePort (an inbox) and a SendPort (the address of someone else's inbox). The usual handshake: the worker first sends back its own SendPort, then both sides can talk.

import 'dart:async';
import 'dart:isolate';

void worker(SendPort toMain) {
  final inbox = ReceivePort();
  toMain.send(inbox.sendPort);            // 1. tell main where to write
  inbox.listen((message) {
    if (message == null) {                // 3. null means "stop"
      inbox.close();
      return;
    }
    final n = message as int;
    toMain.send(n * n);                   // 2. answer each request
  });
}

Future<void> main() async {
  final fromWorker = ReceivePort();
  await Isolate.spawn(worker, fromWorker.sendPort);
  final replies = StreamIterator(fromWorker);
  await replies.moveNext();
  final toWorker = replies.current as SendPort;

  for (final n in [2, 3, 4]) {
    toWorker.send(n);
    await replies.moveNext();
    final square = replies.current;
    print('$n squared is $square');
  }
  toWorker.send(null);
  fromWorker.close();
}

An open ReceivePort keeps an isolate alive, so close ports when you are done. This pattern is more work, so reach for it only when starting a new isolate for each job would be wasteful.

When to use what

SituationTool
Waiting for network, disk, database, timersasync/await on the main isolate. No isolate needed.
One heavy calculation (big JSON, image filter, search over thousands of items)Isolate.run or compute.
Many heavy jobs over time, or a worker that keeps stateIsolate.spawn with ports.
Small work that takes a few millisecondsJust do it. Starting an isolate has its own cost.

Measure before you optimise. Flutter DevTools (lesson 8.4) shows frames that took too long, so you can see whether a function really causes jank.

Example: Prime Counter with a heartbeat

This console app proves that heavy work blocks the event loop. A timer prints a heartbeat every 200 ms. First we count primes on the main isolate, then inside Isolate.run.

import 'dart:async';
import 'dart:isolate';

// countPrimes is the same function as in the Isolate.run section above.

Future<void> main() async {
  var beats = 0;
  final timer = Timer.periodic(
    const Duration(milliseconds: 200),
    (_) => beats++,
  );

  countPrimes(3000000);                       // blocks the main isolate
  await Future.delayed(Duration.zero);
  print('Beats during main-isolate work: $beats');

  beats = 0;
  await Isolate.run(() => countPrimes(3000000)); // main stays free
  print('Beats during Isolate.run work: $beats');
  timer.cancel();
}
  1. While countPrimes runs on the main isolate, the timer cannot fire, because the event loop never gets a turn. The first count is 0 or close to it.
  2. With Isolate.run, the main isolate only waits. The timer keeps firing, so the second count is roughly the job time divided by 200 ms.
  3. In a Flutter app, the "heartbeat" is your animations and frames. The same rule decides whether they stay smooth.

The exact numbers depend on your computer. What matters is the difference between the two lines.

Common mistakes

  • Using an isolate for I/O. An HTTP call is waiting, not computing. await is enough.
  • Capturing big objects in the closure. A closure inside a widget method may capture this and more. Pass plain data to a top-level function.
  • Expecting shared state. Changing a global variable inside the worker does not change it in the main isolate. Return a result instead.
  • Using plugins inside a background isolate without setup. Many plugins talk to the platform through the main isolate. Keep plugin calls on the main isolate unless the plugin's docs say otherwise.
  • Running Isolate.run in DartPad. DartPad compiles to JavaScript for the browser, where dart:isolate is not supported. Run isolate examples with dart run on your machine.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Say it clearly: "async handles waiting, isolates handle heavy computing". Interviewers love that distinction.
  • Explain that isolates share no memory and talk by messages, so there are no data races and no locks.
  • A typical real case: decoding a large API response with Isolate.run or compute inside a repository, so the BLoC and UI stay responsive.
  • Mention the frame budget (about 16 ms at 60 frames per second) when explaining why the UI isolate must stay free.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What does this print? (run with dart run)

import 'dart:isolate';

int sumTo(int n) {
  var sum = 0;
  for (var i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
    sum += i;
  }
  return sum;
}

Future<void> main() async {
  final total = await Isolate.run(() => sumTo(100));
  print('Total: $total');
}
  • A Total: 5050
  • B Total: 100
  • C Total: Instance of 'Future<int>'
  • D Total: 4950

Snippet 2. What does this print? (run with dart run)

import 'dart:isolate';

var counter = 0;

Future<void> main() async {
  final inside = await Isolate.run(() {
    counter += 10;
    return counter;
  });
  print('inside: $inside, main: $counter');
}
  • A inside: 10, main: 10
  • B inside: 10, main: 0
  • C inside: 0, main: 0
  • D A compile error

Snippet 3. What does this print? (run with dart run)

import 'dart:isolate';

Future<void> main() async {
  final future = Isolate.run(() => 42);
  print('waiting');
  print(await future);
}
  • A 42, waiting
  • B waiting
  • C waiting, 42
  • D 42

Snippet 4. What does this print? (run with dart run)

import 'dart:isolate';

Future<void> main() async {
  try {
    await Isolate.run(() => int.parse('abc'));
  } on FormatException {
    print('bad number');
  }
}
  • A bad number
  • B Nothing, the error is lost in the isolate
  • C The program crashes with an uncaught error
  • D abc

Answers

  1. A. Isolate.run returns a Future of the function result, and await unwraps it. 1 + 2 + ... + 100 is 5050.
  2. B. The new isolate has its own copy of the top-level counter. It changes that copy to 10 and returns it; the main isolate copy is still 0.
  3. C. Isolate.run returns a Future immediately, so main prints waiting first and then awaits the result.
  4. A. If the computation throws, Isolate.run throws the same error in the calling isolate, so the on FormatException block runs.

terms.definition: An independent Dart worker with its own memory and event loop. Isolates communicate only by sending messages.
Runs a function in a new isolate, returns its result as a Future, and shuts the isolate down.
Flutter helper that runs a one-argument function in another isolate on native platforms and on the main thread on the web.
A ReceivePort is an inbox (a stream of messages); its SendPort is the address other isolates use to send to it.
Visible stutter when frames take too long because the UI isolate is busy.

lessons.examTip: Remember the one-liner: async handles waiting, isolates handle heavy computing. Network calls do not need an isolate; decoding a huge JSON response might.

quiz.question: Parsing a very large JSON response makes a Flutter list screen stutter. What is the best fix?
options: Run the parsing with Isolate.run or compute
Add more await keywords inside the parser
Call setState more often
Wrap the parser in Future.microtask
quiz.explanation: The work is CPU-bound, so it must leave the UI isolate. await and microtasks still run on the same thread.

quiz.question: A worker isolate changes a top-level variable. What does the main isolate see?
options: The new value immediately
The new value after the next frame
Its own unchanged copy, because isolates do not share memory
A runtime error about a data race
quiz.explanation: Each isolate has its own copy of globals and its own heap. Results must be sent back as messages or returned from Isolate.run.

quiz.question: You need a background worker that stays alive and processes many requests over time. What should you use?
options: A new Isolate.run for every request
Future.wait
A broadcast StreamController on the main isolate
Isolate.spawn with a ReceivePort and SendPort
quiz.explanation: Isolate.spawn with ports creates a long-lived worker you can send messages to repeatedly. Isolate.run is for one-off jobs.

quiz.question: Which task gains nothing from moving to another isolate?
options: Resizing a large photo
Waiting for an HTTP response
Searching 200,000 records with a complex filter
Encrypting a big file in memory
quiz.explanation: Waiting for I/O does not use the CPU, so async/await on the main isolate is enough.

lessons.title: Packages, libraries and testing Dart code
lessons.summaryHtml: Every Dart file is a library. You import libraries with dart:, package: or relative URIs, narrow them with show, hide and as, and publish a clean API by exporting lib/src files from one main file. pub manages packages through pubspec.yaml and pubspec.lock. dart format, dart analyze and lint rules keep code consistent, and package:test with test, group and expect proves it works. You turn the Grade Book logic into a tested package.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

So far most of your Dart code has lived in one file. Real projects are split into many files, reuse code other people wrote, follow a shared style and prove they work with automated tests. This lesson covers the tools for all of that:

  • Libraries: every Dart file is a library. import brings in other libraries, export passes them on.
  • Packages: a folder with a pubspec.yaml, shared through pub, Dart's package manager, and the pub.dev website.
  • Lints and formatting: dart analyze and dart format keep code correct and consistent.
  • Tests: package:test runs small programs that check your code gives the right answers.

Think of a restaurant kitchen. Libraries are the stations (grill, salad, dessert). Packages are ingredients you buy from trusted suppliers. Lints are the head chef's rules. Tests are tasting every dish before it leaves the kitchen.

Why it matters

In a job, you will never work on a one-file project. You will open a codebase with dozens of folders, a pubspec.yaml full of packages, an analysis_options.yaml the team agreed on and a CI pipeline that fails the build if tests or the analyzer fail. Knowing how imports, packages, lints and tests work lets you contribute from day one. Flutter's own tools (flutter pub, flutter analyze, flutter test) are built on exactly what you learn here.

How it works

Project structure

dart create grade_book creates a console project:

grade_book/
  bin/grade_book.dart       entry point with main()
  lib/grade_book.dart       code others can import
  test/grade_book_test.dart tests
  pubspec.yaml              name, SDK range, dependencies
  analysis_options.yaml     lint rules
  pubspec.lock              exact versions pub chose (generated)

A Flutter project has the same idea with lib/main.dart as the entry point, plus platform folders such as android/ and ios/.

pub: adding and updating packages

  • dart pub add http adds a normal dependency and updates pubspec.yaml. In a Flutter project use flutter pub add.
  • dart pub add dev:test adds a dev dependency: needed for development and testing, not shipped in the app.
  • dart pub get downloads everything listed. dart pub upgrade moves to newer allowed versions. dart pub outdated shows what could be updated.

pubspec.yaml says which versions you accept. pubspec.lock records which versions you got. Commit the lock file for apps so every developer and the CI server build with the same versions.

Imports, exports and privacy

import 'dart:math';                          // core library
import 'dart:convert' show jsonDecode;       // only this name
import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;     // prefix: http.get(...)
import 'package:grade_book/grade_book.dart'; // your own lib/ folder
import 'src/helpers.dart' hide debugDump;    // relative, everything but one name
  • dart: for core libraries, package: for packages and for your own lib/ folder.
  • show imports only listed names, hide skips some, as adds a prefix to avoid name clashes.
  • A name starting with an underscore, such as _cache, is private to its library (its file), not to its class. Another class in the same file can see it.

By convention, a package puts its implementation in lib/src/ and offers one main file that exports the public parts. This is often called a barrel file:

// lib/grade_book.dart
export 'src/grades.dart';
export 'src/report.dart' show ReportCard;

Users write one import and get a clean public API. Other packages should not import your src/ files directly.

part and part of

part splits one library across several files that share privacy. Today you mostly see it with code generators: a file user.dart says part 'user.g.dart'; and the generated file starts with part of 'user.dart';. For your own hand-written code, prefer separate libraries with imports.

Lints, analyze, format and fix

analysis_options.yaml chooses the rules. Dart projects usually include package:lints/recommended.yaml; Flutter projects include package:flutter_lints/flutter.yaml. You can turn extra rules on:

include: package:lints/recommended.yaml

linter:
  rules:
    - prefer_final_locals
    - unawaited_futures
CommandWhat it does
dart analyzeReports errors, warnings and lint issues without running the code.
dart format .Rewrites files in the official style. No style debates in code review.
dart fix --applyApplies automatic fixes, for example for deprecated APIs.
dart testRuns every *_test.dart file under test/.

Writing tests with package:test

A test file has a main that registers tests. test describes one behaviour, group bundles related tests, and expect(actual, matcher) checks a result. setUp runs before each test in its group.

import 'package:grade_book/grade_book.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  group('average', () {
    test('returns the mean of the scores', () {
      expect(average([80, 90, 100]), 90);
    });

    test('handles decimals', () {
      expect(average([1, 2]), closeTo(1.5, 0.0001));
    });

    test('throws on an empty list', () {
      expect(() => average([]), throwsArgumentError);
    });
  });
}

Useful matchers: equals (the default), isTrue, isNull, contains, hasLength, closeTo for doubles, isA<T>(), and throwsA(...). Note the () => in the last test: you pass a function so the matcher can call it and catch the error. Async code works too: make the test body async and await inside it, or use expectLater with completion or emitsInOrder for streams.

Example: Grade Book becomes a tested package

The Grade Book console app from lesson 1.1 grows up. We move the logic into lib/src/grades.dart, export it, and test it.

// lib/src/grades.dart
double average(List<num> scores) {
  if (scores.isEmpty) {
    throw ArgumentError('scores must not be empty');
  }
  final total = scores.fold<num>(0, (sum, s) => sum + s);
  return total / scores.length;
}

String letterFor(num score) {
  if (score < 0 || score > 100) {
    throw ArgumentError.value(score, 'score', 'must be 0 to 100');
  }
  return switch (score) {
    >= 90 => 'A',
    >= 80 => 'B',
    >= 70 => 'C',
    >= 60 => 'D',
    _ => 'F',
  };
}
  1. lib/grade_book.dart contains export 'src/grades.dart';.
  2. bin/grade_book.dart imports package:grade_book/grade_book.dart and prints a report.
  3. test/grades_test.dart checks normal values, the boundaries (90, 89.9, 60, 59.9) and the errors.
  4. dart format ., dart analyze and dart test all pass before you commit.

Boundary tests matter most. A bug such as writing > 90 instead of >= 90 only shows up for a score of exactly 90.

Common mistakes

  • Reaching into lib/ with a relative path. An import such as '../lib/src/grades.dart' from bin/ or test/ can make Dart load the same file as two different libraries, which causes confusing type errors. From outside lib/, always use package: imports; inside lib/, relative imports are fine.
  • Thinking _name is class-private. It is library-private.
  • Forgetting the function wrapper in expect. expect(average([]), throwsArgumentError) throws before expect runs and the test fails. Write () => average([]).
  • Comparing doubles with equals. Rounding makes 0.1 + 0.2 not exactly 0.3. Use closeTo.
  • Ignoring analyzer warnings. They are often real bugs, such as an unawaited future or a missing return.
Remember: plain dart run does not check assert statements unless you pass --enable-asserts. dart test and Flutter debug builds do check them.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Expect "What is the difference between dependencies and dev_dependencies?" and "Why commit pubspec.lock?"
  • Explain the test pyramid briefly: many fast unit tests, fewer widget tests, a few integration tests. Lesson 8.3 covers the Flutter side.
  • Teams run dart format --set-exit-if-changed ., dart analyze and the tests in CI, so a pull request cannot be merged if any fails.
  • Before adding a package from pub.dev, look at its publisher, likes, pub points, platform support and how recently it was updated.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What happens when you run this?

import 'dart:math' show max;

void main() {
  print(max(2, 9));
  print(min(2, 9));
}
  • A 9 then 2
  • B 9, then a runtime error
  • C A compile-time error: min is not defined, so nothing prints
  • D 2 then 9

Snippet 2. What does this print?

import 'dart:math' as math;

void main() {
  final values = [3, 8, 5];
  print(values.reduce(math.max));
}
  • A 3
  • B 8
  • C [3, 8, 5]
  • D 16

Snippet 3. You run this with plain dart run (no extra flags). What is printed?

void main() {
  final score = 120;
  assert(score <= 100, 'score too high');
  print('Saved $score');
}
  • A Saved 120
  • B An AssertionError with the message score too high
  • C Nothing
  • D Saved 100

Snippet 4. What does this print?

String initials(String name) => name
    .trim()
    .split(RegExp(r'\s+'))
    .map((part) => part[0].toUpperCase())
    .join();

void main() {
  print(initials('  ada   lovelace '));
  try {
    print(initials(''));
  } on RangeError {
    print('RangeError');
  }
}
  • A AL, RangeError
  • B AL, then an empty line
  • C A L, RangeError
  • D al, RangeError

Answers

  1. C. show max imports only max. min is not in scope, so the program does not compile and nothing runs.
  2. B. The prefix math gives access to max. reduce keeps the larger of each pair, so the result is 8.
  3. A. dart run does not check asserts unless you pass --enable-asserts, so the line is skipped. dart test and Flutter debug builds do check them.
  4. A. The first call splits on runs of whitespace and gives AL. For an empty string, split returns a list holding one empty string, and reading index 0 of it throws a RangeError. A unit test for the empty case would catch this bug.

domains.blurb: How Flutter renders, your first app, stateless and stateful widgets, text and images, buttons and gestures.

lessons.title: How Flutter works
lessons.summaryHtml: In Flutter, everything is a widget: an immutable description of part of the UI. Flutter keeps three trees: short-lived widgets, long-lived elements that hold position and state, and render objects that lay out and paint. build() describes the UI for the current data, setState marks an element dirty so it rebuilds on the next frame, and BuildContext is the element, used to look up ancestors such as the theme. Hot reload keeps state, hot restart resets it.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

In Flutter you describe your screen as a tree of widgets. A widget is a small, immutable description: "a column with an icon and two texts", "padding of 16 around this button". You never say "change that label's text". You say "given this data, the screen looks like this", and Flutter works out what to change on the real screen.

Think of an architect and a builder. Widgets are the architect's drawings: cheap to make, easy to throw away and redraw. Flutter is the builder who compares the new drawing with the building that already stands and only changes what is different. You can hand in a fresh drawing sixty times a second, and the builder will not knock the house down each time.

Why it matters

Almost every confusing Flutter bug comes back to this model: a screen that does not update, state that resets when you did not expect it, a "No MediaQuery found" or "context does not include a Navigator" error, or an app that rebuilds far too often. When you understand the three trees, build() and BuildContext, these errors become easy to read. It also makes you fast: you will know when hot reload is enough and when you need a restart.

How it works

Everything is a widget

Text, icons, padding, alignment, gestures, themes and whole screens are all widgets. Layout is done with widgets too: there is no separate layout file. You compose small widgets into bigger ones.

Screen 1: Everything is a widget lib/main.dart

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

void main() => runApp(const MyApp());

class MyApp extends StatelessWidget {
  const MyApp({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MaterialApp(
      theme: ThemeData(
        colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Colors.lightBlue),
      ),
      home: Scaffold(
        appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Widget tree')),
        body: const Center(
          child: Column(
            mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
            children: [
              Icon(Icons.account_tree, size: 64),
              SizedBox(height: 12),
              Text('Hello, Flutter'),
              Text('Everything here is a widget'),
            ],
          ),
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

Icon, gap, texts, layout, the app bar and the page itself are all widgets in one tree.

The tree for this screen is roughly: MaterialApp → Scaffold → AppBar and Center → Column → Icon, SizedBox, Text, Text. Each widget only knows its own settings and its children.

Three trees: widgets, elements and render objects

TreeWhat it holdsLifetime
Widget treeYour configuration: immutable objects with final fields.Very short. Rebuilt whenever build() runs.
Element treeOne element per widget in use. It remembers where the widget sits in the tree and owns the State of stateful widgets.Long. Survives rebuilds when the widget type and key stay the same.
Render treeRender objects that do layout (sizes and positions) and painting.Long. Updated with new settings, rarely recreated.

When a widget rebuilds, Flutter walks the new widgets alongside the existing elements. For each position it asks: is the new widget the same type with the same key as the old one? If yes, the element stays and simply updates to the new configuration. If no, the old element (and its state) is thrown away and a new one is created. This check is why creating widgets in every build() is cheap: most of the expensive objects are reused.

From build to pixels

Each frame goes through a pipeline:

  1. Build: dirty elements call their widget's build() to get new child widgets.
  2. Layout: parents pass constraints down, children choose a size and pass it up, parents place children.
  3. Paint: render objects record drawing commands.
  4. Composite and rasterise: the Flutter engine turns those commands into pixels on the GPU.

Flutter does not use the platform's native buttons or labels. Its engine (Impeller is the default renderer on iOS and on modern Android) paints every pixel itself. That is why a Flutter app looks the same on Android, iOS, web and desktop, and why you can style anything.

build() and setState

build() should be a pure description: read data, return widgets. It may run many times, for example when a parent rebuilds, the theme changes or the keyboard opens. So never start network calls or create controllers inside it.

A StatefulWidget keeps changing data in its State object. Calling setState marks that element as dirty. On the next frame Flutter rebuilds only the dirty parts.

class _CounterPageState extends State<CounterPage> {
  int _count = 0;

  void _increment() => setState(() => _count++);

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Counter')),
      body: Center(child: Text('Count is $_count')),
      floatingActionButton: FloatingActionButton(
        onPressed: _increment,
        child: const Icon(Icons.add),
      ),
    );
  }
}

Screen 2: setState rebuilds lib/main.dart

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

void main() => runApp(const CounterApp());

class CounterApp extends StatelessWidget {
  const CounterApp({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MaterialApp(
      theme: ThemeData(
        colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Colors.green),
      ),
      home: const CounterPage(),
    );
  }
}

class CounterPage extends StatefulWidget {
  const CounterPage({super.key});

  @override
  State<CounterPage> createState() => _CounterPageState();
}

class _CounterPageState extends State<CounterPage> {
  int _count = 0;

  void _increment() => setState(() => _count++);

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Counter')),
      body: Center(child: Text('Count is $_count')),
      floatingActionButton: FloatingActionButton(
        onPressed: _increment,
        child: const Icon(Icons.add),
      ),
    );
  }
}

Each tap calls setState, which marks the element dirty; the next frame rebuilds the Text with the new count. States: Start → After 3 taps.

Notice the const widgets. A const widget is created once at compile time, and Flutter can skip rebuilding it because it knows it cannot change. Add const wherever the analyzer suggests it.

BuildContext: your address in the tree

The context passed to build is actually the widget's element. It is a handle to "where am I in the tree?". Calls such as Theme.of(context), MediaQuery.of(context), Navigator.of(context) and ScaffoldMessenger.of(context) walk up from that position to find the nearest ancestor of that kind.

So a context only sees what is above it. If you call Navigator.of(context) with the context of the widget that creates MaterialApp, there is no Navigator above it yet, and you get an error. The fix is to use a context from lower in the tree, for example by moving the code into its own widget or wrapping it in a Builder.

Hot reload, hot restart and full restart

In debug mode, Dart runs with a just-in-time compiler that can load changed code into the running app.

ActionWhat happensStateUse it when
Hot reloadInjects changed code and rebuilds the widget tree.KeptYou changed build() methods, styles, texts.
Hot restartReloads code and runs main() again.LostYou changed main(), initState, global or static initialisers, or an enum or class shape and reload misbehaves.
Full restartStops and rebuilds the app.LostYou added a package with native code (a plugin) or changed Android or iOS files.

Screen 3: Hot reload vs hot restart lib/main.dart

// Same CounterApp as before. Only build() was edited:
// a new title and a bigger text style.
class _CounterPageState extends State<CounterPage> {
  int _count = 0;

  void _increment() => setState(() => _count++);

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Tap Counter')),
      body: Center(
        child: Text(
          'Count is $_count',
          style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.headlineMedium,
        ),
      ),
      floatingActionButton: FloatingActionButton(
        onPressed: _increment,
        child: const Icon(Icons.add),
      ),
    );
  }
}

After editing build(), hot reload shows the new title and style but keeps the count; hot restart runs main() again and the count is back to 0. States: Before the edit → After hot reload → After hot restart.

Release builds are compiled ahead of time to native machine code for speed, so hot reload is a debug-only feature.

Example: Widget Tree Explorer

In the lab you run a small counter app that prints a line every time a widget's build() runs:

class Label extends StatelessWidget {
  const Label(this.text, {super.key});
  final String text;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    debugPrint('build Label($text)');
    return Text(text, style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleLarge);
  }
}
  1. Tap + and watch the console. The page's build runs, and so does every non-const Label under it.
  2. Make one Label const. Tap again: its line no longer appears, because Flutter reuses the identical const widget.
  3. Change a text and hot reload: the count stays. Hot restart: the count goes back to 0.
  4. Open Flutter DevTools, choose the Widget Inspector and click a widget on the screen to see where it sits in the tree.

Common mistakes

  • Doing work in build(). Fetching data or creating a TextEditingController there repeats the work on every rebuild. Do it in initState or in a BLoC.
  • Changing a field without setState. The value changes but the screen does not, because nothing marked the element dirty.
  • Using a context from above the thing you look up. The lookup walks up, not down.
  • Expecting hot reload to rerun initState. It does not. Use hot restart.
  • Thinking rebuilds are always expensive. Rebuilding widgets is cheap; the danger is heavy work inside build() or rebuilding huge subtrees for tiny changes.

Interview and real-world notes

  • "Explain the widget, element and render trees" is one of the most common Flutter interview questions. Mention immutability, element reuse by type and key, and layout and paint in render objects.
  • "What is BuildContext?" Answer: the element, a handle to the widget's location, used to look up ancestors.
  • "Hot reload vs hot restart?" Give one example for each.
  • Keys appear in interviews too: they tell Flutter which element belongs to which widget when items move in a list. Lesson 4.3 covers them.

The long-lived object that places a widget in the tree, holds State and decides whether to update or replace on rebuild.
The object that does layout (sizes and positions) and painting.
A handle to a widget’s element, used to look up ancestors with calls such as Theme.of(context).
Injects changed code into the running debug app and rebuilds widgets while keeping state.
Reloads code and runs main() again, resetting all state.

lessons.examTip: When asked about the three trees, say that widgets are cheap blueprints and elements are reused when the widget type and key match. That is why rebuilding is fast.

quiz.question: On rebuild, when does Flutter reuse the existing element for a new widget?
options: When the new widget has the same runtime type and key as the old one
When the new widget has exactly the same field values
Only when the widget is const
Never; elements are recreated on every build
quiz.explanation: Widget.canUpdate compares runtimeType and key. If they match, the element stays and updates to the new configuration, keeping its State.

quiz.question: You change a field in a State object but do not call setState. What happens?
options: Flutter detects the change and rebuilds
The app throws an error
The value changes, but the screen does not update until something else triggers a rebuild
The widget is disposed
quiz.explanation: setState marks the element dirty. Without it, Flutter has no reason to call build again.

quiz.question: You changed code in initState. What do you need to see the change?
options: Hot reload
Nothing, it updates automatically
Change the theme
Hot restart
quiz.explanation: Hot reload rebuilds widgets but does not re-create State objects, so initState is not called again. Hot restart runs main() again.

quiz.question: Calling Navigator.of(context) in the build method of the widget that creates MaterialApp fails. Why?
options: Navigator only works in StatefulWidgets
The context is above MaterialApp, and lookups only search ancestors
MaterialApp does not include a Navigator
build methods cannot use context
quiz.explanation: Lookups walk up from the context. The Navigator is created by MaterialApp, which is below that context. Use a context from a widget under MaterialApp.

lessons.title: Your first app: MaterialApp and Scaffold
lessons.summaryHtml: main() calls runApp() with a root widget, usually a MaterialApp that sets the theme, navigation and title for the whole app. ThemeData(colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(...)) builds a Material 3 palette from one colour, and darkTheme plus ThemeMode.system adds dark mode. Each screen is a Scaffold with slots such as appBar, body and floatingActionButton. Widgets read colours and text styles from Theme.of(context) instead of hard-coding them. You build a Business Card app.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Time to build a real screen. Every Flutter app starts the same way: main() calls runApp() with a root widget. That root is usually a MaterialApp, which sets up the theme, navigation and text direction for the whole app. Each screen is then usually a Scaffold, which gives you the standard page layout: an app bar at the top, a body, and optional slots for a floating button, a navigation bar or a drawer.

Think of MaterialApp as the building (electricity, signs, style rules for every room) and Scaffold as the layout of one room (door at the top, furniture in the middle, a light switch in the corner). In this lesson you build your first mini app: a Business Card with your photo initials, name, job title and contact details.

Why it matters

Every app you build in this course and in your job starts with these two widgets. Getting the theme right at the top means every button, card and text uses consistent colours and fonts without extra work. Using Scaffold slots correctly means snack bars, floating buttons and navigation bars appear in the right place, respect the system bars and animate the way users expect on Android and iOS.

How it works

runApp and the root widget

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

void main() {
  runApp(const BusinessCardApp());
}

runApp takes a widget, makes it fill the screen and starts the rendering pipeline. Import material.dart to get all Material widgets. Mark the root widget const when you can.

MaterialApp

PropertyWhat it does
homeThe first screen.
titleName used by the operating system, for example in the recent apps list or the browser tab.
theme / darkThemeThe light and dark ThemeData.
themeModeThemeMode.system (default), light or dark.
debugShowCheckedModeBannerSet to false to hide the red DEBUG ribbon in screenshots.

Material 3 is the default in current Flutter, so you do not need to switch it on. The simplest good theme is one seed colour:

theme: ThemeData(
  colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Colors.teal),
),

ColorScheme.fromSeed generates a full, accessible palette from that one colour: primary, onPrimary, primaryContainer, surface, outline and more. Widgets pick the right roles automatically. onPrimary means "the colour for text and icons placed on top of primary", so contrast is handled for you.

Scaffold and AppBar

A Scaffold has named slots. You fill only the ones you need:

  • appBar: usually an AppBar with title, optional leading widget and actions (a list of icon buttons on the right).
  • body: the main content.
  • floatingActionButton: the main action of the screen.
  • bottomNavigationBar, drawer: navigation, covered in module 5.
  • backgroundColor: defaults to the theme's surface colour.
import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

void main() => runApp(const MyApp());

class MyApp extends StatelessWidget {
  const MyApp({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MaterialApp(
      theme: ThemeData(
        colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Colors.teal),
      ),
      home: Scaffold(
        appBar: AppBar(
          title: const Text('Business Card'),
          actions: [
            IconButton(icon: const Icon(Icons.share), onPressed: () {}),
          ],
        ),
        body: const Center(child: Text('Hello, Flutter!')),
      ),
    );
  }
}

Screen 1: Scaffold skeleton lib/main.dart

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

void main() => runApp(const MyApp());

class MyApp extends StatelessWidget {
  const MyApp({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MaterialApp(
      theme: ThemeData(
        colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Colors.teal),
      ),
      home: Scaffold(
        appBar: AppBar(
          title: const Text('Business Card'),
          actions: [
            IconButton(icon: const Icon(Icons.share), onPressed: () {}),
          ],
        ),
        body: const Center(child: Text('Hello, Flutter!')),
      ),
    );
  }
}

MaterialApp supplies the teal theme; Scaffold gives the AppBar with a share action and a centred body.

The AppBar already knows to leave room for the status bar. For content without an app bar, wrap the body in SafeArea so it does not hide under a notch or the system bars.

Reading the theme in your widgets

Instead of hard-coding colours and font sizes, read them from the theme:

final colors = Theme.of(context).colorScheme;
final text = Theme.of(context).textTheme;

Text('Asha Kumar', style: text.headlineSmall);
Text('Flutter Developer', style: text.titleMedium?.copyWith(color: colors.primary));

The Material 3 text styles are named by role and size: displayLarge down to displaySmall, then headline, title, body and label, each in Large, Medium and Small. copyWith makes a copy of a style with a few changes. The ?. is there because the styles are nullable.

Example: Business Card app

Here is the whole app in one main.dart, shown in two parts. Paste both parts into DartPad or a new project and run it.

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

void main() => runApp(const BusinessCardApp());

class BusinessCardApp extends StatelessWidget {
  const BusinessCardApp({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MaterialApp(
      title: 'Business Card',
      debugShowCheckedModeBanner: false,
      theme: ThemeData(
        colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Colors.teal),
      ),
      home: const CardPage(),
    );
  }
}

The screen itself goes in its own widget, below MaterialApp, in the same file:

class CardPage extends StatelessWidget {
  const CardPage({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final colors = Theme.of(context).colorScheme;
    final text = Theme.of(context).textTheme;
    return Scaffold(

class CardPage extends StatelessWidget {
  const CardPage({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final colors = Theme.of(context).colorScheme;
    final text = Theme.of(context).textTheme;
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('My Card'), centerTitle: true),
      body: Center(
        child: Column(
          mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
          children: [
            CircleAvatar(
              radius: 48,
              backgroundColor: colors.primary,
              child: Text('AK',
                  style: text.headlineMedium?.copyWith(color: colors.onPrimary)),
            ),
            const SizedBox(height: 16),
            Text('Asha Kumar',
                style: text.headlineSmall?.copyWith(fontWeight: FontWeight.bold)),
            Text('Flutter Developer',
                style: text.titleMedium?.copyWith(color: colors.primary)),
            const SizedBox(height: 24),
            const Card(
              margin: EdgeInsets.symmetric(horizontal: 24),
              child: Column(
                children: [
                  ListTile(leading: Icon(Icons.phone), title: Text('+91 98765 43210')),
                  Divider(height: 1),
                  ListTile(leading: Icon(Icons.email), title: Text('asha@example.com')),
                  Divider(height: 1),
                  ListTile(leading: Icon(Icons.location_on), title: Text('Kochi, India')),
                ],
              ),
            ),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

Every colour and text style comes from the theme: primary for the avatar and job title, titleMedium and headlineSmall for the texts.

  1. BusinessCardApp is the root. It sets the title, hides the debug banner and creates a teal theme.
  2. CardPage is the screen. It reads the colour scheme and text theme once at the top of build.
  3. Column with mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min takes only the height it needs, so Center can centre the whole group.
  4. SizedBox(height: 16) adds a fixed gap. It is the simplest spacer in Flutter.
  5. The Card and everything inside it never change, so the whole card is const.

Now add dark mode. Give MaterialApp a second theme from the same seed with brightness: Brightness.dark:

theme: ThemeData(
  colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Colors.teal),
),
darkTheme: ThemeData(
  colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(
    seedColor: Colors.teal,
    brightness: Brightness.dark,
  ),
),
themeMode: ThemeMode.system,

Screen 3: Dark mode for free lib/main.dart

class BusinessCardApp extends StatelessWidget {
  const BusinessCardApp({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MaterialApp(
      title: 'Business Card',
      debugShowCheckedModeBanner: false,
      theme: ThemeData(
        colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Colors.teal),
      ),
      darkTheme: ThemeData(
        colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(
          seedColor: Colors.teal,
          brightness: Brightness.dark,
        ),
      ),
      themeMode: ThemeMode.system,
      home: const CardPage(), // unchanged
    );
  }
}

With darkTheme and ThemeMode.system, the same CardPage switches to the dark palette when the phone is in dark mode.

Because CardPage reads every colour from the theme, it switches to dark mode with no other changes. That is the pay-off of never hard-coding colours.

Common mistakes

  • Several MaterialApp widgets. Use one at the root. A second one inside a screen creates a separate navigator and theme and causes strange bugs.
  • Hard-coding colours such as Colors.teal in every widget. The app then breaks in dark mode. Use colorScheme roles.
  • Old text style names. headline6 and bodyText2 were removed. Use titleLarge, bodyMedium and the other Material 3 names.
  • Calling Theme.of(context) with the context of the widget that creates MaterialApp. The theme is below that context, so you get the default theme. Read it inside a widget under MaterialApp, such as CardPage.
  • Forgetting const. The analyzer suggests it. Accept the suggestion; it saves rebuild work.
Remember: one MaterialApp per app, one Scaffold per screen, and colours from Theme.of(context).colorScheme.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Interviewers often ask "What is the difference between MaterialApp and Scaffold?" Answer: app-wide setup (theme, navigation, localisation) versus one screen's layout slots.
  • Real apps put the theme in its own file, such as lib/app/theme.dart, and the root widget in lib/app/app.dart, so main.dart stays tiny.
  • Many companies start from a brand colour and use ColorScheme.fromSeed, then adjust a few roles. Lesson 4.2 goes deeper into theming.
  • For a portfolio, take screenshots of your Business Card in light and dark mode. It shows you understand theming from day one.

lessons.title: Stateless and stateful widgets
lessons.summaryHtml:
A StatelessWidget draws itself only from the values it is given, so it never changes on its own. A StatefulWidget is split in two: an immutable widget class and a long-lived State object that holds data which changes over time.

You change that data inside setState, which tells Flutter to call build again on the next frame. The State object has a lifecycle: initState runs once at the start, didUpdateWidget runs when the parent passes new values, and dispose runs once at the end so you can release controllers and subscriptions.

You will build a counter and then a Tip Calculator, and learn why const constructors make rebuilds cheaper.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Think of a printed poster and a whiteboard. The poster shows exactly what was printed on it; to change it, you print a new poster. The whiteboard stays on the wall, and people write on it and wipe it all day. In Flutter, a StatelessWidget is the poster and the State object of a StatefulWidget is the whiteboard.

Every widget object is immutable: its fields are final and never change after it is created. When something must change on screen, Flutter builds new widget objects. A StatefulWidget adds a second, long-lived object, the State, that keeps its data while the widgets around it are rebuilt many times per second if needed.

Why it matters

Almost every screen you will write reacts to the user: a counter goes up, a form shows an error, a list filters as you type. You must decide where each piece of changing data lives. Put it in the wrong place and you get bugs that confuse beginners for days: text that resets when the keyboard opens, values that never update, or the error setState() called after dispose().

Knowing the State lifecycle also prevents memory leaks. Controllers, timers, animation controllers and stream subscriptions must be released when the screen goes away, and dispose is the one correct place to do it. Junior Flutter interviews ask about this lifecycle almost every time.

How it works

We will look at the two widget kinds, then at setState, the lifecycle and const.

StatelessWidget: output from inputs

A StatelessWidget has one job: turn its fields (plus inherited data such as Theme.of(context)) into a widget tree in build. Given the same inputs, it always builds the same thing.

class PriceTag extends StatelessWidget {
  const PriceTag({super.key, required this.label, required this.amount});

  final String label;
  final double amount;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final text = amount.toStringAsFixed(2);
    return ListTile(title: Text(label), trailing: Text('₹$text'));
  }
}

super.key forwards the optional key to the parent class; you will use keys later for lists. Mark the constructor const whenever every field is final, which is almost always.

StatefulWidget: two classes on purpose

A StatefulWidget has a widget class and a State class. The widget holds configuration from the parent and is thrown away and recreated on every parent rebuild. createState is called once, and Flutter attaches the resulting State to an element, the object that represents this spot in the tree. As long as the same widget type (and key) appears in the same place, Flutter reuses that element and its State. That is why data you store in the State survives rebuilds.

Screen 1: Counter: the smallest stateful app lib/main.dart

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

void main() => runApp(const MaterialApp(home: CounterPage()));

class CounterPage extends StatefulWidget {
  const CounterPage({super.key});

  @override
  State<CounterPage> createState() => _CounterPageState();
}

class _CounterPageState extends State<CounterPage> {
  int _count = 0; // survives every rebuild

  void _increment() {
    setState(() => _count++);
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Counter')),
      body: Center(
        child: Column(
          mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
          children: [
            const Text('Taps so far'),
            Text('$_count',
                style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.displayLarge),
          ],
        ),
      ),
      floatingActionButton: FloatingActionButton(
        onPressed: _increment,
        tooltip: 'Add one',
        child: const Icon(Icons.add),
      ),
    );
  }
}

The number lives in the State object. Each tap calls setState, and Flutter rebuilds only this screen with the new value. States: Start → After 3 taps.

Inside the State, widget gives you the current widget object, so widget.label reads a value the parent passed in. The leading underscore in _CounterPageState makes the class private to its file, which is the convention.

What setState really does

setState(fn) runs fn immediately, then marks this element as dirty. On the next frame Flutter calls build for every dirty element and compares the new widgets with the old ones, updating only what changed on screen. Three rules follow:

  • Change the data inside the callback (or just before it). Changing a field without calling setState updates memory but not the screen.
  • The callback must be synchronous. Do the await first, then call setState with the result.
  • After an await, the user may have left the screen. Check if (!mounted) return; before calling setState.
Future<void> _load() async {
  final names = await fetchNames(); // your own async function
  if (!mounted) return;             // screen may be gone
  setState(() => _names = names);
}

The State lifecycle

MethodWhen it runsUse it for
createStateOnce, when the widget is first insertedReturning your State object
initStateOnce, right after the State is createdCreating controllers, starting timers or subscriptions. Always call super.initState() first.
didChangeDependenciesAfter initState, and when an inherited widget it reads changesWork that needs context lookups such as Theme.of
buildAfter the above, and after every setState or parent rebuildDescribing the UI. Keep it fast and free of side effects.
didUpdateWidgetWhen the parent rebuilds with a new widget of the same typeReacting to changed constructor values, for example restarting a timer when a duration changes
disposeOnce, when the State is removed for goodReleasing controllers, timers and subscriptions. Call super.dispose() last.

Screen 2: Lifecycle log lib/main.dart

class Greeting extends StatefulWidget {
  const Greeting({super.key, required this.label});
  final String label;

  @override
  State<Greeting> createState() => _GreetingState();
}

class _GreetingState extends State<Greeting> {
  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    debugPrint('initState');
  }

  @override
  void didUpdateWidget(covariant Greeting oldWidget) {
    super.didUpdateWidget(oldWidget);
    final from = oldWidget.label;
    final to = widget.label;
    if (from != to) debugPrint('didUpdateWidget: $from -> $to');
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    debugPrint('dispose');
    super.dispose();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    debugPrint('build');
    return Text(widget.label,
        style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.headlineMedium);
  }
}

// In the parent State:
// SwitchListTile(title: const Text('Show greeting'), value: _show,
//     onChanged: (v) => setState(() => _show = v)),
// FilledButton.tonal(onPressed: () => setState(() => _label = 'Evening'),
//     child: const Text('Change label')),
// if (_show) Greeting(label: _label),

The grey panel shows the debug console. initState runs once, didUpdateWidget runs when the parent passes a new label, and dispose runs when the switch removes the child. States: First show → New label → Switched off.

Notice that build can run many times, while initState and dispose run exactly once each. Anything expensive or anything that must be cleaned up belongs in those two, never in build.

const constructors and cheap rebuilds

When you write const Text('Taps so far'), Dart creates that object once at compile time and reuses the identical instance. During a rebuild, Flutter sees that the new widget is the very same object as the old one and skips rebuilding that subtree. In a big screen this adds up. Enable the recommended lints (flutter_lints is in every new project) and the analyzer will suggest where const is possible.

Remember: widgets are cheap descriptions. Rebuilding is normal and fast. What you must avoid is losing state or doing slow work inside build.

Example: Tip Calculator

The Tip Calculator has three pieces of state: the bill text, the chosen tip percentage and, in the lab, the number of people. Everything else is derived and computed in build.

  1. Create a StatefulWidget TipCalculator and its State class.
  2. Store a TextEditingController as a final field. It is created once with the State and disposed in dispose.
  3. Store int _tipPercent = 15. The SegmentedButton calls setState(() => _tipPercent = s.first).
  4. The TextField calls setState(() {}) in onChanged. The text is already in the controller; the empty setState just asks for a rebuild.
  5. In build, parse the bill with double.tryParse(...) ?? 0, so an empty or invalid field shows 0.00 instead of crashing.
  6. Format money with toStringAsFixed(2) into local variables and interpolate them with $tipText.

Screen 3: Tip Calculator lib/main.dart

class TipCalculator extends StatefulWidget {
  const TipCalculator({super.key});

  @override
  State<TipCalculator> createState() => _TipCalculatorState();
}

class _TipCalculatorState extends State<TipCalculator> {
  final _bill = TextEditingController();
  int _tipPercent = 15;

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _bill.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final bill = double.tryParse(_bill.text) ?? 0;
    final tip = bill * _tipPercent / 100;
    final tipText = tip.toStringAsFixed(2);
    final totalText = (bill + tip).toStringAsFixed(2);

    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Tip Calculator')),
      body: Padding(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
        child: Column(
          crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.stretch,
          spacing: 16,
          children: [
            TextField(
              controller: _bill,
              keyboardType:
                  const TextInputType.numberWithOptions(decimal: true),
              decoration: const InputDecoration(
                labelText: 'Bill amount',
                prefixIcon: Icon(Icons.receipt_long),
                border: OutlineInputBorder(),
              ),
              onChanged: (_) => setState(() {}),
            ),
            SegmentedButton<int>(
              segments: const [
                ButtonSegment(value: 10, label: Text('10%')),
                ButtonSegment(value: 15, label: Text('15%')),
                ButtonSegment(value: 20, label: Text('20%')),
              ],
              selected: {_tipPercent},
              onSelectionChanged: (s) =>
                  setState(() => _tipPercent = s.first),
            ),
            Card(child: ListTile(title: const Text('Tip'), trailing: Text('₹$tipText'))),
            Card(child: ListTile(title: const Text('Total'), trailing: Text('₹$totalText'))),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

One State object holds the bill controller and the chosen tip. Every change calls setState, and build recomputes the tip and total from scratch. States: Empty → Bill 1200 → 20% tip.

Why not store tip and total as fields too? Because then you must remember to update them every time the bill or percentage changes. Deriving them in build means they can never get out of sync.

Common mistakes

  • Putting changing data on the widget class. Fields there are final and the object is replaced on every parent rebuild. Mutable data goes on the State.
  • Creating controllers in build. TextEditingController() inside build makes a new controller on every rebuild, so typed text disappears and old controllers leak.
  • Forgetting dispose. Every controller, FocusNode, Timer, AnimationController and StreamSubscription you create must be disposed or cancelled.
  • setState after an await without checking mounted. If the user navigated away, Flutter throws an error. Check mounted first.
  • Calling setState inside build. Build must only describe UI. Changing state there causes an error or an endless rebuild loop.
  • Making everything stateful. If a widget has no data of its own that changes, keep it stateless and pass values in.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “Why two classes?” Widgets are immutable configuration and are recreated often; the State lives in the element tree and survives. This split keeps rebuilds cheap and predictable.
  • Be ready to list the lifecycle in order: createState, initState, didChangeDependencies, build, then didUpdateWidget or setState followed by build, then deactivate and dispose.
  • “Ephemeral state” (a tab index, a text field, an animation) is fine in setState. Shared app state, such as a logged-in user or a cart, moves to Provider or BLoC later in this course.
  • In code reviews, seniors look for missing dispose calls, missing mounted checks and missing const. Fixing those three makes your code look professional immediately.

terms.definition: A widget whose output depends only on its constructor arguments and inherited data such as the theme. It has no mutable state of its own.
A widget that creates a separate State object with createState. The widget stays immutable; the State holds what changes.
The long-lived object that keeps data between rebuilds. Flutter keeps it attached to the element tree while the widget stays in the same place.
Runs a callback that changes state, marks the widget as dirty and schedules a rebuild on the next frame.
Lifecycle methods. initState runs once when the State is created; dispose runs once when it is removed for good.
A constructor whose instances can be created at compile time. Flutter can skip rebuilding a const widget because it is the identical object.

lessons.examTip: Interviewers love “why is StatefulWidget two classes?”. Answer: widgets are cheap, immutable and rebuilt often; the State object survives those rebuilds.

lessons.title: Text, images, icons and assets
lessons.summaryHtml:
Most of what users see is text, images and icons. You style text with the theme’s TextTheme (titleLarge, bodyMedium and so on) and adjust it with copyWith. You mix styles in one line with Text.rich and TextSpan.

Images come from your app bundle with Image.asset or from the internet with Image.network. Bundled files and custom fonts must be declared in pubspec.yaml. Icons come from the built-in Icons class.

You will build the menu screen of Brew Lab, a small café app, with a custom font, local photos, a network image with loading and error states, and star icons.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A café menu board has three kinds of content: words (item names, prices, opening hours), pictures (photos of the drinks) and small symbols (a star for favourites, a leaf for vegan). A Flutter screen is the same. Text draws words, Image draws pictures and Icon draws symbols from an icon font.

Some content ships inside your app, like the menu photos printed on the board. These are assets, and you list them in pubspec.yaml so the build tool packs them in. Other content comes from the internet while the app runs, like today’s special, and may be slow or missing.

Why it matters

Good typography and images are the difference between an app that looks like a student project and one a client accepts. They also carry real risks. Hard-coded font sizes ignore the user’s accessibility settings. Missing errorBuilder callbacks show an ugly error box as soon as the network drops. A wrong indent in pubspec.yaml breaks the build. Huge photos slow scrolling and use lots of memory. This lesson gives you the habits that avoid all of these.

How it works

We start with text, then icons, then images and the pubspec entries they need.

Text and TextStyle

Material 3 defines fifteen named styles in TextTheme: display, headline, title, body and label, each in Large, Medium and Small. Read them from the theme and change only what you need with copyWith:

final text = Theme.of(context).textTheme;
final colors = Theme.of(context).colorScheme;

Text('Single-origin beans',
    style: text.titleMedium?.copyWith(color: colors.primary));

The ?. is there because TextTheme styles are nullable. Useful Text parameters are maxLines, overflow: TextOverflow.ellipsis, textAlign and softWrap. Flutter scales text by the user’s system setting through MediaQuery.textScalerOf(context); do not fight it with fixed heights around text.

To mix styles in one run of text, use Text.rich with a tree of TextSpan objects. Child spans inherit the parent span’s style and override parts of it. Prefer Text.rich over the lower-level RichText, because Text.rich also applies the default text style and text scaling for you.

Screen 1: Text styles from the theme lib/main.dart

class AboutPage extends StatelessWidget {
  const AboutPage({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final text = Theme.of(context).textTheme;
    final colors = Theme.of(context).colorScheme;

    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Brew Lab')),
      body: Padding(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
        child: Column(
          crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
          spacing: 8,
          children: [
            Text('Fresh coffee, slow mornings', style: text.headlineSmall),
            Text('Single-origin beans',
                style: text.titleMedium?.copyWith(color: colors.primary)),
            const Text(
              'Roasted in small batches every week and brewed to order.',
              maxLines: 1,
              overflow: TextOverflow.ellipsis,
            ),
            Text.rich(
              TextSpan(
                text: 'Open today ',
                style: text.bodyLarge,
                children: [
                  TextSpan(
                    text: 'until 9 pm',
                    style: TextStyle(
                      fontWeight: FontWeight.bold,
                      color: colors.primary,
                    ),
                  ),
                ],
              ),
            ),
            Text('Prices include tax',
                style: text.labelSmall?.copyWith(fontStyle: FontStyle.italic)),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

Every style comes from the TextTheme; copyWith changes only the colour or style. The long description stops at one line with an ellipsis.

Icons

Icon(Icons.star, size: 18, color: Colors.amber) draws a glyph from the Material icon font that every new project includes (uses-material-design: true in pubspec). Many icons have variants such as Icons.favorite_border or Icons.shopping_bag_outlined. An icon that carries meaning on its own should have a semanticLabel, and an IconButton should have a tooltip, which screen readers also use.

Images from assets and from the network

ConstructorSourceGood for
Image.asset('assets/images/latte.jpg')Bundled in the appLogos, onboarding art, fixed menu photos. Works offline.
Image.network(url)Downloaded at run timeUser avatars, product photos from an API. Needs loading and error states.
Image.file(file)A file on the devicePhotos the user just picked or took (lesson 8.2).
Image.memory(bytes)Bytes in memoryImages you received as data, for example from a database.

The fit parameter decides how the picture fills its box. BoxFit.cover fills and crops, which is what you want for thumbnails and banners. BoxFit.contain shows the whole image with empty bands. BoxFit.fill stretches and distorts, so you rarely want it.

A network image takes time and can fail. loadingBuilder is called while bytes arrive: when its progress argument is null the image is ready, so you return the child. errorBuilder replaces the image when the download fails.

Screen 2: Network image: loading, loaded, failed lib/main.dart

class SpecialCard extends StatelessWidget {
  const SpecialCard({super.key});

  static const url = 'https://picsum.photos/seed/latte/600/400';

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final text = Theme.of(context).textTheme;
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Today’s special')),
      body: Column(
        crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
        children: [
          Image.network(
            url,
            height: 200,
            width: double.infinity,
            fit: BoxFit.cover,
            semanticLabel: 'A latte with leaf art',
            loadingBuilder: (context, child, progress) {
              if (progress == null) return child; // finished
              return const SizedBox(
                height: 200,
                child: Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator()),
              );
            },
            errorBuilder: (context, error, stackTrace) => const SizedBox(
              height: 200,
              child: Center(child: Icon(Icons.broken_image, size: 48)),
            ),
          ),
          Padding(
            padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
            child: Text('Leaf latte · ₹180', style: text.titleLarge),
          ),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}

loadingBuilder shows a spinner until the bytes arrive; errorBuilder shows a fallback icon instead of a red error box when the phone is offline. States: Loading → Loaded → Offline.

Flutter keeps decoded images in an in-memory cache, so showing the same URL twice during a session does not download it twice. If a large photo is shown small, pass cacheWidth (in physical pixels) so Flutter decodes a smaller version and saves memory.

Declaring assets and fonts in pubspec.yaml

Assets and fonts go under the top-level flutter: key. YAML cares about indentation, so use two spaces per level and never tabs.

flutter:
  uses-material-design: true

  assets:
    - assets/images/

  fonts:
    - family: Pacifico
      fonts:
        - asset: assets/fonts/Pacifico-Regular.ttf

A folder entry ending with / includes every file directly in that folder, but not files in subfolders; each subfolder needs its own line. For sharp images on high-density screens, you can add variants in folders named 2.0x and 3.0x next to the main file, and Flutter picks the best one for the device. After you edit pubspec, run flutter pub get and stop and restart the app: hot reload does not bundle new assets.

Use the font with TextStyle(fontFamily: 'Pacifico'), or for the whole app with ThemeData(fontFamily: ...). A font family can list several files with weight and style entries so bold and italic use the real font files instead of a synthetic version.

Example: Brew Lab menu

The Brew Lab menu screen combines everything above.

  1. Create assets/images with four photos and assets/fonts with Pacifico, and declare both in pubspec.
  2. Model the menu with a small MenuItem class. A getter priceLabel returns '₹$price', so widgets never build strings themselves.
  3. Use ListView.builder so rows are built only when they scroll into view.
  4. Each row is a Card with a ListTile. The leading photo is Image.asset with BoxFit.cover, wrapped in ClipRRect for rounded corners.
  5. The trailing rating is a Row with mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min, so it takes only the width it needs inside the tile.

Screen 3: Brew Lab menu lib/main.dart

class MenuItem {
  const MenuItem(this.name, this.price, this.rating, this.image);
  final String name;
  final int price;
  final double rating;
  final String image;

  String get priceLabel => '₹$price';
}

const menu = [
  MenuItem('Leaf latte', 180, 4.8, 'assets/images/latte.jpg'),
  MenuItem('Cold brew', 160, 4.6, 'assets/images/cold_brew.jpg'),
  MenuItem('Masala chai', 90, 4.9, 'assets/images/chai.jpg'),
  MenuItem('Banana cake', 120, 4.4, 'assets/images/cake.jpg'),
];

class MenuPage extends StatelessWidget {
  const MenuPage({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(
        title: const Text('Brew Lab',
            style: TextStyle(fontFamily: 'Pacifico', fontSize: 26)),
        actions: [
          IconButton(
            onPressed: () {},
            icon: const Icon(Icons.shopping_bag_outlined),
            tooltip: 'Cart',
          ),
        ],
      ),
      body: ListView.builder(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(8),
        itemCount: menu.length,
        itemBuilder: (context, i) {
          final item = menu[i];
          return Card(
            child: ListTile(
              leading: ClipRRect(
                borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(8),
                child: Image.asset(item.image,
                    width: 56, height: 56, fit: BoxFit.cover),
              ),
              title: Text(item.name),
              subtitle: Text(item.priceLabel),
              trailing: Row(
                mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
                children: [
                  const Icon(Icons.star, color: Colors.amber, size: 18),
                  Text(item.rating.toString()),
                ],
              ),
            ),
          );
        },
      ),
    );
  }
}

Local photos come from Image.asset inside ClipRRect for rounded corners. The title uses the Pacifico font declared in pubspec.yaml (the preview uses the default font).

Common mistakes

  • Wrong pubspec indentation, or assets: placed at the top level instead of under flutter:. The asset is then silently missing and Image.asset fails at run time.
  • Expecting a folder entry to include subfolders. List assets/images/menu/ separately.
  • Adding an asset and pressing hot reload. Restart the app after changing pubspec.
  • Old style names. headline6 and bodyText2 were removed. Use titleLarge, bodyMedium and the other Material 3 names.
  • No errorBuilder on Image.network. Users on a weak connection see a broken layout.
  • Loading full-size camera photos into small thumbnails. Resize the files or use cacheWidth.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “How do you add a custom font?” Put the file in assets/fonts, declare the family in pubspec, then use fontFamily in a TextStyle or the theme.
  • Real apps usually show network images with a placeholder colour or blur while loading, and they often use a caching package to keep images on disk between launches. Know that Image.network alone caches only in memory.
  • Accessibility matters in client work: give meaningful images a semanticLabel, give icon buttons a tooltip, and test your screens with the largest system text size.
  • Keep all text styles coming from the theme. When the designer changes the font later, you edit one line instead of fifty.
