lessons.title: Buttons, gestures and feedback
lessons.summaryHtml:
Material 3 gives you a button family ordered by emphasis: FilledButton for the main action, FilledButton.tonal and ElevatedButton for secondary ones, OutlinedButton and TextButton for low-emphasis actions, plus IconButton and the FloatingActionButton. Passing onPressed: null disables a button.

For custom tap areas use InkWell (with a ripple) or GestureDetector (no visual feedback, more gestures). Tell the user what happened with a SnackBar, ask for confirmation with showDialog, and offer choices with showModalBottomSheet. Dialogs and sheets return a Future with the user’s answer.

You will build a Habit Tracker screen with tap to complete, long press for options, delete with Undo and a confirm dialog.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A good shop assistant does three things: they respond when you ask for something, they tell you what they did, and they check with you before doing anything you cannot undo. Buttons and gestures are how the user asks. SnackBars tell the user what happened. Dialogs check before a serious action, and bottom sheets offer a short menu of choices.

Why it matters

Users judge an app by how it responds to their fingers. A tap with no ripple feels broken. A delete with no message makes people wonder if it worked. A destructive action with no confirmation, or a confirmation for every small thing, makes the app feel careless or annoying. Picking the right button and the right kind of feedback is a design skill that clients notice, and the async code behind dialogs is a classic source of bugs.

How it works

We cover the buttons, custom gestures, then the three kinds of feedback.

The button family

WidgetEmphasisTypical use
FilledButtonHighestThe one main action: Save, Pay, Continue
FilledButton.tonalMedium-highImportant but secondary actions
ElevatedButtonMediumSecondary action that must stand out from a busy or patterned background
OutlinedButtonMedium-lowAlternatives next to a filled button: Cancel, Skip
TextButtonLowestDialog actions, links such as Learn more
IconButton (also .filled, .filledTonal, .outlined)VariesCompact actions in app bars and list rows; always give a tooltip
FloatingActionButtonHighest on the screenThe primary action of the whole screen, such as New habit

Most buttons also have an .icon constructor that takes icon and label. A button is enabled when onPressed is a function and disabled when it is null, so you usually write onPressed: canSave ? _save : null.

Screen 1: The button family lib/main.dart

class ButtonsDemo extends StatelessWidget {
  const ButtonsDemo({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Buttons')),
      body: Padding(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
        child: Column(
          crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.stretch,
          spacing: 12,
          children: [
            FilledButton(onPressed: () {}, child: const Text('Save habit')),
            FilledButton.tonal(
                onPressed: () {}, child: const Text('Add note')),
            ElevatedButton(
                onPressed: () {}, child: const Text('Share progress')),
            OutlinedButton(
                onPressed: () {}, child: const Text('Skip today')),
            TextButton(onPressed: () {}, child: const Text('Learn more')),
            FilledButton.icon(
              onPressed: () {},
              icon: const Icon(Icons.check),
              label: const Text('Mark done'),
            ),
            const FilledButton(onPressed: null, child: Text('Disabled')),
            Row(
              mainAxisAlignment: MainAxisAlignment.center,
              spacing: 8,
              children: [
                IconButton(onPressed: () {}, tooltip: 'Like',
                    icon: const Icon(Icons.favorite_border)),
                IconButton.filled(onPressed: () {}, tooltip: 'Add',
                    icon: const Icon(Icons.add)),
                IconButton.filledTonal(onPressed: () {}, tooltip: 'Edit',
                    icon: const Icon(Icons.edit)),
              ],
            ),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

From highest to lowest emphasis. The disabled button has onPressed: null; IconButton has filled and tonal variants too.

To restyle one button, use the static styleFrom helper. When a property must change with the button’s state, use ButtonStyle with WidgetStateProperty:

FilledButton(
  onPressed: _save,
  style: ButtonStyle(
    backgroundColor: WidgetStateProperty.resolveWith((states) {
      if (states.contains(WidgetState.disabled)) return Colors.grey.shade300;
      if (states.contains(WidgetState.pressed)) return Colors.green.shade800;
      return Colors.green;
    }),
    minimumSize: const WidgetStatePropertyAll(Size.fromHeight(48)),
  ),
  child: const Text('Save habit'),
)

For app-wide changes, set filledButtonTheme and friends in ThemeData instead (lesson 4.2), so every button stays consistent.

Gestures: InkWell and GestureDetector

Many widgets already handle taps: ListTile and Card combined with InkWell, Chip, Switch. For your own tap areas you have two choices:

  • InkWell gives the Material ripple and supports onTap, onDoubleTap and onLongPress. It paints on the nearest Material ancestor, so an opaque Container between them hides the ripple. Put the colour on Material or Ink instead.
  • GestureDetector shows nothing but recognises more: drags, pans, scales and long presses. Use it for custom interactions such as swiping a card.
Card(
  clipBehavior: Clip.antiAlias, // keeps the ripple inside the corners
  child: InkWell(
    onTap: () => setState(() => _done = !_done),
    onLongPress: _showOptions,
    child: const Padding(
      padding: EdgeInsets.all(16),
      child: Text('Drink water'),
    ),
  ),
)

When several detectors overlap, Flutter runs a gesture arena: each recogniser competes and one wins, which is why a horizontal drag inside a vertical list still works. Keep tap targets at least 48 × 48 logical pixels; Material buttons and IconButtons already meet this.

Feedback: SnackBar

SnackBars are shown by the ScaffoldMessenger, not by the Scaffold, so they survive navigation between screens. Call hideCurrentSnackBar first when the user can trigger several in a row, or they queue up and appear one after another.

Screen 2: Tap to complete, delete with Undo lib/main.dart

class Habit {
  Habit(this.name);
  final String name;
  bool done = false;
}

class _HabitsPageState extends State<HabitsPage> {
  final _habits = [Habit('Drink water'), Habit('Read 10 pages'),
      Habit('Walk after lunch'), Habit('Stretch')];

  void _delete(int index) {
    final removed = _habits[index];
    final name = removed.name;
    setState(() => _habits.removeAt(index));
    ScaffoldMessenger.of(context)
      ..hideCurrentSnackBar()
      ..showSnackBar(SnackBar(
        content: Text('Deleted $name'),
        action: SnackBarAction(
          label: 'Undo',
          onPressed: () => setState(() => _habits.insert(index, removed)),
        ),
      ));
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Habits')),
      body: ListView(
        children: [
          for (final (i, habit) in _habits.indexed)
            ListTile(
              leading: Icon(habit.done
                  ? Icons.check_circle
                  : Icons.radio_button_unchecked),
              title: Text(habit.name),
              onTap: () => setState(() => habit.done = !habit.done),
              trailing: IconButton(
                icon: const Icon(Icons.delete_outline),
                tooltip: 'Delete',
                onPressed: () => _delete(i),
              ),
            ),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}

ListTile has an InkWell inside, so onTap gives a ripple for free. Deleting shows a SnackBar whose Undo action re-inserts the habit. States: Start → Tapped → Deleted.

Feedback: dialogs and bottom sheets

showDialog takes a builder that returns the dialog, usually an AlertDialog. It returns a Future that completes with whatever you pass to Navigator.pop(context, value). If the user taps outside the dialog, the value is null. That is why the code checks ok != true rather than ok == false.

Screen 3: Confirm with a dialog lib/main.dart

Future<void> _confirmReset() async {
  final ok = await showDialog<bool>(
    context: context,
    builder: (context) => AlertDialog(
      icon: const Icon(Icons.restart_alt),
      title: const Text('Reset today?'),
      content: const Text('All habits will be marked as not done.'),
      actions: [
        TextButton(
          onPressed: () => Navigator.pop(context, false),
          child: const Text('Cancel'),
        ),
        FilledButton(
          onPressed: () => Navigator.pop(context, true),
          child: const Text('Reset'),
        ),
      ],
    ),
  );
  if (ok != true || !mounted) return;
  setState(() {
    for (final habit in _habits) {
      habit.done = false;
    }
  });
}

// In the AppBar:
// actions: [IconButton(onPressed: _confirmReset, tooltip: 'Reset',
//     icon: const Icon(Icons.restart_alt))],

showDialog returns a Future. The dialog pops true or false; tapping outside returns null, so the code only resets on true.

After the await, the screen might be gone. Inside a State, check mounted; in other code that holds a BuildContext, check context.mounted. showModalBottomSheet works the same way and is better than a dialog when you offer a list of options. Set showDragHandle: true for the Material 3 handle.

Screen 4: Options in a bottom sheet lib/main.dart

void _showOptions(Habit habit) {
  showModalBottomSheet<void>(
    context: context,
    showDragHandle: true,
    builder: (context) => SafeArea(
      child: Column(
        mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
        children: [
          Text(habit.name,
              style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleMedium),
          ListTile(
            leading: const Icon(Icons.edit),
            title: const Text('Rename'),
            onTap: () => Navigator.pop(context),
          ),
          ListTile(
            leading: const Icon(Icons.notifications_outlined),
            title: const Text('Set reminder'),
            onTap: () => Navigator.pop(context),
          ),
          ListTile(
            leading: const Icon(Icons.delete_outline),
            title: const Text('Delete'),
            onTap: () {
              Navigator.pop(context);
              _delete(_habits.indexOf(habit));
            },
          ),
        ],
      ),
    ),
  );
}

// On each ListTile: onLongPress: () => _showOptions(habit),

A long press on a habit opens a modal bottom sheet with a drag handle. Each option closes the sheet with Navigator.pop before acting.

Example: Habit Tracker

The Habit Tracker uses every kind of feedback, each in the place it fits best.

  1. Store List<Habit> in the State; each Habit has a name and a done flag.
  2. Each habit is a ListTile. onTap toggles done, so the built-in ripple confirms the tap and the icon changes.
  3. The trailing delete IconButton removes the habit immediately and shows a SnackBar with Undo. Undo is friendlier than a dialog because deleting one habit is easy to reverse.
  4. onLongPress opens a bottom sheet with Rename, Set reminder and Delete.
  5. The reset action in the AppBar changes every habit at once, which is harder to undo, so it asks first with a dialog.
  6. A “Mark all done” FilledButton at the bottom is disabled (onPressed: null) when there is nothing left to do.

Common mistakes

  • Using old buttons. RaisedButton, FlatButton and OutlineButton were removed; use the family above.
  • Several FilledButtons side by side. If everything is high emphasis, nothing is. Pair one filled button with outlined or text buttons.
  • Using context after an await without a mounted check. This causes errors when the user leaves the screen while a dialog or request is open.
  • Popping with the wrong context. Inside the dialog builder, the builder’s own context belongs to the dialog route, which is what you want for Navigator.pop.
  • InkWell on a coloured Container. The ripple is hidden behind the colour. Use Material(color: ...) or Ink.
  • Dialogs for everything. Confirm only destructive or expensive actions. For reversible ones, act at once and offer Undo.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “InkWell or GestureDetector?” InkWell when you want Material ripple feedback on taps; GestureDetector for gestures without visuals or beyond taps.
  • Know how to return a value from a dialog and why the result is nullable. Interviewers often ask candidates to write this from memory.
  • Mention the use_build_context_synchronously lint: the analyzer warns when you use a BuildContext after an await without a mounted check.
  • Add small touches that clients notice: tooltips on every IconButton, a SnackBar after saving, and HapticFeedback.lightImpact() from package:flutter/services.dart on important taps.

terms.definition: How strongly a button draws attention. Use one high-emphasis FilledButton per screen area and lower-emphasis buttons for the rest.
A tap area that shows the Material ripple. It needs a Material ancestor, such as the Material inside a Card or Scaffold, to draw on.
Detects taps, long presses, drags and scales without any visual feedback.
The object that shows SnackBars for the app. Reach it with ScaffoldMessenger.of(context).
Opens a modal dialog built by a builder function and returns a Future that completes with the value passed to Navigator.pop.
A value that depends on the widget’s state (pressed, hovered, disabled…). Used in ButtonStyle to style each state.

lessons.examTip: Any time you await a dialog or sheet, check mounted (in a State) or context.mounted before using context or calling setState again.

domains.name: Layout
domains.blurb: Rows, columns, constraints, stacks, lists, grids, slivers and responsive layouts.

lessons.title: Rows, columns and flex
lessons.summaryHtml:
Row lays children out horizontally and Column vertically. Each has a main axis (the direction it lays out) and a cross axis (the other one). mainAxisAlignment distributes free space along the main axis, crossAxisAlignment aligns children across it, and spacing puts a fixed gap between children.

Expanded and Flexible share the leftover space by flex factor, and Spacer fills a gap. When children need more room than the Row or Column has, you get the yellow-and-black overflow stripe; the usual fix is Expanded, Flexible, Wrap or a scroll view.

You will start the Recipe Book app with a recipe detail screen built only from rows and columns.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Picture a bookshelf. A Row is one shelf: books stand side by side from left to right. A Column is a stack of shelves from top to bottom. You decide how to use the empty space on a shelf (push the books to one end, centre them, or spread them out) and how tall books line up (by their tops, middles or bottoms). That is almost all of Flutter’s everyday layout.

Row and Column are both flex layouts. They share the same rules, just turned 90 degrees, and they are also how you will read and write most screens in real projects.

Why it matters

Nearly every screen is rows inside columns inside rows. If you understand the two axes and how space is shared, you can build almost any design from a mockup without guessing. If you do not, you will meet the most common Flutter errors of all: the yellow-and-black overflow stripe and “unbounded height” exceptions. Fixing those quickly is something employers expect even from juniors.

How it works

First the two axes, then how flexible children share space, then why overflows happen.

Main axis and cross axis

The main axis is the direction children are laid out: horizontal for Row, vertical for Column. The cross axis is the other direction. Two properties control them:

mainAxisAlignmentWhere the free space goes
start (default)After the children
endBefore the children
centerSplit before and after
spaceBetweenBetween children only; first and last touch the edges
spaceAroundAround each child, so the edges get half a gap
spaceEvenlyEqual gaps everywhere, including the edges

Screen 1: mainAxisAlignment side by side lib/main.dart

class AlignDemo extends StatelessWidget {
  const AlignDemo({super.key});

  Widget _row(String label, MainAxisAlignment align) {
    return Column(
      crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
      spacing: 4,
      children: [
        Text(label),
        Container(
          color: Colors.orange.shade50,
          child: Row(
            mainAxisAlignment: align,
            children: const [Box('A'), Box('B'), Box('C')],
          ),
        ),
      ],
    );
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Main axis')),
      body: Padding(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
        child: Column(
          spacing: 16,
          children: [
            _row('start', MainAxisAlignment.start),
            _row('center', MainAxisAlignment.center),
            _row('spaceBetween', MainAxisAlignment.spaceBetween),
            _row('spaceEvenly', MainAxisAlignment.spaceEvenly),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

class Box extends StatelessWidget {
  const Box(this.label, {super.key});
  final String label;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) => Container(
        width: 48, height: 48, alignment: Alignment.center,
        color: Colors.deepOrange,
        child: Text(label, style: const TextStyle(color: Colors.white)),
      );
}

The same three boxes in four Rows. Only mainAxisAlignment changes; the free space is placed at the end, at both sides, between the boxes, or evenly around them.

crossAxisAlignment takes start, center (the default), end, stretch (children fill the cross axis, useful for full-width buttons in a Column) and baseline (aligns text baselines in a Row; you must also set textBaseline: TextBaseline.alphabetic).

By default a Row or Column is as long as its parent allows along the main axis (MainAxisSize.max). Set mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min to shrink it to its children, for example a small Row of an icon and a number inside a list tile.

For fixed gaps, current Flutter lets you write spacing: 12 on Row and Column. Before that parameter existed, people inserted SizedBox(width: 12) or SizedBox(height: 12) between children, and you will still see that in older code.

Sharing space: Expanded, Flexible and Spacer

A Row lays out in two passes. First it measures the inflexible children (anything not wrapped in Expanded or Flexible) and lets each be as wide as it wants. Then it divides the space that is left between the flexible children in proportion to their flex factor.

  • Expanded(flex: 2, child: ...) forces the child to fill exactly its share. It is shorthand for Flexible(fit: FlexFit.tight).
  • Flexible(child: ...) allows the child to take up to its share but be smaller if it wants (FlexFit.loose). Good for text that should wrap only when it is long.
  • Spacer() is an empty Expanded. Use it to push the next children to the far end.
Row(
  children: [
    Expanded(flex: 2, child: Container(height: 40, color: Colors.orange)),
    Expanded(child: Container(height: 40, color: Colors.teal)),
    const Spacer(),
    const Icon(Icons.more_vert),
  ],
)
// leftover width after the icon = 4 flex parts:
// orange gets 2, teal gets 1, Spacer gets 1

Why overflows happen

In the first pass, a Row gives inflexible children unbounded width, meaning “take as much as you need”. A long Text happily measures itself as one long line. If the total is wider than the Row, Flutter shows A RenderFlex overflowed by … pixels on the right and paints a warning stripe in debug builds. The fix is to make the greedy child flexible so it only gets the space that is left.

Screen 2: Overflow and the Expanded fix lib/main.dart

const title = 'Grandma’s slow-cooked Malabar chicken biryani';

// BROKEN: a Row lets the Text be as wide as it likes.
Row(
  children: [
    const Icon(Icons.restaurant),
    const SizedBox(width: 8),
    Text(title, style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleLarge),
  ],
)

// FIXED: Expanded gives the Text only the space that is left.
Row(
  children: [
    const Icon(Icons.restaurant),
    const SizedBox(width: 8),
    Expanded(
      child: Text(title, style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleLarge),
    ),
  ],
)

Without Expanded the Text asks for its full width and runs past the edge; Flutter paints the yellow-and-black stripe in debug mode. With Expanded it gets the remaining width and wraps. States: Overflow → With Expanded.

A Column has the same problem vertically, and it causes the famous Vertical viewport was given unbounded height error: a ListView inside a Column wants to be infinitely tall. Wrap the ListView in Expanded, or make the whole screen scroll with a single ListView or SingleChildScrollView instead of a Column. When chips or tags might not fit on one line, use Wrap, which moves children to a new line instead of overflowing.

Watch out: Expanded and Flexible must be direct children of a Row, Column or Flex. Putting Expanded inside a Padding or Container causes an “Incorrect use of ParentDataWidget” error.

Example: Recipe Book detail screen

The Recipe Book is this module’s mini app. It starts with a detail screen, and the next two lessons add styled cards and a hero banner.

  1. The page body is a Column with crossAxisAlignment: start, so headings line up on the left, and spacing: 12 between sections.
  2. The stats Row wraps three InfoTile widgets in Expanded, so each gets exactly one third of the width on any phone.
  3. Each InfoTile is a small Column: icon, bold value, small label.
  4. Each ingredient Row is icon, gap, Expanded name, quantity. The Expanded name pushes the quantity to the right edge and wraps if a name is long.
  5. A Spacer pushes the button Row to the bottom, and two Expanded buttons share its width equally.

Screen 3: Recipe Book: detail screen lib/main.dart

class RecipeDetail extends StatelessWidget {
  const RecipeDetail({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final text = Theme.of(context).textTheme;
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Recipe Book')),
      body: Padding(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
        child: Column(
          crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
          spacing: 12,
          children: [
            Text('Kerala vegetable stew', style: text.headlineSmall),
            const Row(children: [
              Expanded(child: InfoTile(Icons.schedule, '35 min', 'Time')),
              Expanded(child: InfoTile(Icons.people, '4', 'Serves')),
              Expanded(child: InfoTile(Icons.local_fire_department,
                  '280', 'kcal')),
            ]),
            const Divider(),
            Text('Ingredients', style: text.titleMedium),
            for (final (name, qty) in ingredients)
              Row(children: [
                const Icon(Icons.check, size: 18),
                const SizedBox(width: 8),
                Expanded(child: Text(name)),
                Text(qty, style: text.labelLarge),
              ]),
            const Spacer(),
            Row(spacing: 12, children: [
              Expanded(child: OutlinedButton(
                  onPressed: () {}, child: const Text('Share'))),
              Expanded(child: FilledButton(
                  onPressed: () {}, child: const Text('Start cooking'))),
            ]),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

class InfoTile extends StatelessWidget {
  const InfoTile(this.icon, this.value, this.label, {super.key});
  final IconData icon;
  final String value, label;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) => Column(children: [
        Icon(icon, color: Theme.of(context).colorScheme.primary),
        Text(value, style: const TextStyle(fontWeight: FontWeight.bold)),
        Text(label, style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.labelSmall),
      ]);
}

const ingredients = [('Coconut milk', '400 ml'), ('Potatoes', '2'),
    ('Carrots', '2'), ('Green peas', '1 cup')];

Only Rows and Columns: the stats Row splits the width into three equal Expanded tiles, each ingredient Row pushes the quantity to the end, and the buttons share the bottom row.

The ingredients are Dart 3 records such as ('Coconut milk', '400 ml'), and for (final (name, qty) in ingredients) destructures each one inside the Column’s children list.

Common mistakes

  • Confusing the axes. In a Column, mainAxisAlignment.center centres vertically. To centre horizontally you need the cross axis.
  • Long Text in a Row without Expanded or Flexible. It works with short test data and overflows with real data or larger system text.
  • ListView directly inside a Column. Wrap it in Expanded or restructure the screen.
  • Expanded not directly inside a flex widget. Put Padding inside the Expanded, not around it.
  • Using Expanded or Spacer where the width is unbounded, for example in a Row inside a horizontal scroll view. There is no finite leftover space to share, so Flutter throws an error.
  • Using Stack or fixed pixel positions for layouts that Row and Column handle. Flex layouts adapt to screen sizes; hard-coded positions do not.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “Expanded or Flexible?” Expanded forces the child to fill its share (tight); Flexible lets it be smaller (loose). Expanded is Flexible with FlexFit.tight.
  • “How do you fix a RenderFlex overflow?” Find the greedy child, then use Expanded or Flexible, ellipsize the text, switch to Wrap, or make the area scroll. Say which one you would pick and why.
  • Test layouts with long real-world strings (names in several languages, big numbers) and with the largest accessibility text size. Many production bugs are just overflows nobody tested.
  • The Flutter Inspector in DevTools shows constraints and flex values for every widget. Using it in an interview live-coding task makes a strong impression.

terms.definition: The direction a Row or Column lays out its children: horizontal for Row, vertical for Column.
The direction at right angles to the main axis. crossAxisAlignment controls it.
Forces its child to fill a share of the remaining main-axis space, based on flex.
Lets its child take up to a share of the remaining space, but allows it to be smaller (FlexFit.loose).
Makes a Row or Column only as long as its children need, instead of as long as possible.
The debug-mode error and yellow-black stripe shown when a Row or Column’s children do not fit.

lessons.examTip: When a layout breaks, read the error’s first line, then open the Flutter Inspector and turn on the layout explorer: it shows each child’s constraints and flex values.

quiz.question: In a Column, which property moves the children to the horizontal centre of the screen?
options: crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.center
mainAxisAlignment: MainAxisAlignment.center
mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min
textDirection: TextDirection.ltr
quiz.explanation: A Column’s main axis is vertical, so horizontal alignment is its cross axis. The default is already center; start and stretch are the common alternatives.

quiz.question: A Row holds an icon and a long Text. On small phones you see a yellow-and-black stripe. What is the usual fix?
options: Wrap the Row in a Center
Give the Text a bigger font
Wrap the Text in Expanded (or Flexible) so it gets the remaining width and wraps
Set mainAxisAlignment to spaceBetween
quiz.explanation: A Row lets each non-flexible child be as wide as it wants. Expanded limits the Text to the leftover width, so it wraps or ellipsizes.

quiz.question: Two children are wrapped in Expanded with flex: 2 and flex: 1. How is the leftover space shared?
options: Equally
Two thirds and one third
The first child gets it all
By the children’s own widths
quiz.explanation: Leftover space is divided in proportion to flex: 2 + 1 = 3 parts, so the first gets 2/3 and the second 1/3.

quiz.question: Inside a Column you add a ListView and get “Vertical viewport was given unbounded height”. What fixes it?
options: Add mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min to the Column
Wrap the Column in a Row
Set crossAxisAlignment to stretch
Wrap the ListView in Expanded so it gets a bounded height
quiz.explanation: A Column gives its non-flexible children unlimited height, but a ListView wants to be as tall as possible. Expanded gives it exactly the remaining height.

lessons.title: Containers and constraints
lessons.summaryHtml:
Container is a convenience widget that combines padding, margin, size, alignment and a BoxDecoration (colour, gradient, rounded corners, border, shadow). For single jobs, the focused widgets Padding, SizedBox, DecoratedBox and ConstrainedBox are clearer and often const.

All of Flutter layout follows one rule: constraints go down, sizes go up, and the parent sets the position. A parent tells each child the minimum and maximum width and height it may have; the child picks a size inside those limits; the parent then places it. This explains why a Container(width: 100) sometimes fills the whole screen.

You will continue the Recipe Book with a list of decorated recipe cards that also stays readable on a tablet.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Imagine packing boxes for a house move. The removal company tells you, “each box must be between 30 and 60 cm wide”. You choose a size inside that range and report it back. Then the company decides where your box goes in the van. You never choose the position, and you can never ignore the size limits.

Flutter layout works the same way. The parent passes constraints down (a minimum and maximum width and height). The child picks a size inside them and passes it up. The parent then sets the child’s position. Container is the most common box you will pack: it adds padding, margin, colour, rounded corners, borders and shadows around a child.

Why it matters

Most “Flutter is ignoring my width” questions on forums come from not knowing the constraints rule. Once you know it, you can predict layouts instead of trying random widgets until something works. And since almost every card, button background, avatar and badge in a design is a decorated box, mastering BoxDecoration lets you match a designer’s mockup exactly.

How it works

We look at Container and its smaller building blocks first, then at constraints.

What Container really is

Container is not a single primitive. Depending on the parameters you pass, it builds a combination of smaller widgets: Padding for padding, DecoratedBox for colour and decoration, ConstrainedBox for width, height and constraints, Align for alignment, and another Padding for margin. That is why its size rules feel complicated:

  • With a width or height, it tries to be that size (within its constraints).
  • With a child and no size, it shrinks to fit the child plus padding.
  • With no child, no size and no alignment, it tries to be as big as possible.
  • With an alignment, it expands to fill its constraints and positions the child inside.

When you only need one of these jobs, use the focused widget. Padding, SizedBox and DecoratedBox say exactly what you mean and can often be const.

NeedBest widget
Space around a childPadding
A fixed gap or fixed sizeSizedBox (SizedBox.expand fills, SizedBox.shrink is empty)
Background, border, radius, shadowDecoratedBox, or Container when you also need padding or margin
Minimum or maximum sizeConstrainedBox
A fixed shape ratio such as 16:9AspectRatio
A fraction of the parent, such as 80% widthFractionallySizedBox

BoxDecoration

BoxDecoration paints the box: color or gradient, borderRadius, border, boxShadow, an image, and shape: BoxShape.circle for round avatars. For transparent colours, use Colors.black.withValues(alpha: 0.08); the older withOpacity is deprecated.

Screen 1: Container with BoxDecoration lib/main.dart

class DecoratedCard extends StatelessWidget {
  const DecoratedCard({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final colors = Theme.of(context).colorScheme;
    final text = Theme.of(context).textTheme;

    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Decoration')),
      body: Container(
        margin: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12),
        decoration: BoxDecoration(
          color: colors.surface,
          borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(16),
          border: Border.all(color: colors.outlineVariant),
          boxShadow: [
            BoxShadow(
              color: Colors.black.withValues(alpha: 0.08),
              blurRadius: 12,
              offset: const Offset(0, 4),
            ),
          ],
        ),
        child: Row(
          spacing: 12,
          children: [
            Container(
              width: 72,
              height: 72,
              decoration: BoxDecoration(
                gradient: const LinearGradient(
                  colors: [Color(0xFFFFB74D), Color(0xFFE65100)],
                ),
                borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(12),
              ),
              child: const Icon(Icons.rice_bowl, color: Colors.white),
            ),
            Expanded(
              child: Column(
                crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
                children: [
                  Text('Chicken biryani', style: text.titleMedium),
                  Text('Main course', style: text.bodySmall),
                ],
              ),
            ),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

One Container paints a rounded, bordered card with a soft shadow; the inner Container is the gradient thumbnail. Padding is inside the decoration, margin outside.

A decoration does not clip its child. If an image inside a rounded Container shows square corners, set clipBehavior: Clip.antiAlias on the Container (it requires a decoration) or wrap the image in ClipRRect.

Constraints go down, sizes go up, parent sets position

Every layout pass sends a BoxConstraints object from each parent to each child. Three kinds are worth naming:

  • Tight: min equals max, so there is exactly one allowed size. The screen gives the root widget tight constraints, and SizedBox.expand and Expanded pass tight constraints too.
  • Loose: min is zero, so the child may be anything up to the max. Center, Align and Scaffold’s body pass loose constraints.
  • Unbounded: max is infinity. A Row gives inflexible children unbounded width; a ListView gives children unbounded height along its scroll direction.

A child can never break the constraints it receives. That single fact explains the classic surprise below.

Screen 2: Tight versus loose constraints lib/main.dart

import 'package:flutter/widgets.dart';

// Flip this to true and hot restart to compare.
const useCenter = false;

void main() {
  final box = Container(
    width: 100,
    height: 100,
    color: const Color(0xFFE53935),
  );

  // The screen passes TIGHT constraints (min = max = screen size)
  // to the root widget, so width and height above are ignored.
  // Center receives those tight constraints but passes LOOSE ones
  // (0 up to screen size) to its child, so the box can be 100 x 100.
  runApp(useCenter ? Center(child: box) : box);
}

The same 100 × 100 Container. As the root it gets tight constraints and must fill the screen; inside Center it gets loose constraints and can be its own size. States: useCenter = false → useCenter = true.

To see the constraints a widget receives, wrap it in a LayoutBuilder and print them:

LayoutBuilder(
  builder: (context, constraints) {
    debugPrint('$constraints');
    // In a vertical ListView on a phone this prints something like
    // BoxConstraints(w=411.4, 0.0<=h<=Infinity): tight width, unbounded height.
    return const Text('Inside a ListView');
  },
)

ConstrainedBox adds limits on top of the incoming ones. BoxConstraints(maxWidth: 600) means “never wider than 600, but narrower is fine”. That is the standard way to keep forms and cards readable on tablets and the web without breaking phones. Inside an unbounded parent, LimitedBox applies a maximum only when the incoming constraint is infinite.

Remember: a widget’s size request (width, height) is only a wish. The parent’s constraints always win.

Example: Recipe Book list

The Recipe Book now gets a home screen that lists all recipes as cards.

  1. Each RecipeCard is one Container: vertical and horizontal margin separates the cards, padding: 12 keeps content off the edges, and a BoxDecoration gives the surface colour, a radius of 16 and a 1 px outline.
  2. The thumbnail is a 72 × 72 Container with a gradient built from the recipe’s own colour, so every recipe has its own look without photos.
  3. The title Column sits in Expanded (lesson 3.1), so long titles wrap.
  4. The time label is a pill: a Container with small padding and BorderRadius.circular(999), a radius bigger than its height.
  5. The ListView sits in Center and ConstrainedBox(maxWidth: 600). On a phone the cards fill the width; on a tablet or browser they stop at 600 and stay centred.

Screen 3: Recipe Book: recipe list lib/main.dart

class RecipeListPage extends StatelessWidget {
  const RecipeListPage({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Recipe Book')),
      body: Center(
        child: ConstrainedBox(
          constraints: const BoxConstraints(maxWidth: 600),
          child: ListView(
            padding: const EdgeInsets.symmetric(vertical: 8),
            children: [for (final r in recipes) RecipeCard(recipe: r)],
          ),
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

class RecipeCard extends StatelessWidget {
  const RecipeCard({super.key, required this.recipe});
  final Recipe recipe;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final colors = Theme.of(context).colorScheme;
    final text = Theme.of(context).textTheme;
    return Container(
      margin: const EdgeInsets.symmetric(horizontal: 16, vertical: 6),
      padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12),
      decoration: BoxDecoration(
        color: colors.surface,
        borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(16),
        border: Border.all(color: colors.outlineVariant),
      ),
      child: Row(spacing: 12, children: [
        Thumbnail(color: recipe.color, icon: recipe.icon), // 72 x 72
        Expanded(
          child: Column(
            crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
            children: [
              Text(recipe.title, style: text.titleMedium),
              Text(recipe.category, style: text.bodySmall),
            ],
          ),
        ),
        Container(
          padding: const EdgeInsets.symmetric(horizontal: 10, vertical: 4),
          decoration: BoxDecoration(
            color: colors.primaryContainer,
            borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(999),
          ),
          child: Text(recipe.timeLabel, style: text.labelMedium),
        ),
      ]),
    );
  }
}

Each card is a decorated Container. The pill is a Container with a large radius, and ConstrainedBox(maxWidth: 600) keeps cards readable on tablets.

Common mistakes

  • Passing both color and decoration to a Container. This throws an assertion. Put the colour inside the BoxDecoration.
  • Expecting width to work under tight constraints. Inside Expanded, a ListView with stretch, or at the root, width is ignored. Loosen with Center or Align.
  • A Container everywhere. A Container used only for padding hides intent; use Padding or SizedBox.
  • Rounded corners that do not clip the image inside. Add clipBehavior or ClipRRect.
  • Using withOpacity. It is deprecated; use withValues(alpha: ...).
  • Fixed widths for responsive layouts. A SizedBox(width: 600) overflows a 360-wide phone. Use maxWidth instead.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Quote the rule exactly: “Constraints go down. Sizes go up. Parent sets position.” It comes from the Flutter documentation page “Understanding constraints”, which is worth reading end to end.
  • Be able to explain tight, loose and unbounded constraints with one example each.
  • “Container or SizedBox for a gap?” SizedBox: it is lighter, can be const and states the intent.
  • For design-system work, you will turn repeated decorations into theme values or small reusable widgets (lesson 4.3), so a design change touches one place.

terms.definition: Four numbers passed from parent to child: minWidth, maxWidth, minHeight and maxHeight.
Min equals max, so the child has exactly one size it can be. The screen gives the root widget tight constraints.
Min is zero, so the child can be any size up to the max. Center and Align pass loose constraints.
A max of infinity. Rows, Columns and scroll views give some children unbounded space along their main axis.
Describes how to paint a box: color, gradient, borderRadius, border, boxShadow, image and shape.
Adds extra limits, such as a maxWidth, on top of the constraints from its parent.

lessons.examTip: If a widget ignores its width or height, it is being given tight constraints by its parent. Wrap it in Center or Align (loose) or check the parent in the Flutter Inspector.

quiz.question: What is the difference between padding and margin on a Container?

Margin is inside the decoration, padding is outside
Padding is space inside the decoration around the child; margin is empty space outside the decoration

lessons.title: Stack, Positioned and Align
lessons.summaryHtml:
Stack places children on top of each other, painting them in order so later children appear in front. Children without positioning are aligned by the Stack’s alignment; children wrapped in Positioned are pinned by top, left, right and bottom distances. Positioned.fill stretches a layer over the whole Stack.

Align places one child anywhere inside its parent using Alignment(x, y) coordinates from −1 to 1. Material 3’s Badge widget handles the most common overlay, a count on an icon, for you.

You will add a hero banner to the Recipe Book: a photo with a dark gradient, a title on top, a “New” tag and a favourite button, plus a badge on the shopping-list icon.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Think of a noticeboard. You pin a big poster first, then stick a small “SOLD OUT” label on its corner, then a sticky note on top of that. Things pinned later cover things pinned earlier. A Stack is that noticeboard: it puts its children on top of each other in the order you list them.

Positioned is the pin: “16 pixels from the bottom and 16 from the left”. Align is a gentler instruction: “somewhere near the bottom-right corner”. Row and Column put things next to each other; Stack puts things on top of each other.

Why it matters

Modern app designs are full of overlap: text on photos, gradients that make that text readable, unread-count badges, online dots on avatars, play buttons over video thumbnails, floating “New” tags. Every one of these is a Stack or a widget built on one. Knowing how Stack sizes itself and how Positioned works lets you build these without magic numbers that break on other screen sizes.

How it works

We look at how a Stack sizes and paints its children, then at Positioned, Align and Badge.

Painting order and two kinds of children

A Stack paints its children from first to last, so the last child is in front. Each child is one of two kinds:

  • Non-positioned children are placed using the Stack’s alignment (default: top-start, which is top-left in left-to-right languages).
  • Positioned children are wrapped in Positioned and pinned by distances from the Stack’s edges.

The Stack sizes itself from its non-positioned children: it becomes as big as the largest one. Positioned children do not affect the Stack’s size. If every child is positioned, the Stack tries to be as big as its parent allows, so give it a size with a SizedBox or a non-positioned base layer.

Stack propertyWhat it does
alignmentWhere non-positioned children sit, for example Alignment.center
fitStackFit.loose (default): children keep their own size. StackFit.expand: non-positioned children are forced to fill the Stack. StackFit.passthrough: they get the Stack’s own constraints.
clipBehaviorDefault Clip.hardEdge cuts off anything outside the Stack. Clip.none lets badges stick out.

Positioned

Positioned takes top, right, bottom, left, width and height. On each axis you may give at most two of the three values: left, right and width. Setting both left and right stretches the child between them, which is the right way to make a caption span the banner with 16 pixels of margin. Positioned.fill() sets all four edges to zero, and Positioned.directional uses start and end, so the layout mirrors correctly in right-to-left languages such as Arabic.

Watch out: Positioned must be a direct child of a Stack. Wrapping it in Padding or putting it in a Column gives “Incorrect use of ParentDataWidget”.

Screen 1: Recipe hero banner lib/main.dart

class RecipeHeader extends StatelessWidget {
  const RecipeHeader({super.key, required this.recipe});
  final Recipe recipe;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final text = Theme.of(context).textTheme;
    return SizedBox(
      height: 240,
      child: Stack(
        fit: StackFit.expand,
        children: [
          Image.network(recipe.imageUrl, fit: BoxFit.cover,
              errorBuilder: (context, error, stack) =>
                  ColoredBox(color: recipe.color)),
          const DecoratedBox(
            decoration: BoxDecoration(
              gradient: LinearGradient(
                begin: Alignment.topCenter,
                end: Alignment.bottomCenter,
                colors: [Colors.transparent, Colors.black87],
              ),
            ),
          ),
          Positioned(
            left: 16, right: 16, bottom: 16,
            child: Column(
              crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
              mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
              children: [
                Text(recipe.title, style: text.headlineSmall
                    ?.copyWith(color: Colors.white)),
                Text(recipe.timeLabel, style: text.bodyMedium
                    ?.copyWith(color: Colors.white70)),
              ],
            ),
          ),
          Positioned(
            top: 12, left: 12,
            child: Container(
              padding: const EdgeInsets.symmetric(horizontal: 10, vertical: 4),
              decoration: BoxDecoration(color: Colors.amber,
                  borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(999)),
              child: Text('NEW', style: text.labelMedium),
            ),
          ),
          Positioned(
            top: 8, right: 8,
            child: IconButton.filledTonal(onPressed: () {}, tooltip: 'Save',
                icon: const Icon(Icons.favorite_border)),
          ),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}

Five layers in one Stack: photo, gradient, title, “NEW” pill and favourite button. StackFit.expand makes the photo and gradient fill the 240-pixel box.

The gradient layer is what makes the design work. White text on a bright photo is hard to read; a transparent-to-black gradient behind the text guarantees contrast whatever the photo looks like. Because the Stack uses StackFit.expand, the gradient’s DecoratedBox fills the banner without any sizes of its own.

Align and Alignment

Align places a single child inside the space it is given. Alignment(x, y) uses a coordinate system where x and y run from −1 to 1: (−1, −1) is the top-left corner, (0, 0) the centre and (1, 1) the bottom-right. Named constants like Alignment.bottomCenter are just these values. The child’s own edges line up with the parent’s edges at ±1, so a child aligned at (1, 1) touches the bottom-right corner instead of hanging off it.

Screen 2: Alignment coordinates lib/main.dart

class AlignDemo extends StatelessWidget {
  const AlignDemo({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Align')),
      body: Container(
        height: 220,
        margin: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
        color: Theme.of(context).colorScheme.surfaceContainerHigh,
        child: const Stack(
          children: [
            Align(
              alignment: Alignment.topLeft, // Alignment(-1, -1)
              child: Chip(label: Text('topLeft')),
            ),
            Align(
              alignment: Alignment.center, // Alignment(0, 0)
              child: Chip(label: Text('center')),
            ),
            Align(
              alignment: Alignment(0.5, -0.5),
              child: Chip(label: Text('(0.5, -0.5)')),
            ),
            Align(
              alignment: Alignment.bottomRight, // Alignment(1, 1)
              child: Chip(label: Text('bottomRight')),
            ),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

Four Align children in one Stack. Named constants such as topLeft are just Alignment(x, y) values; (0.5, −0.5) sits three quarters across and a quarter down the free space.

Use AlignmentDirectional (topStart, bottomEnd…) when the position should flip in right-to-left languages. Center is simply Align with Alignment.center. Outside a Stack, Align is still useful: for example, Align(alignment: Alignment.centerRight, child: TextButton(...)) puts a “Forgot password?” link on the right of a form without a Row.

Badges

Before Material 3, developers built badges by hand with a Stack, a Positioned circle and Clip.none. Now the Badge widget does it: Badge(label: Text('$count'), child: Icon(...)), with isLabelVisible to hide it, or Badge() with no label for a small dot. It works inside IconButton, NavigationBar destinations and anywhere else an icon goes. Build a custom Stack only for things Badge does not cover, like the online dot on an avatar.

Screen 3: Badges and status dots lib/main.dart

class BadgeDemo extends StatefulWidget {
  const BadgeDemo({super.key});

  @override
  State<BadgeDemo> createState() => _BadgeDemoState();
}

class _BadgeDemoState extends State<BadgeDemo> {
  int _count = 0;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final colors = Theme.of(context).colorScheme;
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Badges')),
      body: Center(
        child: Column(
          mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
          spacing: 32,
          children: [
            Badge(
              label: Text('$_count'),
              isLabelVisible: _count > 0,
              child: const Icon(Icons.shopping_cart, size: 32),
            ),
            Stack(
              children: [
                const CircleAvatar(radius: 40, child: Text('JS')),
                Positioned(
                  right: 2,
                  bottom: 2,
                  child: Container(
                    width: 20,
                    height: 20,
                    decoration: BoxDecoration(
                      color: Colors.green,
                      shape: BoxShape.circle,
                      border: Border.all(color: colors.surface, width: 3),
                    ),
                  ),
                ),
              ],
            ),
            FilledButton(
              onPressed: () => setState(() => _count++),
              child: const Text('Add to cart'),
            ),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

Badge draws the count on the cart icon and hides itself at 0. The green online dot is a Positioned child of a Stack that wraps the avatar. States: Count 0 → Count 3.

One more relative: IndexedStack keeps all its children alive but shows only one, chosen by index. You will use it in lesson 5.4 to keep each bottom-navigation tab’s state.

Example: Recipe Book hero banner

The recipe detail page from lesson 3.1 gets a banner at the top.

  1. A SizedBox(height: 240) gives the Stack a fixed height; the width comes from the screen.
  2. fit: StackFit.expand makes the photo and the gradient fill the box. The photo uses BoxFit.cover and falls back to the recipe’s colour if it cannot load.
  3. A Positioned(left: 16, right: 16, bottom: 16) holds a Column with mainAxisSize.min: the title and time in white.
  4. Two small Positioned children sit in the top corners: a “NEW” pill and an IconButton.filledTonal that toggles the favourite icon with setState.
  5. The AppBar’s shopping-list icon is wrapped in a Badge that counts items added from the page and hides at zero.

Common mistakes

  • A Stack with only Positioned children and no size. It expands to its parent, or causes an error inside unbounded parents such as a ListView. Give it a SizedBox or a base layer.
  • Positioned not directly inside a Stack. Put Padding inside the Positioned instead.
  • Setting left, right and width together. That is three values on one axis; Flutter asserts. Pick two.
  • Using Stack and pixel offsets for layouts that are really rows and columns. They break on other screen sizes and text scales.
  • Badges clipped at the edge. Use the Badge widget, or set clipBehavior: Clip.none on your own Stack, remembering that the part outside the Stack does not receive taps.
  • Text on photos without a scrim. Always add a gradient or a dark overlay behind text on images.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “How does a Stack decide its size?” From its largest non-positioned child, or as large as possible when all children are positioned. Positioned children never affect it.
  • “Align or Positioned?” Align for relative placement inside whatever space exists; Positioned for fixed distances from the Stack’s edges.
  • For RTL markets such as the Gulf region, use Positioned.directional and AlignmentDirectional so the banner layout mirrors automatically.
  • The hero banner here is static. Later, in lesson 3.4, a SliverAppBar with FlexibleSpaceBar makes a banner like this collapse into the app bar as you scroll, and lesson 8.1 animates the photo between screens with a Hero.

terms.definition: Lays its children on top of each other. The first child is at the back, the last at the front.
Pins a Stack child at given distances from the Stack’s edges. It must be a direct child of a Stack.
A Positioned with top, right, bottom and left all set to 0, so the child covers the whole Stack.
A position inside a box where (−1, −1) is the top-left corner, (0, 0) the centre and (1, 1) the bottom-right corner.
How non-positioned children are sized: loose (their own size), expand (fill the Stack) or passthrough (keep the parent’s constraints).
A Material 3 widget that shows a small label or dot on top of a child, usually an icon.

lessons.examTip: Before reaching for Stack, ask whether Row, Column or Align can do it. Use Stack only when things truly overlap: badges, overlays, banners and floating controls.

lessons.title: Lists, grids and slivers
lessons.summaryHtml:
Most real apps are scrolling screens: feeds, catalogues, chats and settings. Flutter gives you ListView for one column of items, GridView for tiles in rows and columns, and slivers for screens that mix several scrolling parts under one scroll bar.

  • Use the builder constructors (ListView.builder, ListView.separated, GridView.builder) for long or unknown lists: they build only the items that are on screen.
  • A grid delegate decides the grid shape: a fixed number of columns, or a maximum tile width that adapts to the screen.
  • CustomScrollView takes a list of slivers such as SliverAppBar, SliverList, SliverGrid and SliverToBoxAdapter, so an app bar, a grid and a list scroll together.

In this lesson the Recipe Book app gets a real home screen: a collapsing app bar, a horizontal row of quick recipes and a grid of all recipes.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A phone screen is small, but your data is not. A recipe app may hold eight recipes today and eight hundred next year. A scrolling list lets the user move through content that is taller than the screen.

Think of a long paper menu in a restaurant. The waiter does not print every page again each time you turn one. You only look at the page in front of you. Flutter’s lazy lists work the same way: they build only the rows you can see, plus a few just outside the screen, and reuse that space as you scroll.

Flutter has three tools for this. ListView shows items in one line, top to bottom or left to right. GridView shows tiles in rows and columns. Slivers are the building blocks under both; you use them directly when one screen needs several scrolling parts, such as a collapsing header, a grid and a list, that move together.

Why it matters

Almost every job-ready Flutter app has at least one long list: products, messages, orders, notifications. Get it wrong and the app feels slow, uses too much memory or throws layout errors. Get it right and a list of ten thousand items scrolls as smoothly as a list of ten.

Lists are also where beginners meet the most confusing Flutter errors, such as “unbounded height”. Understanding why they happen makes you much faster at fixing layouts in general.

How it works

ListView: four constructors

ConstructorBuilds itemsUse it for
ListView(children: [...])All at onceShort, fixed lists such as a settings page with eight rows
ListView.builderLazily, on demandLong or unknown-length lists from data
ListView.separatedLazily, plus separatorsLists with dividers or gaps between rows
ListView.customWith a custom delegateRare, advanced cases

ListView.builder takes an itemCount and an itemBuilder function. Flutter calls itemBuilder(context, index) only for indexes near the visible area. Off-screen rows are thrown away and rebuilt when they come back, so keep itemBuilder fast and never start network calls inside it.

If every row has the same height, tell the list with itemExtent (a number) or prototypeItem (a sample row). The list can then jump to any position without measuring rows, which helps very long lists and scroll bars.

A horizontal list uses scrollDirection: Axis.horizontal. It needs a fixed height from its parent, usually a SizedBox(height: 120, child: ListView...), because a horizontal list inside a vertical one has no natural height of its own.

Screen 1: Recipe list with dividers lib/main.dart

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

void main() => runApp(const RecipeApp());

class Recipe {
  const Recipe(this.name, this.minutes, this.level);
  final String name;
  final int minutes;
  final String level;

  String get info => '$minutes min · $level';
}

const recipes = <Recipe>[
  Recipe('Masala Dosa', 35, 'Easy'),
  Recipe('Lemon Rice', 20, 'Easy'),
  Recipe('Paneer Butter Masala', 45, 'Medium'),
  Recipe('Appam and Stew', 60, 'Medium'),
  Recipe('Kerala Fish Curry', 50, 'Hard'),
];

class RecipeApp extends StatelessWidget {
  const RecipeApp({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MaterialApp(
      theme: ThemeData(
        colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Colors.deepOrange),
      ),
      home: Scaffold(
        appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Recipes')),
        body: ListView.separated(
          itemCount: recipes.length,
          separatorBuilder: (context, index) => const Divider(height: 1),
          itemBuilder: (context, index) {
            final recipe = recipes[index];
            return ListTile(
              leading: CircleAvatar(child: Text(recipe.name[0])),
              title: Text(recipe.name),
              subtitle: Text(recipe.info),
              trailing: const Icon(Icons.chevron_right),
              onTap: () {},
            );
          },
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

ListView.separated builds each row on demand and puts a Divider between rows, but not after the last one.

GridView and grid delegates

A grid needs to know how to size tiles across the screen (the cross axis). That is the job of the gridDelegate:

  • SliverGridDelegateWithFixedCrossAxisCount(crossAxisCount: 2) always shows two columns. Tiles get wider on a tablet.
  • SliverGridDelegateWithMaxCrossAxisExtent(maxCrossAxisExtent: 200) sets the largest tile width and fits as many columns as possible. This is usually the better choice, because it adapts to the screen for free.

Both take mainAxisSpacing, crossAxisSpacing and childAspectRatio (width divided by height, so 3 / 4 gives tiles taller than they are wide). GridView.count and GridView.extent are shortcuts that build all children at once; use GridView.builder for data.

Screen 2: Recipe grid lib/recipe_grid.dart

// Recipe and recipes come from screen 1.
class RecipeGridPage extends StatelessWidget {
  const RecipeGridPage({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Recipe grid')),
      body: GridView.builder(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12),
        gridDelegate: const SliverGridDelegateWithMaxCrossAxisExtent(
          maxCrossAxisExtent: 200,
          mainAxisSpacing: 12,
          crossAxisSpacing: 12,
          childAspectRatio: 3 / 4, // width / height
        ),
        itemCount: recipes.length,
        itemBuilder: (context, index) => RecipeTile(recipe: recipes[index]),
      ),
    );
  }
}

class RecipeTile extends StatelessWidget {
  const RecipeTile({super.key, required this.recipe});
  final Recipe recipe;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final scheme = Theme.of(context).colorScheme;
    final text = Theme.of(context).textTheme;
    return Card(
      clipBehavior: Clip.antiAlias,
      child: Column(
        crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.stretch,
        children: [
          Expanded(
            child: ColoredBox(
              color: scheme.primaryContainer,
              child: Icon(Icons.restaurant, size: 40,
                  color: scheme.onPrimaryContainer),
            ),
          ),
          Padding(
            padding: const EdgeInsets.all(10),
            child: Column(
              crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
              children: [
                Text(recipe.name, style: text.titleSmall,
                    maxLines: 1, overflow: TextOverflow.ellipsis),
                Text(recipe.info, style: text.bodySmall),
              ],
            ),
          ),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}

MaxCrossAxisExtent 200 gives two columns on this narrow phone; the same code shows four or more on a tablet.

Remember: grid tiles get a fixed size from the delegate. If text overflows a tile, give the image area an Expanded so it shrinks, and use maxLines with TextOverflow.ellipsis on titles.

Slivers and CustomScrollView

ListView and GridView are really a scroll view holding one sliver each. When you need more than one kind of content in the same scroll, use CustomScrollView and give it a list of slivers directly:

SliverWhat it does
SliverAppBarAn app bar that can expand, collapse, stay pinned, or float back in. SliverAppBar.medium and SliverAppBar.large are the Material 3 collapsing styles.
SliverList.builderA lazy list of items, like ListView.builder
SliverGrid.builderA lazy grid with a grid delegate
SliverToBoxAdapterHolds one normal widget, such as a heading or a horizontal list
SliverPaddingAdds padding around another sliver
SliverFillRemainingFills the space left, handy for an empty state

The key rule: a CustomScrollView only accepts slivers. A plain widget such as Text must be wrapped in SliverToBoxAdapter. A SliverAppBar has pinned, floating and snap options, and an expandedHeight with a flexibleSpace (often a FlexibleSpaceBar with an image) for a photo header.

Screen 3: Slivers: one scroll, many parts lib/home_page.dart

// Recipe and recipes come from screen 1.
class HomePage extends StatelessWidget {
  const HomePage({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      body: CustomScrollView(
        slivers: [
          const SliverAppBar.large(
            title: Text('Recipe Book'),
            actions: [Icon(Icons.search), SizedBox(width: 12)],
          ),
          SliverToBoxAdapter(
            child: Padding(
              padding: const EdgeInsets.symmetric(horizontal: 16),
              child: Wrap(
                spacing: 8,
                children: [
                  for (final tag in ['Veg', 'Quick', 'Kerala'])
                    Chip(label: Text(tag)),
                ],
              ),
            ),
          ),
          SliverList.builder(
            itemCount: recipes.length,
            itemBuilder: (context, index) {
              final recipe = recipes[index];
              return ListTile(
                leading: const Icon(Icons.restaurant_menu),
                title: Text(recipe.name),
                subtitle: Text(recipe.info),
              );
            },
          ),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}

SliverAppBar.large starts tall and shrinks into a pinned bar as you scroll; the chip row and the list below scroll with it as one. States: At the top → Scrolled.

Example: Recipe Book home screen

The Recipe Book app from lesson 3.1 gets a real home screen. Here is the plan:

  1. A SliverAppBar.large titled Recipe Book that collapses as you scroll.
  2. A section title “Quick (30 min or less)” and a horizontal row of small cards.
  3. A section title “All recipes” and a grid of recipe tiles.
CustomScrollView(
  slivers: [
    const SliverAppBar.large(title: Text('Recipe Book')),
    const SliverToBoxAdapter(child: SectionTitle('Quick (30 min or less)')),
    SliverToBoxAdapter(
      child: SizedBox(
        height: 120,
        child: ListView.separated(
          scrollDirection: Axis.horizontal,
          padding: const EdgeInsets.symmetric(horizontal: 16),
          itemCount: quick.length,
          separatorBuilder: (context, index) => const SizedBox(width: 12),
          itemBuilder: (context, index) => QuickCard(recipe: quick[index]),
        ),
      ),
    ),
    const SliverToBoxAdapter(child: SectionTitle('All recipes')),
    SliverPadding(
      padding: const EdgeInsets.symmetric(horizontal: 16),
      sliver: SliverGrid.builder(
        gridDelegate: const SliverGridDelegateWithMaxCrossAxisExtent(
          maxCrossAxisExtent: 220,
          mainAxisSpacing: 12,
          crossAxisSpacing: 12,
          childAspectRatio: 3 / 4,
        ),
        itemCount: recipes.length,
        itemBuilder: (context, index) => RecipeTile(recipe: recipes[index]),
      ),
    ),
  ],
)

Notice the details. The horizontal list sits inside a SizedBox so it has a height. The grid sits in SliverPadding, not Padding, because only slivers are allowed here. The quick list is computed once at the top of build with recipes.where((r) => r.isQuick).toList(), not inside the item builder. Each text line such as “35 min · Easy” comes from a getter on the model (String get info => '$minutes min · $level';), which keeps the widget code short.

Common mistakes

  • A ListView inside a Column with no bounds. The Column offers unlimited height and the ListView wants all of it, so Flutter throws “Vertical viewport was given unbounded height”. Wrap the list in Expanded.
  • Using shrinkWrap: true as a universal fix. It makes the error go away by measuring every child, which removes laziness. For more than a handful of items, use slivers or Expanded instead.
  • A horizontal ListView without a height. Give it a SizedBox with a fixed height.
  • Heavy work in itemBuilder. Sorting, filtering or parsing inside the builder runs again every time a row scrolls into view. Do it once, before the list.
  • Nested scroll views that fight. Two vertical lists inside each other both try to scroll. Merge them into one CustomScrollView.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Be ready to explain laziness: builder constructors create widgets only for visible items, and elements for off-screen items are disposed. This is why state inside a list row can be lost when it scrolls away; keep important state above the list (you will do this with BLoC later).
  • Know when to use itemExtent or prototypeItem: long lists with equal row heights.
  • Pull-to-refresh (RefreshIndicator) and infinite scrolling with a ScrollController are common tasks; you will build them in the networking module.
  • NestedScrollView exists for screens where a header scrolls with tabbed lists inside it. Reach for CustomScrollView first; it covers most screens.

terms.definition: A lazy list: it calls itemBuilder only for items that are visible or about to be, so thousands of items stay cheap.
A lazy list that also builds a separator widget (such as a Divider) between items.
The object that sets a grid’s layout, for example SliverGridDelegateWithFixedCrossAxisCount or SliverGridDelegateWithMaxCrossAxisExtent.
A scrollable piece of a scroll view that lays itself out lazily along the scroll axis.
A scroll view built from a list of slivers, so different kinds of content share one scroll position.
Wraps one ordinary (box) widget so it can sit inside a list of slivers.

lessons.examTip: Interviewers like to ask why ListView(children: …) is slow for 10,000 items. Answer: it builds every child up front; ListView.builder builds only what is visible.
