lessons.title: Responsive and adaptive layouts
lessons.summaryHtml:
Flutter apps run on small phones, large tablets, foldables, desktop windows and browsers. A responsive layout changes with the space it has; an adaptive layout also fits the device and how people use it (touch or mouse, portrait or landscape).

  • MediaQuery.sizeOf(context) gives the size of the whole window. LayoutBuilder gives the constraints of one part of the screen.
  • Breakpoints turn a width into a layout choice. Material 3 calls these window size classes: compact (under 600), medium (600 to 839) and expanded (840 and up).
  • SafeArea keeps content away from notches, status bars and the home indicator.
  • Navigation adapts: a NavigationBar at the bottom on phones, a NavigationRail at the side on larger screens, and a list–detail view when there is room for both.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

One Flutter codebase can run on a small phone, a folding phone, a tablet, a laptop browser and a desktop window. The same screen must look right in all of them. A layout that only works at 390 pixels wide looks stretched and empty on a tablet, and broken in a phone turned sideways.

Think of water poured into different glasses. The water is the same, but it takes the shape of the glass. A responsive layout is like that: it reshapes itself to the space it has. An adaptive layout goes one step further and fits how the device is used. On a desktop it supports mouse hover and keyboard shortcuts; on a phone it uses big touch targets and a bottom navigation bar.

Why it matters

Clients rarely ask for “phone only” any more. A restaurant owner wants the order screen on a counter tablet. A school wants the same app on students’ phones and on a web dashboard for teachers. Stores also check this: Google Play highlights apps that work well on large screens and foldables, and recent Android versions ignore orientation locks on large screens for apps that target new API levels. Learning to think in available space, not device names, saves you from rewriting screens later.

How it works

Logical pixels and the two ways to measure

Flutter sizes are in logical pixels, not physical pixels. A phone and a tablet with very different pixel densities can both report a width of about 400 logical pixels in portrait. That is why a breakpoint such as 600 works on every device.

ToolMeasuresUse it when
MediaQuery.sizeOf(context)The whole window (the app’s view)Choosing the page skeleton: bottom bar or rail, one pane or two
LayoutBuilderThe constraints the parent gives this widgetA component that adapts to its own box, such as a card that turns from a row into a column
MediaQuery.orientationOf(context)Portrait or landscapeSmall tweaks; prefer width for big decisions
MediaQuery.paddingOf(context)System intrusions such as the status bar and notchUsually hidden behind SafeArea

Prefer the specific methods such as sizeOf over MediaQuery.of(context).size. With sizeOf, the widget only rebuilds when the size changes, not when, for example, the keyboard opens or the text scale changes.

Breakpoints as a Dart 3 switch

Material 3 groups window widths into window size classes. The first three are the ones most apps need:

ClassWidthTypical deviceNavigation
Compactunder 600Phone in portraitBottom NavigationBar
Medium600 to 839Small tablet, unfolded foldableNavigationRail
Expanded840 and upTablet in landscape, desktopExtended rail or navigation drawer, often two panes

Material 3 also defines larger classes for big desktop windows, but these three cover most mobile work. Keep the logic in one small function so every screen agrees. Relational patterns make it read like the table:

enum WindowSize { compact, medium, expanded }

WindowSize windowSizeOf(double width) => switch (width) {
      < 600 => WindowSize.compact,
      < 840 => WindowSize.medium,
      _ => WindowSize.expanded,
    };

Screen 1: Breakpoints with LayoutBuilder lib/size_readout.dart

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

enum WindowSize { compact, medium, expanded }

WindowSize windowSizeOf(double width) => switch (width) {
      < 600 => WindowSize.compact,
      < 840 => WindowSize.medium,
      _ => WindowSize.expanded,
    };

class SizeReadout extends StatelessWidget {
  const SizeReadout({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return LayoutBuilder(
      builder: (context, constraints) {
        final size = windowSizeOf(constraints.maxWidth);
        final width = constraints.maxWidth.round();
        final icon = switch (size) {
          WindowSize.compact => Icons.smartphone,
          WindowSize.medium => Icons.tablet,
          WindowSize.expanded => Icons.desktop_windows,
        };
        return Center(
          child: Column(
            mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
            children: [
              Icon(icon, size: 64),
              Text(size.name,
                  style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.headlineMedium),
              Text('maxWidth: $width'),
            ],
          ),
        );
      },
    );
  }
}

The same widget reports a different window size class as its constraints change. The medium and expanded frames show what it prints in wider windows. States: Compact → Medium → Expanded.

Adaptive navigation

A bottom NavigationBar is easy to reach with a thumb, but on a wide screen it becomes a long, thin strip far from the content. A NavigationRail sits at the side and uses the width better. Both take the same three things: selectedIndex, onDestinationSelected and a list of destinations, so switching between them is simple. The rail has labelType (show labels under icons) and extended (a wider rail with labels beside icons). An extended rail needs labelType left as none.

Screen 2: NavigationBar or NavigationRail lib/adaptive_shell.dart

class AdaptiveShell extends StatefulWidget {
  const AdaptiveShell({super.key});

  @override
  State<AdaptiveShell> createState() => _AdaptiveShellState();
}

class _AdaptiveShellState extends State<AdaptiveShell> {
  int _index = 0;
  static const _labels = ['Home', 'Saved', 'Profile'];
  static const _icons = [Icons.home, Icons.favorite, Icons.person];

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final wide = MediaQuery.sizeOf(context).width >= 600;
    final label = _labels[_index];
    final page = Center(child: Text('$label page'));
    void select(int i) => setState(() => _index = i);

    if (!wide) {
      return Scaffold(
        appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Recipe Book')),
        body: page,
        bottomNavigationBar: NavigationBar(
          selectedIndex: _index,
          onDestinationSelected: select,
          destinations: [
            for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++)
              NavigationDestination(icon: Icon(_icons[i]), label: _labels[i]),
          ],
        ),
      );
    }
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Recipe Book')),
      body: SafeArea(
        child: Row(
          children: [
            NavigationRail(
              selectedIndex: _index,
              onDestinationSelected: select,
              labelType: NavigationRailLabelType.all,
              destinations: [
                for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++)
                  NavigationRailDestination(
                      icon: Icon(_icons[i]), label: Text(_labels[i])),
              ],
            ),
            const VerticalDivider(width: 1),
            Expanded(child: page),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

Under 600 pixels the destinations sit in a bottom NavigationBar; from 600 up they move to a NavigationRail. The rail frame is a scaled-down sketch of a wider window. States: Phone: NavigationBar → Wide: NavigationRail.

List–detail layouts

On a phone, tapping an item opens a new page. On a wide screen, pushing a page wastes space; show the list and the details side by side instead. The trick is to keep the selected item in state, and let the layout decide how to show it: in a second pane when there is room, or on a new route when there is not.

Screen 3: List–detail on wide screens lib/recipes_pane.dart

// Recipe, recipes and RecipeDetail are in the lab files.
class RecipesPane extends StatelessWidget {
  const RecipesPane({
    super.key,
    required this.twoPane,
    required this.selected,
    required this.onSelect,
  });

  final bool twoPane;
  final Recipe? selected;
  final ValueChanged<Recipe> onSelect;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final list = ListView.builder(
      itemCount: recipes.length,
      itemBuilder: (context, index) {
        final recipe = recipes[index];
        return ListTile(
          title: Text(recipe.name),
          subtitle: Text(recipe.info),
          selected: twoPane && recipe == selected,
          onTap: () => onSelect(recipe),
        );
      },
    );
    if (!twoPane) return list;

    final detail = switch (selected) {
      null => const Center(child: Text('Pick a recipe')),
      Recipe recipe => RecipeDetail(recipe: recipe),
    };
    return Row(
      children: [
        SizedBox(width: 320, child: list),
        const VerticalDivider(width: 1),
        Expanded(child: detail),
      ],
    );
  }
}

On a narrow screen tapping a recipe opens a new page; on an expanded window the list and the detail sit side by side and the tapped row is highlighted. States: Narrow: list only → Expanded: list + detail.

SafeArea and orientation

Modern phones have notches, rounded corners, a status bar and a gesture bar. A Scaffold with an AppBar already keeps the top clear, and a NavigationBar handles the bottom. Anything else that reaches an edge needs SafeArea:

Scaffold(
  body: SafeArea(
    child: Row(
      children: [
        NavigationRail(/* ... */),
        const Expanded(child: RecipeGrid()),
      ],
    ),
  ),
)

In landscape, the notch moves to the left or right side, which is exactly where a rail sits. Test landscape on an emulator with a cut-out. Avoid locking orientation to fix layout problems: it hides the bug on phones and is often ignored on tablets and foldables anyway.

Example: an adaptive Recipe Book

The Recipe Book from lessons 3.1 to 3.4 becomes adaptive in four steps:

  1. Measure once. In the home widget: final size = windowSizeOf(MediaQuery.sizeOf(context).width);
  2. Pick the navigation. Compact returns a Scaffold with bottomNavigationBar: NavigationBar(...). Medium and expanded return a Row with a NavigationRail, a VerticalDivider(width: 1) and the page in Expanded. The rail is extended on expanded.
  3. Keep one source of truth. The home state holds int _tab and Recipe? _selected. Both navigation widgets read and write the same _tab, so resizing the window keeps the user on the same tab.
  4. Two panes when expanded. RecipesPane gets twoPane: size == WindowSize.expanded. Tapping a recipe either calls setState to show it on the right, or pushes a detail page on narrow screens.

Because the recipe list is the same widget in both layouts, there is no duplicated code: only the shell around it changes.

Common mistakes

  • Checking the platform for layout. Platform.isAndroid says nothing about width: an Android tablet and an Android phone need different layouts, and dart:io is not available on the web. Use size for layout; use platform checks only for platform behaviour.
  • Hard-coded widths everywhere. width: 360 fits one phone. Use Expanded, Flexible, grids with a max tile width and constraints such as ConstrainedBox(constraints: BoxConstraints(maxWidth: 600)) to keep forms readable on wide screens.
  • Using MediaQuery for a component. A card inside a two-pane layout is narrower than the window. Use LayoutBuilder for component-level decisions.
  • Losing state on resize. If the phone layout and tablet layout build different stateful widgets, rotating the device resets them. Keep state above the layout switch.
  • Forgetting landscape. A tall form that fits in portrait may overflow in landscape. Make long pages scrollable.

Interview and real-world notes

  • A good answer to “how do you support tablets?” names window size classes, MediaQuery.sizeOf for the shell, LayoutBuilder for components, NavigationRail and list–detail.
  • Adaptive also means input: tooltips and hover effects for mouse users, keyboard focus and shortcuts on desktop, and touch targets of at least 48 by 48 logical pixels on touch screens.
  • Test with the device preview options in your IDE, a resizable desktop window, and a foldable or tablet emulator. Run a quick pass in landscape on every release.

terms.definition: A layout that rearranges itself to fit the space available.
A layout that also fits the device and input type, such as touch, mouse or keyboard.
A width at which the layout changes, such as 600 logical pixels.
A widget whose builder receives the parent’s BoxConstraints, so a component can adapt to its own space.
A widget that pads its child to avoid system intrusions such as notches and the status bar.
A vertical Material navigation bar for the side of medium and large screens.

lessons.examTip: Decide layouts by available width, not by device type. “Is it a tablet?” is the wrong question; “how much room do I have?” is the right one.

domains.blurb: Material 3 components, theming and dark mode, and reusable custom widgets.

lessons.title: Material 3 components tour
lessons.summaryHtml:
Material 3 is Google’s current design system and Flutter’s default. It comes with ready-made components that already follow its rules for colour, shape, size and accessibility.

  • Cards come in three variants: elevated (Card), Card.filled and Card.outlined.
  • Chips are small, compact choices: FilterChip for multi-select filters, ChoiceChip for one choice, InputChip for entered tags and ActionChip for quick actions.
  • SegmentedButton picks one (or several) options from a short set. NavigationBar switches top-level destinations. SearchBar and SearchAnchor give a full search experience. Badge marks counts and new items.

You will build the home screen of Travel Explorer, a destination browser that uses all of them.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A design system is a shared kit of parts, like a box of Lego with rules for how pieces fit. Material 3 (sometimes called Material You) is Google’s design system, and it is Flutter’s default. Every new Flutter app already uses its colours, shapes, type sizes and motion.

Material 3 gives you components: buttons, cards, chips, navigation bars, search bars, dialogs and more. Each one already handles the hard parts: touch target size, focus and hover states, screen reader labels, dark mode and right-to-left languages. Your job is to pick the right component for each job and combine them well.

Why it matters

Clients and designers speak in component names. A Figma file may say “filter chips, segmented button, navigation bar with badge”. If you know that each of these is one Flutter widget, you build the screen in an hour instead of drawing everything from Container and GestureDetector. Custom look-alikes also tend to miss accessibility details that the real components get right.

Using standard components also makes theming easy. In the next lesson you change one seed colour and every card, chip and button updates together.

How it works

Buttons: pick by emphasis

Material 3 ranks buttons by how much attention they need. Use one high-emphasis button per area and lower ones for the rest.

WidgetEmphasisTypical use
FilledButtonHighestThe main action: Book now, Save, Pay
FilledButton.tonalMedium-highImportant but secondary: Add to trip
ElevatedButtonMediumWhen a button must stand out from a patterned background
OutlinedButtonMedium-lowAlternatives next to a filled button: Cancel, Details
TextButtonLowestDialog actions, inline links

IconButton also has a toggle mode: set isSelected and selectedIcon to make a favourite heart that switches between outline and filled.

Cards

A card groups content about one thing, such as one destination. Flutter has three variants that match the Material 3 spec: Card (elevated, with a soft shadow), Card.filled (a tinted background, no shadow) and Card.outlined (a border, no shadow). Add clipBehavior: Clip.antiAlias when the card has an image at the top so the image follows the rounded corners.

Screen 1: Cards and navigation lib/main.dart

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

void main() => runApp(MaterialApp(
      theme: ThemeData(colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Colors.teal)),
      home: const CardsDemo(),
    ));

class CardsDemo extends StatelessWidget {
  const CardsDemo({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final scheme = Theme.of(context).colorScheme;
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(
        title: const Text('Travel Explorer'),
        actions: [
          IconButton(
            onPressed: () {},
            icon: const Badge(label: Text('2'), child: Icon(Icons.favorite_border)),
          ),
        ],
      ),
      body: ListView(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12),
        children: [
          Card(
            clipBehavior: Clip.antiAlias,
            child: Column(children: [
              Container(height: 90, color: scheme.primaryContainer,
                  child: const Center(child: Icon(Icons.landscape, size: 40))),
              const ListTile(title: Text('Munnar'), subtitle: Text('Kerala · Mountains')),
            ]),
          ),
          Card.filled(
            child: const ListTile(leading: Icon(Icons.beach_access),
                title: Text('Goa'), subtitle: Text('India · Beach')),
          ),
          Card.outlined(
            child: const ListTile(leading: Icon(Icons.location_city),
                title: Text('Dubai'), subtitle: Text('UAE · City')),
          ),
        ],
      ),
      bottomNavigationBar: NavigationBar(
        selectedIndex: 0,
        destinations: const [
          NavigationDestination(icon: Icon(Icons.explore), label: 'Explore'),
          NavigationDestination(icon: Icon(Icons.favorite_border), label: 'Saved'),
          NavigationDestination(icon: Icon(Icons.map_outlined), label: 'Trips'),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}

The three Card variants side by side: elevated with a header image area, filled and outlined. The favourite icon in the app bar carries a Badge.

Chips and segmented buttons

WidgetBehaviourTravel Explorer example
FilterChipToggles; many can be onBeach, Mountains, City
ChoiceChipOne selected in a groupSort by: Popular or Nearest
InputChipRepresents entered data; can be deletedTravellers added to a trip
ActionChipRuns an action, like a small button“Add to calendar” suggestion
SegmentedButtonConnected options, usually two to fiveBudget, Mid, Luxury

A SegmentedButton<T> works with a set of selected values, even when only one is allowed. You pass segments (each a ButtonSegment with a value and a label or icon), the current selected set and an onSelectionChanged callback. Two flags change its rules: multiSelectionEnabled allows several, and emptySelectionAllowed allows none. An enum is the natural type for T.

Screen 2: Search bar, filter chips and a segmented button lib/filters_panel.dart

enum Budget { budget, mid, luxury }

class FiltersPanel extends StatefulWidget {
  const FiltersPanel({super.key});

  @override
  State<FiltersPanel> createState() => _FiltersPanelState();
}

class _FiltersPanelState extends State<FiltersPanel> {
  static const _types = ['Beach', 'Mountains', 'City', 'Heritage'];
  final _chosen = <String>{};
  Budget _budget = Budget.mid;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Padding(
      padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
      child: Column(
        crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
        spacing: 16,
        children: [
          SearchBar(
            hintText: 'Search destinations',
            leading: const Icon(Icons.search),
          ),
          Wrap(
            spacing: 8,
            children: [
              for (final type in _types)
                FilterChip(
                  label: Text(type),
                  selected: _chosen.contains(type),
                  onSelected: (on) => setState(() {
                    if (on) {
                      _chosen.add(type);
                    } else {
                      _chosen.remove(type);
                    }
                  }),
                ),
            ],
          ),
          SegmentedButton<Budget>(
            segments: const [
              ButtonSegment(value: Budget.budget, label: Text('Budget')),
              ButtonSegment(value: Budget.mid, label: Text('Mid')),
              ButtonSegment(value: Budget.luxury, label: Text('Luxury')),
            ],
            selected: {_budget},
            onSelectionChanged: (set) => setState(() => _budget = set.first),
          ),
          FilledButton(onPressed: () {}, child: const Text('Show results')),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}

FilterChips toggle independently and show a check mark when selected; the SegmentedButton always has exactly one budget selected here. States: Start → Beach + City, Luxury.

Remember: components do not store their own selection. A FilterChip shows whatever selected you pass, and tells you about taps through onSelected. You keep the state (here, a Set<String>) and call setState.

Navigation, search and badges

NavigationBar is the Material 3 bottom bar for three to five top-level destinations. Each NavigationDestination has an icon, an optional selectedIcon (often the filled version) and a label. It replaces the older BottomNavigationBar in Material 3 designs.

Badge wraps an icon and shows a small label or dot. Badge.count(count: 3, child: ...) formats numbers for you, and isLabelVisible hides it at zero.

For search, SearchBar is the pill-shaped input. SearchAnchor.bar combines it with a full search view: tapping the bar opens the view, and your suggestionsBuilder returns widgets for the current text. The builder receives a SearchController; call controller.closeView(text) to close the view with a chosen value.

Screen 3: SearchAnchor with suggestions lib/search.dart

const destinations = [
  (name: 'Munnar', country: 'India'),
  (name: 'Goa', country: 'India'),
  (name: 'Dubai', country: 'UAE'),
  (name: 'Banff', country: 'Canada'),
];

class DestinationSearch extends StatelessWidget {
  const DestinationSearch({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Padding(
      padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
      child: SearchAnchor.bar(
        barHintText: 'Search destinations',
        suggestionsBuilder: (context, controller) {
          final query = controller.text.toLowerCase();
          return destinations
              .where((d) => d.name.toLowerCase().contains(query))
              .map((d) => ListTile(
                    leading: const Icon(Icons.place_outlined),
                    title: Text(d.name),
                    subtitle: Text(d.country),
                    onTap: () => controller.closeView(d.name),
                  ));
        },
      ),
    );
  }
}

Tapping the bar opens a full search view. Typing “ba” matches Dubai and Banff because the filter uses contains, not startsWith. States: Closed → Typing “ba”.

Other components you will meet

The tour does not stop here. FloatingActionButton (and FloatingActionButton.extended) holds the single most important action on a screen, such as “Plan a trip”. Switch, Checkbox and Radio handle settings and forms. DropdownMenu is the Material 3 menu for choosing from a list, and MenuAnchor shows pop-up menus. showDatePicker and showTimePicker open ready-made pickers, showModalBottomSheet slides a panel up from the bottom, and Tooltip explains icon-only buttons. Before building any control yourself, check the widget catalogue on docs.flutter.dev: the component you need very often already exists.

Example: Travel Explorer home

The Travel Explorer app shows six destinations such as Munnar, Goa, Dubai and Banff. The home screen puts the components together:

  1. A SearchAnchor.bar at the top for searching by name.
  2. A Wrap of FilterChips for types, backed by final _types = <String>{};
  3. A SegmentedButton<Budget> with emptySelectionAllowed: true, backed by Budget? _budget.
  4. A DestinationCard per visible destination with a toggle heart.
  5. A NavigationBar with Explore and Saved, and a Badge.count on Saved.

The filtering is plain Dart, kept out of the widgets:

List<Destination> get _visible => destinations
    .where((d) => _types.isEmpty || _types.contains(d.type))
    .where((d) => _budget == null || d.budget == _budget)
    .toList();

Because _budget may be null but the segmented button wants a set, the selected set uses a Dart 3 if-case inside a collection literal: selected: {if (_budget case final budget?) budget}. When _budget is null the set is empty; otherwise it holds one value.

Common mistakes

  • Rebuilding components by hand. A Container with rounded corners and an InkWell is not a chip: it misses selected states, focus, semantics and theming.
  • Too many filled buttons. If everything is high emphasis, nothing is. One FilledButton per section is a good rule.
  • Using ChoiceChip for multi-select. ChoiceChip means “pick one”. Use FilterChip when several can be on.
  • Forgetting that SegmentedButton needs a set. Pass {_budget}, not _budget, and read set.first in the callback.
  • Mixing Material 2 widgets into a Material 3 design. Prefer NavigationBar over BottomNavigationBar, and FilledButton over styled ElevatedButtons for the main action.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Know the button hierarchy and the chip types; interviewers often ask “which widget would you use for…” questions.
  • Explain that components are controlled: they display state you pass and report changes through callbacks. This idea carries straight into Provider and BLoC.
  • The Flutter team keeps a Material 3 demo app and the widget catalogue on docs.flutter.dev; designers often use the Material 3 Figma kit, so component names match one to one.
  • Accessibility comes free with real components, but still add a tooltip to icon-only buttons so screen readers can announce them.

The Material 3 bottom bar for switching between three to five top-level destinations.

lessons.examTip: In a design review, name components by their Material 3 names (filter chip, segmented button, navigation bar). It shows you know the system and makes designer hand-offs faster.

lessons.title: Theming and dark mode
lessons.summaryHtml:
A theme is one central place that decides your app’s colours, text styles and component shapes. Widgets read it with Theme.of(context) instead of hard-coding values, so one change updates the whole app.

  • ColorScheme.fromSeed turns one seed colour into a full Material 3 palette of colour roles (primary, onPrimary, primaryContainer, surface, outline and more), for light or dark.
  • TextTheme holds the type scale (displayLarge down to labelSmall). Component themes such as CardThemeData and FilledButtonThemeData style every card or button at once.
  • MaterialApp takes a theme, a darkTheme and a themeMode (system, light or dark).
  • A ThemeExtension adds your own brand values, such as a “deal” colour, that switch correctly between light and dark.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A theme is your app’s style guide, written as code. Instead of each screen choosing its own colours and fonts, every widget asks the theme: “what is the primary colour?”, “what does a title look like?”, “how round are cards?”.

Think of a school uniform policy. The policy says “navy blazer, white shirt”. Nobody picks their own colour each morning, and if the school changes to green, one announcement updates everyone. ThemeData is that policy for your app, and Theme.of(context) is how each widget reads it.

Dark mode is simply a second policy. You give Flutter a light theme and a dark theme, and it switches between them.

Why it matters

Clients change their minds about colours, and every client has a brand. If colours are scattered across forty files, a rebrand takes days and misses spots. With a theme it takes minutes. Many users also run their phones in dark mode all the time; an app with hard-coded white backgrounds or black text looks broken to them, and some text becomes unreadable. Good theming is also an accessibility issue: Material 3 colour roles are designed so that text on its partner background has enough contrast.

How it works

Colour schemes and roles

ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: ..., brightness: ...) takes one colour and generates a full scheme using Material’s tonal palettes. You never pick forty colours by hand. The result has roles, and each role has a job:

RoleUse it for
primary / onPrimaryKey actions such as filled buttons, and the text or icons on them
primaryContainer / onPrimaryContainerSofter highlighted areas, such as a header block or a selected chip
secondaryContainer, tertiary and partnersAccents that should differ from primary
surface / onSurfacePage backgrounds and normal text
surfaceContainer (lowest to highest)Layered backgrounds for cards, sheets and bars
onSurfaceVariantSecondary text and icons, such as subtitles
outline / outlineVariantBorders and dividers
error / onErrorError states

The golden rule: content on a colour uses the matching “on” colour. Text on primaryContainer uses onPrimaryContainer. Follow it and both light and dark themes are readable automatically. fromSeed also accepts a dynamicSchemeVariant if you want colours that stay closer to the seed than the calm default.

Light, dark and ThemeMode

MaterialApp has three theme properties: theme (light), darkTheme and themeMode. ThemeMode.system, the default, follows the phone setting. To let users choose, keep the mode in state above MaterialApp. A ValueNotifier<ThemeMode> with a ValueListenableBuilder is enough for now; in module 6 you will move it into a Cubit, and in module 7 you will save it with shared_preferences.

Screen 1: Light, dark and system lib/main.dart

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

void main() => runApp(const TravelApp());

final themeMode = ValueNotifier(ThemeMode.system);
const seed = Colors.teal;

class TravelApp extends StatelessWidget {
  const TravelApp({super.key});
  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return ValueListenableBuilder(
      valueListenable: themeMode,
      builder: (context, mode, _) => MaterialApp(
        theme: ThemeData(colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: seed)),
        darkTheme: ThemeData(
          colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(
              seedColor: seed, brightness: Brightness.dark),
        ),
        themeMode: mode,
        home: AppearancePage(mode: mode),
      ),
    );
  }
}

class AppearancePage extends StatelessWidget {
  const AppearancePage({super.key, required this.mode});
  final ThemeMode mode;
  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Appearance')),
      body: ListView(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
        children: [
          Text('Theme', style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleMedium),
          const SizedBox(height: 8),
          SegmentedButton<ThemeMode>(
            segments: const [
              ButtonSegment(value: ThemeMode.system, label: Text('System')),
              ButtonSegment(value: ThemeMode.light, label: Text('Light')),
              ButtonSegment(value: ThemeMode.dark, label: Text('Dark')),
            ],
            selected: {mode},
            onSelectionChanged: (set) => themeMode.value = set.first,
          ),
          const SizedBox(height: 16),
          const Card(
            child: ListTile(
              leading: Icon(Icons.landscape),
              title: Text('Munnar'),
              subtitle: Text('Kerala · Mountains'),
            ),
          ),
          const SizedBox(height: 8),
          FilledButton(onPressed: () {}, child: const Text('Book trip')),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}

The same widgets with theme and darkTheme built from one seed. Changing the segmented button switches ThemeMode and every colour role flips together. States: Light → Dark.

Text themes and component themes

TextTheme holds the Material 3 type scale in five groups (display, headline, title, body, label), each in large, medium and small. Read them with Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleLarge. To change a style, pass a partial TextTheme in ThemeData; Flutter merges it with the defaults. To tweak one use, call copyWith: textTheme.bodyMedium?.copyWith(color: scheme.onSurfaceVariant). A custom font from your assets goes in ThemeData(fontFamily: 'YourFont').

Component themes style every instance of a widget. Current Flutter uses ...ThemeData classes for them, for example cardTheme: CardThemeData(...), filledButtonTheme: FilledButtonThemeData(style: FilledButton.styleFrom(...)), chipTheme: ChipThemeData(...) and navigationBarTheme: NavigationBarThemeData(...). A value set on one widget still overrides the theme for that widget.

Where does Theme.of(context) find the theme? It walks up the widget tree from context to the nearest Theme widget. MaterialApp inserts one for you with the active light or dark theme, so every screen below it sees the same values. When the theme changes, every widget that called Theme.of in its build rebuilds automatically. MaterialApp even animates the change: it blends the old and new ThemeData over a short duration, which is why switching to dark mode fades instead of jumping. That blend is also why your own theme extensions need a proper lerp.

Screen 2: Text theme and component themes lib/app_theme.dart

abstract final class AppTheme {
  static const seed = Color(0xFF00796B);

  static ThemeData light() => _build(Brightness.light);
  static ThemeData dark() => _build(Brightness.dark);

  static ThemeData _build(Brightness brightness) {
    final scheme =
        ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: seed, brightness: brightness);
    return ThemeData(
      colorScheme: scheme,
      textTheme: const TextTheme(
        headlineSmall: TextStyle(fontWeight: FontWeight.w700),
      ),
      cardTheme: CardThemeData(
        clipBehavior: Clip.antiAlias,
        shape: RoundedRectangleBorder(
            borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(20)),
      ),
      filledButtonTheme: FilledButtonThemeData(
        style: FilledButton.styleFrom(minimumSize: const Size(64, 52)),
      ),
    );
  }
}

// In a screen: read the theme, never hard-code.
class DetailBody extends StatelessWidget {
  const DetailBody({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final theme = Theme.of(context);
    return ListView(
      padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
      children: [
        Text('Munnar', style: theme.textTheme.headlineSmall),
        Text('Tea hills in the Western Ghats',
            style: theme.textTheme.bodyMedium
                ?.copyWith(color: theme.colorScheme.onSurfaceVariant)),
        const SizedBox(height: 12),
        Card(
          child: Container(
            height: 120,
            color: theme.colorScheme.primaryContainer,
            child: Icon(Icons.landscape,
                size: 48, color: theme.colorScheme.onPrimaryContainer),
          ),
        ),
        const SizedBox(height: 12),
        FilledButton(onPressed: () {}, child: const Text('Book trip')),
      ],
    );
  }
}

No widget on this screen sets a shape, radius or font weight itself: the rounded card, the bold headline and the tall full-width button all come from ThemeData.

Theme extensions for brand values

Sometimes the colour scheme has no role for what you need: a “deal” highlight, a rating star colour, a map route colour. Do not hijack error or tertiary for it. Create a ThemeExtension: a small immutable class with your values, a copyWith, and a lerp that blends two instances (Flutter uses it to animate between light and dark). Register a light and a dark instance in each theme’s extensions, and read it with Theme.of(context).extension<TravelColors>()!.

Screen 3: A ThemeExtension for brand colours lib/travel_colors.dart

@immutable
class TravelColors extends ThemeExtension<TravelColors> {
  const TravelColors({required this.deal, required this.onDeal});
  final Color deal;
  final Color onDeal;

  static const light =
      TravelColors(deal: Color(0xFFFFE08A), onDeal: Color(0xFF3D2E00));
  static const dark =
      TravelColors(deal: Color(0xFF5B4300), onDeal: Color(0xFFFFE08A));

  @override
  TravelColors copyWith({Color? deal, Color? onDeal}) => TravelColors(
      deal: deal ?? this.deal, onDeal: onDeal ?? this.onDeal);

  @override
  TravelColors lerp(TravelColors? other, double t) {
    if (other is! TravelColors) return this;
    return TravelColors(
      deal: Color.lerp(deal, other.deal, t)!,
      onDeal: Color.lerp(onDeal, other.onDeal, t)!,
    );
  }
}

// Register: ThemeData(..., extensions: const [TravelColors.light])
class DealTag extends StatelessWidget {
  const DealTag(this.label, {super.key});
  final String label;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final travel = Theme.of(context).extension<TravelColors>()!;
    return Container(
      padding: const EdgeInsets.symmetric(horizontal: 10, vertical: 4),
      decoration: BoxDecoration(
        color: travel.deal,
        borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(12),
      ),
      child: Text(label, style: TextStyle(color: travel.onDeal)),
    );
  }
}

The “deal” pill colours come from TravelColors, a ThemeExtension with separate light and dark values, so it stays readable in both modes. States: Light → Dark.

Example: theming Travel Explorer

Travel Explorer gets one AppTheme class that owns every design decision. Dart 3’s abstract final class makes it a pure namespace that nobody can create or extend:

abstract final class AppTheme {
  static const seed = Color(0xFF00796B);
  static ThemeData light() => _build(Brightness.light, TravelColors.light);
  static ThemeData dark() => _build(Brightness.dark, TravelColors.dark);

  static ThemeData _build(Brightness brightness, TravelColors travel) {
    final scheme = ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: seed, brightness: brightness);
    return ThemeData(
      colorScheme: scheme,
      textTheme: const TextTheme(
        headlineSmall: TextStyle(fontWeight: FontWeight.w700),
      ),
      cardTheme: CardThemeData(
        clipBehavior: Clip.antiAlias,
        shape: RoundedRectangleBorder(borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(20)),
      ),
      filledButtonTheme: FilledButtonThemeData(
        style: FilledButton.styleFrom(minimumSize: const Size(64, 52)),
      ),
      extensions: [travel],
    );
  }
}

Then MaterialApp(theme: AppTheme.light(), darkTheme: AppTheme.dark(), themeMode: mode). The screens contain no colour values at all: a destination tile uses scheme.primaryContainer with scheme.onPrimaryContainer, and deal tags read TravelColors. Switching to dark mode now needs zero changes in screen code.

To restyle one part of a screen differently, wrap it in Theme(data: Theme.of(context).copyWith(...), child: ...). Everything inside reads the local override.

Common mistakes

  • Hard-coded colours. Colors.white backgrounds and Colors.black text break in dark mode. Use colour roles.
  • Using old names. background and surfaceVariant in ColorScheme are deprecated: use surface and surfaceContainerHighest. Old text names such as headline6 and bodyText2 are gone: use titleLarge, bodyMedium and friends. For transparency use color.withValues(alpha: 0.5), not withOpacity.
  • A dark theme built from a light scheme. Passing brightness: Brightness.dark to ThemeData while the colorScheme is light causes an assertion error. Build the dark scheme with ColorScheme.fromSeed(..., brightness: Brightness.dark).
  • Reading the theme in initState. Theme.of(context) belongs in build (or didChangeDependencies), so the widget rebuilds when the theme changes.
  • Forcing full width in the button theme. minimumSize: Size.fromHeight(52) makes every filled button infinitely wide, which crashes buttons placed inside a Row. Set a height in the theme and choose full width per layout.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Explain how you would rebrand an app: change the seed or scheme in one theme file, with no screen edits. That answer shows good architecture.
  • Know ThemeMode, theme and darkTheme, and where you would store the user’s choice (state management plus local storage).
  • Designers often hand over a full palette. You can still start from fromSeed and override specific roles with copyWith, or build a ColorScheme directly.
  • Check contrast in both modes and with large text sizes before release; theming bugs are among the most visible ones users report.

terms.definition: The object that holds an app’s colour scheme, text theme and component themes.
Builds a complete, accessible Material 3 colour scheme from one seed colour and a brightness.
A named job for a colour, such as primary or onSurface; “on” colours are for content drawn on top of their partner.
Tells MaterialApp whether to use the light theme, the dark theme, or follow the system setting.
Theme data for one kind of widget, such as CardThemeData for all cards.
A class you add to ThemeData.extensions to carry custom theme values with copyWith and lerp.

lessons.examTip: If you type Colors.something inside a screen widget, stop and ask which colour role it should be. Hard-coded colours are the number one cause of broken dark mode.

lessons.title: Building reusable custom widgets
lessons.summaryHtml:
Professional Flutter code is built from many small, focused widgets rather than one giant build method. A good custom widget is composed from existing widgets, takes its data through constructor parameters, reports user actions through callbacks, and is const where possible.

  • Prefer composition (a widget that contains others) over inheritance (extending a Flutter widget class).
  • Design the API: required named parameters for essential data, defaults for common options, VoidCallback or ValueChanged<T> for events, and Widget “slots” for flexible content.
  • Extract widgets, not helper methods: a widget class gets its own element, can be const and rebuilds on its own.
  • Keys tell Flutter which widget is which when a list changes, so state stays with the right item.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Flutter’s own widgets, such as Card, ListTile and FilledButton, are general parts. Your app also has its own parts: a destination card, a star rating, a price tag, a section header. Writing these once as custom widgets and reusing them is how real Flutter code stays short, consistent and easy to change.

Think of kitchen appliances. A mixer does one job and has a few clear controls: speed, on and off. You do not rebuild a mixer each time you bake; you plug it in and set the speed. A good custom widget is the same: one job, a small set of clear parameters, and it works wherever you plug it in.

Why it matters

As screens grow, a single build method can reach hundreds of lines. It becomes hard to read, easy to break, and slow, because any setState rebuilds all of it. Copy-pasted UI also drifts: the card on the home screen gets a new corner radius, but the copy on the search screen does not.

Small widgets fix all three problems. Teams also share them: many companies keep an internal widget library so every app looks the same. Interviewers regularly ask you to refactor a messy build method, so this skill shows up in hiring too.

How it works

Composition over inheritance

In Flutter you almost never subclass a framework widget such as ElevatedButton or Card to change it. You write a new StatelessWidget (or StatefulWidget) whose build method combines existing widgets. Widgets are cheap, immutable descriptions, so composing many of them is normal and fast.

Designing the widget’s API

The constructor is the widget’s public API. Design it like any other function:

Parameter kindPatternExample
Essential datarequired this.nameThe destination to show
Common optionA default valuethis.max = 5 stars
Optional dataA nullable fieldfinal String? deal;
Event with no dataVoidCallbackonTap, onRemove
Event with a valueValueChanged<T>ValueChanged<int> onChanged
Flexible contentA Widget slotWidget? trailing, Widget child

Use named parameters, mark fields final, pass super.key, and make the constructor const. Then callers can write const DestinationCard(...) and Flutter can skip rebuilding it entirely. Read colours and text styles from Theme.of(context) inside the widget instead of asking for them as parameters, so the widget follows the app theme automatically.

Screen 1: One widget, many uses lib/widgets/destination_card.dart

class DestinationCard extends StatelessWidget {
  const DestinationCard({
    super.key,
    required this.name,
    required this.place,
    this.icon = Icons.place,
    this.onTap,
    this.trailing,
  });

  final String name;
  final String place;
  final IconData icon;
  final VoidCallback? onTap;
  final Widget? trailing; // a slot the caller fills

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final scheme = Theme.of(context).colorScheme;
    return Card(
      child: ListTile(
        onTap: onTap,
        leading: CircleAvatar(
          backgroundColor: scheme.primaryContainer,
          child: Icon(icon, color: scheme.onPrimaryContainer),
        ),
        title: Text(name),
        subtitle: Text(place),
        trailing: trailing,
      ),
    );
  }
}

// Usage: three looks, one widget.
final cards = [
  DestinationCard(
    name: 'Munnar', place: 'Kerala · Mountains', icon: Icons.landscape,
    onTap: () {},
    trailing: const Icon(Icons.favorite),
  ),
  const DestinationCard(
    name: 'Goa', place: 'India · Beach', icon: Icons.beach_access,
    trailing: Text('₹3,500'),
  ),
  const DestinationCard(name: 'Dubai', place: 'UAE · City'),
];

DestinationCard is written once. The caller decides the data, what happens on tap, and what goes in the trailing slot: a heart, a price or nothing.

Callbacks and controlled widgets

A reusable widget should not decide what happens in the app. A heart button does not know about your favourites list; it just says “I was tapped”. That is what callbacks are for. The parent passes a function, and the widget calls it.

A controlled widget goes further: it receives its current value and never stores it. The parent keeps the value in state and passes it back down. Flutter’s own Checkbox, Switch and Slider work this way. Controlled widgets are easy to test, and the value can live anywhere: a State, a Provider, or a Cubit later in the course. A handy convention: when the callback is null, the widget is read-only or disabled, just like a button with onPressed: null.

Screen 2: A controlled StarRating lib/widgets/star_rating.dart

class StarRating extends StatelessWidget {
  const StarRating({
    super.key,
    required this.value,
    this.max = 5,
    this.onChanged,
  });

  final int value;
  final int max;
  final ValueChanged<int>? onChanged; // null means read-only

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final color = Theme.of(context).colorScheme.primary;
    return Row(
      mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
      children: [
        for (var i = 1; i <= max; i++)
          IconButton(
            onPressed: onChanged == null ? null : () => onChanged!(i),
            icon: Icon(i <= value ? Icons.star : Icons.star_border,
                color: color),
          ),
      ],
    );
  }
}

// In the parent State:
// int _rating = 3;
// StarRating(value: _rating,
//     onChanged: (v) => setState(() => _rating = v)),
// Text('$_rating of 5'),

StarRating owns no state: it draws the value it is given and calls onChanged with the tapped star. The parent stores the rating and rebuilds it. States: Value 3 → Tapped star 5.

Widgets versus helper methods

Helper method Widget _buildCard()Widget class DestinationCard
Own element and BuildContextNo, it uses the parent’sYes
Can be constNoYes
RebuildsEvery time the parent rebuildsOnly when needed
Reusable in other filesOnly by copyingYes, just import it
Shows in the DevTools widget treeNoYes, by name

Methods are fine for tiny private pieces that never need their own context. As a default, extract a widget.

Keys: identity for widgets

When a list changes, Flutter compares the new widgets with the old elements. Without keys it matches them by position and type. That is fine for stateless widgets, but a stateful widget’s State lives in the element. Remove the first item and the first element is reused for what is now the first widget, so its state (a tick, typed text, an animation) appears on the wrong item.

  • ValueKey(item.id): the usual choice, based on a stable, unique value.
  • ObjectKey(item): identity of an object when there is no id.
  • UniqueKey(): a new identity every build, which forces a fresh state; use rarely.
  • GlobalKey: unique across the whole app and gives access to a widget’s state, such as GlobalKey<FormState> in forms. It is expensive, so do not use it just to fix lists.

Screen 3: Why keys matter lib/packing_list.dart

class PackingList extends StatefulWidget {
  const PackingList({super.key});

  @override
  State<PackingList> createState() => _PackingListState();
}

class _PackingListState extends State<PackingList> {
  final _items = ['Passport', 'Tickets', 'Charger'];

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Column(
      children: [
        for (final item in _items)
          PackingTile(
            key: ValueKey(item), // remove this line to see the bug
            label: item,
            onRemove: () => setState(() => _items.remove(item)),
          ),
      ],
    );
  }
}

class PackingTile extends StatefulWidget {
  const PackingTile({super.key, required this.label, required this.onRemove});
  final String label;
  final VoidCallback onRemove;

  @override
  State<PackingTile> createState() => _PackingTileState();
}

class _PackingTileState extends State<PackingTile> {
  bool _packed = false;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return ListTile(
      leading: Checkbox(
        value: _packed,
        onChanged: (v) => setState(() => _packed = v ?? false),
      ),
      title: Text(widget.label),
      trailing: IconButton(
          icon: const Icon(Icons.close), onPressed: widget.onRemove),
    );
  }
}

Each PackingTile keeps its own “packed” state. Remove Passport without keys and its tick moves to Tickets; with ValueKey(item) the state follows the right item. States: Start → Removed, no keys → Removed, with keys.

Example: refactoring Travel Explorer

The starter home screen is one long build with _buildCard and _buildHeader helpers. The refactor:

  1. SectionHeader: const SectionHeader({super.key, required this.title, this.actionLabel, this.onAction}). It shows a TextButton only when both action fields are given.
  2. DestinationCard: takes a Destination, an optional onTap and an optional trailing slot, so the explore list shows a heart and the deals list shows a price.
  3. StarRating: controlled, with value, max = 5 and ValueChanged<int>? onChanged. The home state keeps int _rating.
  4. PackingList: adds key: ValueKey(item) to each stateful tile.

Move each widget to its own file, for example lib/widgets/destination_card.dart. In a feature-first project (module 6), widgets used by one feature live in that feature’s folder, and shared ones in a common folder.

Common mistakes

  • Passing BuildContext or whole State objects into widgets. Pass the data and callbacks the widget needs, nothing more.
  • Doing app logic inside a reusable widget. A card that saves to a database cannot be reused. Report events with callbacks instead.
  • Too many parameters. If a widget needs fifteen options, it is probably two widgets. Split it, or use slots.
  • Forgetting const. Add const constructors and use them; the linter will remind you.
  • Using the index as a key. ValueKey(index) changes when items move, so it does not fix the bug. Use a stable id.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Be ready to explain why a widget class beats a helper method: own element, const, targeted rebuilds.
  • Explain keys with a concrete story like the packing list; it shows you understand the element tree from lesson 2.1.
  • Name callback types precisely: VoidCallback, ValueChanged<T>, ValueSetter<T>, or your own typedef when there are several arguments.
  • Reusable widgets are the easiest parts of an app to widget-test. You will test StarRating in lesson 8.3.

terms.definition: Building a widget by combining other widgets inside its build method, instead of subclassing.
A function passed into a widget so it can tell its parent that something happened, such as VoidCallback or ValueChanged<int>.
A Widget parameter (child, leading, trailing) that lets the caller decide part of the content.
A widget that shows a value it receives and reports changes through a callback, without owning the state.
An identity for a widget that Flutter uses to match widgets with existing elements and state when a list changes.
A key based on a value, such as an item id, that stays the same for the same item.

lessons.examTip: In code review, a build method longer than a screen is a smell. Say “let’s extract this into a widget”, and give the new class a name that describes what it shows.

lessons.title: Navigation basics
lessons.summaryHtml:
Apps have many screens. In Flutter each full screen is a route, and a Navigator keeps routes in a stack: push puts a new screen on top, pop removes it and shows the one below.

  • Navigator.of(context).push(MaterialPageRoute(builder: ...)) opens a screen with the platform’s page transition.
  • You pass data forward through the new screen’s constructor, and return data back with Navigator.pop(context, value), which completes the Future that push returned.
  • After an await, check context.mounted (or mounted in a State) before using the context again.
  • pushReplacement and pushAndRemoveUntil change the history; PopScope can block or confirm going back.

You will build the Shop Catalog app: a product list, a product page that returns a quantity, and a cart.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Most apps have more than one screen: a list, a details page, a cart, a checkout. Moving between them is navigation. In Flutter each full screen is a route, and a Navigator manages them.

Picture a stack of plates. The plate on top is the screen you see. Opening a product puts a new plate on top: that is push. Pressing Back takes the top plate off and shows the one underneath: that is pop. You never lose the plates below; the catalog is still there, scrolled to the same place, when you come back.

MaterialApp creates a Navigator for you, and its home is the first route on the stack.

Why it matters

Almost every client project needs a list-to-detail flow, a form that returns a value, a login that should not be reachable with Back, or a checkout that asks before throwing away input. Getting navigation wrong produces real bugs: duplicate screens, a Back button that returns to the login page, crashes when a SnackBar is shown on a screen that has already closed. This lesson uses the imperative Navigator API, which is simple and still widely used. The next lesson adds declarative routing with go_router for deep links and larger apps.

How it works

Push and pop

Navigator.of(context).push(
  MaterialPageRoute(builder: (context) => ProductPage(product: p)),
);

// Later, inside ProductPage:
Navigator.of(context).pop();

MaterialPageRoute builds the page lazily with its builder and animates it in using the platform’s standard transition. It also tells the new page’s AppBar that there is a route below, so the AppBar shows a back arrow automatically. Set fullscreenDialog: true for a task screen such as “New address”, which gets a close button instead.

Screen 1: Push a product page lib/main.dart

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

class Product {
  const Product(this.name, this.price, this.icon);
  final String name;
  final int price;
  final IconData icon;
  String get priceLabel => '₹$price';
}

const products = [
  Product('Headphones', 1999, Icons.headphones),
  Product('Smart watch', 4499, Icons.watch),
  Product('Backpack', 1299, Icons.backpack),
];

void main() => runApp(MaterialApp(
      theme: ThemeData(colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Colors.deepPurple)),
      home: const CatalogPage(),
    ));

class CatalogPage extends StatelessWidget {
  const CatalogPage({super.key});
  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Shop')),
      body: ListView(
        children: [
          for (final p in products)
            ListTile(
              leading: Icon(p.icon),
              title: Text(p.name),
              subtitle: Text(p.priceLabel),
              trailing: const Icon(Icons.chevron_right),
              onTap: () => Navigator.of(context).push(MaterialPageRoute(
                  builder: (context) => ProductPage(product: p))),
            ),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}

class ProductPage extends StatelessWidget {
  const ProductPage({super.key, required this.product});
  final Product product;
  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: Text(product.name)),
      body: Center(
        child: Column(mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min, spacing: 12, children: [
          Icon(product.icon, size: 96),
          Text(product.priceLabel, style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.headlineMedium),
          FilledButton(onPressed: () => Navigator.of(context).pop(),
              child: const Text('Back to shop')),
        ]),
      ),
    );
  }
}

Tapping a row pushes ProductPage on top of the catalog. The AppBar adds a back arrow automatically because there is a route below. States: Catalog → After push.

Passing data forward

The new screen is just a widget, so it receives data through its constructor, like any other widget: ProductPage(product: p). Pass the object or its id; avoid global variables for this, because they make screens depend on hidden state and break when two screens are open at once.

Returning data back

push returns a Future that completes when the pushed route is popped. Whatever you pass to pop becomes the Future’s value. Give push a type so the result is checked: push<int>(...) returns Future<int?>. It is nullable because the user can always leave with Back, which pops with no result.

After the await, the original screen may be gone (the user might have navigated away). Before you use context again, check context.mounted, or mounted inside a State. The Dart analyzer warns about this with the use_build_context_synchronously lint.

Screen 2: Return a result with pop lib/catalog_page.dart

// In CatalogPage (a StatelessWidget): open and wait for a result.
Future<void> openProduct(BuildContext context, Product product) async {
  final qty = await Navigator.of(context).push<int>(
    MaterialPageRoute(builder: (context) => ProductPage(product: product)),
  );
  if (!context.mounted || qty == null) return; // Back pressed: null
  final name = product.name;
  ScaffoldMessenger.of(context).showSnackBar(
    SnackBar(content: Text('Added $qty × $name')),
  );
}

class ProductPage extends StatefulWidget {
  const ProductPage({super.key, required this.product});
  final Product product;

  @override
  State<ProductPage> createState() => _ProductPageState();
}

class _ProductPageState extends State<ProductPage> {
  int _qty = 1;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: Text(widget.product.name)),
      body: Center(
        child: Column(mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min, spacing: 12, children: [
          Icon(widget.product.icon, size: 96),
          Row(mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min, children: [
            IconButton.outlined(
              onPressed: _qty > 1 ? () => setState(() => _qty--) : null,
              icon: const Icon(Icons.remove),
            ),
            Text('  $_qty  ', style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleLarge),
            IconButton.outlined(
              onPressed: () => setState(() => _qty++),
              icon: const Icon(Icons.add),
            ),
          ]),
          FilledButton.icon(
            onPressed: () => Navigator.of(context).pop(_qty),
            icon: const Icon(Icons.add_shopping_cart),
            label: const Text('Add to cart'),
          ),
        ]),
      ),
    );
  }
}

push returns a Future. ProductPage pops with the chosen quantity, the catalog awaits it, checks context.mounted and shows a SnackBar. States: Pick quantity → Back with result.

Changing the history

MethodWhat it doesTypical use
pushAdds a route on topList to details
pop(result)Removes the top route, optionally with a resultBack, Save, Cancel
maybePopPops only if allowed (respects PopScope)Custom back buttons
canPopTells whether there is a route to go back toShowing or hiding a close button
pushReplacementReplaces the current routeLogin to home, splash to home
pushAndRemoveUntilPushes, then removes routes below until a condition is trueAfter logout, or “order placed” back to a clean home
popUntilPops until a condition is trueClose a multi-step flow: popUntil((route) => route.isFirst)

Blocking Back with PopScope

Users go back with the AppBar arrow, the Android back button or gesture, and the iOS swipe. To protect unsaved input, wrap the page in PopScope. Set canPop to false while there are unsaved changes. When the user tries to leave, onPopInvokedWithResult(didPop, result) is called with didPop == false; show a dialog and call Navigator.pop yourself if they confirm. PopScope replaces the deprecated WillPopScope, which does not work well with Android’s predictive back gesture.

Screen 3: Confirm before leaving with PopScope lib/cart_page.dart

class _CartPageState extends State<CartPage> {
  final _note = TextEditingController();

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _note.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }

  Future<bool> _confirmDiscard() async {
    final leave = await showDialog<bool>(
      context: context,
      builder: (context) => AlertDialog(
        title: const Text('Discard your note?'),
        content: const Text('Your delivery note will be lost.'),
        actions: [
          TextButton(onPressed: () => Navigator.pop(context, false),
              child: const Text('Stay')),
          TextButton(onPressed: () => Navigator.pop(context, true),
              child: const Text('Discard')),
        ],
      ),
    );
    return leave ?? false; // tapping outside the dialog returns null
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return PopScope<bool>(
      canPop: _note.text.isEmpty,
      onPopInvokedWithResult: (didPop, result) async {
        if (didPop) return;
        final leave = await _confirmDiscard();
        if (!leave || !mounted) return;
        Navigator.of(context).pop();
      },
      child: Scaffold(
        appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Cart')),
        body: ListView(padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16), children: [
          const ListTile(title: Text('Headphones'), trailing: Text('2 × ₹1999')),
          TextField(
            controller: _note,
            onChanged: (_) => setState(() {}),
            decoration: const InputDecoration(labelText: 'Delivery note'),
          ),
          const SizedBox(height: 16),
          FilledButton(onPressed: () => Navigator.of(context).pop(true),
              child: const Text('Place order')),
        ]),
      ),
    );
  }
}

While the delivery note has text, canPop is false. The back arrow or gesture calls onPopInvokedWithResult, which asks first and pops only if the user agrees. States: Typing a note → Back pressed.

Watch out: PopScope blocks the back button, the back gesture and maybePop. A direct Navigator.pop in your own code still pops, which is why the Place order button works even when the note has text.

Example: Shop Catalog

The Shop Catalog app has three screens and a small cart kept in the catalog’s state as final _cart = <Product, int>{};.

  1. CatalogPage lists products. Tapping one calls _openProduct, which pushes ProductPage and awaits an int?.
  2. ProductPage has a quantity stepper. Add to cart calls Navigator.of(context).pop(_qty).
  3. Back in the catalog: if (!mounted || qty == null) return; then setState(() => _cart.update(product, (old) => old + qty, ifAbsent: () => qty)); and a SnackBar.
  4. A cart IconButton with a Badge pushes CartPage(cart: _cart) and awaits a bool?. Place order pops with true; the catalog then clears the cart and shows “Order placed”.
  5. CartPage lists lines with a Dart 3 pattern, for (final MapEntry(key: p, value: qty) in cart.entries), and protects its delivery note with PopScope.

Every screen gets its data from its constructor and hands results back through pop. No screen reaches into another one’s state.

Common mistakes

  • “Navigator operation requested with a context that does not include a Navigator.” You used a context from above MaterialApp, for example inside the same build that creates it. Move the screen into its own widget so it gets a context below the Navigator.
  • Using context after await without a mounted check. It can throw or show a SnackBar on the wrong screen.
  • Forgetting that results can be null. Always handle the Back case.
  • Calling push inside build. build can run many times; navigate from event handlers such as onTap, or from a listener.
  • Using WillPopScope or named-route strings everywhere. Use PopScope. Named routes with routes: and pushNamed still exist, but Flutter’s docs recommend against them for most apps; go_router is the modern choice for URL-style routes.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Explain the route stack and how results travel back through the Future returned by push.
  • Know when to use pushReplacement (login) and pushAndRemoveUntil (logout).
  • Mention predictive back on Android and that PopScope supports it.
  • Passing whole objects between screens is fine for small apps. Larger apps pass an id and load data from a repository, which also works with deep links. You will see this with go_router and BLoC.

terms.definition: One screen (or dialog) managed by a Navigator, such as a MaterialPageRoute.
A widget that keeps a stack of routes and shows the top one.
A route that builds a page and animates it in with the platform’s standard transition.
push adds a route on top of the stack and returns a Future; pop removes the top route and can send a result back.
Replaces the current route with a new one, so Back does not return to it.
A widget that can stop the current route from being popped by the back button or gesture, for example to confirm unsaved changes.

lessons.examTip: If a Snackbar or navigation call runs after an await, say “I check context.mounted first” in interviews. Missing that check is one of the most common Flutter bugs.
