lessons.title: Declarative routing with go_router
lessons.summaryHtml: With Navigator.push you move between screens by giving commands. With go_router you describe every screen as a URL path once, in a single GoRouter configuration, and then navigate with context.go('/product/3'). Path parameters such as :id carry data in the URL, so the same location works from a button, a browser address bar or a deep link. StatefulShellRoute keeps a bottom navigation bar on screen with its own history per tab, and a redirect function guards private pages by sending signed-out users to the login screen. You upgrade the Shop Catalog app from lesson 5.1 to use all of this.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

In lesson 5.1 you moved between screens by giving orders: "push this page", "pop that page". That is imperative navigation. It works well for small apps, but the app has no idea what "place" the user is in. There is no address.

go_router gives every screen an address, just like pages on a website. You write the list of addresses once: / is the catalog, /product/3 is the detail page for product 3, /cart is the cart. After that, you navigate by saying where you want to be: context.go('/product/3'). The router works out which screens must be on the stack to show that address. This is declarative routing: you describe the result, not the steps.

Think of a city. Imperative navigation is "turn left, walk two blocks, turn right". Declarative navigation is "take me to 12 Market Street". The second form still works if you start from somewhere else, or if someone texts you the address. A deep link is exactly that: someone sends you an address inside the app.

Why it matters

Real apps need things that plain Navigator.push makes awkward:

  • Deep links. A notification or an email opens /product/3 directly, with a working back button.
  • Flutter web. The browser address bar, refresh and back button must match what the user sees.
  • Auth guards. Private pages must send signed-out users to a login screen, and back again afterwards.
  • Bottom navigation with history. Each tab keeps its own stack, so switching tabs does not lose the page you were on.

The Flutter documentation recommends a Router-based approach for apps that need deep linking, and go_router is the package the Flutter team publishes for this. It sits on top of the low-level Router API so you do not have to write a RouterDelegate yourself. Most job postings that mention Flutter navigation expect you to know it.

How it works

1. Install and connect the router

Add the package with flutter pub add go_router. Create one GoRouter in a top-level variable and pass it to MaterialApp.router. Note the different constructor: you no longer pass home.

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:go_router/go_router.dart';

final router = GoRouter(
  initialLocation: '/',
  routes: [
    GoRoute(path: '/', builder: (context, state) => const CatalogScreen()),
    GoRoute(path: '/cart', builder: (context, state) => const CartScreen()),
  ],
);

void main() => runApp(const ShopApp());

class ShopApp extends StatelessWidget {
  const ShopApp({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MaterialApp.router(
      title: 'Shop Catalog',
      theme: ThemeData(colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Colors.teal)),
      routerConfig: router,
    );
  }
}

Every builder receives a GoRouterState. It tells you the matched location, the full uri, the path parameters and any extra object.

2. go, push and pop

CallWhat happens to the stackUse it when
context.go('/cart')Replaced so it matches the location (parents of a sub-route are rebuilt underneath)Moving to a "place": tabs, menu items, after login
context.push('/cart')New page added on top of the current stackA temporary page you will come back from, often returning a value
context.pop()Top page removed (optionally with a result)Closing a pushed page or a dialog
context.goNamed('product', pathParameters: {...})Same as go, but by route nameYou want to change URLs later without hunting for strings

3. Sub-routes, path and query parameters

A route can have child routes. A child path has no leading slash; it is appended to the parent. Going to /product/3 therefore builds the catalog first and puts the product page on top, so the AppBar shows a back arrow automatically.

GoRoute(
  path: '/',
  builder: (context, state) => const CatalogScreen(),
  routes: [
    GoRoute(
      path: 'product/:id',          // full path: /product/:id
      name: 'product',
      builder: (context, state) {
        final id = int.tryParse(state.pathParameters['id'] ?? '');
        final sort = state.uri.queryParameters['sort']; // /product/3?sort=price
        return ProductScreen(id: id, sort: sort);
      },
    ),
  ],
),

Path parameters are always Strings. Parse them with int.tryParse and handle null, because anybody can type /product/abc. You can also pass any Dart object with extra, but extra is not part of the URL. A deep link or a browser refresh will not bring it back, so use it only as an optimisation, never as the only source of data.

Screen 1: Product page from a path parameter lib/main.dart

// Inside GoRouter(routes: [...]):
GoRoute(
  path: '/',
  builder: (context, state) => const CatalogScreen(),
  routes: [
    GoRoute(
      path: 'product/:id', // no leading slash
      name: 'product',
      builder: (context, state) => ProductScreen(
        id: int.tryParse(state.pathParameters['id'] ?? ''),
      ),
    ),
  ],
),

class ProductScreen extends StatelessWidget {
  const ProductScreen({super.key, required this.id});
  final int? id;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final matches = products.where((p) => p.id == id).toList();
    if (matches.isEmpty) {
      return const NotFoundScreen(message: 'Product not found');
    }
    final p = matches.first;
    final text = Theme.of(context).textTheme;
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: Text(p.name)),
      body: Padding(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
        child: Column(
          crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
          spacing: 12,
          children: [
            Text(p.name, style: text.headlineSmall),
            Text(p.priceLabel, style: text.titleLarge),
            FilledButton.icon(
              onPressed: () => context.go('/cart'),
              icon: const Icon(Icons.add_shopping_cart),
              label: const Text('Add to cart'),
            ),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

The same ProductScreen handles a valid id and an unknown one; switch frames to compare /product/2 and /product/99. States: /product/2 → /product/99.

4. Shell routes: shared UI around pages

A ShellRoute wraps its child routes in a common widget, such as a Scaffold with a NavigationBar. Its builder receives (context, state, child), and child is the inner navigator. The better choice for bottom tabs is StatefulShellRoute.indexedStack. Each StatefulShellBranch gets its own navigator, kept alive in an IndexedStack, so every tab remembers its own history and scroll position.

StatefulShellRoute.indexedStack(
  builder: (context, state, shell) => HomeShell(shell: shell),
  branches: [
    StatefulShellBranch(routes: [catalogRoute]),   // tab 0
    StatefulShellBranch(routes: [cartRoute]),      // tab 1
    StatefulShellBranch(routes: [accountRoute]),   // tab 2
  ],
)

// Inside HomeShell.build:
NavigationBar(
  selectedIndex: shell.currentIndex,
  onDestinationSelected: (i) =>
      shell.goBranch(i, initialLocation: i == shell.currentIndex),
  destinations: const [ /* Shop, Cart, Account */ ],
)

Passing initialLocation: i == shell.currentIndex gives the familiar behaviour: tapping the tab you are already on returns to that tab's first page.

Screen 2: Catalog inside a StatefulShellRoute lib/main.dart

class HomeShell extends StatelessWidget {
  const HomeShell({super.key, required this.shell});
  final StatefulNavigationShell shell;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      body: shell, // the current branch's navigator
      bottomNavigationBar: NavigationBar(
        selectedIndex: shell.currentIndex,
        onDestinationSelected: (i) =>
            shell.goBranch(i, initialLocation: i == shell.currentIndex),
        destinations: const [
          NavigationDestination(icon: Icon(Icons.storefront), label: 'Shop'),
          NavigationDestination(icon: Icon(Icons.shopping_cart), label: 'Cart'),
          NavigationDestination(icon: Icon(Icons.person), label: 'Account'),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}

class CatalogScreen extends StatelessWidget {
  const CatalogScreen({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Shop Catalog')),
      body: ListView.builder(
        itemCount: products.length,
        itemBuilder: (context, i) {
          final p = products[i];
          final id = p.id;
          return ListTile(
            leading: const Icon(Icons.shopping_bag),
            title: Text(p.name),
            subtitle: Text(p.priceLabel),
            trailing: const Icon(Icons.chevron_right),
            onTap: () => context.goNamed('product',
                pathParameters: {'id': '$id'}),
          );
        },
      ),
    );
  }
}

HomeShell draws the NavigationBar once; the body is the current branch’s navigator, so the list and its detail pages keep their own history.

5. Redirects and auth guards

A top-level redirect runs before every navigation. Return a new location to send the user elsewhere, or null to let them through. Pass a Listenable (for example a ChangeNotifier that holds the sign-in flag) as refreshListenable, and the router runs the redirect again whenever it notifies. Signing out then moves the user to the login screen without any extra code.

redirect: (context, state) {
  final loc = state.matchedLocation;
  final atLogin = loc == '/login';
  if (!auth.signedIn && loc.startsWith('/account')) {
    final from = Uri.encodeComponent(loc);
    return '/login?from=$from';
  }
  if (auth.signedIn && atLogin) {
    return state.uri.queryParameters['from'] ?? '/';
  }
  return null; // no change
},
refreshListenable: auth,

Individual GoRoutes can also have their own redirect, which is handy for rules that only apply to one area. A redirect can return a Future too, but keep it fast: it runs on every navigation.

Screen 3: Login guard with redirect lib/main.dart

final auth = AuthState(); // extends ChangeNotifier

final router = GoRouter(
  initialLocation: '/',
  refreshListenable: auth, // re-run redirect on sign in/out
  redirect: (context, state) {
    final loc = state.matchedLocation;
    if (!auth.signedIn && loc.startsWith('/account')) {
      final from = Uri.encodeComponent(loc);
      return '/login?from=$from';
    }
    if (auth.signedIn && loc == '/login') {
      return state.uri.queryParameters['from'] ?? '/';
    }
    return null; // allow navigation
  },
  routes: [ /* /login, then the StatefulShellRoute */ ],
);

class LoginScreen extends StatelessWidget {
  const LoginScreen({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Sign in')),
      body: Center(
        child: Column(
          mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
          spacing: 12,
          children: [
            const Text('Sign in to see your account'),
            FilledButton(
                onPressed: auth.signIn, child: const Text('Sign in')),
            TextButton(
                onPressed: () => context.go('/'),
                child: const Text('Keep browsing')),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

Tapping Account while signed out lands on /login?from=/account; after Sign in, refreshListenable re-runs the redirect and the user arrives on the Account tab. States: Signed out → After Sign in.

6. Errors and deep links

errorBuilder: (context, state) => NotFoundScreen(...) shows your own page for unknown paths instead of the default error screen. On the web, routes work straight away (by default the URL uses a hash, such as /#/product/3). On Android you declare an intent filter for your scheme or domain in AndroidManifest.xml; verified App Links also need an assetlinks.json file on your website. On iOS, universal links need the Associated Domains capability and an apple-app-site-association file. Current Flutter versions hand incoming links to the router by default. You can test on an Android emulator with adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "https://yourdomain.example/product/3" and on an iOS simulator with xcrun simctl openurl booted https://yourdomain.example/product/3.

Example: Shop Catalog with go_router

You take the Shop Catalog from lesson 5.1 and replace every Navigator.push with routes.

  1. Define the table: /login outside the shell, then a StatefulShellRoute.indexedStack with three branches: / (with the sub-route product/:id), /cart and /account.
  2. In the catalog list, each ListTile calls context.goNamed('product', pathParameters: {'id': '$id'}), where id is a local variable holding the product id.
  3. ProductScreen receives int? id. If no product matches, it shows "Product not found" instead of crashing.
  4. An AuthState extends ChangeNotifier holds signedIn. The redirect protects /account and remembers where the user wanted to go in ?from=.
  5. Tapping Sign out calls auth.signOut(). Because the router listens to auth, the user lands on /login at once.
  6. Run it on Chrome and type /#/product/3 in the address bar: the detail page opens with a back arrow to the catalog. Type /#/product/99: you see the not-found message.

Common mistakes

  • Creating the GoRouter inside build(). Every rebuild makes a new router, which resets navigation. Keep it in a top-level final, a State field, or a provider.
  • Leading slash on a sub-route. Child paths are relative: write 'product/:id', not '/product/:id'. go_router rejects the slash.
  • Redirect loops. If the redirect sends signed-out users to /login but does not allow /login itself, it keeps redirecting forever. Always return null when the user is already where they should be.
  • Relying on extra. It vanishes on a deep link or web refresh. Put ids in the path and load the data from them.
  • Mixing Navigator.push with go_router. Pages pushed directly on the Navigator are not part of the router's location, so the URL and back button get out of sync. Use context.push instead.
  • Using go when you meant push. After go to a top-level route, the back button may leave the app because the old stack is gone.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Be ready to explain imperative vs declarative navigation and the difference between go and push in one sentence each.
  • "How do you protect routes?" Answer: a top-level redirect that reads auth state, plus refreshListenable so sign-in and sign-out re-run it. With BLoC you can wrap the auth bloc's stream in a small ChangeNotifier for this.
  • "How do you keep tab state?" Answer: StatefulShellRoute.indexedStack, one branch per tab.
  • Teams usually keep route paths as constants or use named routes, and put the router in its own file such as lib/app/router.dart.
  • Turn on debugLogDiagnostics: true while developing: go_router then logs every navigation and redirect, which makes loops easy to spot.

go replaces the stack so it matches the new location; push adds a page on top of the current stack.
A route that wraps its branches in shared UI (like a NavigationBar) and keeps a separate navigation stack for each branch.
A function that runs before navigation and returns a new location (or null to allow it); used for login guards.

lessons.examTip: In interviews, say you keep the GoRouter in one top-level variable (or a provider), never inside build(), and that anything a deep link needs must live in the path or query string, not in extra.

lessons.title: Forms and validation
lessons.summaryHtml: A Form groups input fields so you can check them all at once. Each TextFormField has a validator that returns an error message or null, and a GlobalKey<FormState> lets you call validate(), save() and reset() on the whole form. A TextEditingController reads and changes a field’s text, and a FocusNode moves the cursor between fields. Good forms also pick the right keyboardType, textInputAction and input formatters, validate at the right moment with AutovalidateMode, and show a loading state while submitting. You build an Event Registration app for a meetup.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A form in an app works like a paper form at a reception desk. There are boxes to fill in, some rules for each box ("phone number must have 10 digits"), and one moment when the clerk checks the whole sheet. If a box is wrong, the clerk points at it and says what to fix.

In Flutter, the Form widget is the sheet. Each TextFormField is a box that knows its own rule, called a validator. When the user taps Register, you ask the form to check every box at once with validate(). Fields with a problem show their message in red underneath.

Why it matters

Almost every real app has forms: sign up, login, checkout, profile, booking. Forms are where users feel friction, and where bad data enters your system. A good form:

  • stops bad data early (an email with no domain never reaches your server),
  • shows clear, specific messages at the right moment, not while the user is still typing their first letter,
  • opens the right keyboard (numbers for a phone, @ for email) and moves smoothly from field to field,
  • cannot be submitted twice by an impatient double tap.

Client-side validation is for user experience. Your backend must still validate everything, because anyone can call an API without your app.

How it works

1. Form, GlobalKey and validate()

A Form needs a key so you can reach its FormState from a button. Create the key once as a field of your State, never inside build().

class _RegistrationPageState extends State<RegistrationPage> {
  final _formKey = GlobalKey<FormState>();

  void _submit() {
    final form = _formKey.currentState!;
    if (!form.validate()) return; // shows errors, returns false
    form.save();                  // calls every onSaved
    // send the data...
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Form(
      key: _formKey,
      child: Column(children: [
        TextFormField(
          decoration: const InputDecoration(labelText: 'Full name'),
          validator: (value) =>
              (value == null || value.trim().isEmpty) ? 'Enter your name' : null,
        ),
        FilledButton(onPressed: _submit, child: const Text('Register')),
      ]),
    );
  }
}

The rule is simple: a validator returns null when the value is fine, and a message when it is not. validate() runs every validator in the form, redraws the fields with their errors, and returns true only if all of them returned null.

2. Getting the values: controllers or onSaved

There are two common ways to read what the user typed:

ApproachHowBest for
TextEditingControllerPass controller:; read controller.text, set it, clear() it, or listen to changesFields you also change from code, live character counts, search boxes
onSavedonSaved: (v) => _email = v!, then call form.save() after validate()Simple "fill in and submit" forms
initialValueStarting text without a controllerEdit screens that load an existing value once

You cannot pass both controller and initialValue; set controller.text instead. A controller holds resources, so create it once and call dispose() on it in your State’s dispose() method.

3. Keyboards, actions and formatters

Small details make forms feel professional:

  • keyboardType chooses the on-screen keyboard: TextInputType.emailAddress, .phone, .number, .url, .multiline.
  • textInputAction sets the action key. TextInputAction.next moves focus to the next field in reading order; .done closes the keyboard. Use onFieldSubmitted to submit from the last field.
  • inputFormatters (from package:flutter/services.dart) block bad characters as they are typed: FilteringTextInputFormatter.digitsOnly and LengthLimitingTextInputFormatter(10). The keyboard type alone does not stop pasted letters.
  • obscureText: true for passwords, textCapitalization: TextCapitalization.words for names, and autofillHints so the system can suggest saved emails and addresses.

Screen 1: Registration form lib/main.dart

Form(
  key: _formKey,
  autovalidateMode: _autovalidate,
  child: SingleChildScrollView(
    padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
    child: Column(
      crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.stretch,
      spacing: 16,
      children: [
        TextFormField(
          controller: _name,
          focusNode: _nameFocus,
          decoration: const InputDecoration(
              labelText: 'Full name', prefixIcon: Icon(Icons.person)),
          textCapitalization: TextCapitalization.words,
          textInputAction: TextInputAction.next,
          validator: validateName,
        ),
        TextFormField(
          controller: _email,
          decoration: const InputDecoration(
              labelText: 'Email', prefixIcon: Icon(Icons.email)),
          keyboardType: TextInputType.emailAddress,
          textInputAction: TextInputAction.next,
          autofillHints: const [AutofillHints.email],
          validator: validateEmail,
        ),
        TextFormField(
          controller: _phone,
          decoration: const InputDecoration(
              labelText: 'Phone', prefixIcon: Icon(Icons.phone)),
          keyboardType: TextInputType.phone,
          textInputAction: TextInputAction.done,
          inputFormatters: [
            FilteringTextInputFormatter.digitsOnly,
            LengthLimitingTextInputFormatter(10),
          ],
          validator: validatePhone,
          onFieldSubmitted: (_) => _submit(),
        ),
        DropdownButtonFormField<TicketType>(
          initialValue: TicketType.standard,
          decoration: const InputDecoration(labelText: 'Ticket type',
              prefixIcon: Icon(Icons.confirmation_number)),
          items: [
            for (final t in TicketType.values)
              DropdownMenuItem(value: t, child: Text(t.label)),
          ],
          onChanged: (t) => _ticket = t ?? TicketType.standard,
        ),
        termsField, // FormField<bool> with a CheckboxListTile
        FilledButton(onPressed: _submit, child: const Text('Register')),
      ],
    ),
  ),
)

Outlined fields come from inputDecorationTheme; the dropdown and checkbox take part in the same Form as the text fields.

4. FocusNode

A FocusNode represents keyboard focus for one field. Pass it with focusNode:, then call requestFocus() to put the cursor there from code, or FocusScope.of(context).unfocus() to hide the keyboard. In the example, after a successful registration the cursor jumps back to Full name so the desk can register the next person. Like controllers, focus nodes must be disposed.

5. When to validate: AutovalidateMode

ModeBehaviour
disabled (default)Only when you call validate()
onUserInteractionAfter the user changes a field, on every change
onUnfocusWhen the user leaves a field
alwaysImmediately, even before any typing (usually too noisy)

A friendly pattern: keep the mode in a state variable, start with disabled, and switch to onUserInteraction after the first failed submit. Users are not shouted at on an empty form, but once they have seen the errors, each one disappears as soon as it is fixed.

Screen 2: Validation from empty to valid lib/main.dart

String? validateName(String? value) {
  final v = value?.trim() ?? '';
  if (v.isEmpty) return 'Enter your name';
  return null; // null means valid
}

final _emailPattern = RegExp(r'^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$');
String? validateEmail(String? value) {
  final v = value?.trim() ?? '';
  if (v.isEmpty) return 'Enter your email';
  if (!_emailPattern.hasMatch(v)) return 'Enter a valid email';
  return null;
}

String? validatePhone(String? value) =>
    (value ?? '').length == 10 ? null : 'Enter a 10-digit phone number';

Future<void> _submit() async {
  FocusScope.of(context).unfocus();
  if (!_formKey.currentState!.validate()) {
    setState(() => _autovalidate = AutovalidateMode.onUserInteraction);
    return;
  }
  setState(() => _submitting = true);
  await Future<void>.delayed(const Duration(seconds: 1));
  if (!mounted) return;
  setState(() => _submitting = false);
  // ...show the confirmation dialog
}

// The button:
FilledButton(
  onPressed: _submitting ? null : _submit, // null disables it
  child: _submitting
      ? const SizedBox.square(
          dimension: 20, child: CircularProgressIndicator(strokeWidth: 2))
      : const Text('Register'),
)

The first Register tap shows every error; after that, onUserInteraction re-checks each field as you type, and the button shows a spinner while the request runs. States: Tapped Register → Fixing → Submitting.

6. Fields that are not text

DropdownButtonFormField is a form-aware dropdown; give it initialValue, items and onChanged, and it can have a validator too. For a checkbox, wrap it in a FormField<bool>: its builder gets a FormFieldState with value, didChange(), hasError and errorText, so any widget can join the form.

FormField<bool>(
  initialValue: false,
  validator: (v) => v == true ? null : 'Please accept the code of conduct',
  builder: (field) => Column(
    crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
    children: [
      CheckboxListTile(
        value: field.value ?? false,
        onChanged: field.didChange,
        title: const Text('I accept the code of conduct'),
        controlAffinity: ListTileControlAffinity.leading,
      ),
      if (field.hasError)
        Text(field.errorText ?? '', style: TextStyle(color: errorColor)),
    ],
  ),
)

7. Submitting safely

Real submits are asynchronous. Set a _submitting flag, pass onPressed: null while it is true (this disables the button and prevents double submits), and show a small progress indicator. After every await, check if (!mounted) return; before using context or calling setState, because the user may have left the screen.

Screen 3: Confirmation dialog lib/main.dart

final name = _name.text.trim();
final ticket = _ticket.label;
await showDialog<void>(
  context: context,
  builder: (context) => AlertDialog(
    icon: const Icon(Icons.celebration),
    title: const Text('You are in!'),
    content: Text('$name · $ticket ticket'),
    actions: [
      TextButton(
        onPressed: () => Navigator.pop(context),
        child: const Text('Done'),
      ),
    ],
  ),
);
if (!mounted) return;
_name.clear();
_email.clear();
_phone.clear();
_formKey.currentState!.reset(); // dropdown and checkbox
setState(() {
  _ticket = TicketType.standard;
  _autovalidate = AutovalidateMode.disabled;
});
_nameFocus.requestFocus(); // ready for the next attendee

showDialog with a builder returns a Future; after it completes, the form is cleared and focus returns to Full name for the next attendee.

Example: Event Registration app

The registration desk at "Flutter Meetup Kochi" needs a fast form.

  1. Fields: Full name, Email, Phone, Ticket type (Standard, Student, VIP from an enhanced enum) and a code-of-conduct checkbox.
  2. Validators are top-level functions: validateName, validateEmail (a simple pattern, not a perfect one) and validatePhone (exactly 10 digits). A test file checks them with flutter test.
  3. The phone field uses the phone keyboard, digits-only and a 10-character limit, and submits on the Done key.
  4. _submit() hides the keyboard, validates, switches autovalidate on after a failure, shows a spinner for one second (a stand-in for a network call), then shows a dialog: "Asha Nair · Student ticket".
  5. After Done, it clears the controllers, calls reset() for the dropdown and checkbox, and focuses Full name again.

Common mistakes

  • Returning '' for "valid". Any non-null string is an error, even an empty one. Return null.
  • Creating the GlobalKey or controllers inside build(). They are recreated on each rebuild, so the form loses its state and the text disappears.
  • Forgetting dispose() for controllers and focus nodes, which leaks memory and listeners.
  • Using TextField inside a Form and wondering why validate() ignores it. Only FormField widgets such as TextFormField take part.
  • Not trimming. " " passes an isEmpty check. Trim before checking and before saving.
  • Over-strict email patterns that reject valid addresses. Check the basic shape and let the server confirm by sending an email.
  • Using context after await without checking mounted.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Expect "controller vs onSaved vs onChanged": controllers when code needs to read or change the text at any time, onSaved for a one-time collection after validation, onChanged for live reactions such as search.
  • Explain why validators should be pure functions: they are reusable, and you can unit test them in milliseconds.
  • With BLoC (module 6), the form widget still owns controllers and focus, while the Cubit or Bloc holds the submit status (idle, submitting, success, failure) and the result of the server call.
  • Mention accessibility: labels (not only hints) are read by screen readers, and error messages should say how to fix the problem.
  • Keyboards can cover fields: put the form in a scrolling widget. Scaffold resizes its body for the keyboard by default.

terms.definition: A widget that groups FormFields so they can be validated, saved and reset together through its FormState.
A key that gives you the FormState of a Form, so you can call validate(), save() and reset().
A function that receives the field value and returns an error message, or null when the value is valid.
An object that holds a text field’s current text and selection; you read, set, clear and dispose it.
An object that represents keyboard focus for one field; you can request focus, listen to it and must dispose it.
Decides when fields re-validate on their own: disabled, always, onUserInteraction or onUnfocus.

lessons.examTip: Keep validators as top-level or static functions that take a String? and return a String?. They are then reusable across screens and you can unit test them without building any widgets.

quiz.question: A validator returns an empty string '' when the value is fine. What happens when the form is validated?
options: The field is treated as valid because the message is empty
The validator is ignored
Flutter throws an exception
The field counts as invalid, because any non-null return value is an error
quiz.explanation: Only null means valid. Any String, even an empty one, marks the field invalid, so validate() returns false.

quiz.question: You want errors to stay hidden until the user first presses Register, and then update live while they fix each field. What is the cleanest approach?
options: Start with AutovalidateMode.disabled and switch the Form to onUserInteraction after the first failed validate()
Call validate() inside every onChanged callback
Set AutovalidateMode.always on the Form from the start
Use TextField instead of TextFormField
quiz.explanation: Keeping the mode in state and changing it after the first failed submit gives quiet first contact and live feedback afterwards.

quiz.question: Which object should a StatefulWidget create once in its State and dispose in dispose()?
options: An InputDecoration
A validator function
A TextEditingController
A TextInputType
quiz.explanation: Controllers and FocusNodes hold resources and listeners. Create them once as State fields and dispose them; the others are plain values.

quiz.question: A phone field must accept only digits and at most 10 of them. Which combination is correct?
options: keyboardType: TextInputType.phone alone
keyboardType: TextInputType.phone plus inputFormatters with FilteringTextInputFormatter.digitsOnly and LengthLimitingTextInputFormatter(10)
A validator that deletes letters
obscureText: true and maxLines: 1
quiz.explanation: keyboardType only chooses which keyboard appears; users can still paste letters. Formatters actually block the input, and a validator still checks the final length.

lessons.title: Tabs, drawers and bottom navigation
lessons.summaryHtml: Apps organise their screens with three common patterns. Tabs (TabBar plus TabBarView) switch between related views of one topic. A drawer slides in from the side and holds many or less-used destinations. A NavigationBar at the bottom gives quick access to three to five top-level destinations. DefaultTabController links tabs and pages for you; a TabController gives you full control. Wrapping the destinations in an IndexedStack keeps each one alive, so switching away and back does not lose its state. You build the navigation shell of a Meetup Hub app.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Once an app has more than a couple of screens, users need a map. Material Design offers three main navigation patterns, and each one answers a different question:

  • Tabs are like the dividers in a folder. Everything is about one topic (events), split into related views (upcoming, past, saved). You can swipe between them.
  • A bottom navigation bar is like the floors of a building. Each destination is a separate area of the app, and you jump between them all the time.
  • A drawer is like a cupboard. It holds many items or things you use rarely, hidden until you open it.

Most real apps combine them: a NavigationBar for the main areas, tabs inside one of those areas, and a drawer for account, settings and help.

Why it matters

Navigation decides whether users feel lost. A bottom bar with eight items is cramped; a drawer for something used every minute hides it behind an extra tap. There is also a technical side: when users switch destinations, they expect to find each place exactly as they left it, with the same tab selected, the same scroll position and the same half-filled form. Doing that correctly is a classic junior interview topic and a common source of bugs.

How it works

1. Tabs with DefaultTabController

A TabBar (the row of tabs) and a TabBarView (the swipeable pages) need a shared TabController. The easiest way is DefaultTabController, an inherited widget that creates one for everything below it.

DefaultTabController(
  length: 3, // must equal the number of tabs AND pages
  child: Scaffold(
    appBar: AppBar(
      title: const Text('Events'),
      bottom: const TabBar(tabs: [
        Tab(text: 'Upcoming'),
        Tab(text: 'Past'),
        Tab(icon: Icon(Icons.bookmark), text: 'Saved'),
      ]),
    ),
    body: const TabBarView(children: [
      UpcomingList(),
      PastList(),
      SavedList(),
    ]),
  ),
)

AppBar.bottom is the usual place for a TabBar. For many tabs, set isScrollable: true. Material 3 also has TabBar.secondary for a second level of tabs inside content.

2. When you need a TabController yourself

If you must read the current index, listen to changes or switch tabs from code, create the controller in a State that mixes in SingleTickerProviderStateMixin (the controller animates, so it needs a ticker).

class _EventsPageState extends State<EventsPage>
    with SingleTickerProviderStateMixin {
  late final TabController _tabs = TabController(length: 3, vsync: this);

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    _tabs.addListener(() {
      if (!_tabs.indexIsChanging) debugPrint('Now on tab ' + _tabs.index.toString());
    });
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _tabs.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }

  void showSaved() => _tabs.animateTo(2);
  // Pass controller: _tabs to both the TabBar and the TabBarView.
}

Screen 1: Tabs on the Events destination lib/main.dart

DefaultTabController(
  length: 3,
  child: Scaffold(
    appBar: AppBar(
      title: Text(_titles[_index]),
      bottom: _index == 0
          ? const TabBar(tabs: [
              Tab(text: 'Upcoming'),
              Tab(text: 'Past'),
              Tab(text: 'Saved'),
            ])
          : null,
    ),
    drawer: AppDrawer(onSelect: _select),
    body: IndexedStack(
      index: _index,
      children: const [EventsPage(), TicketsPage(), ProfilePage()],
    ),
    bottomNavigationBar: NavigationBar(/* Events, Tickets, Profile */),
  ),
)

class EventsPage extends StatelessWidget {
  const EventsPage({super.key});
  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final saved = upcoming.where((m) => m.saved).toList();
    return TabBarView(children: [
      EventList(key: const PageStorageKey('upcoming'), items: upcoming),
      EventList(key: const PageStorageKey('past'), items: past),
      EventList(key: const PageStorageKey('saved'), items: saved),
    ]);
  }
}

// EventList: ListView.builder of ListTiles with a CircleAvatar,
// the title, the date and a bookmark icon.

The TabBar sits in AppBar.bottom and shares the DefaultTabController with the TabBarView; switch frames to see the Saved tab. States: Upcoming → Saved.

3. Drawers

Give a Scaffold a drawer: (left side) or endDrawer: (right side). The AppBar adds a menu button automatically, and users can also swipe from the edge. The usual content is a ListView with padding: EdgeInsets.zero, a header such as UserAccountsDrawerHeader, and ListTiles. An open drawer adds an entry to the current route’s history, so Navigator.pop(context) closes it; do that before you change screens. Material 3 also offers NavigationDrawer with NavigationDrawerDestinations and a selectedIndex, which highlights the current item for you.

To open a drawer from your own button, call Scaffold.of(context).openDrawer(). The context must be below the Scaffold: use a Builder, a separate widget, or a GlobalKey<ScaffoldState>.

Screen 2: Drawer with account header lib/main.dart

class AppDrawer extends StatelessWidget {
  const AppDrawer({super.key, required this.onSelect});
  final ValueChanged<int> onSelect;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    void go(int i) {
      Navigator.pop(context); // close the drawer first
      onSelect(i);
    }

    return Drawer(
      child: ListView(
        padding: EdgeInsets.zero,
        children: [
          const UserAccountsDrawerHeader(
            accountName: Text('Asha Nair'),
            accountEmail: Text('asha@example.com'),
            currentAccountPicture: CircleAvatar(child: Text('AN')),
          ),
          ListTile(
              leading: const Icon(Icons.event),
              title: const Text('Events'),
              onTap: () => go(0)),
          ListTile(
              leading: const Icon(Icons.confirmation_number),
              title: const Text('My tickets'),
              onTap: () => go(1)),
          const Divider(),
          ListTile(
            leading: const Icon(Icons.info_outline),
            title: const Text('About'),
            onTap: () {
              Navigator.pop(context);
              showAboutDialog(
                  context: context,
                  applicationName: 'Meetup Hub',
                  applicationVersion: '1.0.0');
            },
          ),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}

Each item closes the drawer with Navigator.pop before switching destination; About uses the built-in showAboutDialog.

4. NavigationBar

NavigationBar is the Material 3 bottom bar. It does not switch pages by itself: you keep the selected index in state and rebuild.

  • selectedIndex and onDestinationSelected connect it to your state.
  • Each NavigationDestination has an icon, an optional selectedIcon (outlined vs filled is the M3 convention) and a label.
  • Wrap an icon in a Badge to show a count, such as unread messages.
  • Use it for three to five destinations. On wide screens, switch to NavigationRail (lesson 3.5). The older BottomNavigationBar still works, but NavigationBar is the M3 component.

5. Keeping state: IndexedStack

BodyWhat happens on switchTrade-off
pages[_index]The old page is disposed; the new one is built from scratchLower memory, but scroll, form input and tab selection are lost
IndexedStack(index: _index, children: pages)All pages stay mounted; only the selected one is visibleState survives; every page is built at start and kept in memory

Inside a TabBarView, pages that scroll off screen are disposed. Give each scrollable a PageStorageKey to restore its scroll offset, or mix AutomaticKeepAliveClientMixin into the page’s State (return true from wantKeepAlive and call super.build(context)) to keep it fully alive. With go_router, StatefulShellRoute.indexedStack from lesson 5.2 gives you the same behaviour plus URLs.

Screen 3: NavigationBar with IndexedStack lib/main.dart

NavigationBar(
  selectedIndex: _index,
  onDestinationSelected: _select, // setState(() => _index = i)
  destinations: const [
    NavigationDestination(
        icon: Icon(Icons.event_outlined),
        selectedIcon: Icon(Icons.event),
        label: 'Events'),
    NavigationDestination(
        icon: Icon(Icons.confirmation_number_outlined),
        selectedIcon: Icon(Icons.confirmation_number),
        label: 'Tickets'),
    NavigationDestination(
        icon: Icon(Icons.person_outline),
        selectedIcon: Icon(Icons.person),
        label: 'Profile'),
  ],
)

// Keeps every page mounted:
body: IndexedStack(
  index: _index,
  children: const [EventsPage(), TicketsPage(), ProfilePage()],
),
// Rebuilds the page from scratch each time (state lost):
// body: const [EventsPage(), TicketsPage(), ProfilePage()][_index],

class _ProfilePageState extends State<ProfilePage> {
  bool _reminders = false;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return ListView(children: [
      const ListTile(
          leading: CircleAvatar(child: Text('AN')),
          title: Text('Asha Nair'),
          subtitle: Text('asha@example.com')),
      SwitchListTile(
        title: const Text('Event reminders'),
        value: _reminders,
        onChanged: (v) => setState(() => _reminders = v),
      ),
    ]);
  }
}

Turn on Event reminders, visit Tickets, come back: IndexedStack kept ProfilePage alive. The last frame shows what body: pages[_index] would do. States: Profile → Tickets → Back to Profile → Without IndexedStack.

6. The Android back button

With a bottom bar, the system back gesture on Android normally closes the app, even if the user is on the third destination. Many apps prefer "back goes to the first destination, then exits". PopScope (the replacement for the deprecated WillPopScope) handles this. Set canPop to allow the pop only on the first destination, and react to blocked pops in onPopInvokedWithResult:

PopScope(
  canPop: _index == 0,
  onPopInvokedWithResult: (didPop, result) {
    if (!didPop) _select(0); // back from Tickets or Profile goes to Events
  },
  child: scaffold,
)

Test this on a real device or emulator, because the behaviour depends on the platform’s back navigation.

Example: Meetup Hub

  1. One Scaffold inside a DefaultTabController(length: 3). Its AppBar title follows the selected destination, and its bottom shows the TabBar only when _index == 0.
  2. EventsPage returns a TabBarView with Upcoming, Past and Saved lists, each with a PageStorageKey.
  3. The body is an IndexedStack of Events, Tickets and Profile. Profile holds a SwitchListTile for reminders, which survives trips to other destinations.
  4. The NavigationBar and the drawer both call the same _select(int) method, so there is one source of truth for the current destination.
  5. The drawer holds the account header, two shortcuts and About, which uses the built-in showAboutDialog.

Common mistakes

  • Length mismatch. DefaultTabController.length, the number of tabs and the number of TabBarView children must be equal.
  • Forgetting to close the drawer before switching or pushing a page, so the drawer is still open when the user comes back.
  • Scaffold.of(context) with the wrong context, which fails with "Scaffold.of() called with a context that does not contain a Scaffold".
  • Losing state with pages[_index] when users expect it to stay. Pick IndexedStack deliberately.
  • Not disposing a manual TabController, or creating it without SingleTickerProviderStateMixin.
  • Too many bottom destinations. More than five becomes hard to tap and read; move the rest into a drawer or a "More" page.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Be ready to justify a pattern: bottom bar for frequent top-level areas, tabs for related views, drawer for many or rare destinations.
  • Explain the IndexedStack trade-off (state kept vs memory and startup cost) and the alternatives: PageStorageKey, AutomaticKeepAliveClientMixin, or lifting state into a Cubit so pages can be rebuilt freely.
  • In production apps with deep links, the bottom bar is usually driven by the router (StatefulShellRoute) rather than a local _index, so each tab has its own URL and back stack.
  • Adaptive layouts switch NavigationBar to NavigationRail on tablets and desktop, using the same destinations list.

domains.name: State management
domains.blurb: setState and lifting state, Provider, BLoC with Cubit and Bloc, and app architecture.

lessons.title: State basics: setState, lifting state, InheritedWidget
lessons.summaryHtml: State is any data that can change while the app runs and changes what the user sees. Ephemeral state belongs to one widget (is this tip expanded?) and setState is perfect for it. App state is needed by several widgets (how many glasses today?), so you lift it up to their closest common ancestor, pass data down as constructor parameters, and send events up through callbacks. When many layers sit in between, an InheritedWidget lets any descendant read the data with of(context) and rebuild when it changes. These tools work, but they mix UI and logic and grow awkward in big apps, which is why the next lessons introduce Provider and BLoC. You build a Water Tracker.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

State is any data that can change while the app is running and that affects what is on screen: a counter, the text in a field, whether a panel is open, the items in a cart. Flutter redraws the UI from state. When state changes, you tell Flutter, and it calls build() again.

The big question is where each piece of state should live. Think of an office. A sticky note on your own desk is fine for a reminder only you need. But the meeting schedule that the whole team reads belongs on the shared whiteboard. Put it on your desk and nobody else can see it; copy it onto every desk and the copies go out of sync.

Why it matters

Most beginner bugs in Flutter apps are state bugs: a header that does not update, two screens showing different totals, a form that forgets what you typed. They almost always come from state living in the wrong place or being duplicated. Understanding the basic tools also explains why packages like Provider and BLoC exist. They do not replace these ideas; they build on them.

How it works

1. setState, properly

setState marks the State object as dirty and schedules a rebuild on the next frame. Only that widget’s build() (and the children it creates) runs again. A few rules:

  • Change the data inside the callback (or just before it), and keep the callback synchronous: setState(() => _count++).
  • Never call setState inside build(); that asks for a rebuild while building.
  • After an await, check if (!mounted) return; first; calling setState after dispose() is an error.
  • Keep stateful widgets small and low in the tree, so a rebuild touches as little UI as possible.

2. Ephemeral state vs app state

The Flutter documentation splits state into two kinds:

Ephemeral (UI) stateApp state
Who needs itOne widgetSeveral widgets or screens
ExamplesExpanded or collapsed, current tab, an animation’s progressSigned-in user, cart, settings, today’s water total
Typical toolsetState in a StatefulWidgetLifted state, InheritedWidget, then Provider or BLoC

There is no strict rule. If only one widget cares today, start with setState. When a second widget needs the value, lift it.

Screen 1: Ephemeral state: the tip card lib/main.dart

class TipCard extends StatefulWidget {
  const TipCard({super.key});
  @override
  State<TipCard> createState() => _TipCardState();
}

class _TipCardState extends State<TipCard> {
  bool _expanded = false; // ephemeral: nobody else needs to know

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Card(
      child: Column(children: [
        ListTile(
          leading: const Icon(Icons.lightbulb_outline),
          title: const Text('Hydration tip'),
          trailing:
              Icon(_expanded ? Icons.expand_less : Icons.expand_more),
          onTap: () => setState(() => _expanded = !_expanded),
        ),
        if (_expanded)
          const Padding(
            padding: EdgeInsets.fromLTRB(16, 0, 16, 16),
            child: Text(
                'Keep a bottle on your desk and refill it after each meeting.'),
          ),
      ]),
    );
  }
}

TipCard keeps _expanded in its own State. Nobody else needs it, so setState inside the card is the right tool. States: Collapsed → Expanded.

3. Lifting state up

When two widgets need the same data, move it to their closest common ancestor. That ancestor owns the value and the methods that change it. It passes the value down as constructor parameters and passes callbacks (VoidCallback, ValueChanged<T>) down so children can report events up.

// Parent owns the state
int _glasses = 0;
void _add() => setState(() => _glasses++);

// Children get data and callbacks
ProgressHeader(glasses: _glasses, goal: 8),   // data down
AddButtons(onAdd: _add, onRemove: _remove),   // events up

The children become stateless and easy to reuse and test: AddButtons does not know or care what "add" means. This is "data down, events up", and it is the same idea you will see in every state management approach.

Screen 2: Lifting state up lib/main.dart

class _WaterHomeState extends State<WaterHome> {
  static const _goal = 8;
  int _glasses = 0; // one owner for the shared value

  void _add() => setState(() => _glasses++);

  void _remove() {
    if (_glasses == 0) return;
    setState(() => _glasses--);
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    // (WaterScope wrapper shown in the next example)
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Water Tracker')),
      body: SingleChildScrollView(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
        child: Column(
          crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.stretch,
          spacing: 16,
          children: [
            ProgressHeader(glasses: _glasses, goal: _goal), // data down
            AddButtons(onAdd: _add, onRemove: _remove), // events up
            const TodayCard(),
            const TipCard(),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

class AddButtons extends StatelessWidget {
  const AddButtons({super.key, required this.onAdd, required this.onRemove});
  final VoidCallback onAdd;
  final VoidCallback onRemove;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Row(spacing: 12, children: [
      Expanded(
          child: OutlinedButton.icon(
              onPressed: onRemove,
              icon: const Icon(Icons.remove),
              label: const Text('Remove'))),
      Expanded(
          child: FilledButton.icon(
              onPressed: onAdd,
              icon: const Icon(Icons.add),
              label: const Text('Add glass'))),
    ]);
  }
}

_WaterHomeState owns _glasses. ProgressHeader receives the value; AddButtons receives callbacks. Tap three times and both stay in sync. States: Start → After 3 taps.

4. The prop drilling problem

Lifting works well for one or two levels. In a real app, the widget that needs the data might be six levels below the owner. Every widget in between must accept and pass on parameters it does not use. This is called prop drilling. It makes constructors noisy, and every change to the data shape touches many files.

5. InheritedWidget

An InheritedWidget puts data into the tree so any descendant can read it directly. You already use this every day: Theme.of(context), MediaQuery.of(context) and Navigator.of(context) all look up inherited widgets.

class WaterScope extends InheritedWidget {
  const WaterScope({super.key, required this.glasses, required this.goal,
      required this.onAdd, required super.child});
  final int glasses;
  final int goal;
  final VoidCallback onAdd;

  static WaterScope of(BuildContext context) {
    final scope = context.dependOnInheritedWidgetOfExactType<WaterScope>();
    assert(scope != null, 'No WaterScope found above this context');
    return scope!;
  }

  @override
  bool updateShouldNotify(WaterScope oldWidget) =>
      glasses != oldWidget.glasses || goal != oldWidget.goal;
}

How the pieces fit:

  • An InheritedWidget is immutable. A StatefulWidget above it holds the real state and builds a new WaterScope with new values after each setState.
  • dependOnInheritedWidgetOfExactType finds the nearest one and registers the caller as a dependent. When a new instance replaces the old one, Flutter calls updateShouldNotify; if it returns true, every dependent rebuilds, even deep inside a const widget.
  • The convention is a static of(context) method, plus maybeOf(context) returning null when the scope is optional.
  • getInheritedWidgetOfExactType reads without registering a dependency. It suits code that runs in callbacks rather than in build().
  • Variants: InheritedNotifier rebuilds dependents when a Listenable notifies, and InheritedModel lets dependents subscribe to only part of the data. MediaQuery.sizeOf(context) is an example: it rebuilds you only when the size changes.

Screen 3: InheritedWidget: WaterScope lib/main.dart

class WaterScope extends InheritedWidget {
  const WaterScope({super.key, required this.glasses,
      required this.goal, required this.onAdd, required super.child});
  final int glasses;
  final int goal;
  final VoidCallback onAdd;

  static WaterScope of(BuildContext context) {
    final scope =
        context.dependOnInheritedWidgetOfExactType<WaterScope>();
    assert(scope != null, 'No WaterScope found above this context');
    return scope!;
  }

  @override
  bool updateShouldNotify(WaterScope oldWidget) =>
      glasses != oldWidget.glasses || goal != oldWidget.goal;
}

// In _WaterHomeState.build:
// return WaterScope(glasses: _glasses, goal: _goal, onAdd: _add,
//     child: Scaffold(...));

class GlassGrid extends StatelessWidget {
  const GlassGrid({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final water = WaterScope.of(context); // registers a dependency
    final color = Theme.of(context).colorScheme.primary;
    return Column(
      crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
      spacing: 8,
      children: [
        const Text('Today'),
        Wrap(spacing: 4, children: [
          for (var i = 0; i < water.goal; i++)
            Icon(i < water.glasses ? Icons.water_drop
                : Icons.water_drop_outlined, color: color),
        ]),
        TextButton(
            onPressed: water.onAdd, child: const Text('Log a glass')),
      ],
    );
  }
}

TodayCard is const and takes no parameters, yet GlassGrid inside it rebuilds because WaterScope.of registered a dependency. Log a glass calls the shared onAdd. States: 3 glasses → Goal reached.

6. Why you need more

These tools are enough for small apps, but they show strain as apps grow. The business logic (adding a glass, saving it, syncing it) lives inside a widget’s State, so it is hard to unit test without building widgets. InheritedWidget needs a stateful wrapper and boilerplate for every piece of shared data. Async work, loading and error states, and sharing between distant screens all get messy. Provider (lesson 6.2) wraps InheritedWidget and ChangeNotifier into a small API. BLoC (lessons 6.3 and 6.4) moves logic into separate classes with explicit states. Both still follow "data down, events up".

Example: Water Tracker

  1. Ephemeral: TipCard keeps _expanded in its own State and toggles it with setState.
  2. The bug: in the starter, the count lives in AddButtons, so ProgressHeader always shows 0.
  3. Lifted: _WaterHomeState owns _glasses, _add and _remove. The header gets the value; the buttons get callbacks.
  4. Inherited: WaterScope wraps the Scaffold. TodayCard is const and takes no parameters, but GlassGrid inside it calls WaterScope.of(context), draws one drop per glass and offers Log a glass through the shared onAdd.
  5. Proof: add a debugPrint to both TodayCard.build and GlassGrid.build. Adding a glass prints only from GlassGrid: the const card is skipped, and the dependency rebuilds only the widget that reads the data.

Common mistakes

  • Changing a field without setState. The data changes but the screen does not.
  • Duplicating state. Keeping the same count in two widgets guarantees they will disagree. Keep one owner.
  • Storing derived values. Do not keep _percent next to _glasses; compute it in build().
  • Copying widget parameters into State in initState and never updating them. If the parent passes a new value, handle it in didUpdateWidget, or just read widget.value directly.
  • Looking up an inherited widget in initState or with a context that sits above it; the lookup fails. Use build or didChangeDependencies, with a context below the scope.
  • updateShouldNotify always returning true, which rebuilds dependents even when nothing they use changed.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Define ephemeral vs app state with one example each, and say when you would move from setState to a state management solution.
  • Explain "data down, events up" and why stateless children with callbacks are easier to test.
  • Know that Theme.of, MediaQuery.of and Provider’s context.watch all rely on the inherited-widget mechanism.
  • In production code, setState is still used a lot for local UI state, even in apps that use BLoC for everything else. Mixing them is normal and healthy.

terms.definition: State used by one widget only, such as a toggle or the current page of a PageView; setState is the right tool.
State shared by many parts of the app or kept between sessions, such as a cart, the signed-in user or today’s total.
Moving state to the closest common ancestor of the widgets that need it, then passing values down and callbacks up.
Passing the same values through many widget constructors that do not use them, only to reach a deep child.
A widget that makes data available to its descendants and rebuilds those that depend on it when updateShouldNotify returns true.
The BuildContext method that finds the nearest InheritedWidget of a type and registers the caller as a dependent.

lessons.examTip: In interviews, say that Theme.of, MediaQuery.of and Navigator.of all work through inherited widgets, and that Provider is essentially a friendlier wrapper around InheritedWidget.

quiz.question: Which piece of state is ephemeral and fits setState inside one widget?
options: Whether a single FAQ item is expanded
The signed-in user

quiz.question: A header and a button row are siblings. The button row holds the counter in its own State, so the header cannot show it. What is the standard fix?
options: Make the counter a global variable

quiz.explanation: Lifting state up gives one owner. Data flows down through constructors and events flow up through callbacks.

quiz.question: What does updateShouldNotify control in an InheritedWidget?
options: Whether the InheritedWidget itself is rebuilt

quiz.explanation: When a new InheritedWidget instance replaces the old one, Flutter calls updateShouldNotify(old). Only if it returns true are the dependents marked for rebuild.

quiz.question: You call MyScope.of(context), which uses dependOnInheritedWidgetOfExactType, inside initState() and get an error. Where should the lookup go instead?

In dispose()

lessons.title: Provider and ChangeNotifier
lessons.summaryHtml: Provider is a small package that puts an object into the widget tree so any widget below can use it. Combined with ChangeNotifier, a class that calls notifyListeners() when its data changes, it gives you shared app state with little code. You create the model once with ChangeNotifierProvider, rebuild widgets with context.watch, call methods without rebuilding using context.read, and limit rebuilds with context.select, Consumer and Selector. Because the model is plain Dart, you can unit test it without any widgets. You build a Shopping Cart app.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

In lesson 6.1 you shared state with an InheritedWidget, and it took a stateful wrapper plus boilerplate. Provider packages that same idea into a few simple calls.

Think of a shop’s notice board. The shop owner (your ChangeNotifier model) keeps the real data and, whenever something changes, rings a bell (notifyListeners()). Staff who care about the board have asked to be told when the bell rings (context.watch), so they look again. Someone who only needs to pin a note does not need to listen for the bell (context.read). The ChangeNotifierProvider is the wall that holds the board where everyone below can reach it.

Why it matters

Provider has long been the approach the Flutter documentation uses to teach simple app state management, and many production apps use it directly or alongside other tools. It also teaches the core ideas you need for every other solution: one owner of the data, widgets that subscribe, and actions that change the data through methods. Even teams that use BLoC use Provider’s ideas every day, because flutter_bloc’s BlocProvider and context.read are built on the provider package.

How it works

1. The model: a ChangeNotifier

Put the state and the operations on it in one plain Dart class. Keep the data private, expose read-only views and computed getters, and call notifyListeners() after every change.

import 'dart:collection';
import 'package:flutter/foundation.dart';

class CartModel extends ChangeNotifier {
  final List<Product> _items = [];

  UnmodifiableListView<Product> get items => UnmodifiableListView(_items);
  int get count => _items.length;
  int get total => _items.fold<int>(0, (sum, p) => sum + p.price);
  bool contains(Product p) => _items.contains(p);

  void add(Product p) {
    if (contains(p)) return;
    _items.add(p);
    notifyListeners();
  }

  void remove(Product p) {
    if (_items.remove(p)) notifyListeners();
  }
}

UnmodifiableListView stops other code from calling cart.items.add(...) behind the model’s back, which would change data without notifying anyone. total is computed, not stored, so it can never disagree with the list.

2. Providing the model

Add the package with flutter pub add provider. Place the provider above every widget that needs it; for app-wide state that means above MaterialApp, so pushed routes can see it too.

void main() {
  runApp(
    ChangeNotifierProvider(
      create: (context) => CartModel(),
      child: const ShopApp(),
    ),
  );
}
  • create runs once (lazily, the first time someone asks), and the provider calls dispose() on the model when it leaves the tree.
  • For several models, use MultiProvider(providers: [...], child: ...) instead of nesting.
  • ChangeNotifierProvider.value(value: existingModel) exposes an object you already own, for example when passing one item to a new route. Never create a new object inside .value.
  • Plain services that never change (an API client) use Provider<ApiClient>. A model that depends on another can use ChangeNotifierProxyProvider.

3. Reading the model

APIRebuilds?Where to use it
context.watch<T>()Yes, on every notificationIn build() when the widget shows T’s data
context.read<T>()NoIn callbacks: onPressed, initState work, event handlers
context.select<T, R>((t) => ...)Only when R changesIn build() when you need one field, such as the count
Consumer<T>Only its builderTo rebuild a small part of a big widget; pass unchanging subtrees as child
Selector<T, R>Only when R changesThe widget form of select

Provider.of<T>(context) is the older form; listen: false makes it behave like read. The extension methods are shorter and clearer.

Screen 1: Catalog: select and read lib/main.dart

void main() {
  runApp(
    ChangeNotifierProvider(
      create: (context) => CartModel(), // created once, disposed for you
      child: MaterialApp(
        theme: ThemeData(
            colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Colors.orange)),
        home: const CatalogPage(),
      ),
    ),
  );
}

class CatalogPage extends StatelessWidget {
  const CatalogPage({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    // Watches nothing, so it never rebuilds when the cart changes.
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Shop')),
      body: ListView(
          children: [for (final p in catalog) ProductTile(product: p)]),
      floatingActionButton: const CartButton(),
    );
  }
}

class CartButton extends StatelessWidget {
  const CartButton({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final count = context.select<CartModel, int>((cart) => cart.count);
    return FloatingActionButton.extended(
      onPressed: () => Navigator.push(context,
          MaterialPageRoute<void>(builder: (context) => const CartPage())),
      icon: const Icon(Icons.shopping_cart),
      label: Text('Cart ($count)'),
    );
  }
}

class ProductTile extends StatelessWidget {
  const ProductTile({super.key, required this.product});
  final Product product;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final inCart =
        context.select<CartModel, bool>((cart) => cart.contains(product));
    return ListTile(
      leading: const Icon(Icons.shopping_bag),
      title: Text(product.name),
      subtitle: Text(product.priceLabel),
      trailing: inCart
          ? const Icon(Icons.check_circle)
          : FilledButton.tonal(
              onPressed: () => context.read<CartModel>().add(product),
              child: const Text('Add'),
            ),
    );
  }
}

CatalogPage watches nothing; CartButton and each tile use context.select, so adding a product rebuilds only the button and that one tile. The Add buttons use context.read. States: Empty cart → After adding two.

4. Controlling rebuilds

When the model notifies, every widget that watches it rebuilds. For small apps this is fine; Flutter is fast. As screens grow, move the subscription down to the widgets that actually show the data. select is the sharpest tool: in the catalog, the page itself watches nothing, a small CartButton selects only the count, and each tile selects only "is my product in the cart?", so adding one product rebuilds one tile and the Cart button, not the whole list. If the page selected the count itself, every count change would rebuild the page and all its tiles. Consumer is useful when you cannot split a widget: only its builder reruns, and a child you pass in is built once and reused.

Screen 2: Cart page: Consumer and watch lib/main.dart

body: Column(children: [
  Expanded(
    child: Consumer<CartModel>(
      builder: (context, cart, child) {
        if (cart.items.isEmpty) {
          return const Center(child: Text('Your cart is empty'));
        }
        return ListView(children: [
          for (final p in cart.items)
            ListTile(
              title: Text(p.name),
              subtitle: Text(p.priceLabel),
              trailing: IconButton(
                icon: const Icon(Icons.remove_circle_outline),
                onPressed: () => cart.remove(p),
              ),
            ),
        ]);
      },
    ),
  ),
  const TotalBar(),
]),

class TotalBar extends StatelessWidget {
  const TotalBar({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final total = context.watch<CartModel>().total;
    return Container(
      color: Theme.of(context).colorScheme.surfaceContainer,
      padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
      child: SafeArea(
        top: false,
        child: Row(
          mainAxisAlignment: MainAxisAlignment.spaceBetween,
          children: [
            Text('Total: ₹$total',
                style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleMedium),
            FilledButton(
              onPressed: total == 0 ? null : () => _checkout(context, total),
              child: const Text('Checkout'),
            ),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

Consumer rebuilds only the list; TotalBar uses context.watch for the total. Removing Canvas Tote updates both, and the catalog’s Cart button, from one notifyListeners(). States: Two items → After removing one.

5. Scoping: app-wide or per screen

Not every model belongs above MaterialApp. A cart or the signed-in user is app-wide. A model that only one screen uses, such as the state of a search page, can be provided in that screen’s route instead. It is then created when the screen opens and disposed automatically when the screen closes, so old search results do not linger in memory or leak into the next visit.

6. Testing the model

Because CartModel is plain Dart, a unit test needs no widgets at all:

test('add updates count and total and notifies listeners', () {
  final cart = CartModel();
  var calls = 0;
  cart.addListener(() => calls++);
  cart.add(catalog[0]); // 499
  cart.add(catalog[1]); // 799
  expect(cart.total, 1298);
  expect(calls, 2);
});

This is the main win over state kept inside widgets: the rules of your app are tested in milliseconds.

Screen 3: Clear dialog and checkout lib/main.dart

Future<void> _confirmClear(BuildContext context) async {
  final cart = context.read<CartModel>(); // grab it before the await
  final count = cart.count;
  final ok = await showDialog<bool>(
    context: context,
    builder: (context) => AlertDialog(
      title: const Text('Clear cart?'),
      content: Text('Remove all $count items?'),
      actions: [
        TextButton(
            onPressed: () => Navigator.pop(context, false),
            child: const Text('Cancel')),
        TextButton(
            onPressed: () => Navigator.pop(context, true),
            child: const Text('Clear')),
      ],
    ),
  );
  if (ok ?? false) cart.clear();
}

void _checkout(BuildContext context, int total) {
  context.read<CartModel>().clear();
  ScaffoldMessenger.of(context).showSnackBar(
      SnackBar(content: Text('Order placed: ₹$total')));
}

The dialog returns a bool through Navigator.pop; checkout clears the model and shows a SnackBar with the total captured before clearing. States: Clear cart? → After checkout.

Example: Shopping Cart app

  1. CartModel holds a private list with add, remove, clear, count, total and contains. A test file checks it.
  2. ChangeNotifierProvider sits above MaterialApp, so both the catalog and the pushed cart page see the same instance.
  3. The catalog’s extended FAB shows Cart (2) with context.select. Each ProductTile selects whether its product is in the cart and shows Add or a check icon.
  4. The cart page lists items in a Consumer with remove buttons. TotalBar watches the total and disables Checkout at 0.
  5. The delete icon asks "Clear cart?" and uses the bool returned by showDialog. Checkout clears the cart and shows "Order placed: ₹1298".

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting notifyListeners(). The data changes but no widget hears about it.
  • watch in a callback. Provider reports an error because callbacks run outside build(). Use read.
  • read in build() for displayed data. The value shows once and never updates.
  • ProviderNotFoundException. The provider is not an ancestor of the widget asking: placed too low (inside a page instead of above MaterialApp) or the context used is above it.
  • Exposing the mutable list, so screens change it directly and skip notifyListeners().
  • Using .value with a new object (ChangeNotifierProvider.value(value: CartModel())): it is recreated on rebuild and never disposed. Use create for objects the provider should own.
  • Calling notifyListeners() during build, for example from a getter, which triggers "setState() or markNeedsBuild() called during build".

Interview and real-world notes

  • Explain watch vs read vs select clearly; it is one of the most common Flutter interview questions.
  • Say that Provider is a dependency-injection and rebuild tool built on InheritedWidget, and ChangeNotifier is the state holder. You can provide any object, not only notifiers.
  • Know its limits: a ChangeNotifier exposes mutable state and methods, so large apps can end up with models that do too much. That is one reason teams move to BLoC or Cubit, where state is immutable and each change is an explicit new state.
  • Riverpod, by the author of Provider, is another popular option you may meet in job listings. The concepts from this lesson carry over.

terms.definition: A Flutter class that keeps a list of listeners and calls them when you call notifyListeners().
A provider that creates a ChangeNotifier, exposes it to descendants, rebuilds dependents when it notifies and disposes it when removed.
Gets T and subscribes: the widget rebuilds whenever T notifies. Use it in build().
Gets T without subscribing. Use it in callbacks such as onPressed.
Subscribes to one derived value R; the widget rebuilds only when that value changes.
A widget whose builder receives T and rebuilds on change, useful to rebuild only a small part of a screen.

lessons.examTip: A one-line interview answer: watch in build to listen, read in callbacks to act, select when you only care about one field.
