lessons.title: BLoC part 1: Cubit
lessons.summaryHtml: A Cubit is a class from the bloc family that holds one immutable state and exposes methods. Each method works out the next state and calls emit(); widgets that listen rebuild. States are plain classes made comparable with equatable, and a sealed class hierarchy (loading, loaded, failure) lets a Dart 3 switch check that every case is handled. With flutter_bloc you create the Cubit with BlocProvider, draw UI with BlocBuilder, and run one-off side effects such as snack bars with BlocListener. Business rules move out of widgets into a class you can test on its own. You build a Task Tracker, the first app in this course that uses the BLoC approach we recommend for production.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Picture a scoreboard at a cricket ground. The crowd does not change the numbers. Someone reports an event ("four runs!"), the scoreboard operator works out the new score and puts up a new board, and everyone watching sees it at once. The operator never scribbles over half the old board.

A Cubit is that operator. It holds exactly one state (the board). Widgets call its methods (add, toggle, delete). Each method computes the next state and calls emit(newState). Widgets that listen rebuild with the new state. The state is immutable: you never change it in place; you replace it.

Why it matters

With setState and ChangeNotifier, logic and data can end up scattered through widgets and mutable models. BLoC (Business Logic Component) gives a clear shape that scales to large teams:

  • Separation: rules live in a Cubit with no widget code, so the UI only draws states and forwards user actions.
  • Predictability: every change is a new, complete state. You can log each one and see exactly what happened.
  • Testability: you can call cubit.add('Read') in a plain test and check cubit.state, with no widgets involved.
  • Explicit async states: loading, loaded and failure are real types, not a tangle of booleans.

This course uses BLoC with flutter_bloc as its production default. A Cubit is the simpler half of the library: methods in, states out. Lesson 6.4 adds the full Bloc with events.

How it works

1. Install

Run flutter pub add flutter_bloc bloc equatable. flutter_bloc adds the Flutter widgets on top of the core bloc package. Listing bloc as well lets plain-Dart files such as a Cubit import package:bloc/bloc.dart without pulling in Flutter. equatable saves you from writing == and hashCode by hand.

2. Design the state

States must be immutable and comparable. Make every field final, give the class a const constructor, extend Equatable and list every field in props. For data that goes through phases, use a sealed hierarchy:

sealed class TasksState extends Equatable {
  const TasksState();
  @override
  List<Object?> get props => [];
}

final class TasksLoading extends TasksState {
  const TasksLoading();
}

final class TasksLoadFailure extends TasksState {
  const TasksLoadFailure(this.message);
  final String message;
  @override
  List<Object?> get props => [message];
}

final class TasksLoaded extends TasksState {
  const TasksLoaded({required this.tasks, this.filter = TaskFilter.all});
  final List<Task> tasks;
  final TaskFilter filter;

  TasksLoaded copyWith({List<Task>? tasks, TaskFilter? filter}) =>
      TasksLoaded(tasks: tasks ?? this.tasks, filter: filter ?? this.filter);

  @override
  List<Object?> get props => [tasks, filter];
}

copyWith builds a new state that keeps the fields you do not pass. Values that can be computed, such as the number of tasks left, are getters, not fields. Equatable compares lists element by element, so two states with equal tasks are equal.

3. Write the Cubit

class TaskCubit extends Cubit<TasksState> {
  TaskCubit(this._loadTasks) : super(const TasksLoading());
  final Future<List<Task>> Function() _loadTasks;
  int _nextId = 100;

  Future<void> load() async {
    emit(const TasksLoading());
    try {
      final tasks = await _loadTasks();
      if (!isClosed) emit(TasksLoaded(tasks: tasks));
    } catch (_) {
      if (!isClosed) emit(const TasksLoadFailure('Could not load tasks'));
    }
  }

  void add(String title) {
    final s = state;
    final text = title.trim();
    if (s is! TasksLoaded || text.isEmpty) return;
    emit(s.copyWith(tasks: [...s.tasks, Task(id: _nextId++, title: text)]));
  }
}
  • super(...) sets the initial state; state always returns the current one.
  • Copy state into a local variable (final s = state;) so the type check s is! TasksLoaded promotes it.
  • Create new lists with spreads or collection for. Never s.tasks.add(...).
  • emit skips a state equal to the current one. That saves rebuilds, and it is why equality must be correct.
  • After an await, check isClosed: emitting after the Cubit is closed throws a StateError.
  • The loader is passed in, not created inside. The real app passes storage or an API call; a test passes a fake. This is the seed of the repository pattern in lesson 6.5.

Screen 1: Sealed states in a BlocBuilder lib/main.dart

// task_cubit.dart
sealed class TasksState extends Equatable {
  const TasksState();
  @override
  List<Object?> get props => [];
}

final class TasksLoading extends TasksState {
  const TasksLoading();
}

final class TasksLoadFailure extends TasksState {
  const TasksLoadFailure(this.message);
  final String message;
  @override
  List<Object?> get props => [message];
}

final class TasksLoaded extends TasksState { /* tasks, filter... */ }

// main.dart
body: BlocBuilder<TaskCubit, TasksState>(
  builder: (context, state) => switch (state) {
    TasksLoading() =>
        const Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator()),
    TasksLoadFailure(:final message) => Center(
        child: Column(
          mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
          spacing: 12,
          children: [
            Text(message),
            FilledButton(
                onPressed: () => context.read<TaskCubit>().load(),
                child: const Text('Retry')),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    TasksLoaded loaded => TaskList(state: loaded),
  },
),

One BlocBuilder draws all three states. The Dart 3 switch is exhaustive, so a forgotten state would not compile. States: Loading → Loaded → Failure.

4. Provide it and build UI

BlocProvider(create: (context) => TaskCubit(fakeLoad)..load(), child: ...) creates the Cubit once, makes it available below, and calls close() when it leaves the tree. The cascade ..load() starts loading right away. To pass an existing Cubit to a new route, use BlocProvider.value(value: cubit, child: ...).

ToolUse it for
BlocBuilder<C, S>Drawing UI from the state; optional buildWhen: (previous, current) => ...
BlocSelector<C, S, T>Rebuilding only when one derived value changes
BlocListener<C, S>Side effects once per change: snack bars, dialogs, navigation; optional listenWhen
context.read<C>()Calling methods from callbacks
context.watch<C>() / context.selectReading state in build() without a builder widget

These are the same read, watch and select ideas from lesson 6.2, because flutter_bloc is built on the provider package.

Screen 2: Toggle and filter lib/task_cubit.dart

class TaskCubit extends Cubit<TasksState> {
  TaskCubit(this._loadTasks) : super(const TasksLoading());
  final Future<List<Task>> Function() _loadTasks;

  void toggle(int id) {
    final s = state;
    if (s is! TasksLoaded) return;
    emit(s.copyWith(tasks: [
      for (final t in s.tasks)
        t.id == id ? t.copyWith(done: !t.done) : t,
    ]));
  }

  void setFilter(TaskFilter filter) {
    final s = state;
    if (s is TasksLoaded) emit(s.copyWith(filter: filter));
  }
  // load, add, delete, undoDelete ...
}

// In TasksLoaded:
List<Task> get visible => switch (filter) {
      TaskFilter.all => tasks,
      TaskFilter.active => tasks.where((t) => !t.done).toList(),
      TaskFilter.done => tasks.where((t) => t.done).toList(),
    };
int get remaining => tasks.where((t) => !t.done).length;

// In TaskList.build (cubit = context.read<TaskCubit>()):
SegmentedButton<TaskFilter>(
  segments: const [
    ButtonSegment(value: TaskFilter.all, label: Text('All')),
    ButtonSegment(value: TaskFilter.active, label: Text('Active')),
    ButtonSegment(value: TaskFilter.done, label: Text('Done')),
  ],
  selected: {state.filter},
  onSelectionChanged: (selection) => cubit.setFilter(selection.first),
),
// ...
ListTile(
  leading: Checkbox(
      value: t.done, onChanged: (_) => cubit.toggle(t.id)),
  title: Text(t.title),
  trailing: IconButton(
      icon: const Icon(Icons.delete_outline),
      onPressed: () => cubit.delete(t.id)),
),

Each tap calls a Cubit method that emits a new TasksLoaded. The Active filter hides done tasks; ticking Buy milk removes it from Active and the counter drops to 1. States: All → Active → Buy milk ticked.

5. Side effects with BlocListener

A builder may run several times for the same state (for example after a theme change), so a snack bar shown from a builder can appear twice. Worse, builders must be pure: they return widgets and do nothing else. BlocListener calls its listener exactly once per new state. In the Task Tracker, delete emits a state carrying lastDeleted; the listener shows "Deleted Call the plumber" with an Undo action, and Undo calls undoDelete().

Screen 3: Delete with Undo lib/main.dart

// task_cubit.dart
void delete(int id) {
  final s = state;
  if (s is! TasksLoaded) return;
  final removed = s.tasks.where((t) => t.id == id).toList();
  if (removed.isEmpty) return;
  emit(TasksLoaded(
      tasks: s.tasks.where((t) => t.id != id).toList(),
      filter: s.filter,
      lastDeleted: removed.first));
}

void undoDelete() {
  final s = state;
  if (s is! TasksLoaded || s.lastDeleted == null) return;
  final tasks = [...s.tasks, s.lastDeleted!]
    ..sort((a, b) => a.id.compareTo(b.id));
  emit(s.copyWith(tasks: tasks)); // copyWith clears lastDeleted
}

// main.dart
BlocListener<TaskCubit, TasksState>(
  listenWhen: (previous, current) =>
      current is TasksLoaded && current.lastDeleted != null,
  listener: (context, state) {
    if (state case TasksLoaded(lastDeleted: final Task deleted)) {
      final title = deleted.title;
      ScaffoldMessenger.of(context)
        ..hideCurrentSnackBar()
        ..showSnackBar(SnackBar(
          content: Text('Deleted $title'),
          action: SnackBarAction(
              label: 'Undo',
              onPressed: () => context.read<TaskCubit>().undoDelete()),
        ));
    }
  },
  child: Scaffold(/* ... */),
)

delete() emits a state carrying lastDeleted; the BlocListener reacts once with a SnackBar, and Undo calls back into the Cubit. States: Deleted → After Undo.

6. Seeing every change: BlocObserver

Set Bloc.observer = const AppObserver(); in main(), where AppObserver extends BlocObserver and overrides onChange. Every state change in every Cubit is then printed with its current and next state, which is a powerful debugging aid and a natural place to report errors in production.

Example: Task Tracker

  1. task_cubit.dart holds Task (Equatable, copyWith), TaskFilter, the sealed TasksState family and TaskCubit with load, add, toggle, delete, undoDelete and setFilter. It imports no Flutter widgets.
  2. main.dart sets the observer and wraps TaskPage in BlocProvider.
  3. TaskPage has a BlocListener for the delete snack bar and a BlocBuilder that switches over the three states.
  4. TaskList shows a text field, a SegmentedButton filter (All, Active, Done), the visible tasks with checkboxes and delete buttons, and "2 tasks left".
  5. The text field’s TextEditingController stays in a small StatefulWidget: it is UI state, so it does not belong in the Cubit.

Common mistakes

  • Mutating state (state.tasks.add(t); emit(state);): nothing rebuilds because the "new" state equals the old one.
  • Incomplete props: a field missing from props makes different states compare equal, so changes are silently ignored.
  • Side effects in BlocBuilder: duplicate snack bars and navigation bugs. Use BlocListener.
  • Creating a Cubit in build() or with BlocProvider.value(value: TaskCubit(...)): it is recreated and never closed. Use create.
  • Emitting after close: check isClosed after awaits in long-running methods.
  • Putting UI objects in the Cubit, such as BuildContext or controllers. A Cubit should run in a plain Dart test.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Explain Cubit vs Bloc: a Cubit exposes methods; a Bloc receives event objects and maps them to states, which adds traceability and event transformers (lesson 6.4). Start with a Cubit and upgrade when you need that.
  • Be ready to write a sealed state family and an exhaustive switch on a whiteboard.
  • State the rules: immutable states, Equatable with complete props, BlocListener for side effects, no Flutter imports in business logic.
  • Mention testing: a Cubit can be tested by calling methods and checking state; the bloc_test package (lesson 6.4) makes the expected sequence of states explicit.

terms.definition: A class that extends Cubit<State>, starts with an initial state and changes it only by calling emit() from its methods.
Replaces the current state and notifies listeners; a state equal to the current one is ignored.
A package that implements == and hashCode from a props list, so two states with the same data count as equal.
Creates a Cubit or Bloc, makes it available below in the tree, and closes it when it is removed.
Rebuilds its builder with the latest state; buildWhen can skip rebuilds.
Runs a listener once per state change for side effects such as snack bars, dialogs or navigation.

lessons.examTip: In interviews, explain why states are immutable: emit compares old and new state, so mutating a list in place and emitting it again changes nothing on screen.

quiz.question: A Cubit method does state.tasks.add(task); emit(state); and nothing changes on screen. Why?
options: emit only works inside async methods
The emitted state is the same object as the current one, so it is treated as no change
BlocBuilder needs buildWhen to rebuild
Cubits cannot hold lists
quiz.explanation: emit ignores a state equal to the current state. Mutating in place and emitting the same object is equal by definition. Build a new list and a new state instead.

quiz.question: Where should a snack bar that confirms "Task deleted" be shown?
options: In a BlocListener listener
In the BlocBuilder builder
Inside the Cubit’s delete method
In the Task constructor
quiz.explanation: A builder may run many times for one state, and the Cubit must not know about widgets. BlocListener runs once per state change and is made for side effects.

quiz.question: Your states are a sealed class TasksState with three subclasses, and the BlocBuilder uses a switch expression over them. What do you gain?
options: Faster rebuilds
Automatic JSON support
The compiler reports an error if a state subclass is not handled
States become mutable
quiz.explanation: Sealed classes let Dart check exhaustiveness. Add a fourth state later and every switch that forgets it stops compiling.

quiz.question: Task extends Equatable with props => [id]. Toggling done emits a new state, but the checkbox does not change. What is the fix?
options: Call setState after emit
Use BlocListener instead of BlocBuilder
Remove Equatable from Task
Include every field in props: [id, title, done]
quiz.explanation: With only id in props, the old and new tasks compare equal, so the lists and states compare equal and emit ignores the change.

lessons.title: BLoC part 2: Bloc, events and testing
lessons.summaryHtml:
A Cubit changes state when you call its methods. A Bloc changes state when you add events to it. Each event type gets a handler registered with on<Event>, and the handler calls emit with new states. Because every change starts as an event object, a Bloc gives you a full log of what happened and control over how events run at the same time (event transformers).

In this lesson you upgrade the Task Tracker to a Bloc with sealed events. You use BlocConsumer to rebuild the list and show a SnackBar, MultiBlocProvider to provide two blocs, and bloc_test to prove each event produces the right states.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

In lesson 6.3 you called methods on a Cubit: cubit.addTask('Buy milk'). A Bloc works like a restaurant kitchen with order tickets. The UI does not tell the kitchen how to cook. It drops a ticket on the counter: “TaskAdded: Buy milk”. The kitchen reads each ticket, does the work and puts out a new plate: the next state.

Those tickets are events. They are plain Dart objects that describe something that happened. The Bloc turns a stream of events into a stream of states. The UI only does two things: it adds events and it draws states.

Why it matters

A Cubit is shorter and is often enough. A Bloc pays off when your app grows:

  • Traceability. Every change starts as an event object, so you can log “what happened, and what state came out” in one place. Support teams love that when a bug report says “the cart emptied itself”.
  • Control over timing. You can decide what happens when the same event arrives many times quickly: queue them, ignore extras or cancel the old one. This fixes double-submits and search-as-you-type bugs.
  • Testability. “Given this state, when this event arrives, expect these states” maps directly onto a test.
CubitBloc
InputMethod callsEvent objects via add()
BoilerplateLowMore: one class per event
Event log and transitionsState changes onlyEvent, current state and next state
Concurrency controlYou write it yourselfBuilt in with event transformers
Good forSimple screens, toggles, formsComplex flows, search, sync, anything you must audit

How it works

Events as a sealed class

Name events in the past tense, from the user’s point of view: TaskAdded, not AddTask. A sealed base class tells Dart the full list of event types, so switches over events are checked for exhaustiveness.

sealed class TaskEvent {
  const TaskEvent();
}

final class TaskAdded extends TaskEvent {
  const TaskAdded(this.title);
  final String title;
}

final class TaskToggled extends TaskEvent {
  const TaskToggled(this.id);
  final int id;
}

final class TaskDeleted extends TaskEvent {
  const TaskDeleted(this.id);
  final int id;
}

Registering handlers with on<Event>

In the constructor you register one handler per event type. A handler receives the event and an Emitter. Calling emit(newState) publishes a state. You read the current state with state. Always build a new state object; never mutate the old list.

class TaskBloc extends Bloc<TaskEvent, TaskState> {
  TaskBloc() : super(const TaskState()) {
    on<TaskAdded>(_onAdded);
    on<TaskToggled>(_onToggled);
    on<TaskDeleted>(_onDeleted);
  }

  int _nextId = 1;

  void _onAdded(TaskAdded event, Emitter<TaskState> emit) {
    final title = event.title.trim();
    if (title.isEmpty) return;
    final task = Task(id: _nextId++, title: title);
    emit(TaskState(tasks: [...state.tasks, task]));
  }

  void _onToggled(TaskToggled event, Emitter<TaskState> emit) {
    emit(TaskState(tasks: [
      for (final t in state.tasks)
        t.id == event.id ? t.copyWith(done: !t.done) : t,
    ]));
  }

  void _onDeleted(TaskDeleted event, Emitter<TaskState> emit) {
    final removed = state.tasks.where((t) => t.id == event.id).firstOrNull;
    if (removed == null) return;
    emit(TaskState(
      tasks: [for (final t in state.tasks) if (t.id != event.id) t],
      lastDeleted: removed,
    ));
  }
}

Because TaskState extends Equatable, emitting a state equal to the current one is skipped, so widgets do not rebuild for nothing.

Async handlers and the Emitter

Handlers can be async. You may call emit several times, for example a loading state before an await and a result after it. Two rules: always await your async work inside the handler, and never keep a reference to emit to call later. Once the handler’s future completes, the emitter is closed. To follow a stream inside a handler, use await emit.forEach(stream, onData: ...), which emits a state for every item and stops cleanly when the bloc closes.

Event transformers

By default, a Bloc processes events concurrently: if two TaskAdded events arrive while an async handler is still running, both handlers run at the same time. You can change this per event type with the transformer argument of on. The four common behaviours are:

  • concurrent (default): run every event at once.
  • sequential: queue events and run them one by one. Good for writes that must stay in order.
  • droppable: ignore new events while one is running. Good for a “Pay” button.
  • restartable: cancel the running one and start the newest. Good for search.

The bloc_concurrency package, from the same authors, ships these four ready-made. A transformer is only a function from a stream of events to a stream of results, so you can also write one in plain Dart:

EventTransformer<E> sequential<E>() =>
    (events, mapper) => events.asyncExpand(mapper);

// in the constructor
on<TaskAdded>(_onAdded, transformer: sequential());

BlocConsumer, listenWhen and buildWhen

BlocBuilder is for drawing. BlocListener is for things that must happen once per change: SnackBars, dialogs, navigation. BlocConsumer is both in one widget. Use listenWhen and buildWhen to react only to the changes you care about; they receive the previous and current state.

MultiBlocProvider

Screens often need more than one bloc. Instead of nesting BlocProvider inside BlocProvider, list them in MultiBlocProvider. MultiBlocListener does the same for listeners. The result is the same tree, just flatter to read.

Testing with bloc_test

Add the packages with flutter pub add flutter_bloc equatable and flutter pub add dev:bloc_test. blocTest builds a fresh bloc, optionally seeds a starting state, runs act, and compares the emitted states with expect. Other parameters include wait (for debounces), skip, errors and verify (for checking mocks afterwards).

blocTest<TaskBloc, TaskState>(
  'deletes a task and remembers it for the SnackBar',
  build: TaskBloc.new,
  seed: () => const TaskState(tasks: [Task(id: 1, title: 'Buy milk')]),
  act: (bloc) => bloc.add(const TaskDeleted(1)),
  expect: () => const [
    TaskState(tasks: [], lastDeleted: Task(id: 1, title: 'Buy milk')),
  ],
);

Equality matters here: expect compares states with ==. Without Equatable (or your own ==), two states with the same tasks would not be equal and the test would fail.

Example: Task Tracker with events

The finished app has a text field, a filter and a list. Every interaction becomes an event.

  1. Typing “Buy milk” and tapping + adds TaskAdded('Buy milk'). The Bloc emits a state with one task.
  2. Ticking the box adds TaskToggled(1). The Bloc emits a new list where that task is done.

    Screen 1: Events in, states out lib/main.dart

    // Typing and tapping + adds TaskAdded('Buy milk')
context.read<TaskBloc>().add(TaskAdded(_controller.text));

// Ticking the box adds TaskToggled(id)
CheckboxListTile(
  controlAffinity: ListTileControlAffinity.leading,
  value: task.done,
  title: Text(task.title),
  onChanged: (_) =>
      context.read<TaskBloc>().add(TaskToggled(task.id)),
  secondary: IconButton(
    icon: const Icon(Icons.delete_outline),
    onPressed: () =>
        context.read<TaskBloc>().add(TaskDeleted(task.id)),
  ),
)

// Empty list message
if (visible.isEmpty) {
  return const Center(child: Text('No tasks here yet'));
}

    Each tap adds an event; the Bloc emits a new TaskState and BlocConsumer rebuilds the list. States: Start → 3 × TaskAdded → TaskToggled(1).

  3. Tapping the bin adds TaskDeleted(2). The new state has lastDeleted set, so the listener shows a SnackBar exactly once.

    Screen 2: BlocConsumer: rebuild and react lib/main.dart

    BlocConsumer<TaskBloc, TaskState>(
  listenWhen: (prev, curr) =>
      curr.lastDeleted != null &&
      curr.lastDeleted != prev.lastDeleted,
  listener: (context, state) {
    final title = state.lastDeleted!.title;
    ScaffoldMessenger.of(context)
      ..hideCurrentSnackBar()
      ..showSnackBar(SnackBar(content: Text('Deleted "$title"')));
  },
  builder: (context, state) {
    // ...builds the ListView of CheckboxListTiles
  },
)

    The builder redraws the list; the listener runs once per deletion and shows the SnackBar.

  4. The filter is a tiny FilterCubit. A Cubit is the right tool here: one method, no history needed. MultiBlocProvider provides both, and a switch expression picks the visible tasks.

Screen 3: Two blocs, one screen lib/main.dart

MultiBlocProvider(
  providers: [
    BlocProvider(create: (_) => TaskBloc()),
    BlocProvider(create: (_) => FilterCubit()),
  ],
  child: MaterialApp(home: const TaskPage()),
)

// In TaskPage.build
final filter = context.watch<FilterCubit>().state;

SegmentedButton<TaskFilter>(
  segments: const [
    ButtonSegment(value: TaskFilter.all, label: Text('All')),
    ButtonSegment(value: TaskFilter.active, label: Text('Active')),
    ButtonSegment(value: TaskFilter.done, label: Text('Done')),
  ],
  selected: {filter},
  onSelectionChanged: (s) =>
      context.read<FilterCubit>().select(s.first),
)

final visible = switch (filter) {
  TaskFilter.all => state.tasks,
  TaskFilter.active => [for (final t in state.tasks) if (!t.done) t],
  TaskFilter.done => [for (final t in state.tasks) if (t.done) t],
};

MultiBlocProvider supplies TaskBloc and FilterCubit; the Done segment shows only finished tasks.

Common mistakes

  • Mutating state. state.tasks.add(task); emit(state); changes the old list and emits an equal state, so nothing rebuilds. Always build a new list.
  • Forgetting to await in async handlers. If you fire a future without awaiting and call emit in its callback, the handler has already finished and the emit throws.
  • Side effects in the builder. Showing a SnackBar inside builder repeats it on every rebuild. Put it in a listener.
  • Events named like commands. LoadData, SetFlag and one “do everything” event hide what really happened. Name events after user actions or system facts.
  • Using Bloc everywhere. A theme toggle does not need three event classes. Mixing Cubits and Blocs in one app is normal.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Be ready to explain the data flow: UI adds event, handler runs, emit produces state, BlocBuilder rebuilds. Mention that states should be immutable and comparable.
  • A BlocObserver set with Bloc.observer = MyObserver(); can log every event, transition and error across the app. Teams use it to send errors to crash reporting.
  • Explain one transformer with a real case: restartable for search, droppable for payment buttons.
  • Show that you test blocs without widgets: blocTest runs in milliseconds and covers most business logic. Widget tests (lesson 8.3) can use MockBloc from bloc_test with whenListen to feed fake states.

terms.definition: An object that describes something that happened, such as TaskAdded. You add it to a Bloc with bloc.add().
A function registered with on<Event>() that receives the event and an Emitter and emits new states.
Controls how events of one type are processed over time: all at once (the default), one after another, dropping new ones, or restarting.
A widget that combines BlocBuilder (rebuild UI) and BlocListener (run one-off side effects) for the same bloc.
Provides several blocs to the subtree without deep nesting of BlocProvider widgets.
A helper from bloc_test that builds a bloc, acts on it and checks the exact list of states it emits.

lessons.examTip: In interviews, explain Cubit vs Bloc as “methods vs events”: pick Bloc when you need traceability or control over event timing (search-as-you-type, preventing double submits).

quiz.question: A Bloc receives an event but no handler is registered for that event type. What happens?
options: The event is silently ignored
A StateError is thrown telling you to register a handler with on<Event>
The Bloc emits its initial state again
The event is forwarded to the nearest Cubit
quiz.explanation: Every event type a Bloc can receive needs a handler registered with on<Event>() in the constructor. Adding an unhandled event throws a StateError (the check runs as an assert, so you see it in debug builds).

quiz.question: You want to show a SnackBar once when a task is deleted, and also rebuild the task list. Which widget fits best?
options: BlocSelector
BlocProvider
RepositoryProvider
BlocConsumer
quiz.explanation: BlocConsumer has a builder for UI and a listener for one-off side effects such as SnackBars, navigation and dialogs.

quiz.question: A search bloc should cancel the previous request when the user types a new letter, so only the latest query wins. Which transformer behaviour is that?
options: Restartable
Sequential
Droppable
Concurrent
quiz.explanation: Restartable cancels the handler that is still running and starts one for the newest event. Droppable ignores new events while one is running; sequential queues them.

quiz.question: In a blocTest, what does the seed parameter do?
options: Adds an event before act runs
Sets a random number generator for the test
Sets the state the bloc starts from before act runs
Skips the first emitted state
quiz.explanation: seed returns a state the bloc is put into before act, so you can test a handler without replaying earlier events. skip is the parameter that ignores emitted states.

lessons.title: App architecture
lessons.summaryHtml:
Architecture is about deciding where code lives and who may talk to whom. A common Flutter layout has three layers: presentation (widgets and blocs), domain (models and repository contracts) and data (repository implementations, API clients, databases). Dependencies point inwards: the UI knows the bloc, the bloc knows a repository interface, and only the composition root in main.dart chooses the real implementation.

You organise folders feature-first, inject dependencies through constructors and RepositoryProvider, and test blocs with fake repositories. You refactor the Task Tracker into these layers.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Think of a restaurant again. The waiter (the UI) takes orders and serves plates. The chef (the bloc) decides what to cook. The pantry manager (the repository) gets ingredients, whether from the fridge, a supplier or the market. The chef never drives to the market, and the waiter never opens the fridge. Each person has one job and a clear way to ask the next person for help.

App architecture is the same idea for code: decide which part does what, and which part may call which. Nothing here is Flutter magic. It is plain Dart classes, interfaces and constructors.

Why it matters

Small apps survive without structure. Real apps do not. After a few months, a widget that fetches data, parses JSON, caches results and draws a list becomes impossible to test and scary to change. Typical pain:

  • The backend renames a field and you must edit twelve widgets.
  • You cannot test the “retry on failure” logic without a real server.
  • Two developers edit the same 900-line file every day.

Layers and repositories fix this. Each change has one obvious home, and each piece can be tested alone. Employers expect junior developers to recognise and follow this structure from day one.

How it works

The three layers

LayerContainsKnows aboutMust not
PresentationWidgets, pages, blocs and cubitsDomain models, repository interfacesCall HTTP or SQL directly
DomainModels (Task), repository contracts, optional use casesNothing else in the appImport Flutter widgets or packages like http
DataRepository implementations, API clients, database helpers, JSON parsingDomain contracts, packages such as http or sqfliteImport widgets or blocs

The arrows point towards the domain. That is the dependency rule: the inner layer never imports the outer one. Flutter’s own architecture guide on docs.flutter.dev describes a very similar split: a UI layer, a data layer made of repositories and services, and an optional domain layer for logic shared by many screens. Names differ between teams; the direction of the arrows is what matters.

Repositories: one door to the data

A repository is the only way the rest of the app gets tasks. Define it as an interface in the domain layer:

abstract interface class TaskRepository {
  Future<List<Task>> fetchTasks();
  Future<Task> addTask(String title);
}

Then implement it in the data layer. Today it keeps tasks in memory; in lesson 7.1 you will write one that calls an API, and in 7.3 one that uses SQLite. The cubit never changes.

class InMemoryTaskRepository implements TaskRepository {
  final List<Task> _tasks = [
    const Task(id: 1, title: 'Plan sprint'),
    const Task(id: 2, title: 'Review pull request', done: true),
  ];

  @override
  Future<List<Task>> fetchTasks() async {
    await Future<void>.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 600));
    return List<Task>.unmodifiable(_tasks);
  }

  @override
  Future<Task> addTask(String title) async {
    await Future<void>.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 300));
    final task = Task(id: _tasks.length + 1, title: title);
    _tasks.add(task);
    return task;
  }
}

Larger apps often split the data layer further: a small API client or service that only talks HTTP, and a repository that combines it with a local cache. Start simple and split when a class grows two jobs.

Dependency injection with constructors

The cubit asks for its repository instead of creating one:

class TasksCubit extends Cubit<TasksState> {
  TasksCubit(this._repository) : super(const TasksInitial());
  final TaskRepository _repository;

  Future<void> load() async {
    emit(const TasksLoading());
    try {
      emit(TasksLoaded(await _repository.fetchTasks()));
    } catch (_) {
      emit(const TasksFailure('Could not load tasks.'));
    }
  }
}

This is dependency injection. It needs no package: a constructor parameter is enough. The type is the interface, so any implementation fits.

RepositoryProvider and the composition root

Somebody must create the real objects. That place is the composition root: main.dart and the top-level App widget. RepositoryProvider from flutter_bloc puts one repository instance into the widget tree, and blocs read it when they are created.

void main() {
  runApp(App(taskRepository: InMemoryTaskRepository()));
}

class App extends StatelessWidget {
  const App({super.key, required this.taskRepository});
  final TaskRepository taskRepository;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return RepositoryProvider<TaskRepository>.value(
      value: taskRepository,
      child: MaterialApp(
        home: BlocProvider(
          create: (context) =>
              TasksCubit(context.read<TaskRepository>())..load(),
          child: const TasksPage(),
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

Use MultiRepositoryProvider when you have several. Because App takes the repository as a parameter, a widget test can pump App(taskRepository: FakeTaskRepository()). Some teams use a service locator package instead; the idea is the same.

Feature-first folders

Group by feature, then by layer inside it:

lib/
  main.dart
  app.dart
  features/
    tasks/
      domain/        task.dart, task_repository.dart
      data/          in_memory_task_repository.dart
      presentation/  tasks_cubit.dart, tasks_page.dart
    auth/
      ...
  core/              shared widgets, theme, utilities

Layer-first folders (lib/blocs, lib/screens) are fine for tiny apps, but a feature ends up spread across the whole tree. Feature-first keeps code that changes together in one place.

Where does logic go?

A useful test: if the rule would still be true in a web version or a command-line version of your app, it does not belong in a widget. “A task title cannot be blank” is a business rule, so the cubit (or a domain class) checks it. “The Add button is disabled while saving” is a UI rule, so the page decides it from the state. “Retry twice on a network error” is a data rule, so the repository handles it.

Some teams add a use case class between blocs and repositories, such as AddTask or CompleteCheckout. It is worth it when one action touches several repositories or when many blocs share the same steps. For a single repository call it only adds a layer of forwarding, so keep it optional.

Finally, keep models immutable. A Task with final fields and Equatable can be passed between layers safely: nobody can change it behind your back, and comparing two states is reliable.

Example: Task Tracker, layered

The starter works, but TasksPage holds the data, fakes the network and draws the UI. After the refactor, the page is a pure function of TasksState. It shows a spinner, the list, or a failure with Retry.

Screen 1: One UI, three states lib/features/tasks/presentation/tasks_page.dart

BlocBuilder<TasksCubit, TasksState>(
  builder: (context, state) => switch (state) {
    TasksInitial() || TasksLoading() =>
      const Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator()),
    TasksFailure(:final message) => Center(
        child: Column(
          mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
          children: [
            Text(message),
            const SizedBox(height: 12),
            FilledButton(
              onPressed: () => context.read<TasksCubit>().load(),
              child: const Text('Retry'),
            ),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    TasksLoaded(:final tasks) => ListView(
        children: [
          for (final task in tasks)
            ListTile(
              leading: Icon(task.done
                  ? Icons.check_circle
                  : Icons.radio_button_unchecked),
              title: Text(task.title),
            ),
        ],
      ),
  },
)

TasksPage only switches on TasksState; it has no idea whether data came from memory, HTTP or a fake. States: Loading → Loaded → Failure.

Adding a task shows the flow across layers: the dialog returns text, the page calls cubit.add, the cubit calls repository.addTask and then emits the reloaded list.

Screen 2: Adding goes through the cubit lib/features/tasks/presentation/tasks_page.dart

Future<void> _showAddDialog(BuildContext context) async {
  final cubit = context.read<TasksCubit>();
  var text = '';
  final title = await showDialog<String>(
    context: context,
    builder: (dialogContext) => AlertDialog(
      title: const Text('New task'),
      content: TextField(autofocus: true, onChanged: (v) => text = v),
      actions: [
        TextButton(onPressed: () => Navigator.pop(dialogContext), child: const Text('Cancel')),
        FilledButton(onPressed: () => Navigator.pop(dialogContext, text), child: const Text('Add')),
      ],
    ),
  );
  if (title != null) await cubit.add(title);
}

The dialog only returns text; the cubit saves it through the repository and emits the new list. States: Dialog → After Add.

The real payoff is the test. A FakeTaskRepository implements the same interface in ten lines. It can return data instantly or throw on purpose, so you can test the failure path without switching off your Wi-Fi.

blocTest<TasksCubit, TasksState>(
  'load emits a failure when the repository throws',
  build: () => TasksCubit(FakeTaskRepository(fail: true)),
  act: (cubit) => cubit.load(),
  expect: () => const [
    TasksLoading(),
    TasksFailure('Could not load tasks.'),
  ],
);

Common mistakes

  • Creating repositories inside widgets or blocs. final repo = HttpTaskRepository(); inside a bloc makes it untestable. Inject it.
  • Leaking data types upwards. Passing raw Map<String, dynamic> JSON or database rows into widgets couples the UI to the API. Convert to models in the data layer.
  • Over-engineering on day one. A use case class for every single call, three model copies per entity and five folders per button slow a small team down. Add layers when they solve a real problem.
  • Providing repositories too low. If two screens need the same repository, provide it above both, usually above MaterialApp, or pushed routes will not find it.
  • Catching errors in the UI. Convert exceptions into failure states in the bloc. Widgets should only switch on state.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Be ready to sketch the arrows and to explain the dependency rule in one sentence.
  • Explain the difference between a fake (a simple working implementation) and a mock (records calls and returns stubbed answers, for example with mocktail). Both rely on injected interfaces.
  • Mention that the same cubit worked unchanged when you swapped memory for HTTP or SQLite. That sentence shows you understand why repositories exist.
  • Many companies follow a variation of this layout. When you join a team, read one full feature from page to repository before writing code.

terms.definition: A group of code with one job, such as drawing UI or fetching data, that may only depend on certain other layers.
A class that hides where data comes from (API, database, memory) behind simple methods like fetchTasks().
Giving an object the things it needs through its constructor instead of letting it create them.
A flutter_bloc widget that makes one instance of a repository available to the subtree via context.read.
The single place, usually main.dart, where concrete implementations are created and wired together.
A folder structure grouped by feature (tasks, auth, cart) with layers inside each feature.

lessons.examTip: When asked “how do you structure a Flutter app?”, draw the arrows: widget → bloc → repository interface ← implementation → API or database. Then say how you test each box.

quiz.question: Your TasksCubit creates an HttpTaskRepository inside its constructor. What is the main problem?
options: Cubits cannot make HTTP calls
It will not compile
The cubit is tied to one implementation, so tests cannot swap in a fake
The UI will rebuild too often
quiz.explanation: Creating dependencies inside a class hard-wires them. Passing a TaskRepository into the constructor lets main.dart choose the real one and tests choose a fake.

quiz.question: Which layer should know about JSON field names such as "userId"?
options: The data layer
The presentation layer
The domain models used by widgets
The theme
quiz.explanation: Parsing and API details belong in the data layer. The rest of the app works with clean models and does not change when the API does.

quiz.question: What does RepositoryProvider give you that a global variable does not?
options: Faster network calls
Automatic caching of all responses
Hot reload support
A scoped instance you can replace per widget tree, for example in tests
quiz.explanation: RepositoryProvider puts one instance into the widget tree. Tests and previews can provide a different instance without touching global state.

quiz.question: A team has folders lib/blocs, lib/screens and lib/repositories, each with 60 files. What is the usual argument for feature-first instead?
options: It makes the app smaller
Code that changes together sits together, so a feature is easy to find, own and delete
Dart requires feature folders
It removes the need for repositories
quiz.explanation: Feature-first keeps a feature’s UI, logic and data side by side. Layer-first spreads one feature across many distant folders.

lessons.title: HTTP and JSON
lessons.summaryHtml:
Most apps talk to a server. With the http package you send a request such as GET /posts, check the status code, and decode the JSON body with jsonDecode. You then turn the raw maps into typed models with a fromJson factory (and back with toJson), using Dart 3 map patterns to validate the shape.

Networks fail, so you handle timeouts, lost connections, bad status codes and malformed data, and you show clear loading, data and error states. You build a News Reader that lists posts from JSONPlaceholder and opens each one.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

An API is a waiter for data. Your app sends a request: “GET me the posts, please”. The server sends back a response with a status code (200 means OK) and a body, usually text in JSON format. Your job is to ask politely, check the answer, and turn that text into Dart objects the rest of the app can trust.

In this lesson you use the free test API https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com. Its /posts endpoint returns a list of 100 fake posts, each with userId, id, title and body. Other free APIs such as Hacker News and Open-Meteo are good for practice later.

Why it matters

Almost every job app loads data from a backend: products, orders, messages, bookings. Networking bugs are also the ones users notice most: endless spinners, blank screens, crashes on bad data. A junior developer who handles errors and loading states carefully stands out quickly.

How it works

Add the package and make a request

Run flutter pub add http. Import it with a prefix so names like get and Client stay clear: import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;. On Android, release builds also need the INTERNET permission in AndroidManifest.xml; debug builds have it already. macOS apps need the outgoing network entitlement.

final response = await client
    .get(Uri.parse('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts'))
    .timeout(const Duration(seconds: 10));

if (response.statusCode != 200) {
  final code = response.statusCode;
  throw ApiException('The server answered with status $code.');
}
final data = jsonDecode(response.body); // from dart:convert

Important: the http package does not throw for 404 or 500. It returns a normal response. Checking statusCode is your job.

From JSON to a model

jsonDecode returns dynamic: maps become Map<String, dynamic>, arrays become List<dynamic>. Passing those raw maps around is fragile. Instead, convert them once into a model. Dart 3 map patterns check the keys and the types in one step:

class Post {
  const Post({required this.id, required this.userId,
      required this.title, required this.body});
  final int id;
  final int userId;
  final String title;
  final String body;

  factory Post.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) => switch (json) {
        {'id': int id, 'userId': int userId,
         'title': String title, 'body': String body} =>
          Post(id: id, userId: userId, title: title, body: body),
        _ => throw FormatException('Unexpected post JSON: $json'),
      };

  Map<String, dynamic> toJson() =>
      {'id': id, 'userId': userId, 'title': title, 'body': body};
}

If a field is missing or has the wrong type, the pattern does not match and you get a clear FormatException right at the edge of the app, not a null error three screens later. For big APIs, teams often generate this code with json_serializable; writing it by hand first teaches you what the generator does.

Handling failures

Four things commonly go wrong. Catch each one and turn it into your own exception with a message a user understands:

ProblemWhat you seeHow to handle it
No internet, DNS failurehttp.ClientException“No connection. Check your internet.”
Server too slowTimeoutException from .timeout()“The server took too long to answer.”
Bad status (401, 404, 500)A normal response with that codeCheck statusCode; 401 often means “sign in again”
Unexpected bodyFormatException“The server sent data we could not read.”
Future<List<Post>> fetchPosts() async {
  try {
    final response = await _client
        .get(Uri.parse('$_base/posts'))
        .timeout(const Duration(seconds: 10));
    if (response.statusCode != 200) {
      final code = response.statusCode;
      throw ApiException('The server answered with status $code.');
    }
    final data = jsonDecode(response.body);
    if (data is! List) throw const FormatException('Expected a JSON list');
    return [for (final item in data) Post.fromJson(item as Map<String, dynamic>)];
  } on TimeoutException {
    throw const ApiException('The server took too long to answer.');
  } on http.ClientException {
    throw const ApiException('No connection. Check your internet.');
  } on FormatException {
    throw const ApiException('The server sent data we could not read.');
  }
}

Sending data

To create something, send JSON with POST. Set the content type header and encode the body with jsonEncode. A successful create usually answers 201. JSONPlaceholder pretends to save the post and returns it with a new id, but nothing is really stored.

final response = await client.post(
  Uri.parse('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts'),
  headers: {'Content-Type': 'application/json; charset=UTF-8'},
  body: jsonEncode({'userId': 1, 'title': 'Hello', 'body': 'First post'}),
);
if (response.statusCode != 201) {
  throw const ApiException('Could not create the post.');
}
final created = Post.fromJson(jsonDecode(response.body) as Map<String, dynamic>);

Query parameters, headers and the Uri class

Many endpoints take options in the query string, such as /posts?userId=1. Build the address with Uri.https instead of joining strings: it encodes spaces and special characters for you, and it keeps the host, path and parameters readable. Headers carry extra information such as the content type, the language or an access token.

final uri = Uri.https('jsonplaceholder.typicode.com', '/posts', {'userId': '1'});
final response = await client.get(uri, headers: {'Accept': 'application/json'});

Query parameter values are always strings, so convert numbers with toString().

Testing without the network

Because PostsApi receives its http.Client, a test can pass a fake one. The http package ships MockClient for exactly this. You decide what the “server” answers, so you can test success, a 500 error and broken JSON in milliseconds, with no internet and no flaky results.

import 'package:http/testing.dart';

final client = MockClient((request) async =>
    http.Response('[{"id":1,"userId":1,"title":"Hi","body":"Text"}]', 200));
final posts = await PostsApi(client).fetchPosts();
expect(posts.single.title, 'Hi');

Write one test per branch of fetchPosts: status 200, a non-200 status, invalid JSON and a timeout. That covers every message the user can see.

Loading states in the UI

Following lesson 6.5, the API class lives in the data layer and a cubit turns results into a sealed state: PostsLoading, PostsLoaded or PostsFailure. The page switches on that state. Nothing in a widget touches http.

Example: News Reader

  1. Create the project, run flutter pub add http flutter_bloc, and write Post with fromJson and toJson.
  2. Write PostsApi with an injected http.Client, a timeout, a status check and friendly exceptions.
  3. Add PostsCubit with load(), provide it with BlocProvider, and call load() when it is created.
  4. Build the page as a switch over the state. Turn on airplane mode and tap Retry to see the failure screen.

Screen 1: Loading, data, error lib/main.dart

BlocBuilder<PostsCubit, PostsState>(
  builder: (context, state) => switch (state) {
    PostsLoading() => const Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator()),
    PostsFailure(:final message) => Center(
        child: Column(
          mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
          children: [
            const Icon(Icons.cloud_off, size: 48),
            const SizedBox(height: 12),
            Text(message, textAlign: TextAlign.center),
            const SizedBox(height: 12),
            FilledButton.icon(
              onPressed: () => context.read<PostsCubit>().load(),
              icon: const Icon(Icons.refresh),
              label: const Text('Retry'),
            ),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    PostsLoaded(:final posts) => ListView.separated(
        itemCount: posts.length,
        separatorBuilder: (context, index) => const Divider(height: 1),
        itemBuilder: (context, index) {
          final post = posts[index];
          return ListTile(
            leading: CircleAvatar(child: Text(post.id.toString())),
            title: Text(post.title, maxLines: 1, overflow: TextOverflow.ellipsis),
            subtitle: Text(post.body, maxLines: 2, overflow: TextOverflow.ellipsis),
          );
        },
      ),
  },
)

One sealed PostsState drives three screens; the switch expression makes sure none is forgotten. States: Loading → Loaded → Offline.

Each tile opens a detail page. The list already holds the full Post, so you pass the object to the new route instead of downloading it again.

Screen 2: Post details lib/main.dart

class PostPage extends StatelessWidget {
  const PostPage({super.key, required this.post});
  final Post post;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final text = Theme.of(context).textTheme;
    final id = post.id;
    final author = post.userId;
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: Text('Post $id')),
      body: ListView(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
        children: [
          Text(post.title, style: text.titleLarge),
          const SizedBox(height: 8),
          Text('By user $author', style: text.labelMedium),
          const SizedBox(height: 16),
          Text(post.body, style: text.bodyLarge),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}

Tapping a tile pushes PostPage with the Post object; no second request is needed.

A note on the platforms. On Android and iOS the same code works unchanged. On the web, the browser adds its own rules: the server must allow your site through CORS headers, and some errors look different. JSONPlaceholder allows browser requests, so the News Reader also runs on the web.

Common mistakes

  • Skipping the status check. Decoding an error page throws a confusing FormatException, or worse, parses an error object as if it were data.
  • Using json['title'] everywhere. A typo such as 'titel' silently gives null. Parse once into a model.
  • No timeout. On a bad connection a request can hang for a long time and the spinner never stops.
  • Building URLs by string concatenation with user input. Use Uri.https(host, path, queryParameters) so spaces and symbols are encoded.
  • Calling the API inside build(). build can run many times a second. Start requests from a bloc, initState or a user action (lesson 7.2 goes deeper).

Interview and real-world notes

  • Explain the full path: request, status check, decode, model, state, UI. Mention where each error is caught.
  • Show you can test it: MockClient from package:http/testing.dart returns fixed responses, so PostsApi can be tested for 200, 500 and bad JSON without a network.
  • Real APIs need authentication headers, such as Authorization: Bearer <token>. Never hard-code secrets in the app; anything in the app bundle can be extracted.
  • Large JSON responses can be parsed off the main thread with Isolate.run or compute (lesson 1.13) to avoid janky scrolling.
  • Many teams use the dio package for interceptors and retries. The concepts in this lesson transfer directly.

terms.definition: A number the server sends with every response: 2xx success, 4xx a problem with the request, 5xx a problem on the server.
A text format for data made of objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. jsonDecode turns it into Dart maps and lists.
A typed Dart class, such as Post, that replaces raw Map<String, dynamic> data in the rest of the app.
A factory that builds a model from a decoded map, and a method that turns it back into a map for sending.
An object that sends requests. Injecting it lets tests replace the network with MockClient.
A limit on how long you wait for a response before giving up and showing an error.

lessons.examTip: In code reviews, look for three things in every network call: a status code check, a timeout, and a typed model instead of raw maps reaching the UI.

lessons.title: Async UI: FutureBuilder and StreamBuilder
lessons.summaryHtml:
FutureBuilder and StreamBuilder rebuild part of the UI whenever a Future completes or a Stream emits. Their builder receives an AsyncSnapshot with a connection state (none, waiting, active, done), the latest data and any error.

The golden rule: create the future or stream once, in initState or in a bloc, never inside build, or every rebuild starts a new request. You also add pull-to-refresh with RefreshIndicator and a live “Updated N s ago” label driven by a stream.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A Future is a parcel that will arrive once. A Stream is a newspaper subscription: new issues keep arriving until it is cancelled. Your UI must look sensible before the parcel arrives, when it arrives, and if it gets lost.

FutureBuilder and StreamBuilder are widgets that watch a future or a stream and call your builder again whenever something changes. Your builder looks at a snapshot and decides what to show: a spinner, the data or an error.

Why it matters

Every screen that loads something has at least three states. Beginners often handle only the happy path, which leads to a list that is blank forever when the network fails. Another classic bug is a screen that downloads the same data again every time the user types a letter. Both are fixed by understanding how these builders work.

How it works

AsyncSnapshot and ConnectionState

connectionStateFutureBuilderStreamBuilder
nonefuture is nullstream is null
waitingstarted, not finishedsubscribed, no event yet
activenot usedhas emitted, still open
donecompleted with data or errorstream closed

Besides the state, the snapshot has data, error, hasData and hasError. A useful detail: when you give a builder a new future or stream, the snapshot goes back to waiting but keeps the previous data. That lets a refresh keep the old list on screen instead of flashing a spinner.

The order of checks

A reliable pattern is: error first, then “no data yet”, then data.

builder: (context, snapshot) {
  if (snapshot.hasError) {
    return const _Message('Could not load posts. Pull down to try again.');
  }
  if (!snapshot.hasData) {
    return const Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator());
  }
  final posts = snapshot.data!;
  return ListView.builder(/* ... */);
}

If you need to tell states apart exactly, you can switch on the state instead:

return switch (snapshot.connectionState) {
  ConnectionState.none || ConnectionState.waiting =>
    const Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator()),
  ConnectionState.active || ConnectionState.done => snapshot.hasError
      ? Text('Error: ' + snapshot.error.toString())
      : Text('Loaded ' + snapshot.data!.length.toString() + ' posts'),
};

The golden rule: never create the future in build

build can run many times: on setState, on theme changes, when the keyboard opens. This code starts a new download every time:

// BAD: a new Future on every rebuild
FutureBuilder<List<Post>>(
  future: fetchPosts(),
  builder: ...,
)

Create it once and store it in the state object:

late Future<List<Post>> _postsFuture;

@override
void initState() {
  super.initState();
  _postsFuture = fetchPosts();
}

// in build
FutureBuilder<List<Post>>(future: _postsFuture, builder: ...)

The same rule applies to streams. Stream.periodic(...) in build would restart the stream on each rebuild.

Pull-to-refresh

RefreshIndicator wraps a scrollable. When the user pulls down it shows a spinner and calls onRefresh, which must return a Future. The spinner hides when that future completes. To refresh, create a new future, store it with setState so the FutureBuilder switches to it, and await it:

Future<void> _refresh() async {
  final future = fetchPosts();
  setState(() => _postsFuture = future);
  try {
    await future;
  } on Exception {
    // The FutureBuilder shows the error.
  }
}

Two details: the child must be scrollable even when the list is short or empty, so use AlwaysScrollableScrollPhysics; and the error view must be scrollable too, or the user cannot pull to retry.

StreamBuilder

StreamBuilder rebuilds for every event. Typical sources: a StreamController you own, Firestore snapshots (lesson 7.5), authentication changes (lesson 7.4), or timers. It subscribes when it is built and cancels the subscription when it is removed, so you do not have to.

Stream<int> _ticker() =>
    Stream.periodic(const Duration(seconds: 1), (i) => i + 1);

StreamBuilder<int>(
  stream: _secondsSinceRefresh,
  builder: (context, snapshot) {
    final seconds = snapshot.connectionState == ConnectionState.waiting
        ? 0
        : snapshot.data ?? 0;
    return Text('Updated $seconds s ago');
  },
)

initialData lets you show a value before the first event, but it is only used when the builder is first created, not when you swap in a new stream.

Streams you own: StreamController

Sometimes you produce events yourself, for example a download progress value or messages from a socket. A StreamController gives you a sink to add values and a stream to listen to. A normal controller allows only one listener. If several widgets must listen, create it with StreamController.broadcast(). Whoever creates a controller must also close it, usually in dispose, or the stream stays open and keeps memory alive.

final _progress = StreamController<double>.broadcast();

void _onChunk(double value) => _progress.add(value);

@override
void dispose() {
  _progress.close();
  super.dispose();
}

FutureBuilder or a bloc?

SituationGood fit
One screen shows data loaded once, no sharingFutureBuilder with the future in initState
A simple live value such as a timer or auth stateStreamBuilder
Data shared by several screens, with retry, caching or paginationA bloc or cubit and BlocBuilder
Values that combine several sourcesA bloc that listens to each source

Both builders are good tools as long as you know their limits. When a FutureBuilder starts to collect flags such as “is refreshing” and “last error”, that logic is asking to move into a cubit.

Example: News Reader, async UI

This version of the News Reader keeps things local to one screen, which is exactly where FutureBuilder shines.

  1. The state object creates _postsFuture and a ticker stream in initState.
  2. The FutureBuilder shows a spinner, then the posts, or an error message.

    Screen 1: Three snapshots, three screens lib/main.dart

    FutureBuilder<List<Post>>(
  future: _postsFuture, // created in initState
  builder: (context, snapshot) {
    if (snapshot.hasError) {
      return const _Message(
          'Could not load posts. Pull down to try again.');
    }
    if (!snapshot.hasData) {
      return const Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator());
    }
    final posts = snapshot.data!;
    return ListView.builder(
      physics: const AlwaysScrollableScrollPhysics(),
      itemCount: posts.length,
      itemBuilder: (context, index) => ListTile(
        leading: CircleAvatar(
            child: Text(posts[index].id.toString())),
        title: Text(posts[index].title,
            maxLines: 1, overflow: TextOverflow.ellipsis),
      ),
    );
  },
)

    Check hasError first, then hasData; while waiting with no data yet, show a spinner. States: waiting → done + data → done + error.

  3. Pulling down calls _refresh. The old posts stay visible under the spinner because the snapshot keeps its data while waiting.

    Screen 2: Pull to refresh lib/main.dart

    Future<void> _refresh() async {
  final future = fetchPosts();
  setState(() {
    _postsFuture = future;
    _secondsSinceRefresh = _ticker();
  });
  try {
    await future; // keeps the refresh spinner until the data arrives
  } on Exception {
    // The FutureBuilder shows the error; nothing else to do here.
  }
}

// in build
RefreshIndicator(
  onRefresh: _refresh,
  child: FutureBuilder<List<Post>>(/* ... */),
)

    The spinner stays until the Future from onRefresh completes; the old list stays visible because the snapshot keeps its data while waiting.

  4. A StreamBuilder above the list counts the seconds since the last refresh and restarts at 0 when a new stream is set.

Screen 3: A live label with StreamBuilder lib/main.dart

Stream<int> _ticker() =>
    Stream.periodic(const Duration(seconds: 1), (i) => i + 1);

StreamBuilder<int>(
  stream: _secondsSinceRefresh, // created in initState and _refresh
  builder: (context, snapshot) {
    // After a new stream is set, the old value is kept while
    // waiting, so treat "waiting" as 0.
    final seconds =
        snapshot.connectionState == ConnectionState.waiting
            ? 0
            : snapshot.data ?? 0;
    return Text('Updated $seconds s ago',
        style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.labelMedium);
  },
)

Stream.periodic emits every second; a refresh swaps in a new stream, so the count starts again. States: After 3 s → After 41 s → Just refreshed.

Notice how little the page knows. It holds two objects, a future and a stream, and describes what to draw for each snapshot. The loading, success and failure paths are all visible in one builder, which makes the screen easy to review. The price is that this logic lives in a widget; when the screen grows, move it into a cubit and keep the same three visual states.

Common mistakes

  • Creating the future or stream in build. Causes repeated requests, flicker and lost stream position.
  • Checking only connectionState == done. A finished future can hold an error. Treating it as data gives an empty list or a null crash.
  • Using snapshot.data! without checking. On the first frame data is null.
  • A non-scrollable child inside RefreshIndicator. Pull-to-refresh silently does nothing.
  • Returning before the work finishes in onRefresh. If onRefresh does not await the load, the spinner disappears immediately.
  • Listening to a single-subscription stream twice. Two builders on one plain stream throw “Stream has already been listened to”. Use a broadcast stream or a bloc.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Know the four ConnectionState values and which builder uses active.
  • Explain when you would not use FutureBuilder: shared data, retry logic, caching or pagination belong in a bloc. BlocBuilder is effectively a StreamBuilder over the bloc’s state stream, with the loading logic moved out of the widget.
  • Mention the “keeps previous data while waiting” behaviour. It is a small detail that shows you have read the docs.
  • For a single async value used in several places, cache the future in a repository instead of calling the API again.

terms.definition: The value a FutureBuilder or StreamBuilder passes to its builder: connectionState, data, error and helpers like hasData.
none (no future or stream), waiting (started, nothing yet), active (a stream has emitted and is still open), done (finished).
A widget that subscribes to one Future and rebuilds when it completes with data or an error.
A widget that subscribes to a Stream and rebuilds for every event until the stream closes.
A Material widget that shows a spinner when the user pulls a scrollable down and calls onRefresh, which returns a Future.

lessons.examTip: If an interviewer shows you FutureBuilder(future: api.fetch(), ...) inside build, the expected answer is “that refetches on every rebuild; move the future to initState or a bloc”.
