quiz.question: A FutureBuilder uses future: fetchPosts() directly inside build. The user types in a search box on the same screen. What happens?
options: Nothing, FutureBuilder caches the result automatically
Each rebuild creates a new future, so the request runs again and the spinner flashes
The app does not compile
Only the first keystroke triggers a request
quiz.explanation: build runs on every setState. Calling fetchPosts() there creates a new Future each time, and FutureBuilder subscribes to the new one. Create it once in initState or a bloc.

quiz.question: A StreamBuilder shows live stock prices. The stream has emitted a price and stays open. What is snapshot.connectionState?
options: ConnectionState.active
ConnectionState.waiting
ConnectionState.done
ConnectionState.none
quiz.explanation: active means the stream has delivered at least one event and is still open. done means it has closed; waiting means no event has arrived yet.

quiz.question: Pull-to-refresh does nothing on the error screen, which is a Center with a Text. Why?
options: RefreshIndicator only works with FutureBuilder
onRefresh must return void
RefreshIndicator needs a scrollable child that can be pulled, so the error view must be scrollable with AlwaysScrollableScrollPhysics
Errors disable RefreshIndicator
quiz.explanation: RefreshIndicator listens to overscroll from a scrollable. A Center has nothing to pull, so wrap the message in a ListView with AlwaysScrollableScrollPhysics.

quiz.question: In a production app that uses BLoC, where should the list of posts usually be loaded?
options: In a FutureBuilder inside each widget
In main() before runApp
In the widget’s dispose method
In a bloc or cubit, with BlocBuilder drawing its states
quiz.explanation: FutureBuilder is fine for small, local cases. For app data, a bloc owns the loading, retry and caching logic, and BlocBuilder plays the role of StreamBuilder.

lessons.title: Local storage
lessons.summaryHtml:
Apps must remember things between launches. For small settings, such as a theme choice, use shared_preferences: simple key-value pairs saved on the device. For structured data you create, search and update, such as notes or orders, use a real database. sqflite gives you SQLite on Android and iOS with query, insert, update and delete.

You build a Notes app that stores notes in SQLite, remembers dark mode with SharedPreferencesAsync, and deletes with a swipe. You also learn how to choose between storage options.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

When an app closes, everything in memory is gone. Local storage is the app’s notebook on the device. Different notebooks suit different jobs: a sticky note for one setting, a filing cabinet with labelled drawers for hundreds of records, and a locked safe for secrets.

In Flutter, the sticky note is shared_preferences and the filing cabinet is an SQLite database through sqflite.

Why it matters

Users expect an app to remember their theme, their draft, their last search and their offline data. A notes, expenses or inventory app is useless if it forgets everything on restart. Local storage also makes apps fast and usable offline: show saved data instantly, then sync with the server when possible.

How it works

Choosing storage

NeedGood choiceWhy
A few settings: theme, language, onboarding seenshared_preferencesSimple key-value, no schema
Many records you search, sort and updateSQLite via sqflite (or a type-safe layer on top, such as drift)Tables, indexes, queries, transactions
Tokens and passwordsA secure storage plugin that uses the Keychain on iOS and Keystore-backed encryption on AndroidPreferences and SQLite files are not encrypted
Large files: images, PDFsFiles in the app’s documents directoryDatabases are not meant for big blobs
Data shared across devices and usersA backend such as Cloud Firestore (lesson 7.5)Local storage lives on one device only

shared_preferences

Add it with flutter pub add shared_preferences. The package offers three APIs. The original SharedPreferences class is now called the legacy API and is planned for deprecation. New code should use SharedPreferencesAsync (always reads from the platform) or SharedPreferencesWithCache (keeps a local cache for fast synchronous reads).

final prefs = SharedPreferencesAsync();

await prefs.setBool('darkMode', true);
final bool? dark = await prefs.getBool('darkMode'); // null if never set
await prefs.remove('darkMode');

Keys are plain strings, so keep them in constants to avoid typos. Values are limited to bool, int, double, String and List<String>.

sqflite: opening the database

Add flutter pub add sqflite path. sqflite runs on Android, iOS and macOS; it does not run in DartPad or on the web, and Windows and Linux need a different setup, so use a phone or emulator for this lesson. Plugins need the Flutter engine ready, so call WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized() before using them in main.

static Future<NotesDatabase> open() async {
  final path = p.join(await getDatabasesPath(), 'notes.db');
  final db = await openDatabase(
    path,
    version: 1,
    onCreate: (db, version) => db.execute(
      'CREATE TABLE notes(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, '
      'title TEXT NOT NULL, body TEXT NOT NULL, updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL)',
    ),
  );
  return NotesDatabase._(db);
}

onCreate runs only the first time the file is created. When you later change the schema, raise version and add an onUpgrade callback that runs ALTER TABLE for existing users. Import path with a prefix (as p): it has a top-level context that can confuse you inside widgets.

Mapping rows to models

SQLite only stores simple types: integers, real numbers, text and blobs. There is no DateTime or bool, so store dates as milliseconds and booleans as 0 or 1. Rows come back as Map<String, Object?>; convert them with a map pattern, just like JSON:

Map<String, Object?> toMap() => {
      if (id != null) 'id': id,
      'title': title,
      'body': body,
      'updated_at': updatedAt.millisecondsSinceEpoch,
    };

factory Note.fromMap(Map<String, Object?> map) => switch (map) {
      {'id': int id, 'title': String title, 'body': String body,
       'updated_at': int ms} =>
        Note(id: id, title: title, body: body,
            updatedAt: DateTime.fromMillisecondsSinceEpoch(ms)),
      _ => throw FormatException('Bad note row: $map'),
    };

CRUD

Future<List<Note>> all() async {
  final rows = await _db.query('notes', orderBy: 'updated_at DESC');
  return rows.map(Note.fromMap).toList();
}

Future<int> insert(Note note) => _db.insert('notes', note.toMap());

Future<int> update(Note note) =>
    _db.update('notes', note.toMap(), where: 'id = ?', whereArgs: [note.id]);

Future<int> delete(int id) =>
    _db.delete('notes', where: 'id = ?', whereArgs: [id]);

insert returns the new row id; update and delete return how many rows changed. Always pass values through whereArgs. For several writes that must succeed or fail together, use db.transaction.

Migrations with onUpgrade

Your app will change after release. Suppose version 2 lets users pin notes. New users get the new table from onCreate, but existing users already have version 1 on their phones. Raise the version number and describe how to move from each old version to the new one:

final db = await openDatabase(
  path,
  version: 2,
  onCreate: (db, version) => db.execute(
    'CREATE TABLE notes(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, title TEXT NOT NULL, '
    'body TEXT NOT NULL, updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL, pinned INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0)',
  ),
  onUpgrade: (db, oldVersion, newVersion) async {
    if (oldVersion < 2) {
      await db.execute('ALTER TABLE notes ADD COLUMN pinned INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0');
    }
  },
);

Checking oldVersion < 2 instead of == 1 means a user who skips several releases still runs every step in order. Test upgrades by installing the old build, adding data, then installing the new build over it.

When several writes must succeed or fail together, such as moving a note to another folder and updating a counter, wrap them in db.transaction((txn) async { ... }) and use txn for every call inside it. If any statement throws, SQLite rolls all of them back.

Example: Notes app

  1. main ensures the binding, opens the database and reads darkMode before runApp.
  2. NotesPage loads all notes in initState. After a restart the notes are still there.

    Screen 1: Notes list lib/main.dart

    Future<List<Note>> all() async {
  final rows = await _db.query('notes', orderBy: 'updated_at DESC');
  return rows.map(Note.fromMap).toList();
}

// NotesPage.build
Scaffold(
  appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Notes'), actions: [
    IconButton(
      icon: Icon(widget.dark ? Icons.light_mode : Icons.dark_mode),
      onPressed: () => widget.onDarkChanged(!widget.dark),
    ),
  ]),
  floatingActionButton: FloatingActionButton(
      onPressed: () => _openEditor(), child: const Icon(Icons.add)),
  body: _notes.isEmpty
      ? const Center(child: Text('No notes yet. Tap + to write one.'))
      : ListView(children: [
          for (final note in _notes)
            ListTile(
              title: Text(note.title),
              subtitle: Text(note.body,
                  maxLines: 1, overflow: TextOverflow.ellipsis),
              onTap: () => _openEditor(note),
            ),
        ]),
)

    Notes come from SELECT ... ORDER BY updated_at DESC, so the latest edit is on top. States: First launch → After restart.

  3. Tapping + or a note opens EditNotePage. It returns a Note; if the id is null the page inserts, otherwise it updates.

    Screen 2: Editing a note lib/main.dart

    Scaffold(
  appBar: AppBar(
    title: Text(widget.note == null ? 'New note' : 'Edit note'),
    actions: [IconButton(icon: const Icon(Icons.check), onPressed: _save)],
  ),
  body: Padding(
    padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
    child: Column(children: [
      TextField(controller: _title,
          decoration: const InputDecoration(labelText: 'Title')),
      const SizedBox(height: 12),
      Expanded(
        child: TextField(
          controller: _body,
          decoration: const InputDecoration(labelText: 'Note',
              alignLabelWithHint: true, border: OutlineInputBorder()),
          maxLines: null,
          expands: true,
          textAlignVertical: TextAlignVertical.top,
        ),
      ),
    ]),
  ),
)

    The editor returns a Note with the same id, so NotesPage calls db.update instead of insert.

  4. The sun and moon button flips the theme and saves the choice, so the app opens in the same mode next time. Swiping a note left deletes it.

Screen 3: Dark mode remembered lib/main.dart

Future<void> main() async {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  final db = await NotesDatabase.open();
  final prefs = SharedPreferencesAsync();
  final dark = await prefs.getBool('darkMode') ?? false;
  runApp(NotesApp(db: db, prefs: prefs, initialDark: dark));
}

// _NotesAppState
Future<void> _setDark(bool value) async {
  setState(() => _dark = value);
  await widget.prefs.setBool('darkMode', value);
}

MaterialApp(
  theme: ThemeData(colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Colors.amber)),
  darkTheme: ThemeData(colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(
      seedColor: Colors.amber, brightness: Brightness.dark)),
  themeMode: _dark ? ThemeMode.dark : ThemeMode.light,
  home: NotesPage(db: widget.db, dark: _dark, onDarkChanged: _setDark),
)

The toggle is saved with SharedPreferencesAsync and read in main() before runApp, so the app starts dark next time.

In a larger app, NotesDatabase would sit behind a NotesRepository interface and a cubit would own the list (lesson 6.5). This lesson keeps the UI simple so you can focus on storage.

Why not keep the notes in shared_preferences as one big JSON string? It works for a handful of items, but every change rewrites the whole string, you cannot sort or search without loading everything, and one corrupt write can lose all notes. A database stores each note as its own row, updates only what changed, and lets SQLite do the sorting with orderBy.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting ensureInitialized. Awaiting plugin calls before runApp without it throws a binding error.
  • Storing secrets in preferences. Preferences are plain files; rooted or backed-up devices can expose them.
  • Editing onCreate for a schema change. Existing installs never run it again, so the new column is missing and queries fail.
  • String-building SQL. Use ? placeholders and whereArgs.
  • Async removal in Dismissible. Remove the item from the list synchronously in onDismissed, then delete from the database.
  • Opening the database many times. Open it once and share the instance.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Expect “how would you make this app work offline?” Answer: store data locally, show it first, sync changes when online, and resolve conflicts with timestamps or server rules.
  • Know the schema migration story: version, onCreate, onUpgrade.
  • Mention that shared_preferences has newer async and cached APIs; it shows you keep up with package changes.
  • For bigger apps, teams often add a type-safe query layer on top of SQLite. The ideas here, tables, migrations and repositories, still apply.

terms.definition: A plugin that stores small key-value data (bool, int, double, String, List<String>) using the platform’s preferences storage.
The asynchronous shared_preferences API: every get and set returns a Future and reads directly from platform storage.
A small SQL database stored in a single file on the device. sqflite is the Flutter plugin that uses it.
Create, read, update, delete: the four basic operations on stored data.
The number passed to openDatabase. Raising it runs onUpgrade so you can change tables without losing data.
Values passed separately from the SQL where clause (id = ?), so they are escaped safely.

lessons.examTip: Say “preferences for settings, a database for records, secure storage for secrets”. Then add: never put tokens or passwords in shared_preferences.

quiz.question: You need to remember whether the user chose dark mode. Which storage is the simplest good fit?
options: shared_preferences
A SQLite table with one row
A JSON file you parse by hand
Cloud Firestore
quiz.explanation: A single flag is exactly what key-value preferences are for. A database would work but adds schema and code for no benefit.

quiz.question: Why write db.delete('notes', where: 'id = ?', whereArgs: [id]) instead of building the string 'id = ' + id.toString()?
options: It runs faster on iOS only
Placeholders keep values separate from SQL, which prevents SQL injection and quoting bugs
sqflite does not accept strings in where
It deletes all rows
quiz.explanation: With ? placeholders, sqflite binds the values safely. Concatenating user input into SQL is a classic injection risk and breaks on quotes.

quiz.question: Version 2 of your app adds a pinned column to notes. Users already have version 1 installed. What should you do?
options: Delete the app’s data on every launch
Change the CREATE TABLE in onCreate only
Raise the version to 2 and add the column in onUpgrade
Create a second database file
quiz.explanation: onCreate only runs for fresh installs. Existing users get onUpgrade(oldVersion, newVersion), where you run ALTER TABLE to add the column.

quiz.question: After swiping a note away, Flutter reports that a dismissed Dismissible is still part of the tree. What is the fix?
options: Give each Dismissible the same key
Wait for the database delete, then call setState
Wrap the list in a FutureBuilder
Remove the item from the list with setState in onDismissed straight away, then delete it from the database
quiz.explanation: Dismissible expects its item to be removed in the same frame. Update the in-memory list synchronously, then let the async delete run.

lessons.title: Firebase setup and authentication
lessons.summaryHtml:
Firebase is Google’s app platform: authentication, the Cloud Firestore database, storage, analytics and more, without running your own server. You connect a Flutter app with the FlutterFire CLI: flutterfire configure generates firebase_options.dart, and Firebase.initializeApp starts it in main.

Firebase Authentication handles accounts. You register and sign in with email and password, turn FirebaseAuthException codes into friendly messages, and use the authStateChanges() stream to show the right screen automatically. This starts the Chat app you finish in lesson 7.5.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Building your own login system means storing passwords safely, sending reset emails, blocking brute-force attacks and keeping sessions alive. Firebase Authentication is a ready-made reception desk that does all of that. Your app asks it “please sign in this person” and it answers with a User or an error.

Firebase itself is a set of backend services from Google. Your app connects to a Firebase project, and then any service you enable (Auth now, Cloud Firestore in the next lesson) can be used from Dart.

Why it matters

Nearly every real app has accounts. Firebase lets a small team ship sign-in in an afternoon, and many startups and agencies use it for MVPs and production apps alike. Knowing the setup steps and the auth flow is a common requirement in junior Flutter job posts.

How it works

Setup, once per app

  1. In the Firebase console, create a project. Under Authentication, click Get started and enable the Email/Password sign-in method.
  2. Install the Firebase CLI and log in (firebase login), then install the FlutterFire CLI: dart pub global activate flutterfire_cli.
  3. In your project folder, add the packages: flutter pub add firebase_core firebase_auth.
  4. Run flutterfire configure. Choose the project and platforms. It registers the apps in Firebase and writes lib/firebase_options.dart plus platform config files.

Run flutterfire configure again when you add a platform or switch project. The values in firebase_options.dart identify your project; they are not a secret password. Your data is protected by security rules on the server (lesson 7.5), not by hiding this file.

Initialise in main

Future<void> main() async {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  await Firebase.initializeApp(options: DefaultFirebaseOptions.currentPlatform);
  runApp(ChatApp(auth: AuthRepository(FirebaseAuth.instance)));
}

ensureInitialized is needed because you await a plugin before runApp. Firebase plugins do not run in DartPad; use an emulator or device.

Wrap Firebase in a repository

Following lesson 6.5, widgets should not call FirebaseAuth.instance directly. A small AuthRepository hides it, so later you can add a bloc and test with a fake.

class AuthRepository {
  AuthRepository(this._auth);
  final FirebaseAuth _auth;

  Stream<User?> authStateChanges() => _auth.authStateChanges();

  Future<void> signIn(String email, String password) =>
      _auth.signInWithEmailAndPassword(email: email, password: password);

  Future<void> register(String email, String password) =>
      _auth.createUserWithEmailAndPassword(email: email, password: password);

  Future<void> signOut() => _auth.signOut();
}

Creating an account also signs the user in. Firebase keeps the session on the device, so users stay signed in after a restart until they sign out.

Errors: FirebaseAuthException codes

Every auth failure throws FirebaseAuthException. Its code is a short string. Map codes to messages in one place:

static String messageFor(FirebaseAuthException e) => switch (e.code) {
      'invalid-email' => 'That email address looks wrong.',
      'invalid-credential' || 'wrong-password' || 'user-not-found' =>
        'Wrong email or password.',
      'email-already-in-use' => 'An account already exists for that email.',
      'weak-password' => 'Choose a stronger password (at least 6 characters).',
      'too-many-requests' => 'Too many attempts. Try again later.',
      'network-request-failed' => 'No connection. Check your internet.',
      _ => 'Something went wrong. Please try again.',
    };

Newer projects have email enumeration protection on by default. It stops attackers from checking which emails have accounts, so a wrong email and a wrong password usually both come back as invalid-credential. Handle all three codes with one neutral message; never say “this email is not registered”.

authStateChanges: the auth gate

authStateChanges() emits the current user (or null) when you listen, then again on every sign-in and sign-out. Put a StreamBuilder at the top of the app and let it choose the screen. The sign-in page never navigates; it only calls the repository.

class _ChatAppState extends State<ChatApp> {
  late final Stream<User?> _authStream = widget.auth.authStateChanges();

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MaterialApp(
      home: StreamBuilder<User?>(
        stream: _authStream,
        builder: (context, snapshot) {
          if (snapshot.connectionState == ConnectionState.waiting) {
            return const Scaffold(body: Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator()));
          }
          final user = snapshot.data;
          return user == null
              ? SignInPage(auth: widget.auth)
              : HomePage(auth: widget.auth, user: user);
        },
      ),
    );
  }
}

There are two related streams: idTokenChanges() also fires when the token refreshes, and userChanges() also fires when profile data such as the display name changes. For an auth gate, authStateChanges() is enough. In a BLoC app, an AuthBloc would listen to this stream (with emit.forEach) and go_router could redirect based on its state.

More account features

Real sign-in screens usually add a “Forgot password?” link and email verification. Both are one call each. Firebase sends the emails from templates you can edit in the console under Authentication.

await FirebaseAuth.instance.sendPasswordResetEmail(email: email);

final user = FirebaseAuth.instance.currentUser;
if (user != null && !user.emailVerified) {
  await user.sendEmailVerification();
}

currentUser gives you the signed-in user synchronously, which is handy inside a button handler. Do not use it to decide which screen to show at start-up, though: right after launch Firebase may still be restoring the saved session, so it can be null for a moment. The authStateChanges() stream waits for that and then tells you the truth.

Also think about what happens to local data on sign-out. If a different person signs in on the same phone, they must not see the previous user’s cached chats or settings. Clear per-user storage when the stream emits null.

Example: Chat app, part 1

  1. Follow the setup steps, then start the app. The gate shows a spinner for a moment, then the sign-in page because no user is signed in.
  2. Enter an email and password and tap Sign in. The button shows a small spinner while busy. A wrong password shows the mapped message under the field.

    Screen 1: Sign in lib/main.dart

    Future<void> _submit() async {
  setState(() {
    _busy = true;
    _error = null;
  });
  final email = _email.text.trim();
  final password = _password.text;
  try {
    if (_register) {
      await widget.auth.register(email, password);
    } else {
      await widget.auth.signIn(email, password);
    }
  } on FirebaseAuthException catch (e) {
    if (mounted) setState(() => _error = AuthRepository.messageFor(e));
  } finally {
    if (mounted) setState(() => _busy = false);
  }
}

// in build
TextField(
  controller: _password,
  obscureText: true,
  decoration: InputDecoration(
    labelText: 'Password',
    prefixIcon: const Icon(Icons.lock_outline),
    errorText: _error,
  ),
),
FilledButton(
  onPressed: _busy ? null : _submit,
  child: _busy
      ? const SizedBox.square(dimension: 20,
          child: CircularProgressIndicator(strokeWidth: 2))
      : Text(action),
),

    The error comes from FirebaseAuthException.code mapped to a friendly message and shown as the field’s errorText. States: Empty → Busy → Wrong password.

  3. Tap “Create an account” to switch the same form into register mode. A 5-character password returns weak-password.

    Screen 2: Create account lib/main.dart

    static String messageFor(FirebaseAuthException e) => switch (e.code) {
      'invalid-email' => 'That email address looks wrong.',
      'invalid-credential' || 'wrong-password' || 'user-not-found' =>
        'Wrong email or password.',
      'email-already-in-use' => 'An account already exists for that email.',
      'weak-password' => 'Choose a stronger password (at least 6 characters).',
      'too-many-requests' => 'Too many attempts. Try again later.',
      'network-request-failed' => 'No connection. Check your internet.',
      _ => 'Something went wrong. Please try again.',
    };

// the toggle under the button
TextButton(
  onPressed: _busy ? null : () => setState(() => _register = !_register),
  child: Text(_register ? 'I already have an account' : 'Create an account'),
),

    The same form in register mode; weak-password and email-already-in-use get their own messages.

  4. A successful sign-up signs the user in. authStateChanges() emits the User, the gate shows HomePage, and the new account appears in the console under Authentication, Users. The logout button calls signOut, the stream emits null and the sign-in page returns.

Screen 3: Signed in lib/main.dart

StreamBuilder<User?>(
  stream: _authStream, // widget.auth.authStateChanges(), created once
  builder: (context, snapshot) {
    if (snapshot.connectionState == ConnectionState.waiting) {
      return const Scaffold(body: Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator()));
    }
    final user = snapshot.data;
    return user == null
        ? SignInPage(auth: widget.auth)
        : HomePage(auth: widget.auth, user: user);
  },
)

// HomePage.build
final email = user.email ?? 'unknown';
Scaffold(
  appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Chat'), actions: [
    IconButton(tooltip: 'Sign out', icon: const Icon(Icons.logout),
        onPressed: auth.signOut),
  ]),
  body: Center(
    child: Column(mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min, children: [
      CircleAvatar(radius: 32, child: Text(email[0].toUpperCase())),
      const SizedBox(height: 12),
      Text('Signed in as $email'),
      const SizedBox(height: 4),
      Text('Messages arrive in lesson 7.5',
          style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.bodySmall),
    ]),
  ),
)

authStateChanges() emitted a User, so the StreamBuilder shows HomePage; the logout button emits null and returns to sign-in.

Keep testing in mind from the start. Because every widget receives an AuthRepository, a widget test can pass a fake one whose stream emits a user straight away, and check that HomePage appears, without any Firebase project. Firebase also offers a local Emulator Suite, so you can try sign-up flows without creating real accounts in your production project.

Common mistakes

  • Using Firebase before initializeApp completes. Always await it in main.
  • Forgetting to enable the provider. If Email/Password is off in the console, sign-in fails with an “operation not allowed” style error.
  • Navigating after sign-in. Pushing HomePage manually leaves the sign-in page underneath and breaks sign-out. Let the auth stream decide.
  • Calling setState after the page is gone. On success the gate removes the sign-in page, so check mounted before updating state.
  • Showing raw error codes. Users should never see invalid-credential. Map codes to plain sentences.
  • Creating the auth stream in build. Store it once, as in lesson 7.2.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Be ready to explain the auth gate pattern and why it beats manual navigation.
  • Know the other common features: sendPasswordResetEmail, user.sendEmailVerification(), updateDisplayName, and social sign-in providers.
  • Authentication says who the user is; security rules say what they may read and write. You need both.
  • Many teams keep separate Firebase projects for development and production, linked through build flavors (lesson 8.5).
  • For testing, depend on AuthRepository, not FirebaseAuth. A fake repository lets widget and bloc tests run without a network.

lessons.title: Cloud Firestore and real-time data
lessons.summaryHtml: Cloud Firestore is Firebase’s NoSQL document database. Data lives in documents (sets of fields) grouped into collections, and a document can hold its own subcollections. You can read data once with get() or listen with snapshots(), which pushes a fresh result every time the data changes, on every device. In this lesson the Chat app gets real-time messages: a typed Message model with withConverter, a query ordered by a server timestamp, a StreamBuilder that shows loading, empty, live and sending states, and security rules that decide who may read and write.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Cloud Firestore is a database that lives in Google’s cloud and talks directly to your Flutter app. It is a NoSQL document database: there are no tables with fixed columns. Instead you store documents, and each document is a small set of named fields, a bit like a Dart Map. Documents live inside collections, and a document can hold its own collections, called subcollections.

Think of a set of folders. The rooms folder holds one card per chat room. Each room card has its own messages folder inside it, with one card per message. You find any card by its path, such as rooms/general/messages/abc123.

The special part is real time. Instead of asking “give me the messages” once, your app can say “keep me posted”. Firestore then pushes a new result to every listening device the moment anything changes. That is how a chat message typed on one phone appears on another phone a moment later, with no refresh button.

Why it matters

Many apps need shared, live data: chat, order tracking, a team task board, a live score. Building that yourself means a server, a database, WebSockets, authentication and offline handling. Firestore gives you all of that as a managed service, and the FlutterFire plugin cloud_firestore exposes it as ordinary Dart Futures and Streams, which you already know from module f1.

It also works offline. On Android and iOS, Firestore keeps a local cache by default. Writes made offline show up in the UI at once and are sent when the connection returns. For users on patchy mobile data, that alone makes an app feel far more reliable.

In job terms, Firebase is common in start-ups and agency projects because a small team can ship a backend fast. Knowing how to model data, query it, secure it and keep reads under control is exactly what a junior Flutter developer is expected to handle.

How it works

Data model: collections, documents, fields

A document has an id (you choose it, or Firestore generates one) and fields. Field values can be strings, numbers, booleans, null, maps, arrays, Timestamps, geo points and references to other documents. A collection contains only documents, and a document can contain subcollections.

SQL ideaFirestore ideaChat app example
TableCollectionrooms
RowDocumentrooms/general
ColumnField (no fixed schema)name, members, updatedAt
Child table with a foreign keySubcollectionrooms/general/messages
JOINNo joins: copy the data you need (denormalise)lastMessage copied onto the room

The golden rule is to design for your screens. The rooms list needs each room’s name and latest message, so we store lastMessage on the room document too. That duplicates a little data, but the rooms screen reads one document per room instead of scanning messages.

Set it up by creating a Firestore database in the Firebase console for the project you connected in lesson 7.4, then run flutter pub add cloud_firestore. The entry point is FirebaseFirestore.instance.

Writing data

final db = FirebaseFirestore.instance;
final room = db.collection('rooms').doc('general');

// Create or overwrite a whole document with a known id.
await room.set({'name': 'General', 'members': [uid], 'updatedAt': FieldValue.serverTimestamp()});

// Add a document with a generated id.
await room.collection('messages').add({'text': 'Hi!', 'senderId': uid, 'createdAt': FieldValue.serverTimestamp()});

// Change some fields; fails if the document does not exist.
await room.update({'members': FieldValue.arrayUnion([otherUid])});

// Merge: create if missing, otherwise change only these fields.
await room.set({'lastMessage': 'Hi!'}, SetOptions(merge: true));

await room.delete(); // note: this does NOT delete its subcollections

FieldValue has server-side helpers: serverTimestamp(), increment(1), arrayUnion and arrayRemove. Use a batch (db.batch()) when several writes must succeed or fail together, and a transaction (db.runTransaction) when a write depends on a value you must read first, such as a stock count.

Typed models with withConverter

Raw maps mean string keys and casts everywhere. withConverter puts that conversion in one place, so the rest of the app works with a real class.

class Message {
  const Message({required this.text, required this.senderId, required this.senderName, this.createdAt});
  final String text;
  final String senderId;
  final String senderName;
  final DateTime? createdAt; // null while the server time is still pending

  factory Message.fromFirestore(DocumentSnapshot<Map<String, dynamic>> doc, SnapshotOptions? options) {
    final data = doc.data() ?? const <String, dynamic>{};
    return Message(
      text: data['text'] as String? ?? '',
      senderId: data['senderId'] as String? ?? '',
      senderName: data['senderName'] as String? ?? 'Guest',
      createdAt: (data['createdAt'] as Timestamp?)?.toDate(),
    );
  }

  Map<String, Object?> toFirestore() => {
        'text': text,
        'senderId': senderId,
        'senderName': senderName,
        'createdAt': FieldValue.serverTimestamp(),
      };
}

Notice createdAt is nullable. When you write a server timestamp, the local copy has no time yet, so the first snapshot delivers null for that field. Code that does createdAt! will crash on your own freshly sent message.

Reading once versus listening

CallReturnsUse it for
doc.get() / query.get()Future of one snapshotData that rarely changes: a profile screen, a settings document
doc.snapshots() / query.snapshots()Stream of snapshotsLive data: chat, order status, a shared list

A QuerySnapshot has docs (the current result), docChanges (what was added, modified or removed since the last snapshot) and metadata. Each document’s metadata.hasPendingWrites is true while a local write has not reached the server yet, which is perfect for a “Sending…” label.

In Flutter, show a stream with StreamBuilder. Create the stream once, in initState or in a repository, never inside build().

Screen 1: Live chat room lib/chat_page.dart

class ChatPage extends StatefulWidget {
  const ChatPage({super.key, required this.roomId});
  final String roomId;

  @override
  State<ChatPage> createState() => _ChatPageState();
}

class _ChatPageState extends State<ChatPage> {
  late final Stream<QuerySnapshot<Message>> _messages;

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    // Build the query ONCE. A new stream in build() restarts the listener.
    _messages = FirebaseFirestore.instance
        .collection('rooms').doc(widget.roomId).collection('messages')
        .withConverter<Message>(
          fromFirestore: Message.fromFirestore,
          toFirestore: (m, _) => m.toFirestore(),
        )
        .orderBy('createdAt', descending: true)
        .limit(50)
        .snapshots();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final me = FirebaseAuth.instance.currentUser!.uid;
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('General')),
      body: Column(children: [
        Expanded(
          child: StreamBuilder<QuerySnapshot<Message>>(
            stream: _messages,
            builder: (context, snap) {
              if (snap.hasError) return Center(child: Text('Error: ' + snap.error.toString()));
              if (!snap.hasData) return const Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator());
              final docs = snap.data!.docs;
              if (docs.isEmpty) return const Center(child: Text('No messages yet. Say hi!'));
              return ListView.builder(
                reverse: true, // index 0 (newest) sits at the bottom
                padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12),
                itemCount: docs.length,
                itemBuilder: (context, i) => MessageBubble(
                  message: docs[i].data(),
                  mine: docs[i].data().senderId == me,
                  pending: docs[i].metadata.hasPendingWrites,
                ),
              );
            },
          ),
        ),
        Composer(roomId: widget.roomId),
      ]),
    );
  }
}

One StreamBuilder drives four states. Notice the grey “Sending…” line: the message shows instantly from the local cache while the server write is still pending. States: Loading → Empty → Live → Sending.

The list uses reverse: true. The query returns the newest message first, and a reversed list draws item 0 at the bottom, so the newest message sits just above the text field and the list starts scrolled to the end, just like a messaging app.

Queries and indexes

Queries combine where filters (isEqualTo, isGreaterThan, arrayContains, whereIn and more), orderBy, limit, and cursors such as startAfterDocument for paging. Firestore indexes every single field automatically. A query that filters on one field and sorts by another needs a composite index. The first time you run it, the error message in the debug console contains a link that creates the index for you.

Screen 2: Rooms list from a query lib/rooms_page.dart

class RoomsPage extends StatefulWidget {
  const RoomsPage({super.key});

  @override
  State<RoomsPage> createState() => _RoomsPageState();
}

class _RoomsPageState extends State<RoomsPage> {
  final _uid = FirebaseAuth.instance.currentUser!.uid;
  late final Stream<QuerySnapshot<Map<String, dynamic>>> _rooms =
      FirebaseFirestore.instance
          .collection('rooms')
          .where('members', arrayContains: _uid)
          .orderBy('updatedAt', descending: true)
          .snapshots();

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Chats')),
      body: StreamBuilder(
        stream: _rooms,
        builder: (context, snap) {
          if (!snap.hasData) {
            return const Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator());
          }
          final rooms = snap.data!.docs;
          return ListView.separated(
            itemCount: rooms.length,
            separatorBuilder: (_, __) => const Divider(height: 1),
            itemBuilder: (context, i) {
              final data = rooms[i].data();
              final name = data['name'] as String? ?? 'Room';
              return ListTile(
                leading: CircleAvatar(child: Text(name[0])),
                title: Text(name),
                subtitle: Text(data['lastMessage'] as String? ?? ''),
                trailing: const Icon(Icons.chevron_right),
                onTap: () => Navigator.of(context).push(MaterialPageRoute(
                  builder: (_) => ChatPage(roomId: rooms[i].id),
                )),
              );
            },
          );
        },
      ),
    );
  }
}

The list only contains rooms whose members array includes the signed-in user, newest activity first. This where + orderBy pair needs a composite index.

There is no full-text search and no LIKE '%word%'. If you need search, you usually add a search service later. Plan queries before you plan data.

Security rules basics

Your app talks to the database directly, so anyone can extract your project config. Security rules are the real gatekeeper. They run on Google’s servers for every read and write. Everything is denied unless a rule allows it.

rules_version = '2';
service cloud.firestore {
  match /databases/{database}/documents {
    match /rooms/{roomId} {
      allow read, write: if request.auth != null; // the batch also updates the room
    }
    match /rooms/{roomId}/messages/{messageId} {
      allow read: if request.auth != null;
      allow create: if request.auth != null
        && request.resource.data.senderId == request.auth.uid
        && request.resource.data.text is string
        && request.resource.data.text.size() > 0
        && request.resource.data.text.size() <= 500
        && request.resource.data.createdAt == request.time;
      allow update, delete: if false;
    }
  }
}

request.auth is the signed-in user, request.resource.data is the document as it would look after the write, and resource.data is the document as it is now. The last line forces clients to use serverTimestamp(), so nobody can backdate a message. When a write breaks a rule, the local copy disappears and the Future fails with a FirebaseException whose code is permission-denied.

Screen 3: Security rules reject a write lib/composer.dart

Future<void> _send() async {
  final text = _controller.text.trim();
  if (text.isEmpty) return;
  final user = FirebaseAuth.instance.currentUser!;
  final db = FirebaseFirestore.instance;
  final room = db.collection('rooms').doc(widget.roomId);
  final messages = room.collection('messages').withConverter<Message>(
        fromFirestore: Message.fromFirestore,
        toFirestore: (m, _) => m.toFirestore(),
      );

  final batch = db.batch()
    ..set(messages.doc(), Message(
      text: text,
      senderId: user.uid,
      senderName: user.displayName ?? 'Guest',
    ))
    ..set(room, {
      'lastMessage': text,
      'updatedAt': FieldValue.serverTimestamp(),
    }, SetOptions(merge: true));

  _controller.clear(); // do not wait: the local cache shows it at once
  try {
    await batch.commit();
  } on FirebaseException catch (e) {
    if (!mounted) return;
    final msg = e.code == 'permission-denied'
        ? 'Not sent: messages must be 1 to 500 characters.'
        : 'Not sent: ' + e.code;
    ScaffoldMessenger.of(context)
        .showSnackBar(SnackBar(content: Text(msg)));
  }
}

The rules allow messages of 1 to 500 characters. A longer one is shown locally for a moment, then removed, and the commit fails with permission-denied, which the app turns into a SnackBar.

Example: Chat app real-time messages

  1. Keep the sign-in flow from lesson 7.4. Once a user is signed in, open ChatPage(roomId: 'general').
  2. Add the Message model above, with fromFirestore and toFirestore.
  3. In ChatPage.initState, build the query: rooms/general/messages, withConverter, orderBy('createdAt', descending: true), limit(50), snapshots().
  4. In build, a StreamBuilder shows an error text, a spinner, an empty message, or a reversed ListView.builder of bubbles. Mine go right in the primary container colour; others go left with the sender’s name.
  5. The composer sends with a batch: set a new message document and set the room’s lastMessage and updatedAt with merge: true.
  6. Clear the text field before awaiting commit(). The snapshot listener already shows the message from the local cache; the await only finishes when the server confirms.
  7. Publish the rules and test with two devices: one on the emulator, one on the web or a phone.

Common mistakes

  • Creating the stream in build(). Every rebuild starts a new listener, the screen flashes back to loading, and you may pay for the initial reads again.
  • Leaving test-mode rules in place. Test mode allows everyone to read and write for a limited time. Replace it with real rules before anyone else uses the app.
  • Using DateTime.now() for ordering. Device clocks drift. Use FieldValue.serverTimestamp() and handle the null it gives in the first local snapshot.
  • Unbounded queries. Listening to a whole collection without limit reads every document. Firestore bills per document read, so always limit and page.
  • One giant document. A document has a 1 MiB size limit and is always read whole. Growing lists (messages, orders) belong in a subcollection.
  • Treating rules as filters. A query that could return a document the user may not read is rejected as a whole. Add the matching where clause to the query.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Expect “How would you model a chat in Firestore?” Answer with rooms, a messages subcollection, a server timestamp, a limited query and denormalised lastMessage.
  • Explain get() versus snapshots() and when you would use each. Mention that listeners should be cancelled when a screen closes; StreamBuilder does that for you.
  • In a BLoC architecture, wrap Firestore in a repository that exposes Stream<List<Message>>. In the Bloc, emit.forEach turns each stream event into a state. Widgets never import cloud_firestore.
  • Know that rules validate data on the server. Client-side validation is for user experience; rules are for security. Heavier logic, such as sending push notifications, usually goes in Cloud Functions.
  • Mention offline support and hasPendingWrites: interviewers like candidates who think about bad networks.

terms.definition: A named group of documents, such as rooms or messages. It holds no data of its own.
A record with an id and fields (strings, numbers, maps, arrays, timestamps). It can contain subcollections.
Returns a Stream that emits a new snapshot whenever the query result or document changes.
A placeholder the server replaces with its own time when the write arrives, so clocks on phones do not matter.
Wraps a reference or query so reads return your model class and writes accept it, instead of raw maps.
Server-side rules that allow or deny each read and write, based on the signed-in user and the data.

lessons.examTip: Interviewers like “rules are not filters”: a query must only ask for documents the rules allow, or the whole query fails with permission-denied.

quiz.question: Your chat screen creates the Firestore query inside build(). What is the main problem?
options: build() cannot return a StreamBuilder
Each rebuild creates a new stream, so the listener restarts and flickers back to loading
Firestore streams only work in initState()
Queries created in build() ignore security rules
quiz.explanation: A new query object gives StreamBuilder a new stream, so it unsubscribes and resubscribes. Create the stream once (initState or a repository) and reuse it.

quiz.question: Why use FieldValue.serverTimestamp() for createdAt instead of DateTime.now()?
options: DateTime values cannot be stored in Firestore
It is cheaper to write
Phone clocks can be wrong, so ordering by server time keeps messages in the real order
It makes the field required by the rules
quiz.explanation: The server fills in its own time when the write arrives. Device clocks can be off by minutes, which would scramble the message order.

quiz.question: A query asks for all messages in a room, but the rules only allow reading messages the user sent. What happens?
options: The query fails with permission-denied
The query returns only the allowed messages
The query returns everything because reads are always allowed
The app crashes at compile time
quiz.explanation: Rules are not filters. Firestore checks whether the query could return a forbidden document; if so, the whole query is rejected.

quiz.question: A room stores every message in one array field. What is the best reason to move messages to a subcollection?
options: Arrays cannot hold strings
Subcollections are free to read
Arrays are sorted randomly
A document has a size limit and is read in full, so one ever-growing document becomes slow, costly and eventually impossible
quiz.explanation: A document has a maximum size of 1 MiB and is always read whole. A messages subcollection lets you query, page and listen to only the newest messages.

lessons.title: Animations
lessons.summaryHtml: Flutter has two families of animation. Implicit widgets such as AnimatedContainer, AnimatedOpacity and AnimatedSwitcher animate on their own whenever a property changes: you just call setState with a new value. Explicit animations use an AnimationController with a Tween and a Curve, so you decide when to start, stop, reverse or repeat, and you feed the result into widgets like FadeTransition, SlideTransition or AnimatedBuilder. A Hero flies a shared widget from one screen to the next. You will combine all three in an Onboarding app with swipeable slides, animated page dots and a hero hand-off to the home screen.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

An animation is just a value that changes a little on every frame. A box that is 140 pixels wide now and 240 pixels wide 400 milliseconds later looks like it grows, because Flutter draws every step in between. Your job is to say what changes, how long it takes and how the speed feels (the curve). Flutter does the frame-by-frame work.

Think of a dimmer switch versus a light switch. setState alone is a light switch: the UI jumps from one state to the next. An animation is a dimmer: the same change, spread over time, so the eye can follow it.

Flutter gives you two tools. Implicit animations are “set and forget”: you change a property, and the widget animates to it. Explicit animations give you a remote control, an AnimationController, that you start, stop, reverse and repeat yourself.

Why it matters

Good motion is not decoration. It tells users what happened: a card that expands shows where the details came from, a page that slides shows which way to go back, and a button label that fades from “Next” to “Get started” signals that the next tap is different. Apps without motion feel abrupt, and apps with too much motion feel slow.

Clients often ask for “something like the onboarding in app X”. Knowing which tool to pick, and doing it without jank or leaked controllers, is a real junior-level skill that shows up in take-home tests and code reviews.

How it works

Implicit animations

Every widget named AnimatedSomething is implicit. You give it a duration and optionally a curve. When a rebuild gives it a new value, it animates from the old value to the new one.

WidgetAnimatesTypical use
AnimatedContainerSize, padding, colour, decoration, alignmentExpanding cards, selected states
AnimatedOpacityOpacityFade a hint or label in and out
AnimatedAlign, AnimatedPadding, AnimatedPositionedPositionMoving an element inside a layout or a Stack
AnimatedSwitcherReplaces one child with another (fade by default)Swapping a label, an icon, or loading and content
AnimatedCrossFadeCross-fades between two given childrenCollapsed versus expanded views
TweenAnimationBuilderAny value you can tweenA custom property with no ready-made widget

Screen 1: Implicit: AnimatedContainer lib/main.dart

class GrowBox extends StatefulWidget {
  const GrowBox({super.key});

  @override
  State<GrowBox> createState() => _GrowBoxState();
}

class _GrowBoxState extends State<GrowBox> {
  bool _open = false;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final scheme = Theme.of(context).colorScheme;
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Implicit animation')),
      body: Center(
        child: Column(mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min, children: [
          GestureDetector(
            onTap: () => setState(() => _open = !_open),
            child: AnimatedContainer(
              duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 400),
              curve: Curves.easeOutCubic,
              width: _open ? 240 : 140,
              height: _open ? 180 : 90,
              padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
              decoration: BoxDecoration(
                color: _open ? scheme.primary : scheme.primaryContainer,
                borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(_open ? 28 : 12),
              ),
              child: AnimatedOpacity(
                opacity: _open ? 1 : 0,
                duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 300),
                child: Text('Tap again to close',
                    style: TextStyle(color: scheme.onPrimary)),
              ),
            ),
          ),
          const SizedBox(height: 16),
          const Text('Tap the box'),
        ]),
      ),
    );
  }
}

One bool in setState changes size, colour and corner radius; AnimatedContainer tweens between them over 400 ms. The middle frame is a moment during the animation. States: Closed → Mid-animation → Open.

Notice there is no controller and no dispose. The state is one bool. That is why implicit widgets should be your first choice.

AnimatedSwitcher needs one extra detail: it decides whether the child is “new” by comparing the type and key. Swapping Text('Next') for Text('Get started') looks like the same widget, so nothing animates. Give each child a key, for example Text(label, key: ValueKey(label)).

Explicit animations: controller, tween, curve

An explicit animation has three parts that snap together:

  • AnimationController produces a number from 0.0 to 1.0 over a duration. You call forward(), reverse(), repeat(), stop() or forward(from: 0).
  • CurvedAnimation reshapes that 0–1 progress with a Curve, such as Curves.easeOutCubic (fast start, gentle stop) or Curves.elasticOut (overshoots, then settles).
  • Tween maps 0–1 onto real values: Tween(begin: 0.8, end: 1.0) for a scale, or Tween(begin: Offset(0, 0.5), end: Offset.zero) for a slide. tween.animate(parent) gives you an Animation<T>.

The controller needs a vsync, which is a TickerProvider. Add SingleTickerProviderStateMixin to your State (or TickerProviderStateMixin if you have several controllers) and pass this. The ticker fires once per frame and is muted when the widget is not visible. Always call dispose() on the controller: it leaks otherwise, and if it is still running when the widget is removed, Flutter reports that the State “was disposed with an active Ticker”.

Screen 2: Explicit: controller, tween, curve lib/main.dart

class WelcomeBanner extends StatefulWidget {
  const WelcomeBanner({super.key});

  @override
  State<WelcomeBanner> createState() => _WelcomeBannerState();
}

class _WelcomeBannerState extends State<WelcomeBanner>
    with SingleTickerProviderStateMixin {
  late final AnimationController _controller = AnimationController(
    vsync: this, // ticks only while this widget is visible
    duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 800),
  );
  late final Animation<double> _curve =
      CurvedAnimation(parent: _controller, curve: Curves.easeOutCubic);
  late final Animation<Offset> _slide =
      Tween(begin: const Offset(0, 0.5), end: Offset.zero).animate(_curve);

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    _controller.forward();
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _controller.dispose(); // always dispose controllers
    super.dispose();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final theme = Theme.of(context);
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Explicit animation')),
      body: Center(
        child: Column(mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min, children: [
          FadeTransition(
            opacity: _curve,
            child: SlideTransition(
              position: _slide,
              child: Column(children: [
                Icon(Icons.waving_hand,
                    size: 64, color: theme.colorScheme.primary),
                Text('Welcome back!', style: theme.textTheme.headlineSmall),
              ]),
            ),
          ),
          const SizedBox(height: 24),
          FilledButton.tonal(
            onPressed: () => _controller.forward(from: 0),
            child: const Text('Replay'),
          ),
        ]),
      ),
    );
  }
}

The controller runs from 0 to 1 in 800 ms; the curve shapes the pace; FadeTransition and SlideTransition read the values without calling setState. Replay restarts it from 0. States: t = 0.0 → t = 0.3 → t = 1.0.

To show an animation, prefer the ready-made transition widgets: FadeTransition, SlideTransition, ScaleTransition, RotationTransition, SizeTransition. They listen to the animation and repaint only what they need, without calling setState. For anything else, use AnimatedBuilder:

AnimatedBuilder(
  animation: _controller,
  child: const Icon(Icons.sync, size: 48), // built once, reused every frame
  builder: (context, child) => Transform.rotate(
    angle: _controller.value * 2 * math.pi, // needs import 'dart:math' as math;
    child: child,
  ),
)

The child parameter is a performance trick: the part that does not change is built once and passed into every frame.

Hero: shared elements between screens

Wrap a widget on the first route in Hero(tag: 'x', child: ...) and a widget on the second route in a Hero with the same tag. When you push or pop, Flutter lifts the widget into an overlay and flies it from one position and size to the other. Tags must be unique on each screen, so use an id, not a constant, in lists.

Screen 3: Hero: shared element between routes lib/main.dart

class Plant {
  const Plant(this.name, this.color);
  final String name;
  final Color color;
}

class PlantGrid extends StatelessWidget {
  const PlantGrid({super.key, required this.plants});
  final List<Plant> plants;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Plants')),
      body: GridView.count(
        crossAxisCount: 2,
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12),
        mainAxisSpacing: 12,
        crossAxisSpacing: 12,
        children: [
          for (final p in plants)
            GestureDetector(
              onTap: () => Navigator.of(context).push(MaterialPageRoute(
                  builder: (_) => PlantDetail(plant: p))),
              child: Column(children: [
                Expanded(child: Hero(tag: p.name, child: _Tile(p, 40))),
                Text(p.name),
              ]),
            ),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}

class PlantDetail extends StatelessWidget {
  const PlantDetail({super.key, required this.plant});
  final Plant plant;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) => Scaffold(
        appBar: AppBar(title: Text(plant.name)),
        body: Column(crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.stretch, children: [
          SizedBox(height: 220, child: Hero(tag: plant.name, child: _Tile(plant, 96))),
          const Padding(padding: EdgeInsets.all(16), child: Text('Water once a week. Bright, indirect light.')),
        ]),
      );
}

class _Tile extends StatelessWidget {
  const _Tile(this.plant, this.iconSize);
  final Plant plant;
  final double iconSize;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) => Container(
        decoration: BoxDecoration(color: plant.color, borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(16)),
        child: Center(child: Icon(Icons.local_florist, size: iconSize)),
      );
}

Both routes wrap the coloured tile in a Hero with the same tag (the plant name). On push, Flutter flies the tile from its grid cell to the top of the detail screen. States: Grid → Detail.

Choosing a tool

You needUse
A property changes in response to stateAn Animated... implicit widget
Swap one widget for anotherAnimatedSwitcher with keys
Play on screen open, repeat, reverse, chain or staggerAnimationController + transitions
Follow a finger (drag to dismiss)Controller whose value you set from the gesture
Element travels between routesHero
Custom route transitionPageRouteBuilder with transitionsBuilder

Example: Onboarding app

The Onboarding app shows three slides (Discover, Plan, Grow), then opens a home screen.

  1. A PageView.builder with a PageController holds the slides. onPageChanged stores the current page in state.
  2. Three page dots are AnimatedContainers. The active one is 24 pixels wide, the others 8, so the pill slides as you swipe.
  3. The main button calls _pager.nextPage(duration: ..., curve: Curves.easeOutCubic). On the last slide its label changes to “Get started” through an AnimatedSwitcher with a ValueKey.
  4. Each slide is a small StatefulWidget with its own controller. When it is built, the icon scales in with Curves.elasticOut and the text slides up and fades in.
  5. “Get started” pushes the home screen with pushReplacement and a PageRouteBuilder that fades. The last slide’s icon and the home app bar’s icon share Hero(tag: 'logo'), so the logo flies into place.

Screen 4: Onboarding app lib/onboarding_page.dart

@override
Widget build(BuildContext context) {
  final scheme = Theme.of(context).colorScheme;
  return Scaffold(
    body: SafeArea(
      child: Column(children: [
        Align(
          alignment: Alignment.centerRight,
          child: TextButton(
            onPressed: _isLast ? null : _skip,
            child: const Text('Skip'),
          ),
        ),
        Expanded(
          child: PageView.builder(
            controller: _pager,
            itemCount: slides.length,
            onPageChanged: (i) => setState(() => _page = i),
            itemBuilder: (context, i) => SlideView(slide: slides[i]),
          ),
        ),
        Row(mainAxisAlignment: MainAxisAlignment.center, children: [
          for (var i = 0; i < slides.length; i++)
            AnimatedContainer(
              duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 250),
              margin: const EdgeInsets.symmetric(horizontal: 4),
              width: i == _page ? 24 : 8,
              height: 8,
              decoration: BoxDecoration(
                color: i == _page ? scheme.primary : scheme.outlineVariant,
                borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(4),
              ),
            ),
        ]),
        Padding(
          padding: const EdgeInsets.all(24),
          child: SizedBox(
            width: double.infinity,
            child: FilledButton(
              onPressed: _next,
              child: AnimatedSwitcher(
                duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 200),
                child: Text(_isLast ? 'Get started' : 'Next',
                    key: ValueKey(_isLast)),
              ),
            ),
          ),
        ),
      ]),
    ),
  );
}

A PageView of slides. The dots are AnimatedContainers (the active one is wider), and the button label cross-fades from Next to Get started with an AnimatedSwitcher. States: Slide 1 → Slide 2 → Last slide.

void _next() {
  if (_isLast) {
    Navigator.of(context).pushReplacement(PageRouteBuilder(
      transitionDuration: const Duration(milliseconds: 600),
      pageBuilder: (_, __, ___) => const HomePage(),
      transitionsBuilder: (_, animation, __, child) =>
          FadeTransition(opacity: animation, child: child),
    ));
  } else {
    _pager.nextPage(
      duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 350),
      curve: Curves.easeOutCubic,
    );
  }
}

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting dispose() on an AnimationController. The controller leaks, and if it is still running when the widget is removed, Flutter reports an error about an active Ticker.
  • Calling setState in a controller listener to rebuild the whole screen every frame. Use a transition widget or AnimatedBuilder so only the animated part rebuilds.
  • Creating the controller in build(). Every rebuild makes a new controller that restarts the animation and leaks the old one. Create it in initState or a late final field.
  • No keys on AnimatedSwitcher children, so it never animates.
  • Duplicate Hero tags on one screen, for example a constant tag inside a list. Flutter throws an error about multiple heroes sharing a tag.
  • Overdoing it. Most UI motion lasts roughly 150 to 500 milliseconds. Long, bouncy animations on every tap make the app feel slow.

Interview and real-world notes

  • A classic question: “Implicit versus explicit animations?” Answer: implicit animates property changes automatically and needs no controller; explicit uses an AnimationController for full control over timing and playback.
  • Be ready to explain vsync and why SingleTickerProviderStateMixin exists: it ties ticks to frames and pauses off-screen animations.
  • Respect accessibility. Some users turn off animations in system settings. MediaQuery.disableAnimationsOf(context) tells you, so you can shorten or skip decorative motion.
  • Animate cheap properties (opacity, transforms) where you can, and profile on a real device in profile mode, which lesson 8.4 covers.
  • Designers may hand you vector animation files made in tools like After Effects. Third-party packages can play them; the controller concepts you learned here still apply.

terms.definition: A widget such as AnimatedContainer that animates from its old value to its new value whenever you rebuild it with different properties.
An object that produces values from 0.0 to 1.0 over a duration, which you can forward, reverse, repeat or stop.
Maps the controller’s 0.0–1.0 range onto the values you need, such as 0.0 to 1.0 opacity or an Offset.
A function that changes the pace of an animation, such as Curves.easeOutCubic (fast then slow) or Curves.elasticOut (overshoot).
Links a controller to the screen refresh, so the animation only ticks while its widget is visible. Usually SingleTickerProviderStateMixin.
A widget that animates between two routes when both contain a Hero with the same tag.
