quiz.question: You want a card to smoothly grow and change colour when the user taps it, and nothing else. What is the simplest correct tool?
options: An AnimationController with a Tween for each property
A Timer that calls setState every 16 ms
AnimatedContainer with new width, height and colour set in setState
A Hero widget
quiz.explanation: Implicit widgets are made for this: change the properties in setState and AnimatedContainer animates from the old values to the new ones.

quiz.question: Why do you pass vsync: this to an AnimationController?
options: So the controller ticks in step with frames and pauses when its widget is not on screen
So the animation runs on a background isolate
So the animation can use a Curve
So the widget rebuilds without setState
quiz.explanation: vsync connects the controller to a Ticker. The TickerProvider mixin (SingleTickerProviderStateMixin) mutes the ticker when the widget is not visible, which saves battery.

quiz.question: An AnimatedSwitcher that swaps two Text widgets shows no animation. What is the usual fix?
options: Wrap it in a Hero
Increase the duration to 2 seconds
Use AnimatedOpacity instead of Text
Give each child a different key, such as ValueKey(label)
quiz.explanation: AnimatedSwitcher compares the old and new child by type and key. Two Text widgets without keys look like the same widget, so it only updates the text instead of cross-fading.

quiz.question: A Hero animation does not run when you push the detail screen. What is the most likely cause?
options: Hero only works with named routes
The two Hero widgets have different tags
Hero needs an AnimationController
The detail screen is a StatelessWidget
quiz.explanation: Flutter pairs Heroes on the old and new route by tag. The tags must be equal (and unique on each screen) for the flight to happen.

lessons.title: Device features and plugins
lessons.summaryHtml: Flutter draws the UI itself, but cameras, photo libraries, sensors and battery data belong to Android and iOS. Plugins bridge that gap: a Dart API on top, with native code for each platform underneath. You will use image_picker to take or choose a photo, learn how permissions work on each platform (Info.plist usage strings on iOS, the manifest and runtime prompts on Android), and see how a platform channel (MethodChannel) sends a message from Dart to Kotlin or Swift and back. The mini app is a Profile Photo screen with a source picker sheet and a battery tile.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Flutter paints every pixel of your UI itself, which is why the same code looks the same on Android and iOS. But the camera, the photo library, the battery, GPS and notifications belong to the operating system. Dart cannot touch them directly.

A plugin is the translator. It is a package with a friendly Dart API on top and native code underneath: Kotlin or Java for Android, Swift or Objective-C for iOS, JavaScript for the web. You call pickImage() in Dart; the plugin opens the real system photo picker and hands the chosen file back.

Think of an embassy. Your app speaks Dart. The operating system speaks Kotlin or Swift. A plugin is the embassy staff who pass messages between the two and translate the answers. A platform channel is the phone line they use, and you can install your own line when no plugin exists.

Why it matters

Almost every real app needs at least one device feature: a profile photo, a scanned receipt, a map pin, a phone call button, a push notification. Clients also ask for features with no ready-made plugin, such as talking to a custom Bluetooth device or a vendor SDK. Knowing how plugins, permissions and channels fit together lets you pick good packages, set up each platform correctly, and fall back gracefully when something is not available.

Permissions are also where apps get rejected or crash. A missing iOS usage string, or a prompt shown with no explanation, is a classic junior mistake that reviewers and app stores catch.

How it works

How a plugin is built

Most official plugins are federated. The package you depend on (for example image_picker) is the app-facing Dart API. Behind it is a platform interface package and one implementation package per platform. You just add the main package; Flutter wires in the right implementation when it builds for each platform.

When you choose a plugin on pub.dev, check:

  • The platform badges (Android, iOS, Web, desktop). A plugin without Web support will throw on the web.
  • The publisher (verified publishers such as flutter.dev), the pub points and how recently it was updated.
  • The setup section of the README. Many plugins need changes in Info.plist or AndroidManifest.xml.

image_picker in practice

Add it with flutter pub add image_picker. The main methods are pickImage, pickMultiImage, pickVideo and pickMedia. pickImage returns Future<XFile?>: an XFile if the user chose something, or null if they cancelled.

  • source: ImageSource.gallery or ImageSource.camera.
  • maxWidth / maxHeight / imageQuality: shrink the photo on the device. Phone cameras produce large files; resizing saves memory and upload time.
  • file.readAsBytes() works on every platform, including the web. File(file.path) from dart:io does not work on the web.

Screen 1: Profile Photo: pick and show lib/profile_page.dart

class _ProfilePageState extends State<ProfilePage> {
  final _picker = ImagePicker();
  Uint8List? _photo;

  Future<void> _pick(ImageSource source) async {
    try {
      final file = await _picker.pickImage(
        source: source,
        maxWidth: 1024, // resize on the device: smaller memory and uploads
        imageQuality: 85,
      );
      if (file == null) return; // the user cancelled: not an error
      final bytes = await file.readAsBytes();
      if (!mounted) return;
      setState(() => _photo = bytes);
    } on PlatformException {
      if (!mounted) return; // e.g. no camera, or access denied
      ScaffoldMessenger.of(context).showSnackBar(SnackBar(
        content: Text('Could not open ' + source.name + '. Check permissions.'),
      ));
    }
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final photo = _photo;
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Profile')),
      body: Center(
        child: Column(mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min, children: [
          CircleAvatar(
            radius: 64,
            backgroundImage: photo == null ? null : MemoryImage(photo),
            child: photo == null ? const Icon(Icons.person, size: 64) : null,
          ),
          const SizedBox(height: 16),
          Text('Asha Nair', style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleLarge),
          const Text('Flutter developer'),
          const SizedBox(height: 24),
          Row(mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min, children: [
            FilledButton.tonalIcon(
              onPressed: () => _pick(ImageSource.gallery),
              icon: const Icon(Icons.photo_library),
              label: const Text('Gallery'),
            ),
            const SizedBox(width: 12),
            OutlinedButton.icon(
              onPressed: () => _pick(ImageSource.camera),
              icon: const Icon(Icons.photo_camera),
              label: const Text('Camera'),
            ),
          ]),
        ]),
      ),
    );
  }
}

The photo is read with readAsBytes(), which works on Android, iOS and the web. Cancelling the picker returns null and leaves the screen unchanged. States: No photo → Photo chosen → Camera error.

Camera photos are saved to a temporary cache. If you need the file later, copy it somewhere permanent or upload it. On Android, the system can kill your activity while the camera app is open on low-memory devices; the plugin offers retrieveLostData() to recover the result when the app restarts.

A bottom sheet is a tidy way to offer both sources from one tap target. showModalBottomSheet returns whatever value you pass to Navigator.pop, so it can return the chosen ImageSource directly.

Screen 2: Choose a source in a bottom sheet lib/profile_page.dart

Future<void> _chooseSource() async {
  final source = await showModalBottomSheet<ImageSource>(
    context: context,
    showDragHandle: true,
    builder: (context) => SafeArea(
      child: Column(mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min, children: [
        ListTile(
          leading: const Icon(Icons.photo_camera),
          title: const Text('Take a photo'),
          onTap: () => Navigator.pop(context, ImageSource.camera),
        ),
        ListTile(
          leading: const Icon(Icons.photo_library),
          title: const Text('Choose from gallery'),
          onTap: () => Navigator.pop(context, ImageSource.gallery),
        ),
      ]),
    ),
  );
  if (source != null) await _pick(source);
}

// In build(): tap the avatar to open the sheet.
GestureDetector(
  onTap: _chooseSource,
  child: CircleAvatar(radius: 64, child: const Icon(Icons.person, size: 64)),
)

showModalBottomSheet returns the ImageSource the user tapped, or null if they dismissed the sheet. One tap target replaces two buttons.

Permissions: the concept

Both platforms protect sensitive features, but in different ways.

iOSAndroid
Where you declare itios/Runner/Info.plist usage descriptions, such as NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription, NSCameraUsageDescription, NSMicrophoneUsageDescriptionandroid/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml <uses-permission> entries
When the user is askedThe first time the feature is used, with your usage text in the dialogAt runtime for “dangerous” permissions (camera, location, microphone and others)
If you forget to declare itThe app is terminated when the feature is usedThe request fails or the feature is unavailable
After the user says noYou cannot ask again; the user must change it in SettingsYou can ask again, until the user chooses not to be asked; then only Settings can change it

Modern system pickers reduce the need for permissions. On recent Android versions image_picker uses the system Photo Picker, and on iOS it uses the system picker (PHPicker) for the library. For the camera and other features, follow each plugin’s README exactly. When you need to check or request permissions yourself, community packages exist for that job.

Good permission UX follows three rules. Ask in context (when the user taps Camera, not at app start). Explain first with a short sentence of your own. Handle “no” gracefully: disable the feature, show why, and offer another path such as the gallery.

Platform channels

When no plugin exists, you write the bridge yourself. A MethodChannel has a unique name. Dart calls invokeMethod; native code registers a handler with the same channel name and replies with result.success, result.error or result.notImplemented. Calls are asynchronous, and values are encoded by a standard codec that supports null, booleans, numbers, strings, byte data, lists and maps.

// android/app/src/main/kotlin/.../MainActivity.kt
class MainActivity : FlutterActivity() {
    override fun configureFlutterEngine(flutterEngine: FlutterEngine) {
        super.configureFlutterEngine(flutterEngine)
        MethodChannel(flutterEngine.dartExecutor.binaryMessenger, "academy.ralfiz/battery")
            .setMethodCallHandler { call, result ->
                if (call.method == "getBatteryLevel") {
                    val manager = getSystemService(Context.BATTERY_SERVICE) as BatteryManager
                    result.success(manager.getIntProperty(BatteryManager.BATTERY_PROPERTY_CAPACITY))
                } else {
                    result.notImplemented()
                }
            }
    }
}

The Kotlin file also needs imports for Context, BatteryManager, FlutterActivity, FlutterEngine and MethodChannel. On the Dart side, catch PlatformException (the native code reported an error) and MissingPluginException (no handler on this platform).

Screen 3: Platform channel: battery level lib/battery_page.dart

class _BatteryPageState extends State<BatteryPage> {
  static const _channel = MethodChannel('academy.ralfiz/battery');
  String _status = 'Unknown';

  Future<void> _read() async {
    String status;
    try {
      final level = await _channel.invokeMethod<int>('getBatteryLevel');
      status = 'Battery: $level%';
    } on PlatformException catch (e) {
      status = 'Failed: ' + (e.message ?? e.code);
    } on MissingPluginException {
      status = 'Not available here';
    }
    if (!mounted) return;
    setState(() => _status = status);
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Battery')),
      body: Center(
        child: Column(mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min, children: [
          const Icon(Icons.battery_std, size: 64),
          const SizedBox(height: 12),
          Text(_status, style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.headlineSmall),
          const SizedBox(height: 24),
          FilledButton(onPressed: _read, child: const Text('Get battery level')),
        ]),
      ),
    );
  }
}

Dart calls getBatteryLevel on a named MethodChannel. Android answers from Kotlin; on a platform with no handler (such as the web) the call throws MissingPluginException and the app shows a fallback. States: Start → Android → Web.

Related tools: an EventChannel streams events from native code to Dart (sensor readings, for example). Pigeon, from the Flutter team, generates type-safe channel code from a Dart definition so you do not match strings by hand. dart:ffi calls C libraries directly.

Other everyday plugins

The url_launcher plugin opens web links, the phone dialer (tel:), email (mailto:) and maps with launchUrl(Uri.parse(...)). Its README explains the extra manifest and Info.plist entries needed to check which apps can handle a link. Location, notifications, sharing and connectivity each have well-known plugins; the same checklist applies: platforms, setup, permissions, fallback.

Example: Profile Photo app

  1. Run flutter pub add image_picker.
  2. Add NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription and NSCameraUsageDescription with clear sentences to ios/Runner/Info.plist, for example “Used to set your profile photo.”
  3. Build the profile screen: a 64-radius CircleAvatar, the name, and Gallery and Camera buttons.
  4. In _pick, call pickImage with maxWidth: 1024 and imageQuality: 85. Return early on null. Read the bytes and show them with MemoryImage. Check mounted after every await.
  5. Catch PlatformException and show a SnackBar, so a picker failure or a denied permission does not crash the app.
  6. Make the avatar tappable and open the source sheet.
  7. Add the battery tile with a MethodChannel. Without native code it shows “Not available here”; add the Kotlin handler to see a real level on Android.

Common mistakes

  • Treating cancel as an error, or forgetting the null check and crashing with a null-check operator on XFile.
  • Missing iOS usage descriptions. Everything works on Android, then the iOS build is terminated the first time the camera opens.
  • Using dart:io File everywhere. It is not available on the web. Prefer readAsBytes() or check kIsWeb.
  • Using context after an await without checking mounted. The user may have left the screen while the picker was open.
  • Requesting every permission at startup. Users deny prompts that have no context, and some permissions cannot be requested again.
  • Channel name typos between Dart and native code, which show up as MissingPluginException.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “How does Flutter talk to native code?” Answer: through platform channels (method, event and basic message channels), usually wrapped in plugins; mention Pigeon for type safety and FFI for C libraries.
  • Explain the permission flow on both platforms, and how you would handle a permanently denied permission (explain, then guide the user to Settings).
  • Test device features on real devices. Emulators have simulated cameras, and some features, such as HEIC photos, behave differently on simulators.
  • Wrap plugins behind your own small class (for example PhotoService). Your widgets and Blocs depend on that class, which makes them easy to test with a fake in lesson 8.3.
  • After adding a plugin, do a full restart (and for iOS sometimes pod install through a fresh build). Hot reload does not load new native code.

lessons.title: Testing Flutter apps
lessons.summaryHtml: Flutter has three levels of automated tests. Unit tests check plain Dart logic and Cubits in milliseconds. Widget tests build one screen in a fake test environment with pumpWidget, find widgets with find, act with tester.tap and enterText, then expect what should be on screen. Integration tests (integration_test) run the whole app on a real device or emulator. mocktail replaces real dependencies such as repositories with controllable fakes, and bloc_test checks exactly which states a Cubit or Bloc emits. You will test a small Tasks app at all three levels.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A test is a small program that uses your app the way a person would, then checks the result. “Build the Tasks screen, type Walk dog, tap +, and check that Walk dog is in the list.” If a later change breaks that behaviour, the test fails and tells you before your users do.

Think of a pre-flight checklist. The pilot does not trust memory; they tick every item before each flight. Automated tests are your checklist, and the computer runs it in seconds every time you change code.

Flutter ships the tools in the SDK. flutter_test gives you test, testWidgets, finders and matchers. The integration_test package runs the full app on a device. Two community favourites fill the gaps: mocktail for fake dependencies and bloc_test for Cubits and Blocs.

Why it matters

Every app grows. After a few months, nobody can manually re-check every screen after every change. Tests give you the confidence to refactor, upgrade packages and ship on a Friday. They also document how code is meant to behave.

For a junior developer, tests are a hiring signal. Take-home assignments often say “tests are a plus”, and many teams will not merge a pull request that lowers test coverage. The BLoC architecture you learned in module f6 was designed with testing in mind: logic lives in Cubits you can test without any widgets at all.

How it works

The three levels

LevelWhat it runsSpeedNeeds a deviceUse it for
Unit testA function, class, Cubit or BlocFastestNoLogic, calculations, state changes, models and JSON parsing
Widget testOne widget or screen in a test environmentFastNoWhat appears on screen and how it reacts to taps and typing
Integration testThe whole app, real pluginsSlowestYes (device, emulator or desktop)Critical journeys: sign in, checkout, onboarding

A healthy project has many unit tests, a good number of widget tests and a few integration tests. That shape is often called the test pyramid. Test files live in test/, end in _test.dart, and run with flutter test.

Unit tests

import 'package:flutter_test/flutter_test.dart';
import 'package:tasks_app/main.dart';

void main() {
  group('summary', () {
    test('counts open tasks', () {
      expect(summary(const [Task('a'), Task('b', done: true), Task('c')]), '2 tasks left');
    });
    test('uses singular and celebrates zero', () {
      expect(summary(const [Task('a')]), '1 task left');
      expect(summary(const [Task('a', done: true)]), 'All done!');
    });
  });
}

Each test follows arrange, act, assert: set up the input, run the code, check the output with expect(actual, matcher). Common matchers include equals, isTrue, isNull, contains, hasLength(3) and throwsA(isA<FormatException>()). Use group to organise tests, and setUp to create fresh objects before each one.

Widget tests

Here is the Tasks screen we will test. It uses a Cubit with a sealed state, exactly the pattern from lesson 6.3.

Screen 1: The app under test lib/main.dart

@override
Widget build(BuildContext context) {
  return Scaffold(
    appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Tasks')),
    body: BlocBuilder<TasksCubit, TasksState>(
      builder: (context, state) => switch (state) {
        TasksInitial() || TasksLoading() =>
          const Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator()),
        TasksError(:final message) => Center(
            child: Column(mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min, children: [
              Text(message),
              TextButton(
                onPressed: () => context.read<TasksCubit>().load(),
                child: const Text('Retry'),
              ),
            ]),
          ),
        TasksLoaded(:final tasks) => Column(children: [
            Padding(
              padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
              child: Row(children: [
                Expanded(
                  child: TextField(
                    key: const Key('newTask'),
                    controller: _controller,
                    decoration: const InputDecoration(labelText: 'New task'),
                  ),
                ),
                const SizedBox(width: 8),
                IconButton.filled(
                  key: const Key('addTask'),
                  icon: const Icon(Icons.add),
                  onPressed: _add,
                ),
              ]),
            ),
            Text(summary(tasks)),
            Expanded(
              child: ListView.builder(
                itemCount: tasks.length,
                itemBuilder: (context, i) => CheckboxListTile(
                  value: tasks[i].done,
                  title: Text(tasks[i].title),
                  onChanged: (_) => context.read<TasksCubit>().toggle(i),
                ),
              ),
            ),
          ]),
      },
    ),
  );
}

One BlocBuilder switches over a sealed state. The keys on the text field and the + button are there for the tests. States: Loading → Loaded → Error.

A widget test gets a WidgetTester. The core loop is pump, find, act, pump, expect:

  • await tester.pumpWidget(widget) builds the widget tree. Wrap screens in MaterialApp (our TasksApp already does) so themes, text direction and navigation work.
  • Finders locate widgets: find.text, find.byKey, find.byType, find.byIcon, find.widgetWithText.
  • Actions: tester.tap, tester.enterText, tester.drag, tester.longPress.
  • await tester.pump() renders the next frame after a state change. pumpAndSettle() keeps pumping until animations and pending timers are finished. A test with an endless animation never settles, so use pump(duration) there.
  • Matchers for finders: findsOneWidget, findsNothing, findsNWidgets(2), findsWidgets.

Screen 2: A widget test, frame by frame test/tasks_page_test.dart

class MockTaskRepository extends Mock implements TaskRepository {}

void main() {
  testWidgets('shows tasks, adds one and toggles it', (tester) async {
    final repo = MockTaskRepository();
    when(() => repo.fetchTasks())
        .thenAnswer((_) async => const [Task('Buy milk')]);

    await tester.pumpWidget(TasksApp(repository: repo));
    expect(find.byType(CircularProgressIndicator), findsOneWidget);

    await tester.pumpAndSettle(); // the Future completes, spinner goes
    expect(find.text('Buy milk'), findsOneWidget);
    expect(find.text('1 task left'), findsOneWidget);

    await tester.enterText(find.byKey(const Key('newTask')), 'Walk dog');
    await tester.tap(find.byKey(const Key('addTask')));
    await tester.pump();
    expect(find.text('Walk dog'), findsOneWidget);
    expect(find.text('2 tasks left'), findsOneWidget);

    await tester.tap(find.text('Buy milk'));
    await tester.pump();
    expect(find.text('1 task left'), findsOneWidget);
    verify(() => repo.fetchTasks()).called(1);
  });
}

What the test “sees” after each step. The mock repository returns one task, so the first expectation is exact. Every action is followed by pump() so the tree rebuilds. States: pumpWidget → pumpAndSettle → enterText + tap → tap Buy milk.

Widget tests run in a fake environment: no real network, no real plugins, and time is simulated. That is why the repository is replaced by a mock, and why pumpAndSettle can “wait” for a Future without really waiting.

Mocks with mocktail

A dependency such as TaskRepository might call an API or a database. In tests you want full control, so you create a mock:

class MockTaskRepository extends Mock implements TaskRepository {}

final repo = MockTaskRepository();
when(() => repo.fetchTasks()).thenAnswer((_) async => const [Task('Buy milk')]); // success
when(() => repo.fetchTasks()).thenThrow(Exception('offline'));                 // failure
verify(() => repo.fetchTasks()).called(1);                                     // was it called once?

Use thenAnswer for anything that returns a Future or Stream, and thenReturn for plain values. A method you did not stub returns null, which usually causes a type error, so stub everything the code under test calls. If you match arguments with any() for a custom type, call registerFallbackValue once in setUpAll.

Testing Cubits and Blocs with bloc_test

blocTest builds the Cubit, runs act, collects every emitted state and compares the list with expect. seed sets a starting state, setUp stubs mocks, wait handles debounced events, errors checks thrown errors, and verify runs final checks. States need value equality (Equatable or your own ==), or two identical states will not match.

Screen 3: bloc_test and the test runner test/tasks_cubit_test.dart

class MockTaskRepository extends Mock implements TaskRepository {}

void main() {
  late MockTaskRepository repo;
  setUp(() => repo = MockTaskRepository());

  blocTest<TasksCubit, TasksState>(
    'load emits [loading, loaded] on success',
    setUp: () => when(() => repo.fetchTasks())
        .thenAnswer((_) async => const [Task('Test me')]),
    build: () => TasksCubit(repo),
    act: (cubit) => cubit.load(),
    expect: () => const [TasksLoading(), TasksLoaded([Task('Test me')])],
  );

  blocTest<TasksCubit, TasksState>(
    'load emits [loading, error] when the repository throws',
    setUp: () => when(() => repo.fetchTasks()).thenThrow(Exception('offline')),
    build: () => TasksCubit(repo),
    act: (cubit) => cubit.load(),
    expect: () => const [TasksLoading(), TasksError('Could not load tasks')],
  );

  blocTest<TasksCubit, TasksState>(
    'add appends a trimmed task',
    build: () => TasksCubit(repo),
    seed: () => const TasksLoaded([Task('a')]),
    act: (cubit) => cubit.add('  b  '),
    expect: () => const [TasksLoaded([Task('a'), Task('b')])],
  );
}

blocTest checks the exact list of states. The console shows what flutter test prints for a pass and for a failing finder (timings and file paths trimmed). States: All pass → One fails.

Integration tests

Add the SDK package to dev_dependencies in pubspec.yaml (integration_test: sdk: flutter), create integration_test/app_test.dart, and run flutter test integration_test with a device or emulator connected.

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:flutter_test/flutter_test.dart';
import 'package:integration_test/integration_test.dart';
import 'package:tasks_app/main.dart';

void main() {
  IntegrationTestWidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();

  testWidgets('add a task end to end', (tester) async {
    await tester.pumpWidget(TasksApp(repository: InMemoryTaskRepository()));
    await tester.pumpAndSettle();
    await tester.enterText(find.byKey(const Key('newTask')), 'Ship it');
    await tester.tap(find.byKey(const Key('addTask')));
    await tester.pumpAndSettle();
    expect(find.text('Ship it'), findsOneWidget);
  });
}

The API is the same WidgetTester you already know, but now the app runs for real, with real timing and real plugins.

Example: testing the Tasks app

  1. Create the project with flutter create tasks_app and add packages: flutter pub add flutter_bloc equatable, then flutter pub add dev:bloc_test dev:mocktail.
  2. The app depends on an abstract TaskRepository, and TasksApp takes it as a constructor parameter. This small design choice is what makes every test below possible.
  3. Unit-test summary: two open tasks, one open task, none open.
  4. Write three blocTests: load succeeds, load fails, and add trims the title.
  5. Write two widget tests: the happy path (load, add, toggle) and the error path (the repository throws, the screen shows “Could not load tasks” and a Retry button).
  6. Run flutter test and expect All tests passed!. Then break the app on purpose (change “task left” to “tasks left”) and watch a test fail with a clear message.
  7. Optionally add the integration test and run it on an emulator.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to pump after tap or enterText. The state changed but the tree was not rebuilt, so the expectation fails.
  • pumpAndSettle timing out because something animates forever, such as a spinner that never goes away. Fix the stub so loading finishes, or use pump(const Duration(seconds: 1)).
  • Testing against a real API. Tests become slow and fail when the network is down. Inject a repository and mock it.
  • Hard-coding dependencies inside widgets (final repo = HttpTaskRepository(); in build), which leaves nothing to replace in tests.
  • States without equality. blocTest reports “expected [TasksLoaded] but got [TasksLoaded]” because two instances are not equal. Use Equatable.
  • Testing implementation details, such as private fields or exact widget nesting, instead of what the user sees. Such tests break on every refactor.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Be ready to name the three test types, what each is for, and why most tests should be unit and widget tests.
  • Explain pump versus pumpAndSettle in one sentence each. This is a very common question.
  • Explain dependency injection as the reason code is testable: the Cubit takes a repository in its constructor, and tests pass a mock.
  • Golden tests compare a widget’s rendering with a saved image (matchesGoldenFile), which catches visual regressions.
  • flutter test --coverage writes a coverage report. Teams often run flutter analyze and flutter test on every pull request in CI, which lesson 8.5 touches on.

terms.definition: A test that builds widgets with pumpWidget in a headless test environment and interacts with them through a WidgetTester.
An object that locates widgets, such as find.text('Save'), find.byType(ListTile), find.byKey(Key('addTask')) or find.byIcon(Icons.add).
pump() renders one new frame; pumpAndSettle() keeps pumping until no more frames are scheduled (animations and timers finish).
A stand-in object whose answers you set with when(...) and whose calls you check with verify(...).
A bloc_test helper that builds a Cubit or Bloc, runs act, and compares the emitted states with expect.
A test that drives the complete app on a device or emulator using the integration_test package.

lessons.examTip: Put Keys on the widgets you test (Key('addTask')). Tests that find by key survive text and translation changes.

quiz.question: In a widget test you tap the + button, but expect(find.text('Walk dog'), findsOneWidget) fails even though the app works. What is the most likely fix?
options: Call await tester.pump() after the tap so a new frame is built
Replace testWidgets with test
Use findsNothing instead

quiz.question: Why pass a MockTaskRepository to the Cubit in tests instead of the real repository?
options: Mocks make the test run on a device
Real repositories cannot be used with Cubits
The test controls the data and errors, runs fast and does not depend on the network
Mocks automatically generate the UI
quiz.explanation: A mock returns exactly what you set with when(...), including errors, with no network or disk. That makes the test fast and repeatable, and lets you test failure paths.

quiz.question: Which test type is the best fit for “log in, add three items to the cart and check out on a real Android phone”?
options: A unit test
An integration test with integration_test
A blocTest
A golden test

quiz.question: A blocTest for load() expects [TasksLoaded(...)] but fails with an extra TasksLoading() first. What does this tell you?
options: bloc_test is broken
TasksLoaded needs a const constructor
The mock was not called
The Cubit really emits a loading state before the data, so expect must list both states in order
quiz.explanation: blocTest compares the full list of emitted states. If load() emits TasksLoading and then TasksLoaded, the expected list must contain both, in that order.

lessons.title: Performance and debugging
lessons.summaryHtml: A smooth app finishes each frame within the display’s budget (about 16 ms at 60 Hz). When build, layout, paint or your own Dart code take longer, frames are dropped and users see jank. You will learn to measure before you fix: run in profile mode on a real device and use DevTools (Inspector, Performance, CPU profiler, Memory). Then apply the fixes that matter most: const widgets and small widgets to limit rebuilds, ListView.builder for long lists, keys so state stays with the right item, cacheWidth so images decode at display size, and Isolate.run for heavy work. The mini app is a Photo Feed that starts slow and ends smooth.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A screen that “feels smooth” is a screen that draws a new frame on time, every time. On a 60 Hz display Flutter has about 16 milliseconds per frame (1000 ÷ 60); on a 120 Hz display, about 8. In that time it must run your build methods, lay widgets out, paint them, and hand the result to the GPU. If one frame takes longer, it is dropped, and the user sees a stutter called jank.

Think of a flip-book. If one page is missing, the drawing jumps. Performance work means finding out which pages are slow and why, then removing the waste.

Debugging is the twin skill: finding out why the app does the wrong thing, not just the slow thing. Flutter gives you one toolbox for both, called DevTools.

Why it matters

Users forgive a plain design far more easily than a stuttering scroll. Reviews mention “laggy” quickly, and low-end Android phones, common in many markets, expose every inefficiency. Clients also notice battery drain and memory crashes on older devices.

Most real-world slowness comes from a handful of patterns: rebuilding too much, building lists eagerly, decoding huge images, and doing heavy work on the UI thread. Once you can spot these in DevTools, you can fix most problems in minutes. The key habit is measure first: optimising without measuring often changes the wrong thing.

How it works

Where frames are made

Each frame passes through two main threads. The UI thread runs your Dart code: build, layout, paint, and any other Dart work such as parsing or sorting. The raster thread turns the painted layers into GPU commands. A slow UI thread usually means too much Dart work or too many rebuilds. A slow raster thread usually means expensive effects: large blurs, many clips, Opacity over big subtrees, or huge images. Flutter’s Impeller renderer, the default on iOS and modern Android, removed the shader-compilation stutter that older apps saw on first animations.

Build modes

ModeCommandWhat it is for
Debugflutter runHot reload, asserts, breakpoints. Slow on purpose. Never judge performance here.
Profileflutter run --profileCompiled like release, with tracing for DevTools. Use a real device.
Releaseflutter run --release / flutter buildWhat users get. No debugging tools.

DevTools tour

Open DevTools from VS Code or Android Studio (the Flutter extension has an “Open DevTools” command), or from the link flutter run prints.

  • Flutter Inspector: the live widget tree, the selected widget’s properties and a layout explorer for Rows, Columns and constraints. “Select widget mode” lets you tap something on the device and jump to it in the tree.
  • Performance: a bar per frame, split into UI and raster time, with slow frames highlighted. Select a frame to see the timeline of events. Tracing options can add every widget build, layout and paint to the timeline, and rebuild statistics show which widgets rebuild most.
  • CPU Profiler: records which functions used the most time. Perfect for finding the one slow method.
  • Memory: heap usage over time and snapshots. A graph that only goes up as you open and close a screen hints at a leak (for example a controller that is never disposed).
  • Network and Logging: HTTP calls and log output in one place.

For plain debugging, set breakpoints in the IDE, use debugPrint or log from dart:developer, and read the full error in the console: messages such as “A RenderFlex overflowed” or “setState() called after dispose()” name the widget and usually suggest the fix.

Rebuild less

  • Use const wherever the analyzer allows it. A const widget is one shared instance, so when its parent rebuilds, Flutter sees the same object and skips it.
  • Push state down. Call setState in the smallest widget that owns the changing value, not at the top of the screen.
  • Extract widgets as classes, not helper methods. A separate StatelessWidget can be const and rebuilds on its own; a _buildHeader() method always rebuilds with its parent.
  • Select only what you need: BlocSelector, buildWhen, context.select, and the child parameter of AnimatedBuilder and Consumer.
  • Keep build cheap. No sorting, parsing, network calls or object creation that could happen once in initState or a Cubit.

Lists, keys and images

ListView(children: [...]) builds every child immediately. ListView.builder builds only what is visible (plus a small cache area) and disposes items that scroll far off screen. If every row has the same height, itemExtent or prototypeItem saves layout work. Avoid shrinkWrap: true on long lists inside other scroll views: it forces every item to be laid out.

Screen 1: A lazy, cache-friendly feed lib/feed_page.dart

class FeedPage extends StatelessWidget {
  const FeedPage({super.key, required this.posts});
  final List<Post> posts;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final px = MediaQuery.sizeOf(context).width *
        MediaQuery.devicePixelRatioOf(context);
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Photo Feed')),
      body: ListView.builder(
        itemCount: posts.length, // 1,000 posts, only visible ones are built
        itemBuilder: (context, i) => PostCard(
          key: ValueKey(posts[i].id),
          post: posts[i],
          cacheWidth: px.round(),
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

class PostCard extends StatelessWidget {
  const PostCard({super.key, required this.post, required this.cacheWidth});
  final Post post;
  final int cacheWidth;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Card(
      margin: const EdgeInsets.fromLTRB(12, 6, 12, 6),
      clipBehavior: Clip.antiAlias,
      child: Column(children: [
        Image.network(
          post.imageUrl,
          height: 160,
          width: double.infinity,
          fit: BoxFit.cover,
          cacheWidth: cacheWidth, // decode at display size
          errorBuilder: (_, __, ___) => const SizedBox(
              height: 160, child: Center(child: Icon(Icons.broken_image))),
        ),
        ListTile(
          leading: CircleAvatar(child: Text(post.author[0])),
          title: Text(post.author),
          subtitle: Text(post.caption),
          trailing: const Icon(Icons.favorite_border),
        ),
      ]),
    );
  }
}

ListView.builder builds only the cards on screen, each card has a stable key, and cacheWidth decodes each photo at the width it is shown, not at full camera resolution.

Keys tell Flutter which widget is which. Without keys, Flutter matches old and new children by position and type. That is fine for static lists, but when items are removed, inserted or reordered, State objects (and their data, such as a “liked” flag or text in a field) can end up on the wrong item. Give such items a stable key from your data, like ValueKey(post.id). Do not use UniqueKey() in build: a new key every frame throws the state away each time.

Screen 2: Why keys matter lib/main.dart

class FruitTile extends StatefulWidget {
  const FruitTile({super.key, required this.name, required this.onDelete});
  final String name;
  final VoidCallback onDelete;

  @override
  State<FruitTile> createState() => _FruitTileState();
}

class _FruitTileState extends State<FruitTile> {
  bool _liked = false; // state lives in the State object, not the widget

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return ListTile(
      title: Text(widget.name),
      leading: IconButton(
        icon: Icon(_liked ? Icons.favorite : Icons.favorite_border),
        color: _liked ? Colors.red : null,
        onPressed: () => setState(() => _liked = !_liked),
      ),
      trailing: IconButton(
        icon: const Icon(Icons.delete),
        onPressed: widget.onDelete,
      ),
    );
  }
}

// In the parent's build():
ListView(children: [
  for (final f in fruits)
    FruitTile(
      key: ValueKey(f), // remove this line to see the bug
      name: f,
      onDelete: () => setState(() => fruits.remove(f)),
    ),
])

Each card keeps its own liked state. Delete Apple: without keys the State objects stay in their positions, so Banana inherits Apple’s red heart. With ValueKey(name) the state moves with its item. States: Apple liked → Deleted, no keys (bug) → Deleted, with keys.

Images are the most common memory problem. A 12-megapixel photo shown in a 400-pixel-wide card is still decoded at full size unless you pass cacheWidth or cacheHeight. Flutter keeps decoded images in an in-memory ImageCache, so scrolling back does not decode again; precacheImage warms that cache before a screen appears. Ship assets at sensible sizes, with 2.0x and 3.0x variants instead of one giant file.

Heavy work off the UI thread

Dart runs your code on one isolate, the same one that builds frames. A long loop, a large JSON decode or image processing blocks frames until it finishes. Move such work to another isolate with Isolate.run (lesson 1.13) or Flutter’s compute, which also works on the web by running the work on the main thread. Pass a top-level or static function: whatever a closure captures is copied to the new isolate, and capturing a State object fails.

Screen 3: Heavy work: UI thread vs isolate lib/main.dart

int countPrimes(int below) {
  var count = 0;
  for (var n = 2; n < below; n++) {
    var prime = true;
    for (var d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
      if (n % d == 0) { prime = false; break; }
    }
    if (prime) count++;
  }
  return count;
}

// Top-level, so the isolate does not capture the State object.
int primesBelow3M() => countPrimes(3000000);

class _PrimeScreenState extends State<PrimeScreen> {
  String _result = 'Tap a button';
  bool _busy = false;

  Future<void> _run({required bool isolate}) async {
    setState(() { _busy = true; _result = 'Counting...'; });
    await Future<void>.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 50)); // show spinner
    final count = isolate
        ? await Isolate.run(primesBelow3M) // UI stays free
        : primesBelow3M(); // blocks the UI thread: frames are dropped
    if (!mounted) return;
    setState(() { _busy = false; _result = 'Found $count primes'; });
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Heavy work')),
      body: Center(
        child: Column(mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min, children: [
          SizedBox(height: 48, child: _busy ? const CircularProgressIndicator() : null),
          Text(_result, style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleMedium),
          const SizedBox(height: 24),
          OutlinedButton(onPressed: _busy ? null : () => _run(isolate: false), child: const Text('Run on UI thread')),
          const SizedBox(height: 8),
          FilledButton(onPressed: _busy ? null : () => _run(isolate: true), child: const Text('Run in isolate')),
        ]),
      ),
    );
  }
}

On the UI thread the spinner stops turning until counting finishes (dropped frames). With Isolate.run the same work runs in parallel and the spinner keeps spinning. States: Idle → UI thread: frozen → Isolate: smooth → Done.

Example: Photo Feed

The starter feed shows 1,000 posts and feels sluggish. Fix it in the order you measure it.

  1. Run flutter run --profile on a phone, open DevTools, go to Performance and scroll the feed. Note slow frames and look at the timeline.
  2. The feed uses ListView(children: ...) with 1,000 cards: switch to ListView.builder. Startup gets faster.
  3. build sorts all posts each time: sort once when the sort toggle changes and keep the result in state.
  4. Photos decode at full size: add cacheWidth based on the screen width and MediaQuery.devicePixelRatioOf.
  5. Like a post, delete it, and watch the next post turn red: add key: ValueKey(post.id).
  6. The Stats button freezes the spinner: move the calculation into Isolate.run.
  7. Add const wherever the analyzer suggests it (flutter analyze lists them with the recommended lints). Profile again and compare.

Common mistakes

  • Measuring in debug mode or only on a fast emulator, then “fixing” problems that do not exist in release.
  • Optimising blind. Adding RepaintBoundary or const everywhere without checking what is actually slow.
  • Calling setState high in the tree for a tiny change, rebuilding the whole screen on every keystroke.
  • Creating Futures, streams or controllers in build, which restarts work and leaks memory.
  • Using index or UniqueKey() as keys for lists that change. Keys must be stable and come from the data.
  • Forgetting dispose for controllers, focus nodes, stream subscriptions and timers, which shows up as rising memory.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “How would you investigate a janky screen?” Answer: reproduce in profile mode on a real device, open the DevTools Performance view, check whether UI or raster time is high, then use the timeline, rebuild stats and CPU profiler to find the cause.
  • Know why const helps and why widget classes beat helper methods; this is asked very often.
  • Be able to explain what keys do, and when you need ValueKey, ObjectKey or a GlobalKey (rarely: to reach a FormState or move state across the tree).
  • flutter build apk --analyze-size (and the equivalent for other targets) produces a size report that DevTools can open, useful when an app download is too large.
  • In production, add crash reporting: FlutterError.onError catches framework errors and PlatformDispatcher.instance.onError catches uncaught async errors, so you can send them to a reporting service.

A build (flutter run --profile) that is compiled like release but keeps enough tooling for DevTools. Measure performance here, never in debug.
Flutter’s browser-based suite: Inspector, Performance, CPU profiler, Memory, Network and Logging views.
A widget created at compile time and reused; Flutter can skip rebuilding it because the instance is identical.
An identity for a widget, such as ValueKey(post.id), so Flutter matches state to the right item when a list changes.
An Image parameter that decodes the picture at a given pixel width, saving memory and decode time for large photos.

quiz.question: A teammate says the feed is janky because the frame chart looks red while running flutter run on an emulator. What should you do first?
options: Rewrite the feed with CustomPaint
Measure again in profile mode on a real device
Remove all animations
Switch the state management to BLoC
quiz.explanation: Debug mode and emulators distort performance. Profile mode on a physical device shows what users will actually see.

quiz.question: A list of 5,000 products is built with ListView(children: [...]). What is the main problem?
options: ListView cannot scroll more than 1,000 items
Keys are not allowed in ListView
The items are drawn in reverse order
Every item is created up front, even those far off screen
quiz.explanation: A children list creates all widgets immediately. ListView.builder creates items lazily as they scroll into view, which saves time and memory.

quiz.question: You delete the first post in a list of stateful cards. Now the second post shows the first post’s “liked” heart. What fixes it?
options: Give each card a key such as ValueKey(post.id)
Make the card a StatelessWidget with const
Call setState twice
Wrap the list in a RepaintBoundary
quiz.explanation: Without keys, Flutter matches old state to new widgets by position and type. A stable key ties each State object to its post.

quiz.question: Parsing a large JSON file makes the loading spinner freeze for a moment. Which fix addresses the cause?
options: Wrap the spinner in const
Use a smaller font
Run the parsing in another isolate, for example with Isolate.run or compute
Call setState before parsing
quiz.explanation: Dart code runs on the UI isolate; long work blocks frames. Moving it to another isolate keeps the UI thread free to animate.

lessons.title: Build and publish
lessons.summaryHtml: Shipping turns your project into signed packages the stores accept. You set the app’s identity (application id and bundle identifier), generate launcher icons with flutter_launcher_icons, understand the splash screen, and manage versions: in version: 1.2.0+5, 1.2.0 is what users see and 5 is the build number that must grow with every upload. For Android you create an upload key, sign the release and upload an .aab to the Play Console; for iOS you sign in Xcode, run flutter build ipa and upload to App Store Connect and TestFlight. Finally you configure dev and prod builds with --dart-define (the idea behind flavors) and see how CI can automate it all.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Until now you have run apps from your editor in debug mode. Publishing means turning the same code into a release build that is fast, small and signed, then giving it to a store that checks it and delivers it to users. Signing is like a wax seal on a letter: it proves the update really comes from you, so nobody else can publish a fake update of your app.

A release has three layers. The app identity (id, name, icon, version). The binary (an Android App Bundle or an iOS archive, signed with your keys). The store listing (screenshots, description, privacy answers, testers). Flutter handles the binary; the rest is configuration and paperwork you learn once and reuse for every client.

Why it matters

For a junior Flutter developer, “can you publish it?” is part of the job. Clients expect you to handle the Play Console and App Store Connect, to ship updates without breaking the build number, and to keep signing keys safe. A lost Android key or a mismatched bundle identifier can block updates for days. A clean, repeatable release process also lets a team ship small updates often instead of big risky ones.

How it works

1. App identity

WhatAndroidiOS
Unique idapplicationId in android/app/build.gradle.ktsBundle Identifier on the Runner target in Xcode
Name under the iconandroid:label in AndroidManifest.xmlCFBundleDisplayName in Info.plist
Can it change later?The id: no, not after the first releaseThe id: no, not after the first release

Pick a reverse-domain id you control, such as academy.ralfiz.notes, before the first upload. The com.example id that flutter create generates is not accepted by Google Play.

2. Launcher icons and splash

Every platform needs icons in many sizes. The flutter_launcher_icons package generates them from one image. Add it with flutter pub add dev:flutter_launcher_icons, then configure it in pubspec.yaml:

flutter_launcher_icons:
  android: "launcher_icon"
  ios: true
  image_path: "assets/icon/icon.png"          # square PNG, 1024 x 1024
  remove_alpha_ios: true                       # the App Store rejects icons with transparency
  adaptive_icon_background: "#1565C0"
  adaptive_icon_foreground: "assets/icon/foreground.png"

Run dart run flutter_launcher_icons and rebuild. Android adaptive icons use a separate foreground and background layer so each launcher can mask them into circles or squircles; keep the important part in the centre.

The splash screen is what the OS shows while Flutter starts. On Android 12 and later the system draws it from your icon and a background colour; on iOS it comes from LaunchScreen.storyboard. Packages exist that generate both from one config, but keep it simple: a colour and a logo. Do not add an artificial delay; make the first screen load fast instead.

3. Versions and build numbers

The version line in pubspec.yaml drives both platforms:

version: 1.2.0+5AndroidiOSRule
1.2.0 (build name)versionNameCFBundleShortVersionStringWhat users see; follow major.minor.patch
5 (build number)versionCodeCFBundleVersionMust increase with every upload

You can override both at build time with --build-name=1.2.1 --build-number=6, which is how CI systems usually set them.

4. Android: sign and upload

  1. Create an upload keystore once (the Flutter docs give this command for macOS and Linux): 
    keytool -genkey -v -keystore ~/upload-keystore.jks -keyalg RSA \
        -storetype JKS -keysize 2048 -validity 10000 -alias upload
  2. Create android/key.properties with storePassword, keyPassword, keyAlias=upload and storeFile (the full path to the .jks). Add it to .gitignore.
  3. In android/app/build.gradle.kts, load key.properties and point the release build at it: 
    val keystoreProperties = Properties()   // import java.util.Properties
val keystorePropertiesFile = rootProject.file("key.properties")
if (keystorePropertiesFile.exists()) {
    keystoreProperties.load(FileInputStream(keystorePropertiesFile)) // import java.io.FileInputStream
}

android {
    // ...
    signingConfigs {
        create("release") {
            keyAlias = keystoreProperties.getProperty("keyAlias")
            keyPassword = keystoreProperties.getProperty("keyPassword")
            storeFile = keystoreProperties.getProperty("storeFile")?.let { file(it) }
            storePassword = keystoreProperties.getProperty("storePassword")
        }
    }
    buildTypes {
        release {
            signingConfig = signingConfigs.getByName("release")
        }
    }
}
  4. Run flutter build appbundle. The signed .aab appears under build/app/outputs/bundle/release/.
  5. In the Play Console, create the app, complete the store listing, content rating, data safety form, target audience and privacy policy, and enrol in Play App Signing: Google keeps the key that signs what users download, and your key only proves uploads are yours.
  6. Upload the bundle to a testing track (internal, closed or open) before production. New personal developer accounts must run a closed test with real testers for a period before they can publish to production; check the current requirements in the Play Console.

5. iOS: sign and upload

  • You need a paid Apple Developer Program membership and a Mac with Xcode.
  • Open ios/Runner.xcworkspace, select the Runner target, set the Bundle Identifier and your Team under Signing and Capabilities. Automatic signing creates the certificates and profiles for you.
  • Create the app record in App Store Connect with the same bundle id.
  • Run flutter build ipa. It creates an archive and an .ipa under build/ios/. Upload it with Apple’s Transporter app or from Xcode’s Organizer.
  • Test with TestFlight, fill in the privacy details, screenshots and review notes (include a demo login if the app needs one), then submit for App Review.

6. Dev and prod: defines and flavors

Apps usually need at least two configurations: a development build that talks to a test server, and a production build that talks to the live one. The lightest tool is --dart-define, read with String.fromEnvironment. With several values, put them in a JSON file and pass --dart-define-from-file=config/prod.json. Do not put real secrets here: anything compiled into an app can be extracted.

Screen 1: Dev and prod from one codebase lib/main.dart

// flutter run --dart-define=FLAVOR=dev
// flutter build appbundle --dart-define=FLAVOR=prod --dart-define=API_URL=https://api.example.com
const flavor = String.fromEnvironment('FLAVOR', defaultValue: 'dev');
const apiUrl = String.fromEnvironment('API_URL',
    defaultValue: 'https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com');
const isProd = flavor == 'prod';

void main() => runApp(const NotesApp());

class NotesApp extends StatelessWidget {
  const NotesApp({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MaterialApp(
      title: isProd ? 'Notes' : 'Notes DEV',
      theme: ThemeData(
        colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: const Color(0xFF1565C0)),
      ),
      home: const HomePage(),
    );
  }
}

class HomePage extends StatelessWidget {
  const HomePage({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Notes')),
      body: Column(children: [
        if (!isProd)
          Container(
            width: double.infinity,
            color: Colors.orange,
            padding: const EdgeInsets.all(6),
            child: const Text('DEV BUILD',
                textAlign: TextAlign.center,
                style: TextStyle(fontWeight: FontWeight.bold)),
          ),
        const ListTile(
            leading: Icon(Icons.flag),
            title: Text('Flavor'),
            subtitle: Text(flavor)),
        const ListTile(
            leading: Icon(Icons.cloud),
            title: Text('API'),
            subtitle: Text(apiUrl)),
      ]),
    );
  }
}

The same code built twice. With --dart-define=FLAVOR=dev the app shows an orange DEV BUILD strip and uses the test API; with FLAVOR=prod the strip disappears and the live API is used. The values are compile-time constants. States: FLAVOR=dev → FLAVOR=prod.

Flavors go further. Android product flavors and iOS schemes give each variant its own application id, name and icon, so “Notes DEV” and “Notes” can be installed side by side. You then run flutter run --flavor dev. Set them up when a project needs them; the Flutter docs have a step-by-step guide for each platform.

Show the version somewhere in the app, such as an About dialog. When a user reports a bug, support can ask which build they have.

Screen 2: Show the version to users and support lib/home_page.dart

// flutter build appbundle --build-name=1.2.0 --build-number=5 \
//   --dart-define=APP_VERSION=1.2.0+5
const appVersion =
    String.fromEnvironment('APP_VERSION', defaultValue: 'dev build');

class HomePage extends StatelessWidget {
  const HomePage({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(
        title: const Text('Notes'),
        actions: [
          IconButton(
            icon: const Icon(Icons.info_outline),
            tooltip: 'About',
            onPressed: () => showAboutDialog(
              context: context,
              applicationName: 'Notes',
              applicationVersion: appVersion,
              applicationIcon: const Icon(Icons.sticky_note_2, size: 40),
              children: const [Text('Made with Flutter by Ralfiz Academy.')],
            ),
          ),
        ],
      ),
      body: const Center(child: Text('Your notes appear here')),
    );
  }
}

showAboutDialog builds a standard About dialog. Here the version comes from a define set by the build script, so support staff can match a bug report to a build.

Before release, consider --obfuscate --split-debug-info=build/symbols. It makes the Dart code harder to reverse-engineer; keep the symbol files, because you need them to read crash stack traces.

7. CI: let a machine do it

Continuous integration runs your checks on every push: flutter analyze, flutter test, then a release build. Services such as GitHub Actions or Codemagic can store the keystore and passwords as encrypted secrets, set the build number automatically, and upload to a testing track. Tools such as fastlane automate store uploads and screenshots. Start small: analyze and test on every pull request is already a big win.

Example: releasing the Notes app

  1. Set the id to academy.ralfiz.notes on both platforms and the display name to “Notes”.
  2. Add assets/icon/icon.png, configure flutter_launcher_icons and run it. Check the icon on a device.
  3. Set version: 1.0.0+1. Add the About dialog with APP_VERSION.
  4. Run the dev build: flutter run --dart-define=FLAVOR=dev shows the orange strip.
  5. Create the upload keystore and key.properties, wire up signing, and run flutter build appbundle --dart-define=FLAVOR=prod --dart-define=APP_VERSION=1.0.0+1.
  6. Upload to the Play Console internal testing track and install it from the tester link. For iOS, repeat with flutter build ipa and TestFlight.
  7. For the next update: fix, bump to 1.0.1+2, build, upload.

Common mistakes

  • Reusing a build number. The upload is rejected. Every upload needs a higher number, even for the same version name.
  • Losing the upload key or committing it to Git. Back up the keystore and passwords securely; keep key.properties and *.jks out of source control.
  • Shipping with com.example or changing the id after release, which creates a different app in the store.
  • Missing iOS usage descriptions or privacy answers, a common reason for App Review rejection.
  • Putting API secrets in --dart-define and thinking they are hidden. Keep secrets on a server.
  • Testing only debug builds. Always install and try the release build before submitting: release mode can reveal problems such as a missing internet permission on Android.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Be ready to explain versionName versus versionCode and how the pubspec version maps to both platforms.
  • Explain Play App Signing: the upload key proves an upload is yours, and Google signs the final APKs. If the upload key is lost, it can be reset through Play support; the app signing key stays safe with Google.
  • Know the difference between --dart-define (compile-time values) and full flavors (separate app ids, icons and native config).
  • Mention staged rollouts on Play and phased releases on the App Store: shipping to a small percentage first limits the damage from a bad release.
  • For your portfolio, publish at least one of the course apps to a testing track. Walking an interviewer through your release process is a strong signal.

terms.definition: The permanent, unique id of the app in the stores, such as academy.ralfiz.notes. It cannot change after the first release.
The part after + in pubspec version. Stores reject an upload whose build number is not higher than the last one.
The key you sign Android uploads with. With Play App Signing, Google re-signs the app for users with its own app signing key.
The publishing format for Google Play; Play generates optimised APKs for each device from it.
Apple’s beta testing service for builds uploaded to App Store Connect.
A build flag that sets compile-time constants, read in Dart with String.fromEnvironment; the simplest way to separate dev and prod settings.

lessons.examTip: Back up the upload keystore and its passwords somewhere safe, and never commit key.properties or the .jks file to Git.

domains.name: Professional API and architecture
domains.blurb: Dio and interceptors, token auth with refresh, a robust API layer, freezed and json_serializable, dependency injection and clean architecture.

lessons.title: Dio in depth
lessons.summaryHtml:
Dio is an HTTP client that you configure once and use everywhere. BaseOptions sets the base URL, timeouts and default headers. Interceptors run code around every request, response and error, for headers, logging and later tokens and retries. A CancelToken stops requests the user no longer needs, and progress callbacks drive upload and download bars.

You start TaskFlow, the team task app for modules 9 to 12, by building its ApiClient against DummyJSON. Every DioException is translated into a small sealed family of app exceptions, so the rest of the app never depends on Dio.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

In lesson 7.1 you called http.get and parsed the answer yourself. That works for a small app. In a professional app, every request needs the same things: a base URL, timeouts, headers, a token, logging and a clean error when something fails. Writing that by hand at every call site is how bugs creep in.

Dio is an HTTP client for Dart that gives you one configured object for all of that. Think of it as the post room of a company. Every letter (request) goes through the same room. The room stamps the return address (headers), writes it in the log book (logging), attaches the security badge (token) and sorts the replies. The people who write the letters (your repositories) never think about stamps.

In this module you build the API layer of TaskFlow, a team task app that grows until the end of the course. This lesson creates its ApiClient against https://dummyjson.com.

Why it matters

Both packages are good. The difference is how much structure you get for free.

Needhttp packageDio
Base URL and default headersYou build full URIs yourselfBaseOptions(baseUrl:, headers:)
Timeouts.timeout() on each FutureConnect, send and receive timeouts in options
JSON decodingjsonDecode(response.body) by handAutomatic for JSON responses
Cross-cutting logic (tokens, logs, retries)Wrap the client yourselfInterceptors
Cancelling a requestNot built in for a single requestCancelToken
Upload and download progressManual with streamed requestsonSendProgress, onReceiveProgress
Error typesStatus codes plus platform exceptionsOne DioException with a type

For a two-screen app, http is fine and has fewer moving parts. When you add login tokens, retries and many endpoints, Dio’s interceptors save a lot of repeated code. That is why many teams choose it.

How it works

One Dio, configured once

Install it with flutter pub add dio. Create one Dio for the app, not one per request. BaseOptions holds the defaults every request inherits. A single request can still override them with Options.

final dio = Dio(BaseOptions(
  baseUrl: 'https://dummyjson.com',
  connectTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 10),
  receiveTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 15),
  headers: {'Accept': 'application/json'},
));

// Path is joined to baseUrl; query parameters are encoded for you.
final response = await dio.get<Map<String, dynamic>>(
  '/todos',
  queryParameters: {'limit': 10, 'skip': 0},
);
final todos = response.data!['todos'] as List<dynamic>;

// Override one option for one call only.
await dio.get<dynamic>('/todos',
    options: Options(receiveTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 2)));

The three timeouts measure different things:

  • connectTimeout: how long to wait to open the connection to the server.
  • sendTimeout: how long sending the request body may take. It matters for uploads, not for a GET without a body.
  • receiveTimeout: how long to wait for data to arrive once connected.

Without timeouts, a request on a bad network can hang until the operating system gives up, and your spinner spins forever.

Interceptors: a pipeline around every request

An interceptor is a class with three hooks: onRequest, onResponse and onError. Dio runs the interceptors in the order you added them. Each hook receives a handler and must call exactly one of its methods:

CallMeaning
handler.next(x)Pass the request, response or error to the next interceptor.
handler.resolve(response)Finish now with this response (for example from a cache or a retry).
handler.reject(error)Finish now with this error.
class HeadersInterceptor extends Interceptor {
  @override
  void onRequest(RequestOptions options, RequestInterceptorHandler handler) {
    options.headers['Accept-Language'] = 'en';
    options.headers['X-Client'] = 'TaskFlow-Flutter';
    handler.next(options); // forget this and the request never leaves
  }
}

dio.interceptors.add(HeadersInterceptor());

Dio ships a LogInterceptor. Add it last, so it prints the request after every other interceptor has changed it. In Flutter, pass logPrint so lines go through debugPrint, and only add it in debug builds. Response bodies can contain personal data, so keep responseBody off unless you are debugging a specific call.

if (kDebugMode) {
  dio.interceptors.add(LogInterceptor(
    requestBody: true,
    responseBody: false,
    logPrint: (line) => debugPrint(line.toString()),
  ));
}

Cancelling with CancelToken

A user opens a screen, it starts loading, and they press Back. Without cancelling, the response still arrives and your code may call setState on a disposed widget. A CancelToken lets you stop the request. Several requests can share one token, and cancel() stops them all. The awaiting code receives a DioException whose type is cancel.

final token = CancelToken();
try {
  await dio.get<dynamic>('/todos', queryParameters: {'delay': 4000},
      cancelToken: token);
} on DioException catch (e) {
  if (CancelToken.isCancel(e)) debugPrint('Cancelled: nothing to show');
}

// In dispose() or on a Cancel button:
token.cancel('User left the screen');

DummyJSON accepts a delay query parameter (0 to 5000 ms), which is handy for testing spinners, cancel buttons and timeouts.

From DioException to app exceptions

Every Dio failure is a DioException. Its type says what went wrong, response holds the server’s answer when there was one, and error holds the original low-level error. The rest of your app should not know Dio exists, so the API layer translates these into your own exceptions.

DioExceptionTypeWhat happenedTaskFlow exception
connectionTimeout, sendTimeout, receiveTimeoutA timeout ran outRequestTimeoutException
connectionErrorNo connection (offline, DNS failure, server down)NetworkException
badResponseThe server answered with a status that failed validation (by default, outside 200 to 299)Unauthorized or ServerException, by status code
cancelYou cancelled itCancelledException
badCertificate, unknown, othersCertificate check failed, or something unexpectedUnknownException
AppException mapDioException(DioException e) {
  return switch (e.type) {
    DioExceptionType.connectionTimeout ||
    DioExceptionType.sendTimeout ||
    DioExceptionType.receiveTimeout =>
      const RequestTimeoutException(),
    DioExceptionType.connectionError => const NetworkException(),
    DioExceptionType.cancel => const CancelledException(),
    DioExceptionType.badResponse => _fromResponse(e.response),
    _ => const UnknownException(),
  };
}

The final _ case matters. Dio has added enum values over time, so a wildcard keeps your switch compiling when a new type appears. AppException itself is a sealed class, so later switches over it are checked for exhaustiveness.

Upload and download progress

For uploads, send a FormData built fresh for each request (Dio cannot reuse a finalised one). Both post and download report progress as bytes so far and total bytes. The total is -1 when the server does not send a length, so guard the division.

final form = FormData.fromMap({
  'title': 'Sprint notes',
  'file': await MultipartFile.fromFile(path, filename: 'notes.pdf'),
});
await dio.post<dynamic>('/upload', data: form,
    onSendProgress: (sent, total) {
  if (total > 0) setState(() => _progress = sent / total);
});

await dio.download(url, savePath, cancelToken: token,
    onReceiveProgress: (received, total) {
  if (total > 0) setState(() => _progress = received / total);
});

A LinearProgressIndicator(value: _progress) then shows real progress instead of an endless spinner. (DummyJSON has no upload endpoint, so this part is for your real projects.)

Example: TaskFlow’s ApiClient

TaskFlow gets one ApiClient class in lib/api/api_client.dart. It owns the Dio, adds the headers and log interceptors, and exposes get and post methods that throw only AppExceptions. It also accepts extra interceptors, which lesson 9.2 uses for the auth token.

class ApiClient {
  ApiClient({Dio? httpClient, List<Interceptor> interceptors = const []})
      : dio = httpClient ?? Dio(_defaultOptions) {
    dio.interceptors.add(HeadersInterceptor());
    dio.interceptors.addAll(interceptors);
    if (kDebugMode) {
      dio.interceptors.add(LogInterceptor(
          logPrint: (line) => debugPrint(line.toString())));
    }
  }

  static final _defaultOptions = BaseOptions(
    baseUrl: 'https://dummyjson.com',
    connectTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 10),
    receiveTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 15),
  );

  final Dio dio;

  Future<T> get<T>(String path,
      {Map<String, dynamic>? query, CancelToken? cancelToken}) async {
    try {
      final response = await dio.get<T>(path,
          queryParameters: query, cancelToken: cancelToken);
      return response.data as T;
    } on DioException catch (e) {
      throw mapDioException(e);
    }
  }
}

A TaskRepository calls _api.get('/todos', query: {'limit': 10}) and maps each JSON item to a Task. DummyJSON calls the text field todo, so Task.fromJson reads json['todo'] into title. The screen loads on start and shows a spinner, then the list.

Screen 1: Loading, then data lib/main.dart

Widget _buildBody() {
  if (_loading) {
    return Center(
      child: Column(
        mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
        spacing: 16,
        children: [
          const CircularProgressIndicator(),
          OutlinedButton(
            onPressed: () => _cancelToken?.cancel('User tapped Cancel'),
            child: const Text('Cancel'),
          ),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
  // ... error branch, see the next mock
  return ListView.builder(
    itemCount: _tasks.length,
    itemBuilder: (context, i) {
      final task = _tasks[i];
      return ListTile(
        leading: Icon(task.completed
            ? Icons.check_circle
            : Icons.radio_button_unchecked),
        title: Text(task.title),
        subtitle: Text('#' + task.id.toString()),
      );
    },
  );
}

The page starts a request in initState, shows a spinner with Cancel, then the parsed DummyJSON todos. States: Loading → Loaded.

The app bar has a “slow load” button that asks DummyJSON for a 4-second delay. While it waits, a Cancel button calls cancelToken.cancel(). The page also cancels its token in dispose(), and it ignores answers from a request that a newer one replaced.

Screen 2: Cancelling a slow request lib/main.dart

Future<void> _load({int delayMs = 0, Duration? receiveTimeout}) async {
  _cancelToken?.cancel('Replaced by a new request');
  final token = CancelToken();
  setState(() {
    _cancelToken = token;
    _loading = true;
    _error = null;
  });
  try {
    final tasks = await widget.repository.fetchTasks(
      delayMs: delayMs,
      cancelToken: token,
      receiveTimeout: receiveTimeout,
    );
    if (!mounted || !identical(token, _cancelToken)) return;
    setState(() => _tasks = tasks);
  } on AppException catch (e) {
    if (!mounted || !identical(token, _cancelToken)) return;
    setState(() => _error = e.message); // 'Request cancelled.'
  } finally {
    if (mounted && identical(token, _cancelToken)) {
      setState(() => _loading = false);
    }
  }
}

@override
void dispose() {
  _cancelToken?.cancel('Page closed');
  super.dispose();
}

The slow load asks DummyJSON for a 4 s delay; Cancel stops it and the client maps the cancel to a calm message. States: Slow load → After Cancel.

Finally, the “timeout test” button sends the same slow request with a 2-second receive timeout. Dio throws a receiveTimeout exception, the client maps it, and the page shows the friendly message with a Retry button. Turn on airplane mode and tap Retry to see the connectionError path.

Screen 3: Errors become messages lib/main.dart

// Timeout test button: 4 s delay, 2 s receive timeout
IconButton(
  tooltip: 'Timeout test',
  icon: const Icon(Icons.timer_off),
  onPressed: () => _load(
    delayMs: 4000,
    receiveTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 2),
  ),
),

// Error branch of _buildBody()
final error = _error;
if (error != null) {
  return Center(
    child: Column(
      mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
      spacing: 12,
      children: [
        const Icon(Icons.cloud_off, size: 48),
        Text(error, textAlign: TextAlign.center),
        FilledButton(onPressed: _load, child: const Text('Retry')),
      ],
    ),
  );
}

receiveTimeout and connectionError arrive as different DioException types; the mapper turns each into a friendly AppException message. States: receiveTimeout → Airplane mode.

Common mistakes

  • Creating a new Dio in every method. You lose shared interceptors and connection reuse. Create one and inject it.
  • Forgetting to call the handler. An interceptor that returns without next, resolve or reject leaves the request hanging with no error.
  • Catching DioException in widgets. Then every screen knows about Dio and repeats the same mapping. Translate errors once in the API layer.
  • Treating a cancel as an error. A cancelled request is usually intentional. Do not show a red error banner for it.
  • Logging everything in release. Full request and response logs can leak tokens and personal data. Log in debug builds only, and keep bodies off by default.
  • Dividing by the progress total without a check. The total can be -1.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “Why Dio over http?” A good answer: interceptors for cross-cutting concerns, typed errors, timeouts, cancellation and progress. Also say that http is simpler and fine for small apps. Interviewers like trade-offs, not fan loyalty.
  • Be ready to explain the interceptor order. Headers and auth first, retries next, logging last.
  • Explain the three timeouts and which one fires when the server is slow to answer (usually receiveTimeout).
  • Mention that DioException types map to user-facing messages in one place, so the UI stays simple and the mapping is unit-testable without a network.
  • On Flutter web, custom headers make the browser send a CORS preflight request, and the server must allow them. Test this lesson’s app on an emulator, a device or desktop.

terms.definition: Default settings for every request a Dio instance sends: base URL, timeouts, headers and more.
A class with onRequest, onResponse and onError hooks that runs around every request in the order interceptors were added.
The object an interceptor hook receives; call next() to continue, resolve() to finish with a response or reject() to finish with an error.
An object you pass to one or more requests; calling cancel() on it stops them with a DioException of type cancel.
The single exception type Dio throws; its type (timeout, connectionError, badResponse, cancel and so on) says what failed.
How long Dio waits for response data once connected before failing with a receiveTimeout error.

lessons.examTip: Say “translate DioException once, in the API layer” in interviews: widgets and blocs should only ever see your own exception or failure types.
