quiz.question: You add a HeadersInterceptor, an AuthInterceptor and a LogInterceptor. Where should the LogInterceptor go, and why?
options: Last, so it logs the request after the other interceptors have changed it
First, so it sees the request before anything can change it
Anywhere: Dio sorts interceptors by type
It must be in a separate Dio instance
quiz.explanation: Interceptors run in the order they were added. Adding the logger last means it prints the final headers and body that actually go to the server.

quiz.question: A user leaves a screen while its request is still loading. What is the cleanest way to handle this with Dio?
options: Set receiveTimeout to one second
Wrap setState in try/catch
Pass a CancelToken to the request and cancel it in dispose()
Create a new Dio instance for each screen
quiz.explanation: Cancelling in dispose() stops the request, and the awaiting code gets a DioException of type cancel, which you treat as a normal, silent outcome.

quiz.question: The server answers a request with status 503. Which DioExceptionType does Dio report with the default settings?
options: connectionError
badResponse
receiveTimeout
unknown
quiz.explanation: By default Dio treats any status outside 200 to 299 as a failure and throws a DioException of type badResponse, with the response attached so you can read the status code.

quiz.question: Why does the TaskFlow ApiClient convert every DioException into an AppException?
options: Dio exceptions cannot be caught with try/catch
AppException is required by Flutter for error widgets
It makes requests faster
So the UI and business logic depend on the app’s own error types, not on the HTTP library
quiz.explanation: Mapping in one place keeps Dio an implementation detail. You can change the HTTP library, test the mapping without a network and switch over a sealed type in the UI.

lessons.title: Authentication with tokens
lessons.summaryHtml:
After login the server returns a short-lived access token, sent as Authorization: Bearer … on every protected request, and a longer-lived refresh token used only to get a new access token. An auth interceptor attaches the token in onRequest and, on a 401, refreshes it once and replays the request.

Because several requests can fail at the same moment, TaskFlow uses a QueuedInterceptor: the first 401 refreshes, the others wait and retry with the new token. If the refresh fails, the tokens are cleared, an AuthCubit emits Unauthenticated, and a go_router redirect sends the user to the login screen.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

At a music festival you show your ticket once at the gate. You get a wristband that works for one day. Every stage checks the wristband, not your ticket. When the wristband expires, you go to the help desk with your membership card and get a new wristband without buying a new ticket.

Token authentication works the same way. You log in once with a username and password. The server gives you two tokens:

  • The access token is the wristband. It is short-lived, and you send it with every request in the Authorization: Bearer <token> header.
  • The refresh token is the membership card. It lives longer, and you only send it to one endpoint to get a fresh access token.

In this lesson TaskFlow gets a login screen, an interceptor that attaches and refreshes tokens, and an auth state that decides which screen the router shows.

Why it matters

Almost every job app has a login. The hard part is not the form. It is what happens 15 minutes later, when the access token expires in the middle of a screen that fires five requests at once. A weak implementation logs the user out, refreshes the token five times, or crashes with a pile of 401 errors. Users see that as “the app keeps kicking me out”.

A good implementation is invisible. Expired tokens are refreshed once, the failed requests are replayed, and the user only goes back to the login screen when the refresh token itself is no longer valid.

How it works

The login flow against DummyJSON

  1. The app sends POST /auth/login with username, password and an optional expiresInMins. DummyJSON’s test user is emilys with password emilyspass.
  2. The response contains the user’s profile fields plus accessToken and refreshToken. The app saves both in a TokenStorage.
  3. Protected requests, such as GET /auth/me or any resource under the /auth/ prefix like /auth/todos, carry Authorization: Bearer <accessToken>.
  4. When the access token has expired, the server answers 401 Unauthorized. The app calls POST /auth/refresh with the refresh token and gets a new pair.
  5. If the refresh call fails too, the session is over. The app clears the tokens and shows the login screen.
Access tokenRefresh token
Sent withEvery protected requestOnly the refresh endpoint
LifetimeShort (minutes)Longer (days or weeks, set by the server)
If stolenUseful to an attacker until it expiresCan mint new access tokens, so protect it even more
Where TaskFlow keeps itIn TokenStorage: in memory for now, in secure storage from lesson 11.1. Never in shared_preferences.

Attaching the token in onRequest

You never add the header by hand in repositories. An interceptor reads the current token and sets the header on every request. Requests that must not carry a token, like login itself, are marked with Options(extra: {skipAuth: true}). The extra map travels with the request but is never sent to the server, so it is the right place for flags like this.

@override
Future<void> onRequest(
    RequestOptions options, RequestInterceptorHandler handler) async {
  if (options.extra[skipAuth] != true) {
    final access = await tokens.readAccessToken();
    if (access != null) {
      options.headers['Authorization'] = 'Bearer $access';
    }
  }
  handler.next(options);
}

The 401 problem: refresh once, queue the rest

Imagine the task screen fires three requests just after the token expired. All three get a 401. A normal Interceptor handles errors concurrently, so you would start three refresh calls. Many servers rotate refresh tokens: each refresh invalidates the previous refresh token. The second and third refresh calls then fail, and the user is logged out for no reason.

Dio’s QueuedInterceptor solves this. It handles one callback of each kind at a time and makes the others wait in a queue. The first 401 refreshes. The second and third wait, then see that the token has changed since they were sent, and simply retry with the new one.

TimeRequest ARequest BRequest C
1401 with the old token401, waits in the queue401, waits in the queue
2Calls /auth/refresh, saves the new pair, retries: 200waitingwaiting
3doneSees a newer token, retries: 200waiting
4doneSees a newer token, retries: 200
@override
Future<void> onError(
    DioException err, ErrorInterceptorHandler handler) async {
  final request = err.requestOptions;
  if (err.response?.statusCode != 401 || request.extra[skipAuth] == true) {
    handler.next(err);
    return;
  }
  // Did another request refresh the token while this one waited?
  final current = await tokens.readAccessToken();
  final sentWith = request.headers['Authorization'];
  if (current != null && sentWith != 'Bearer $current') {
    await _retry(request, current, handler);
    return;
  }
  final fresh = await _refresh(); // POST /auth/refresh on _plainDio
  if (fresh == null) {
    await tokens.clear();
    onSessionExpired(); // tells the AuthCubit
    handler.next(err);
    return;
  }
  await _retry(request, fresh, handler);
}

Future<void> _retry(RequestOptions request, String token,
    ErrorInterceptorHandler handler) async {
  request.headers['Authorization'] = 'Bearer $token';
  try {
    handler.resolve(await _plainDio.fetch<dynamic>(request));
  } on DioException catch (e) {
    handler.next(e);
  }
}

Two details are easy to miss. First, the refresh call and the retries use a separate Dio without the auth interceptor. If you retried through the main Dio and the retry failed again, its error would join the queue behind the error that is waiting for it, and nothing would ever finish. Second, the refresh request must never trigger another refresh. Using the plain Dio guarantees that.

Logout when refresh fails

The interceptor lives in the data layer and must not import widgets or blocs. So it only calls a plain callback, onSessionExpired. In main() that callback adds an event to a broadcast StreamController. The AuthRepository exposes that stream, and the AuthCubit listens to it and emits Unauthenticated with a message.

Auth state in a Cubit

Auth has three real states, which is a perfect fit for a sealed class. AuthUnknown means the app has just started and has not checked stored tokens yet. Authenticated carries the user. Unauthenticated carries an optional message and a submitting flag for the login button.

sealed class AuthState extends Equatable {
  const AuthState();
  @override
  List<Object?> get props => [];
}
final class AuthUnknown extends AuthState { const AuthUnknown(); }
final class Authenticated extends AuthState {
  const Authenticated(this.user);
  final User user;
  @override
  List<Object?> get props => [user];
}
final class Unauthenticated extends AuthState {
  const Unauthenticated({this.message, this.submitting = false});
  final String? message;
  final bool submitting;
  @override
  List<Object?> get props => [message, submitting];
}

On start, restore() checks for a stored token and calls /auth/me. login() emits Unauthenticated(submitting: true), then Authenticated or Unauthenticated with the error message. A Cubit is enough here. If your team prefers events, the same logic fits a Bloc with AuthLoginRequested and AuthLogoutRequested events.

go_router redirect

Screens should not push the login page themselves. Instead, the router asks the auth state on every navigation and whenever the state changes. refreshListenable takes a Listenable, so a small StreamListenable class turns the cubit’s stream into one.

GoRouter buildRouter(AuthCubit auth) => GoRouter(
      initialLocation: '/splash',
      refreshListenable: StreamListenable(auth.stream),
      redirect: (context, state) {
        final loc = state.matchedLocation;
        return switch (auth.state) {
          AuthUnknown() => loc == '/splash' ? null : '/splash',
          Unauthenticated() => loc == '/login' ? null : '/login',
          Authenticated() =>
            loc == '/login' || loc == '/splash' ? '/tasks' : null,
        };
      },
      routes: [/* /splash, /login, /tasks */],
    );

Returning null means “stay where you are”. Because the switch is over a sealed type, adding a new auth state later forces you to decide where it goes.

Example: signing in to TaskFlow

The login page watches the AuthCubit. The fields are prefilled with DummyJSON’s test user. A wrong password comes back as a 4xx error, which the repository turns into its own clear message instead of the “session expired” text.

Screen 1: Login with AuthCubit lib/main.dart

final state = context.watch<AuthCubit>().state;
final submitting = state is Unauthenticated && state.submitting;
final message = state is Unauthenticated ? state.message : null;
return Scaffold(
  appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Sign in to TaskFlow')),
  body: ListView(
    padding: const EdgeInsets.all(24),
    children: [
      TextField(
          controller: _user,
          decoration: const InputDecoration(
              labelText: 'Username', prefixIcon: Icon(Icons.person))),
      const SizedBox(height: 12),
      TextField(
          controller: _pass,
          obscureText: true,
          decoration: InputDecoration(
              labelText: 'Password',
              prefixIcon: const Icon(Icons.lock),
              errorText: message)),
      const SizedBox(height: 24),
      FilledButton(
        onPressed: submitting
            ? null
            : () => context.read<AuthCubit>().login(_user.text.trim(), _pass.text),
        child: Text(submitting ? 'Signing in…' : 'Sign in'),
      ),
    ],
  ),
);

The page watches AuthCubit: submitting disables the button, and a failed login shows the message under the password field. States: Ready → Wrong password → Submitting.

After login the router moves to /tasks. The page loads three pages of /auth/todos in parallel with Future.wait. Tap the timer icon to replace the access token with a broken one: the three requests fail with 401. The interceptor’s debugPrint lines show one “refreshing” and two “token already refreshed”, and the list comes back without the user noticing. (The refresh and the retries go through the plain Dio, so the main Dio’s LogInterceptor does not print them.)

Screen 2: Expired token, one refresh lib/main.dart

/// Three parallel requests: after a 401 they all wait for ONE refresh.
Future<List<Task>> _loadThreeAtOnce() async {
  final repo = context.read<TaskRepository>();
  final pages = await Future.wait(
      [for (final skip in [0, 5, 10]) repo.fetchTasks(skip: skip)]);
  return [for (final page in pages) ...page];
}

// AppBar actions
IconButton(
    tooltip: 'Expire access token',
    icon: const Icon(Icons.timer_off),
    onPressed: () => _breakTokens(keepRefresh: true)),
IconButton(
    tooltip: 'Break both tokens',
    icon: const Icon(Icons.key_off),
    onPressed: () => _breakTokens(keepRefresh: false)),
IconButton(
    tooltip: 'Sign out',
    icon: const Icon(Icons.logout),
    onPressed: () => context.read<AuthCubit>().logout()),

Three parallel requests hit a 401; the QueuedInterceptor refreshes once and replays all three, so the user never notices. States: Signed in → Debug log.

The key icon breaks both tokens. Now the refresh fails, the interceptor clears the tokens and calls onSessionExpired. The cubit emits Unauthenticated with a message, and the redirect sends the user to the login page.

Screen 3: Session expired lib/auth/auth_cubit.dart

// main.dart: the interceptor only knows a callback
final expired = StreamController<void>.broadcast();
final api = ApiClient(interceptors: [
  AuthInterceptor(tokens: tokens, onSessionExpired: () => expired.add(null)),
]);

// auth_cubit.dart: the cubit listens to the repository's stream
AuthCubit(this._repository) : super(const AuthUnknown()) {
  _expiredSub = _repository.sessionExpired.listen((_) => emit(
      const Unauthenticated(
          message: 'Your session has expired. Please sign in again.')));
}

// router: Unauthenticated always lands on /login
Unauthenticated() => loc == '/login' ? null : '/login',

When the refresh fails, the interceptor calls onSessionExpired, the cubit emits Unauthenticated with a message and the redirect shows /login. States: Key icon tapped → Redirected.

Common mistakes

  • Refreshing with a plain Interceptor. Parallel 401s start parallel refreshes, and rotating refresh tokens then log the user out.
  • Retrying through the same Dio inside a QueuedInterceptor. This can deadlock. Use a separate Dio for refresh and retries.
  • Refreshing on every error. Only a 401 means “your token is not accepted”. A 403 means “you are known but not allowed”, and refreshing will not help.
  • Navigating from the interceptor. The data layer should not know about routes. Emit state and let the router redirect.
  • Storing tokens in shared_preferences. It is plain text on the device. Lesson 11.1 moves TaskFlow to secure storage.
  • Treating a wrong password as an expired session. Login errors need their own message.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Be ready to draw the refresh flow and explain why only one refresh may run at a time. Mention refresh token rotation.
  • Explain why access tokens are short-lived: a leaked one is only useful for a short time.
  • Know that a JWT access token is only signed, not encrypted: anyone who has it can read its claims. Never put secrets in it.
  • For deep links, a common upgrade is to pass the original location to the login page (for example /login?from=/tasks/42) and go there after sign-in.
  • Some teams use packages that wrap this pattern. Knowing how to build it yourself shows you understand what they do.

terms.definition: A short-lived credential sent with every protected request, usually as Authorization: Bearer <token>.
A longer-lived credential sent only to the refresh endpoint to obtain a new access token.
The status a server returns when the request has no valid credentials, for example an expired access token.
A Dio interceptor that handles one request, response or error callback at a time, so waiting callbacks can reuse the result of the first one.
A server policy where each refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one.
A go_router callback that runs on navigation (and when refreshListenable fires) and returns a new location or null to stay.

lessons.examTip: Interviewers love “five requests get a 401 at once: what happens?” Answer: one refresh, the others wait in a queue and retry with the new token.

quiz.question: Three requests fail with 401 at the same time. Why does TaskFlow use a QueuedInterceptor for the refresh logic?
options: QueuedInterceptor makes requests faster
Only QueuedInterceptor can read response status codes
So only the first error refreshes the token while the others wait and then retry with the new token
Because a normal Interceptor cannot call handler.resolve
quiz.explanation: A normal interceptor handles the three errors in parallel and starts three refreshes. With rotating refresh tokens, the extra refreshes fail and log the user out.

quiz.question: The refresh call itself must not pass through the auth interceptor. What is the simplest way to guarantee that?
options: Send the refresh request and the retries with a separate Dio that has no auth interceptor
Set receiveTimeout to zero on the refresh request
Call the refresh endpoint from the login page
Put the refresh token in the Authorization header
quiz.explanation: A plain Dio avoids refresh loops and avoids a deadlock where a retried request’s error waits in the queue behind the error that is waiting for it.

quiz.question: Which response should make the app try a token refresh?
options: 403 Forbidden
401 Unauthorized
404 Not Found
500 Internal Server Error
quiz.explanation: 401 means the credentials were missing or not accepted, as with an expired access token. 403 means the user is known but not allowed, so a new token will not help.

quiz.question: The refresh token has been revoked. What should TaskFlow do?
options: Retry the refresh forever with backoff
Keep using the old access token
Show a dialog asking for the refresh token
Clear the tokens, emit Unauthenticated and let the router redirect to the login page
quiz.explanation: A failed refresh ends the session. The data layer reports it through onSessionExpired, the AuthCubit emits Unauthenticated with a message, and the redirect handles navigation.

lessons.title: A robust API layer
lessons.summaryHtml:
A robust API layer treats failure as a normal result. Repositories return a sealed Result<T> (Ok or Err) holding a typed Failure, and one function in the UI turns each failure into a message. A RetryInterceptor retries temporary problems with exponential backoff, but only for idempotent requests such as GET.

TaskFlow’s task list becomes a paginated TaskListBloc: a ScrollController requests the next page near the bottom, a footer shows loading, retry or “all caught up”, RefreshIndicator reloads, and a small time-based cache in the repository avoids repeating requests.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

So far TaskFlow can talk to the server and stay logged in. Real networks are messy, though. Trains go into tunnels, servers restart, and lists have hundreds of items. A robust API layer is one that expects this. It returns failures as normal values instead of surprises, retries only when that is safe, loads long lists page by page and avoids asking the server the same question twice a second.

Think of a good delivery service. When a parcel cannot be delivered, you get a clear note (“nobody home”, “address unknown”), not silence. The driver tries again later for some problems but not for others. Big orders arrive in several boxes. That is what this lesson builds.

Why it matters

In lesson 9.1 the repository threw AppExceptions. That works, but nothing in the method signature tells the caller that it can fail, so it is easy to forget a try. Error messages also lived in the data layer, which makes translation hard.

Production apps also need:

  • Lists that load 20 items at a time as you scroll, instead of downloading everything.
  • Automatic retries for short network glitches, without ever sending the same payment twice.
  • Pull-to-refresh, and an error screen with a Retry button that actually works.
  • Fewer duplicate requests when the user goes back and forth between screens.

How it works

Typed failures and a Result type

A Result<T> is a value that is either a success holding a T or a failure holding a Failure. Because it is a sealed class, the compiler forces every caller to handle both cases. The failure itself is also sealed, so the UI can switch over every kind of problem.

sealed class Result<T> {
  const Result();
}
final class Ok<T> extends Result<T> {
  const Ok(this.value);
  final T value;
}
final class Err<T> extends Result<T> {
  const Err(this.failure);
  final Failure failure;
}

/// Runs body and turns expected errors into Err.
Future<Result<T>> guard<T>(Future<T> Function() body) async {
  try {
    return Ok(await body());
  } on AppException catch (e) {
    return Err(failureFromException(e));
  } on FormatException {
    return Err(const UnknownFailure()); // unexpected JSON
  }
}

Notice what guard does not catch: programming errors such as a null check on a missing value. Those should crash in development so you find and fix them, not turn into a vague “something went wrong”.

A small detail: Err(const UnknownFailure()) is not written as const Err(...). Inside guard the result type is Err<T>, and a constant cannot depend on a type parameter.

Mapping failures to messages in one place

The data layer says what went wrong. The presentation layer decides how to say it. One function does the translation, so wording stays consistent and you can later swap it for localized strings.

String failureMessage(Failure failure) => switch (failure) {
      NetworkFailure() => 'You are offline. Check your connection.',
      TimeoutFailure() => 'The server is slow right now. Try again.',
      UnauthorizedFailure() => 'Please sign in again.',
      CancelledFailure() => 'Cancelled.',
      ServerFailure(statusCode: final int code) when code >= 500 =>
        'TaskFlow is having trouble. Try again soon.',
      ServerFailure() => 'That request did not work.',
      UnknownFailure() => 'Something went wrong.',
    };

Retries with exponential backoff

Some failures are temporary: a timeout, a dropped connection, or a 502, 503 or 504 from an overloaded gateway. Retrying those often works. But you may only retry requests that are idempotent, meaning that sending them twice has the same effect as sending them once.

MethodIdempotent?Auto-retry?
GET, HEAD, OPTIONSYes: they only readYes
PUT, DELETEYes by definition: same final stateYes, if your API follows the rules
POST, PATCHNot guaranteed: a retry may create a second task or charge twiceNo (unless the API supports idempotency keys)

Exponential backoff waits longer before each attempt, for example 0.5 s, 1 s, then 2 s. A little random jitter is added so thousands of phones do not retry at the same instant after an outage.

class RetryInterceptor extends Interceptor {
  RetryInterceptor(this._dio, {this.maxRetries = 3});
  final Dio _dio;
  final int maxRetries;
  final _random = Random(); // from dart:math
  static const _idempotent = {'GET', 'HEAD', 'OPTIONS', 'PUT', 'DELETE'};

  bool _isTemporary(DioException e) => switch (e.type) {
        DioExceptionType.connectionTimeout ||
        DioExceptionType.receiveTimeout ||
        DioExceptionType.connectionError => true,
        DioExceptionType.badResponse =>
          const {502, 503, 504}.contains(e.response?.statusCode),
        _ => false,
      };

  @override
  Future<void> onError(
      DioException err, ErrorInterceptorHandler handler) async {
    final options = err.requestOptions;
    final attempt = options.extra['retryAttempt'] as int? ?? 0;
    final method = options.method.toUpperCase();
    if (attempt >= maxRetries ||
        !_idempotent.contains(method) ||
        !_isTemporary(err)) {
      handler.next(err);
      return;
    }
    final delayMs = 500 * pow(2, attempt).toInt() + _random.nextInt(250);
    await Future<void>.delayed(Duration(milliseconds: delayMs));
    options.extra['retryAttempt'] = attempt + 1;
    try {
      handler.resolve(await _dio.fetch<dynamic>(options));
    } on DioException catch (e) {
      handler.next(e);
    }
  }
}

The retry goes through the same Dio, so the auth interceptor attaches the current token again. Because it needs that Dio, you add it after creating the client: api.dio.interceptors.add(RetryInterceptor(api.dio));. That puts it after the LogInterceptor, which is fine: the logger prints each failed attempt, and every retry runs through the whole chain again, so it is logged too. A cancelled request has type cancel, so it is never retried.

Pagination with a BLoC

DummyJSON pages with limit and skip and returns total. There are more items while skip + items.length < total. The TaskListState tracks everything the list screen must show:

FieldUsed for
statusinitial, loading, success or failure of the first page
tasksEverything loaded so far
isLoadingMoreThe spinner in the footer, and a guard against double loads
hasReachedMaxStop asking; show “You are all caught up”
isRefreshingLets pull-to-refresh know when to stop spinning
failureThe latest error, for the error page, footer or SnackBar
Future<void> _onNextPage(
    TaskListNextPageRequested e, Emitter<TaskListState> emit) async {
  if (state.status != LoadStatus.success ||
      state.isLoadingMore ||
      state.hasReachedMax) {
    return; // one page at a time, nothing after the end
  }
  emit(state.copyWith(isLoadingMore: true, failure: () => null));
  final result = await _repository.fetchTasks(
      skip: state.tasks.length, limit: pageSize);
  switch (result) {
    case Ok(value: final page):
      emit(state.copyWith(
          tasks: [...state.tasks, ...page.tasks],
          hasReachedMax: !page.hasMore,
          isLoadingMore: false));
    case Err(:final failure):
      emit(state.copyWith(isLoadingMore: false, failure: () => failure));
  }
}

The guard matters because the scroll listener fires many times per second near the bottom. The first event sets isLoadingMore before its first await, so the events behind it return early. The bloc_concurrency package offers a droppable() transformer that does the same job at the event level. copyWith takes failure as a function so you can explicitly set it back to null.

Infinite scroll and pull-to-refresh

A ScrollController tells you how far the user has scrolled. When they are within about 300 pixels of the end, ask for the next page. The list has one extra item at the end, the footer, which shows a spinner, a retry button or “You are all caught up”.

void _onScroll() {
  final bloc = context.read<TaskListBloc>();
  final pos = _scroll.position;
  if (pos.pixels >= pos.maxScrollExtent - 300 && bloc.state.failure == null) {
    bloc.add(const TaskListNextPageRequested());
  }
}

Future<void> _refresh() async {
  final bloc = context.read<TaskListBloc>()..add(const TaskListRefreshed());
  // RefreshIndicator keeps spinning until this Future completes.
  await bloc.stream.firstWhere((s) => !s.isRefreshing);
}

RefreshIndicator needs a Future that completes when the refresh is done. Waiting for “the next state” is a trap: Bloc does not emit a state equal to the current one, so a refresh that returns the same data would spin forever. The isRefreshing flag always changes from true to false, so the wait always ends. Give the list AlwaysScrollableScrollPhysics, or a short list cannot be pulled.

Simple caching

ApiTaskRepository keeps each page in a map with the time it arrived. A request for the same page within two minutes returns the cached page without touching the network. Pull-to-refresh passes forceRefresh: true, which clears the cache. This is an in-memory cache that disappears when the app closes. Module 10 replaces it with a Drift database for real offline support.

Example: the TaskFlow task list

The /tasks route now creates a TaskListBloc with ApiTaskRepository and adds TaskListStarted. The first 20 todos appear. Scrolling near the end shows the loading footer and appends the next 20, until the footer says you are all caught up.

Screen 1: Infinite scroll lib/tasks/task_list_page.dart

ListView.builder(
  controller: _scroll,
  physics: const AlwaysScrollableScrollPhysics(),
  itemCount: state.tasks.length + 1,
  itemBuilder: (context, i) =>
      i < state.tasks.length ? _TaskTile(state.tasks[i]) : _Footer(state),
)

// _Footer.build
final Widget child;
if (state.hasReachedMax) {
  child = const Text('You are all caught up');
} else if (state.failure != null && !state.isLoadingMore) {
  child = TextButton.icon(
    onPressed: () => context
        .read<TaskListBloc>()
        .add(const TaskListNextPageRequested()),
    icon: const Icon(Icons.refresh),
    label: const Text('Could not load more. Retry'),
  );
} else {
  child = const CircularProgressIndicator();
}
return Padding(
    padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16), child: Center(child: child));

The list has one extra item, the footer: a spinner while the next page loads, then “You are all caught up” when hasReachedMax is true. States: First page → Loading more → The end.

With airplane mode on, the first page fails and the page shows the failure message with Retry. If a later page fails, the list stays visible and the footer offers a retry instead.

Screen 2: Failures in the right place lib/tasks/task_list_page.dart

builder: (context, state) => switch (state.status) {
  LoadStatus.initial || LoadStatus.loading =>
    const Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator()),
  LoadStatus.failure => Center(
      child: Column(
        mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
        spacing: 12,
        children: [
          const Icon(Icons.cloud_off, size: 48),
          Text(failureMessage(state.failure!)),
          FilledButton(
            onPressed: () => context
                .read<TaskListBloc>()
                .add(const TaskListStarted()),
            child: const Text('Retry'),
          ),
        ],
      ),
    ),
  LoadStatus.success => RefreshIndicator(
      onRefresh: _refresh,
      child: ListView.builder(/* tasks + footer */),
    ),
},

An empty list that fails becomes an error page with Retry; a failed later page keeps the list and moves the retry into the footer. States: First page failed → Later page failed.

Pulling down refreshes. If the refresh fails while tasks are on screen, the list stays and a SnackBar explains why. A BlocConsumer listener fires only when a refresh ends with a failure (isRefreshing goes from true to false), so a failed later page uses the footer instead.

Screen 3: Pull-to-refresh lib/tasks/task_list_page.dart

Future<void> _refresh() async {
  final bloc = context.read<TaskListBloc>()
    ..add(const TaskListRefreshed());
  // RefreshIndicator keeps spinning until this Future completes.
  await bloc.stream.firstWhere((s) => !s.isRefreshing);
}

BlocConsumer<TaskListBloc, TaskListState>(
  // Only a failed refresh: the end of a refresh with a failure set.
  listenWhen: (prev, curr) =>
      prev.isRefreshing && !curr.isRefreshing && curr.failure != null,
  listener: (context, state) => ScaffoldMessenger.of(context)
      .showSnackBar(SnackBar(
          content: Text(failureMessage(state.failure!)))),
  builder: (context, state) => /* see previous mock */,
)

RefreshIndicator waits for isRefreshing to become false; a failed refresh keeps the list and a BlocConsumer listener shows a SnackBar for it. States: Pulling down → Refresh failed.

Because the bloc depends on the TaskRepository interface, testing it needs no network. A mocktail mock returns canned results:

class MockTaskRepository extends Mock implements TaskRepository {}

TaskPage pageOf(int from, int count, int total) => TaskPage(
      tasks: [
        for (var i = from; i < from + count; i++)
          Task(id: i, title: 'Task $i', completed: false),
      ],
      total: total,
      skip: from,
    );

void main() {
  late MockTaskRepository repo;
  setUp(() => repo = MockTaskRepository());

  blocTest<TaskListBloc, TaskListState>(
    'appends the next page and stops at the end',
    setUp: () {
      when(() => repo.fetchTasks(
              skip: 0, limit: 2, forceRefresh: any(named: 'forceRefresh')))
          .thenAnswer((_) async => Ok(pageOf(0, 2, 3)));
      when(() => repo.fetchTasks(skip: 2, limit: 2))
          .thenAnswer((_) async => Ok(pageOf(2, 1, 3)));
    },
    build: () => TaskListBloc(repo, pageSize: 2),
    act: (bloc) async {
      bloc.add(const TaskListStarted());
      await Future<void>.delayed(Duration.zero);
      bloc.add(const TaskListNextPageRequested());
    },
    skip: 3, // loading, first page, isLoadingMore
    expect: () => [
      TaskListState(
          status: LoadStatus.success,
          tasks: [...pageOf(0, 2, 3).tasks, ...pageOf(2, 1, 3).tasks],
          hasReachedMax: true),
    ],
  );

  blocTest<TaskListBloc, TaskListState>(
    'shows a failure when the first page fails',
    setUp: () => when(() => repo.fetchTasks(
            skip: 0, limit: 20, forceRefresh: any(named: 'forceRefresh')))
        .thenAnswer((_) async => Err(const NetworkFailure())),
    build: () => TaskListBloc(repo),
    act: (bloc) => bloc.add(const TaskListStarted()),
    expect: () => [
      const TaskListState(status: LoadStatus.loading),
      const TaskListState(
          status: LoadStatus.failure, failure: NetworkFailure()),
    ],
  );
}

Common mistakes

  • Retrying POST requests automatically. A timeout does not mean the server did nothing. A retry can create duplicate tasks or orders.
  • Retrying without delay or limit. Instant, endless retries hammer a server that is already struggling.
  • No guard on “load more”. The same page is fetched several times and the list shows duplicates.
  • Replacing the list with an error page when page 5 fails. Keep what the user already has and show the error in the footer.
  • A first page that does not fill the screen. Then the user cannot scroll, so the next page never loads. Choose a page size that fills a tall screen, or load another page when the footer is built.
  • Error text in the data layer. Return typed failures and map them to words in the UI.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Explain idempotency with an example: “DELETE task 7 twice leaves the same result; POST create task twice makes two tasks.”
  • Know offset pagination (skip/limit, used here) and cursor pagination (the server returns a “next” token). Cursors do not skip or repeat items when rows are added while you scroll.
  • Many teams use a Result or Either type. Packages exist, but a sealed class with Dart 3 patterns is short and needs no dependency.
  • Say where caching lives (the repository) and how it is invalidated (time to live, pull-to-refresh, or after a write).

terms.definition: A sealed type that is either a success with a value (Ok) or a failure with a reason (Err), so callers must handle both.
A request that has the same effect whether it is sent once or several times, such as GET, PUT or DELETE.
Waiting longer before each retry (for example 0.5 s, 1 s, 2 s), usually with random jitter.
Loading a list in pages with skip (or offset) and limit, using the total to know when to stop.
A state flag that says the last page has loaded, so the list stops requesting more.
How long a cached response is considered fresh before the app fetches it again.

lessons.examTip: When asked “would you retry this request?”, answer with idempotency first: GET yes, POST no unless the API supports idempotency keys.

quiz.question: A POST /tasks request times out. Why should the RetryInterceptor NOT retry it automatically?
options: Dio cannot resend a request body
POST is not idempotent: the server may already have created the task, so a retry could create a duplicate
Timeouts are never temporary
POST requests are always cached
quiz.explanation: A timeout only tells you the answer did not arrive in time. The server may have done the work, so only idempotent requests are safe to repeat blindly.

quiz.question: Why does the repository return Result<TaskPage> instead of throwing exceptions?
options: The return type shows that the call can fail, and a switch over the sealed Result forces callers to handle Err
Exceptions cannot cross async gaps in Dart
Result objects are faster than exceptions
BLoC cannot catch exceptions
quiz.explanation: With a sealed Result the compiler checks that both Ok and Err are handled. Unexpected programming errors still throw, so they are found during development.

quiz.question: Page 3 fails to load while pages 1 and 2 are on screen. What does TaskFlow show?
options: A full-screen error that replaces the list
Nothing: the error is ignored
The existing list, with a footer that offers “Could not load more. Retry”
A dialog that blocks the screen until the network is back
quiz.explanation: Keeping loaded data visible is better for the user. The failure is stored in state and the footer offers a manual retry.

quiz.question: Pull-to-refresh sometimes spins forever when the refreshed data is identical. What is the cause?
options: RefreshIndicator only works with StreamBuilder
The ScrollController was disposed
ListView.builder cannot be refreshed
The page awaited the next emitted state, but Bloc does not emit a state equal to the current one
quiz.explanation: Equatable states that compare equal are not emitted again. An isRefreshing flag that always goes from true to false gives the page a state change it can wait for.

lessons.title: JSON at scale: freezed and json_serializable
lessons.summaryHtml:
Hand-written fromJson, toJson, ==, hashCode and copyWith are fine for one model and painful for twenty. json_serializable generates the JSON code from annotations such as @JsonKey(name: 'todo'), and freezed generates immutable data classes with value equality, copyWith, toString and sealed unions.

You run dart run build_runner build -d to create the .g.dart and .freezed.dart part files, handle renamed fields, enums, defaults and nested lists, and decide whether generated files go into git. You convert TaskFlow’s Task and DummyJSON page models to freezed.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

In lesson 7.1 you wrote fromJson and toJson by hand. That is like filling in a paper form by hand for every customer: fine for three customers, slow and error-prone for three hundred. Code generation is a rubber stamp. You describe the model once with annotations, and a tool writes the boring code for you, the same way every time.

Two packages do this in most professional Flutter code bases. json_serializable writes the JSON conversion. freezed writes immutable data classes: equality, hashCode, toString, copyWith and sealed unions. They work together, and both run through build_runner.

Why it matters

TaskFlow already has Task, the DummyJSON page wrapper, the auth tokens and a user profile. Modules 10 to 12 add projects, sync records and Supabase rows. For each model, a correct hand-written version needs a constructor, fields, fromJson, toJson, ==, hashCode, copyWith and toString. Every new field must be added in six places. Typical bugs that reach production:

  • A typo in a JSON key ('userID') that only fails at runtime.
  • A field added to the constructor but forgotten in ==, so a bloc state that did change is treated as equal and the UI does not rebuild.
  • A copyWith that cannot set a nullable field back to null, because dueDate ?? this.dueDate ignores the null.

Generated code removes whole classes of these bugs, and the model file becomes a short, readable description of the data.

How it works

Installing and the build_runner workflow

flutter pub add freezed_annotation json_annotation
flutter pub add dev:build_runner dev:freezed dev:json_serializable

dart run build_runner build -d     # generate once
dart run build_runner watch -d     # regenerate on every save

The annotation packages are normal dependencies because your code uses them at runtime. The generators are dev dependencies: they run on your machine and in CI, never inside the app. -d is short for --delete-conflicting-outputs. Recent build_runner versions already behave this way by default, so the flag is harmless there and still useful on older projects.

Each model file declares where its generated code goes:

FileWritten byContains
task.dartYouAnnotated model, part directives, custom getters
task.freezed.dartfreezedImplementation class, ==, hashCode, toString, copyWith
task.g.dartjson_serializable_$TaskFromJson and _$TaskToJson

Until you run the generator, the editor shows errors such as “Target of URI hasn’t been generated”. That is expected: generate, and they disappear.

json_serializable on its own

You can use json_serializable without freezed. Here is the DummyJSON login response, which uses camelCase keys:

import 'package:json_annotation/json_annotation.dart';

part 'auth_tokens.g.dart';

@JsonSerializable()
class AuthTokens {
  const AuthTokens({required this.accessToken, required this.refreshToken});

  final String accessToken;
  final String refreshToken;

  factory AuthTokens.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) =>
      _$AuthTokensFromJson(json);
  Map<String, dynamic> toJson() => _$AuthTokensToJson(this);
}

When a backend uses snake_case, as Supabase tables usually do, add @JsonSerializable(fieldRename: FieldRename.snake) and userId maps to user_id without a single @JsonKey.

Controlling fields with @JsonKey

OptionUse it when
name: 'todo'The JSON key differs from your Dart name
defaultValue: falseThe key may be missing (with freezed, prefer @Default)
unknownEnumValue: …The server may send enum values your app does not know yet
includeFromJson: false / includeToJson: falseA field is local only, or must not be sent back
fromJson: / toJson:You need a custom conversion, for example seconds to Duration

Enums are matched by name by default. Use @JsonValue('high') on each value, or @JsonEnum(fieldRename: …), when the wire format differs. DateTime fields are read from and written as ISO 8601 strings automatically.

Nested models work if each has its own fromJson. For toJson, set explicit_to_json: true in build.yaml (or explicitToJson: true on the annotation) so nested objects become maps too, not objects that only turn into maps when jsonEncode runs.

freezed data classes

This is TaskFlow’s Task with freezed. Since freezed 3, a class using factory constructors must be declared abstract or sealed.

import 'package:freezed_annotation/freezed_annotation.dart';

part 'task.freezed.dart';
part 'task.g.dart';

enum TaskPriority {
  @JsonValue('low') low,
  @JsonValue('normal') normal,
  @JsonValue('high') high,
}

@freezed
abstract class Task with _$Task {
  const Task._(); // lets you add getters and methods

  const factory Task({
    required int id,
    @JsonKey(name: 'todo') required String title,
    @Default(false) bool completed,
    required int userId,
    @JsonKey(unknownEnumValue: TaskPriority.normal)
    @Default(TaskPriority.normal)
    TaskPriority priority,
    DateTime? dueDate,
  }) = _Task;

  factory Task.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) => _$TaskFromJson(json);

  bool get isOverdue {
    final due = dueDate;
    return !completed && due != null && due.isBefore(DateTime.now());
  }
}

What you get for free:

  • Value equality. Two tasks with the same fields are ==, which bloc relies on to skip identical states. Lists inside freezed classes are compared by content.
  • copyWith, including task.copyWith(dueDate: null), which really clears the date.
  • Immutability. Fields are final, and list fields are exposed as unmodifiable views.
  • A readable toString: Task(id: 1, title: …, completed: false, …).

The private constructor const Task._(); is only needed when you add your own members, like isOverdue. freezed also supports a “mixed mode” with a normal constructor and your own final fields; the factory style above is the one you will see most often in existing code.

Putting @JsonKey on factory parameters triggers the analyzer warning invalid_annotation_target. The freezed documentation recommends silencing it in analysis_options.yaml with invalid_annotation_target: ignore under analyzer: errors:.

Unions with sealed classes

Several named factories create a union. Each redirect name becomes a real subclass:

@freezed
sealed class TasksState with _$TasksState {
  const factory TasksState.loading() = TasksLoading;
  const factory TasksState.loaded(List<Task> tasks) = TasksLoaded;
  const factory TasksState.failure(String message) = TasksFailure;
}

String describe(TasksState s) => switch (s) {
      TasksLoading() => 'Loading…',
      TasksLoaded(:final tasks) => 'Tasks: ' + tasks.length.toString(),
      TasksFailure(:final message) => 'Error: ' + message,
    };

Because the class is sealed, the compiler checks the switch is exhaustive. freezed 3.0 removed the old when and map helpers; a later 3.x release added them back, but the documentation calls them legacy and recommends Dart’s own switch. Compare this with the hand-written sealed states from lesson 6.3: same idea, a quarter of the code, with equality included.

Generated files and git

OptionProsCons
Commit generated filesClone and run immediately; diffs show what changed; CI is simplerNoisy pull requests; merge conflicts in generated files
Ignore them (*.g.dart, *.freezed.dart in .gitignore)Clean history; generated code always matches the generatorEvery developer and CI job must run build_runner first

Both are common. Pick one per project, write it in the README and make CI enforce it. A package you publish on pub.dev must include its generated files, because users do not run your generators. Many teams also exclude generated files from analysis with exclude: ["**/*.g.dart", "**/*.freezed.dart"] under analyzer:.

Example: TaskFlow models

DummyJSON’s /todos?limit=30&skip=0 returns {"todos": [...], "total": 254, "skip": 0, "limit": 30}. Wrap it in a freezed page class:

@freezed
abstract class TodosPage with _$TodosPage {
  const factory TodosPage({
    required List<Task> todos,
    required int total,
    required int skip,
    required int limit,
  }) = _TodosPage;

  factory TodosPage.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) =>
      _$TodosPageFromJson(json);
}

// In the ApiClient from lesson 9.1:
final response = await dio.get<Map<String, dynamic>>('/todos',
    queryParameters: {'limit': 30, 'skip': 0});
final page = TodosPage.fromJson(response.data!);

The list screen only sees Task objects. DummyJSON sends no priority, so every task shows normal through @Default.

Screen 1: Parsed with generated fromJson lib/tasks_page.dart

class TasksList extends StatelessWidget {
  const TasksList({super.key, required this.page});
  final TodosPage page;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('TaskFlow')),
      body: ListView.builder(
        itemCount: page.todos.length,
        itemBuilder: (context, i) {
          final task = page.todos[i];
          final info = 'User ' + task.userId.toString() +
              ' · ' + task.priority.name;
          return ListTile(
            leading: Icon(task.completed
                ? Icons.check_circle
                : Icons.radio_button_unchecked),
            title: Text(task.title),
            subtitle: Text(info),
          );
        },
      ),
    );
  }
}

The UI only sees clean Task objects: title comes from the "todo" key and a missing priority falls back to normal.

Changing a task never mutates it. The page replaces it with a copy, so blocs and setState see a new value and equality stays reliable.

Screen 2: copyWith keeps Task immutable lib/tasks_page.dart

class _EditableTasksState extends State<EditableTasks> {
  late List<Task> _tasks = widget.initial;

  void _toggle(int i, bool done) {
    setState(() {
      _tasks = [
        for (var j = 0; j < _tasks.length; j++)
          if (j == i) _tasks[j].copyWith(completed: done) else _tasks[j],
      ];
    });
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('TaskFlow')),
      body: ListView(
        children: [
          for (var i = 0; i < _tasks.length; i++)
            CheckboxListTile(
              value: _tasks[i].completed,
              onChanged: (v) => _toggle(i, v ?? false),
              title: Text(_tasks[i].title),
            ),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}

Ticking a box replaces the Task with task.copyWith(completed: true); the old object never changes. States: Before → After ticking row 1.

The screen state is a freezed union. Adding a fourth case later, such as TasksState.offline(), makes every incomplete switch a compile error instead of a runtime surprise.

Screen 3: A freezed union drives the screen lib/tasks_view.dart

Widget buildBody(TasksState state, VoidCallback onRetry) {
  return switch (state) {
    TasksLoading() =>
      const Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator()),
    TasksLoaded(:final tasks) => ListView(
        children: [
          for (final t in tasks)
            ListTile(
              leading: const Icon(Icons.task_alt),
              title: Text(t.title),
            ),
        ],
      ),
    TasksFailure(:final message) => Center(
        child: Column(
          mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
          spacing: 12,
          children: [
            Text(message),
            FilledButton(onPressed: onRetry, child: const Text('Retry')),
          ],
        ),
      ),
  };
}

TasksState is a sealed freezed union, so the switch must cover loading, loaded and failure or it will not compile. States: Loading → Loaded → Failure.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the part directives or the _$Task mixin. The generator then produces nothing, or the class misses its members. Check the file name in part matches exactly.
  • Leaving out abstract or sealed on factory-style freezed classes with freezed 3 or later. Older tutorials omit it and no longer compile.
  • Editing generated files. The next build overwrites them. Change the source file instead.
  • Making every field required and non-nullable without checking the real API. One missing key and fromJson throws for the whole list. Use @Default or nullable types where the API is not strict.
  • Forgetting explicit_to_json for nested models, then being surprised that toJson() contains objects instead of maps.
  • Using generated models everywhere, including the UI and database. Lesson 9.6 separates API models from domain entities for good reasons.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Know the costs: build time grows with the number of models, generated files are large, and a broken generator blocks the team. Tell interviewers when you would still hand-write a class.
  • Be ready to explain why value equality matters for bloc: identical states are skipped, changed states rebuild.
  • Mention that json_serializable works without freezed, and that freezed can be used without JSON for pure state classes.
  • Code reviewers look at the model file, not the generated file. Keep model files small and well named.

terms.definition: The Dart build tool that runs code generators such as freezed and json_serializable and writes the generated part files.
A file such as task.g.dart that belongs to task.dart through a part directive and can use its private names.
Annotation that customises one field: its JSON name, default value, unknown enum value or custom converter.
freezed annotation that gives a field a default value, used by the constructor and by fromJson when the key is missing.
Generated method that returns a new object with some fields changed and the rest copied.
A freezed class with several named factory constructors, each becoming a subclass you can switch over exhaustively.

lessons.examTip: In interviews, say what you would NOT generate: tiny value objects and one-off parsing stay hand-written. Codegen pays off for many models that change often.

quiz.question: DummyJSON returns a todo’s text under the key "todo", but your Dart field is title. What is the cleanest fix with json_serializable?
options: Rename the Dart field to todo
Write fromJson by hand for that class
Add @JsonKey(name: 'todo') to the title field
Post-process the map before calling fromJson
quiz.explanation: @JsonKey(name: …) maps a JSON key to a Dart field with a different name, so the rest of the app keeps a clear name.

quiz.question: Why does freezed need the part 'task.freezed.dart'; directive and the _$Task mixin?
options: The generated code lives in a separate part file, and the mixin adds the generated fields, equality and copyWith to your class
They make the class mutable
They are only needed on Flutter web
They register the class with get_it
quiz.explanation: build_runner writes the implementation into the part file. The part directive joins it to your library, and the mixin connects your class to the generated members.

quiz.question: The server adds a new priority value "urgent" that your enum does not know yet. Which setting stops fromJson from throwing?
options: includeIfNull: false
explicitToJson: true
@JsonKey(includeToJson: false)
@JsonKey(unknownEnumValue: TaskPriority.normal)
quiz.explanation: unknownEnumValue tells the generated code which value to use when the JSON holds a value that is not in the enum.

quiz.question: You have a freezed TasksState union with loading, loaded and failure cases. What is the recommended way to handle each case in Dart 3?
options: A chain of is checks with casts
A switch expression over the generated subclasses, which the compiler checks for exhaustiveness
A Map from Type to widget
Catching a StateError for unknown cases
quiz.explanation: Declared as sealed, the union’s subclasses can be matched with a switch expression, and the compiler reports any case you forgot. freezed 3.0 removed the old when/map helpers; 3.1 added them back for legacy code, but switch is the recommended style.

lessons.title: Dependency injection
lessons.summaryHtml:
Dependency injection means an object receives the things it needs instead of creating them. Constructor injection is the foundation: TaskRepository takes an ApiClient, which takes a Dio. Someone still has to build that graph once, in the composition root.

You use get_it as a service locator there, choosing between registerSingleton, registerLazySingleton, registerFactory and async registrations. You hand objects to widgets with BlocProvider and RepositoryProvider, switch dev, staging and prod with --dart-define, see what injectable adds, and swap in fakes for tests.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A restaurant kitchen does not grow its own tomatoes or forge its own knives. Suppliers deliver them, and the chef just cooks. If a supplier changes, the recipes stay the same.

Dependency injection (DI) is that idea for code. A class says what it needs, usually as constructor parameters, and someone else delivers it. TasksCubit needs a TaskRepository. It should not care whether that repository talks to DummyJSON, a Drift database or a fake in a test.

You already did simple DI in lesson 6.5 with constructors and RepositoryProvider. This lesson scales it to a real app with many objects, several environments and a test suite.

Why it matters

By now TaskFlow has a Dio instance with interceptors, an ApiClient, a TokenStorage, an AuthRepository, a TaskRepository and several blocs. They depend on each other in a specific order. If each class builds its own dependencies:

  • You get several Dio instances, some without the auth interceptor from lesson 9.2.
  • Tests hit the real network because nothing can be swapped.
  • Switching from the staging API to production means editing code in many places.

With DI, the graph is built in one place, every class is testable on its own, and changing an implementation is a one-line change.

How it works

Constructor injection first

The most important DI tool is not a package. It is a constructor parameter typed as an interface:

class RemoteTaskRepository implements TaskRepository {
  RemoteTaskRepository(this._api);
  final ApiClient _api;
  // ...
}

class TasksCubit extends Cubit<TasksState> {
  TasksCubit(this._tasks) : super(const TasksLoading());
  final TaskRepository _tasks;
}

Neither class knows who creates it or which concrete class it receives. That already makes both testable. What is left is the composition root: the single place where real objects are created and connected, just before runApp.

TaskFlow’s object graph

ObjectDepends onLifetime
AppConfigBuild flagsOne for the whole run
DioAppConfig (base URL)Shared, created on first use
ApiClientDioShared
TaskRepositoryApiClientShared
TasksCubitTaskRepositoryNew per screen

The lifetime column decides how you register each object.

get_it: a service locator for the composition root

get_it is a registry of objects by type. You register how to build each type once, then ask for it with getIt<T>(). It needs no BuildContext and no code generation.

import 'package:get_it/get_it.dart';

final getIt = GetIt.instance;

void setupDependencies(AppConfig config, {TaskRepository? taskRepository}) {
  getIt
    ..registerSingleton<AppConfig>(config)
    ..registerLazySingleton<Dio>(() => Dio(BaseOptions(
          baseUrl: config.apiBaseUrl,
          connectTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 10),
          receiveTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 10),
        )))
    ..registerLazySingleton<ApiClient>(() => ApiClient(httpClient: getIt<Dio>()))
    ..registerLazySingleton<TaskRepository>(
        () => taskRepository ?? RemoteTaskRepository(getIt<ApiClient>()))
    ..registerFactory<TasksCubit>(() => TasksCubit(getIt<TaskRepository>()));
}

void main() {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  setupDependencies(AppConfig.fromEnvironment());
  runApp(const App());
}
RegistrationBehaviourUse for
registerSingleton(instance)You pass a ready object; the same one is returned every timeConfig, objects that must exist at startup
registerLazySingleton(() => …)Built on the first request, then sharedDio, API clients, repositories, databases
registerFactory(() => …)A new instance on every requestCubits, blocs, form controllers
registerSingletonAsync(() async => …)Built by an async function; wait with await getIt.allReady()Objects that need async setup

Notice the factory for TasksCubit. BlocProvider(create: …) closes the bloc it created when the screen goes away. If get_it handed out a singleton cubit, the second visit would receive an already closed cubit.

Async dependencies

Some objects need await before they exist, such as a preferences cache. The simplest option is to await them in main and register the result:

Future<void> main() async {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  final prefs = await SharedPreferencesWithCache.create(
    cacheOptions: const SharedPreferencesWithCacheOptions(
      allowList: {'compactList'},
    ),
  );
  getIt.registerSingleton<SharedPreferencesWithCache>(prefs);
  setupDependencies(AppConfig.fromEnvironment());
  runApp(const App());
}

When several async objects depend on each other, registerSingletonAsync with its dependsOn list and await getIt.allReady() handle the ordering. Keep startup work small: every await here delays the first frame.

Where get_it meets the widget tree

The golden rule: call getIt only at the edges, in main, in route builders and in BlocProvider(create: …). Classes below that receive dependencies through constructors, and widgets read blocs with context.read and BlocBuilder as before.

GoRoute(
  path: '/tasks',
  builder: (context, state) => BlocProvider(
    create: (_) => getIt<TasksCubit>()..load(),
    child: const TasksPage(),
  ),
),

You can also use flutter_bloc’s MultiRepositoryProvider as the composition root and skip get_it entirely:

MultiRepositoryProvider(
  providers: [
    RepositoryProvider<ApiClient>(create: (_) => ApiClient(httpClient: dio)),
    RepositoryProvider<TaskRepository>(
      create: (context) => RemoteTaskRepository(context.read<ApiClient>()),
    ),
  ],
  child: const App(),
)
get_itRepositoryProvider
Needs BuildContextNoYes
Usable outside widgets (background tasks, services)YesNo
Scoped to part of the treeVia scopes (pushNewScope)Naturally
Main riskHidden global lookupsDeep provider nesting

Many teams combine them: get_it builds the graph, BlocProvider hands blocs to screens.

injectable: optional code generation

In large apps the setup function grows long. injectable generates it from annotations such as @injectable (factory), @lazySingleton and @singleton on your classes, plus @module for third-party types like Dio. You annotate a top-level configureDependencies() with @InjectableInit(), run build_runner, and call getIt.init(). It also supports environment annotations. It is convenient, but it adds a generator and hides the wiring; many teams start with plain get_it and add injectable only when registrations become a chore.

Environments with --dart-define

TaskFlow needs dev, staging and prod builds that talk to different APIs. Pass values at build time and read them as compile-time constants:

enum AppEnv { dev, staging, prod }

class AppConfig {
  const AppConfig({required this.env, required this.apiBaseUrl});

  factory AppConfig.fromEnvironment() {
    const envName = String.fromEnvironment('ENV', defaultValue: 'dev');
    const baseUrl = String.fromEnvironment('API_BASE_URL',
        defaultValue: 'https://dummyjson.com');
    return AppConfig(env: AppEnv.values.byName(envName), apiBaseUrl: baseUrl);
  }

  final AppEnv env;
  final String apiBaseUrl;
  bool get isProd => env == AppEnv.prod;
}
flutter run --dart-define=ENV=staging --dart-define=API_BASE_URL=https://staging.example.com
flutter build apk --dart-define-from-file=config/prod.json

String.fromEnvironment only works when evaluated as const, which is why the locals above are const. byName throws on an unknown name, so a typo fails at startup instead of silently using the wrong server. Combine this with the build flavors from lesson 8.5 when you also need different app IDs and icons.

Watch out: dart-define values are compiled into the app. Anyone can extract them from an APK or IPA. Use them for configuration such as URLs and feature flags, never for secrets. Lesson 11.1 covers what to do with real secrets.

Swapping fakes in tests

Unit tests usually need no get_it at all: TasksCubit(FakeTaskRepository()). Widget tests that pump the whole App reset the locator and register fakes:

setUp(() async {
  await getIt.reset();
  setupDependencies(
    const AppConfig(env: AppEnv.dev, apiBaseUrl: 'http://fake'),
    taskRepository: FakeTaskRepository(),
  );
});

Without reset(), the second test fails because the types are already registered, or worse, reuses state from the first test.

Example: wiring TaskFlow

The starter creates Dio and the repository inside the cubit, with a hard-coded URL. After the refactor, setupDependencies builds everything, and the app reads AppConfig to show a banner outside production.

Screen 1: One build, three environments lib/main.dart

class App extends StatelessWidget {
  const App({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final config = getIt<AppConfig>();
    final envName = config.env.name.toUpperCase();
    final baseUrl = config.apiBaseUrl;
    return MaterialApp(
      theme: ThemeData(colorSchemeSeed: const Color(0xFF00897B)),
      home: Scaffold(
        appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('TaskFlow')),
        body: Column(
          children: [
            if (!config.isProd)
              Container(
                width: double.infinity,
                padding: const EdgeInsets.all(8),
                color: Colors.amber.shade200,
                child: Text('$envName · $baseUrl'),
              ),
            Expanded(
              child: BlocProvider(
                create: (_) => getIt<TasksCubit>()..load(),
                child: const TasksView(),
              ),
            ),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

The same code shows a coloured banner for dev and staging and nothing in prod, based on AppConfig registered in get_it. States: ENV=staging → ENV=prod.

The widget test passes a fake repository. Nothing in the UI or the cubit changed, which proves the wiring is the only thing that knows about DummyJSON.

Screen 2: Real repository or fake, same UI test/tasks_page_test.dart

class FakeTaskRepository implements TaskRepository {
  @override
  Future<List<Task>> fetchTasks() async => const [
        Task(id: 1, title: 'Fake task A', completed: false),
        Task(id: 2, title: 'Fake task B', completed: true),
      ];
}

void main() {
  setUp(() async {
    await getIt.reset();
    setupDependencies(
      const AppConfig(env: AppEnv.dev, apiBaseUrl: 'http://fake'),
      taskRepository: FakeTaskRepository(),
    );
  });

  testWidgets('shows tasks from the injected repository',
      (tester) async {
    await tester.pumpWidget(const App());
    await tester.pumpAndSettle();
    expect(find.text('Fake task A'), findsOneWidget);
    expect(find.text('DEV · http://fake'), findsOneWidget);
  });
}

In the test, setupDependencies gets a FakeTaskRepository; TasksView and TasksCubit do not change at all. States: Real (DummyJSON) → Fake (widget test).

Testers appreciate an “About this build” screen. It also reminds everyone how visible these values are.

Screen 3: About this build lib/about_page.dart

class AboutBuildPage extends StatelessWidget {
  const AboutBuildPage({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final config = getIt<AppConfig>();
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('About this build')),
      body: ListView(
        children: [
          ListTile(
            leading: const Icon(Icons.layers),
            title: const Text('Environment'),
            subtitle: Text(config.env.name),
          ),
          ListTile(
            leading: const Icon(Icons.link),
            title: const Text('API base URL'),
            subtitle: Text(config.apiBaseUrl),
          ),
          const ListTile(
            leading: Icon(Icons.info_outline),
            title: Text('Values from --dart-define are not secret'),
          ),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}

A small debug screen reads AppConfig from get_it. Handy for testers, and it shows the values are visible to anyone.

Common mistakes

  • Registering cubits or blocs as singletons. The first screen closes them, the next one crashes. Use registerFactory.
  • Calling getIt everywhere. A repository that does getIt<Dio>() inside a method hides its dependency. Pass it in the constructor.
  • Using an object before it is registered, for example calling getIt in a global variable initialiser that runs before setupDependencies.
  • Forgetting await getIt.reset() between tests.
  • Treating dart-define as a vault for API secrets.
  • Circular dependencies, such as AuthRepository needing ApiClient and ApiClient needing AuthRepository. Break the cycle with a smaller interface, such as TokenStorage, that both can use.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Explain the difference between DI (the principle) and a service locator (one way to implement the composition root).
  • Know the three lifetimes and give an example of each from a real app.
  • Mention how you run the same code against dev, staging and prod, and why those values are not secret.
  • Show a test that swaps a fake in one line. It proves the design, not just the tool.

terms.definition: Passing an object the collaborators it needs, usually through its constructor, instead of letting it create them.
The one place, near main(), where concrete classes are created and connected.
A registry you ask for objects by type, such as getIt<TaskRepository>(). get_it is one.
One shared instance that is created the first time someone asks for it.
A registration that builds a new instance every time it is requested; right for cubits and blocs.
A flutter run/build flag that compiles a key=value pair into the app, read with String.fromEnvironment.

lessons.examTip: A good interview line: “Classes ask for what they need through constructors; only the composition root knows get_it.” It shows you know both DI and the service-locator trap.
