quiz.question: You register TasksCubit with registerSingleton and create it with BlocProvider(create: (_) => getIt<TasksCubit>()). After leaving and reopening the screen the app throws “Cannot emit new states after calling close”. Why?
options: BlocProvider closed the shared cubit when the first screen was disposed, and the same closed instance was handed out again
get_it cannot store cubits
The cubit needs a const constructor
BlocProvider requires RepositoryProvider above it
quiz.explanation: BlocProvider(create: …) owns and closes what it creates. A singleton cubit is closed once and then reused. Register cubits and blocs with registerFactory so each screen gets a fresh instance.

quiz.question: Which registration fits a Dio client that should be shared by the whole app but only built when first needed?
options: registerFactory
registerLazySingleton
registerFactoryParam
Creating it inside each repository
quiz.explanation: A lazy singleton is created on first use and then shared. A factory would create a new Dio, with new interceptors and connection pools, on every request.

quiz.question: You build the release app with --dart-define=MAPS_KEY=abc123. What is true about that value?
options: It is encrypted inside the app
It is only available in debug builds
It is removed by --obfuscate
It is compiled into the app binary and can be extracted, so it is configuration, not a secret
quiz.explanation: dart-define values become compile-time constants in the app. Anyone with the APK or IPA can find them. Secrets belong on a server, as lesson 11.1 shows.

quiz.question: What is the main risk of calling getIt<TaskRepository>() deep inside many widgets and classes?
options: It is slow because lookups are O(n)
It does not work on iOS
Dependencies become hidden, so you cannot see or replace what a class needs from its constructor
get_it forbids it
quiz.explanation: A class that fetches its own dependencies from a global locator hides them. Keeping get_it calls in the composition root and route builders keeps dependencies visible and easy to fake.

lessons.title: Clean architecture in practice
lessons.summaryHtml:
Clean architecture applies the layers you met in lesson 6.5 at production scale. The domain layer holds pure Dart entities, repository interfaces and optional use cases. The data layer holds models (DTOs) that mirror the API, mappers, data sources and repository implementations. The presentation layer holds widgets and cubits.

The dependency rule says source code only points inwards, towards the domain. You restructure TaskFlow’s tasks feature into feature-first folders, decide where a use case earns its place and where it is ceremony, and wire everything with get_it.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Think of a hospital. Doctors (the domain) decide what treatment a patient needs. They do not care which supplier delivers the medicine or which brand of syringe arrives. The pharmacy and the suppliers (the data layer) handle that. The reception desk (the presentation layer) talks to patients and shows them what the doctor decided. If the hospital changes supplier, the doctors keep working as before.

Clean architecture is this idea applied to code. You met its basic form in lesson 6.5. Here you add the parts that production apps use: entities separate from API models, mappers, data sources, use cases and a strict rule about which code may import which.

Why it matters

TaskFlow’s backend will change twice in this course. Module 10 adds a Drift database as a local cache, and module 12 moves everything to Supabase, where a task row looks different again (is_done, project_id, created_at). If TasksPage reads json['todo'] directly, each change touches the UI, the logic and the tests. With clean boundaries, each change stays inside the data layer.

Real teams also gain:

  • Parallel work: one developer builds the screen against a fake repository while another builds the API code.
  • Fast tests: business rules are plain Dart and test in milliseconds, without Flutter or a network.
  • Onboarding: every feature has the same shape, so a new developer knows where to look.

How it works

The three layers and the dependency rule

LayerTaskFlow contentsMay import
PresentationTasksPage, TasksCubit, ErrorViewDomain, Flutter, flutter_bloc
DomainTask entity, TaskRepository and AuthRepository interfaces, GetMyTasks, Result, FailureOnly Dart and small pure-Dart helpers
DataTaskDto, mappers, TaskRemoteDataSource, TaskRepositoryImplDomain, dio, drift, supabase_flutter…

The dependency rule: imports point towards the domain. The domain never imports presentation or data code. The data layer implements domain interfaces, which is why its arrow points up, not down.

Screen 1: The layer map lib/layer_diagram.dart

class LayerDiagram extends StatelessWidget {
  const LayerDiagram({super.key});

  Widget _box(BuildContext context, String title, String body, Color c) {
    return Container(
      width: double.infinity,
      padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12),
      decoration: BoxDecoration(
        color: c, borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(12)),
      child: Column(children: [
        Text(title, style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleMedium),
        Text(body, textAlign: TextAlign.center),
      ]),
    );
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final s = Theme.of(context).colorScheme;
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('TaskFlow layers')),
      body: Padding(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
        child: Column(spacing: 4, children: [
          _box(context, 'Presentation', 'TasksPage · TasksCubit', s.primaryContainer),
          const Icon(Icons.arrow_downward),
          _box(context, 'Domain', 'Task · TaskRepository · GetMyTasks', s.tertiaryContainer),
          const Icon(Icons.arrow_upward),
          _box(context, 'Data', 'TaskDto · mapper · TaskRepositoryImpl', s.secondaryContainer),
        ]),
      ),
    );
  }
}

A tiny widget that draws the rule: presentation and data both point at the domain, and the domain points at nothing.

Entities versus models (DTOs)

In lesson 9.4 one freezed Task did two jobs: it described the business idea and it parsed DummyJSON. That is fine for small apps. In a clean setup you split it:

Entity: TaskModel: TaskDto
LayerDomainData
ShapeWhat the app means: title, isCompleted, ownerIdWhat the API sends: todo, completed, userId
JSON codeNonefromJson/toJson (hand-written or generated)
Changes whenBusiness rules changeThe API or database changes
// domain: pure Dart
class Task {
  const Task({required this.id, required this.title,
      required this.isCompleted, required this.ownerId});
  final int id;
  final String title;
  final bool isCompleted;
  final int ownerId;

  Task copyWith({bool? isCompleted}) => Task(id: id, title: title,
      isCompleted: isCompleted ?? this.isCompleted, ownerId: ownerId);
}

Later a Drift row and a Supabase row get their own models. All of them map to the same Task.

Mappers

A mapper converts a model into an entity and back. An extension in the data layer keeps it close to the DTO and out of the domain:

extension TaskDtoMapper on TaskDto {
  Task toEntity() => Task(
        id: id,
        title: todo.trim(),
        isCompleted: completed,
        ownerId: userId,
      );
}

Mappers are also the right place for small clean-ups: trimming text, turning an empty string into null, or converting a status string into an enum.

Repository interfaces and implementations

The domain declares what it needs. It returns the Result type from lesson 9.3 (Ok with a value or Err with a typed Failure), so callers must handle failure:

abstract interface class TaskRepository {
  Future<Result<List<Task>>> tasksForUser(int userId);
  Future<Result<Task>> setCompleted(Task task, bool completed);
}

The data layer implements it with a data source, a class that only knows one source (here, the REST API through Dio). The repository combines data sources, maps DTOs to entities and turns exceptions into domain failures:

class TaskRepositoryImpl implements TaskRepository {
  TaskRepositoryImpl(this._remote);
  final TaskRemoteDataSource _remote;

  @override
  Future<Result<List<Task>>> tasksForUser(int userId) => _guard(() async {
        final dtos = await _remote.fetchForUser(userId);
        return [for (final dto in dtos) dto.toEntity()];
      });

  @override
  Future<Result<Task>> setCompleted(Task task, bool completed) =>
      _guard(() async {
        final saved = await _remote.updateCompleted(task.id, completed);
        return task.copyWith(isCompleted: saved);
      });

  Future<Result<T>> _guard<T>(Future<T> Function() body) async {
    try {
      return Ok(await body());
    } on DioException catch (e) {
      return Err(failureFromDio(e));
    } catch (_) {
      return Err(const UnknownFailure()); // unexpected JSON
    }
  }
}

In module 10 this class gains a second data source, a local Drift database, and decides when to read from each. Nothing above it changes.

Use cases: helpful or ceremony?

A use case is one application action in the domain layer. GetMyTasks earns its place: it combines two repositories and holds a business rule (open tasks first) that both the task list and a future home-screen widget need.

class GetMyTasks {
  GetMyTasks(this._auth, this._tasks);
  final AuthRepository _auth;
  final TaskRepository _tasks;

  Future<Result<List<Task>>> call() async {
    final userId = await _auth.currentUserId();
    final result = await _tasks.tasksForUser(userId);
    return switch (result) {
      Ok(:final value) => Ok(sortOpenFirst(value)),
      Err() => result,
    };
  }

  static List<Task> sortOpenFirst(List<Task> tasks) => [...tasks]
    ..sort((a, b) => a.isCompleted == b.isCompleted
        ? a.title.compareTo(b.title)
        : (a.isCompleted ? 1 : -1));
}

The call() method lets the cubit write await _getMyTasks(). Compare it with a ToggleTask class whose call only forwards to setCompleted: that adds a file, a registration and a test with no behaviour. Skip it and let the cubit call the repository.

Write a use case when…Skip it when…
It combines two or more repositoriesIt forwards a single repository call
It holds a business rule you want to test aloneThe “rule” is only UI state, such as a loading flag
Several blocs or screens need the same stepsOnly one cubit will ever use it

Feature-first folders

lib/
  main.dart                 composition root (get_it setup, runApp)
  core/                     Result, Failure, ApiClient, theme
  features/
    auth/
      domain/  data/  presentation/
    tasks/
      domain/               task.dart, task_repository.dart, get_my_tasks.dart
      data/                 task_dto.dart, task_mapper.dart,
                            task_remote_data_source.dart, task_repository_impl.dart
      presentation/         tasks_cubit.dart, tasks_page.dart, error_view.dart

Shared building blocks such as Result usually live in core/. The lab solution groups each layer into one file so it is easy to paste; split it once it works.

Wiring with get_it

Register from the outside in: data sources, repositories, use cases, then cubits. Only main.dart knows the concrete classes.

void setupDependencies() {
  getIt
    ..registerLazySingleton<Dio>(() => Dio(BaseOptions(baseUrl: 'https://dummyjson.com')))
    ..registerLazySingleton<TaskRemoteDataSource>(() => TaskRemoteDataSource(getIt()))
    ..registerLazySingleton<TaskRepository>(() => TaskRepositoryImpl(getIt()))
    ..registerLazySingleton<AuthRepository>(() => const DemoAuthRepository(152))
    ..registerFactory<GetMyTasks>(() => GetMyTasks(getIt(), getIt()))
    ..registerFactory<TasksCubit>(() => TasksCubit(getIt(), getIt()));
}

getIt() without a type argument infers the type from the constructor parameter. DemoAuthRepository stands in for the real AuthRepository from lesson 9.2, which would ask /auth/me for the user id.

Keeping the rule honest

Rules that nobody checks decay. Review imports in pull requests: a domain file that imports package:dio or package:flutter is a red flag. Some teams go further and move each layer into its own Dart package inside a pub workspace, so a forbidden import does not even resolve. Start with folders and reviews; move to packages when the team grows.

Example: TaskFlow “My tasks”

The starter page calls Dio, reads json['todo'], sorts and handles errors inside setState. After the refactor the page only switches on state. GetMyTasks supplies the sorted list, and ticking a task goes straight to TaskRepository.

Screen 2: My tasks, open first lib/features/tasks/presentation/tasks_page.dart

class TasksPage extends StatelessWidget {
  const TasksPage({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('My tasks')),
      body: BlocBuilder<TasksCubit, TasksState>(
        builder: (context, state) => switch (state) {
          TasksLoading() =>
            const Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator()),
          TasksError(:final message) => ErrorView(
              message: message,
              onRetry: () => context.read<TasksCubit>().load(),
            ),
          TasksLoaded(:final tasks) when tasks.isEmpty =>
            const Center(child: Text('No tasks yet.')),
          TasksLoaded(:final tasks) => ListView(
              children: [
                for (final task in tasks)
                  CheckboxListTile(
                    value: task.isCompleted,
                    title: Text(task.title),
                    onChanged: (v) => context
                        .read<TasksCubit>()
                        .toggle(task, v ?? false),
                  ),
              ],
            ),
        },
      ),
    );
  }
}

GetMyTasks loads the signed-in user’s tasks and sorts open ones first; ticking one goes through TaskRepository and the list re-sorts. States: Loading → Loaded → After ticking row 1.

Failures arrive as typed Failure objects, and the cubit turns them into words with failureMessage, the one mapping function from lesson 9.3. The page never sees a DioException, so moving to Supabase will not change this screen.

Screen 3: Failures become messages lib/features/tasks/presentation/error_view.dart

class ErrorView extends StatelessWidget {
  const ErrorView({super.key, required this.message, required this.onRetry});
  final String message;
  final VoidCallback onRetry;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Center(
      child: Column(
        mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
        spacing: 12,
        children: [
          const Icon(Icons.cloud_off, size: 48),
          Text(message),
          FilledButton.icon(
            onPressed: onRetry,
            icon: const Icon(Icons.refresh),
            label: const Text('Retry'),
          ),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}

TaskRepositoryImpl turns a DioException into a NetworkFailure; the cubit shows failureMessage(failure). The empty list gets its own state. States: Offline → No tasks.

Common mistakes

  • Returning DTOs from repositories. The API shape then leaks into cubits and widgets, and the split buys nothing.
  • Importing data or Flutter code into the domain, for example catching DioException in a use case.
  • A use case for every call. Pass-through classes slow everyone down. Add them where they hold logic.
  • Three identical classes per concept. If entity, DTO and table row are truly the same, it is fine to start with one and split when they diverge.
  • Putting business rules in widgets, such as sorting in build(). It cannot be tested without Flutter and runs on every rebuild.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Draw the three layers and the arrows, then explain the dependency rule in one sentence.
  • Explain entity versus DTO with a concrete field rename, such as todo to title.
  • Give one example where a use case helps and one where it is ceremony. Pragmatism is what senior reviewers look for.
  • Mention that Flutter’s own architecture guide on docs.flutter.dev recommends a UI layer and a data layer with an optional domain layer. Clean architecture is a family of similar ideas, not one fixed recipe; follow your team’s conventions.

terms.definition: A domain object such as Task that describes the business idea in pure Dart, with no JSON or database details.
A data transfer object that mirrors an external format, such as DummyJSON’s todo JSON, and lives in the data layer.
Code that converts between a DTO and an entity, for example TaskDto.toEntity().
A domain class with one application action, such as GetMyTasks, often exposed through a call() method.
A data-layer class that talks to one source only, such as the REST API or the local database.
Imports point inwards: presentation and data depend on domain, and domain depends on nothing in the app.

lessons.examTip: When an interviewer asks about clean architecture, also say when you would not use a layer. “I skip pass-through use cases” sounds more senior than reciting three circles.

lessons.title: Drift: a typed SQLite database
lessons.summaryHtml: Drift is a library that sits on top of SQLite and lets you describe tables as Dart classes. A code generator (build_runner) turns them into row classes, insert helpers (companions) and a typed query API, so a misspelled column is a compile error, not a crash on a user’s phone. Queries can be read once with get() or watched with watch(), which gives a Stream that emits again whenever the data changes. You group queries in DAOs, keep multi-step writes safe with transactions, and change the schema over time with migrations. In this lesson TaskFlow gets its local database, AppDatabase, with projects, tasks, a join and a first migration.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

In lesson 7.3 you used sqflite: you wrote SQL as strings and got rows back as Map<String, Object?>. That works, but nothing checks your strings. Type 'updated_at' in one place and 'updatedAt' in another, and you only find out when a user’s app crashes.

Drift keeps SQLite underneath but moves the description of your data into Dart. You write each table as a class. A code generator reads those classes and writes the boring, error-prone code for you: a row class per table, helpers for inserts, and a query API where columns are real Dart objects. If a column does not exist, your code does not compile.

Think of it as the difference between writing directions on a napkin and using a map app. Both can get you there, but only one warns you before you take a wrong turn.

Why it matters

From module 9, TaskFlow loads tasks from an API. Every screen waits for the network, and with no signal the app is empty. A professional app keeps a local copy: it opens instantly, works on a train, and syncs later (lesson 10.3). That local copy needs real queries: “open tasks in project X, newest first, with the project name”. That is relational data, which is what SQLite is good at.

Drift adds three things that matter in production:

  • Compile-time safety. Queries use generated column objects, so renames and typos show up in the analyzer.
  • Reactive queries. watch() returns a Stream, which plugs straight into StreamBuilder or a Cubit. Write anywhere, and every screen showing that data updates.
  • Managed migrations. Your schema will change after release. Drift tracks a version number and gives you tools to upgrade old databases and to test those upgrades.

How it works

Setup

Add the runtime packages and the generators:

flutter pub add drift drift_flutter dev:drift_dev dev:build_runner
dart run build_runner build -d      # after every change to tables
dart run build_runner watch -d      # or keep it running while you work

drift_flutter gives you driftDatabase(name: ...), which opens the database file in a sensible app directory on Android, iOS and desktop. The web works too, but needs two extra files in web/, described in the Drift docs.

Tables as Dart classes

import 'package:drift/drift.dart';
import 'package:drift_flutter/drift_flutter.dart';

part 'app_database.g.dart';

@DataClassName('ProjectRow')
class Projects extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();
  TextColumn get name => text().withLength(min: 1, max: 60)();
}

@DataClassName('TaskRow')
class Tasks extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();
  TextColumn get title => text().withLength(min: 1, max: 200)();
  BoolColumn get done => boolean().withDefault(const Constant(false))();
  IntColumn get projectId => integer()
      .nullable()
      .references(Projects, #id, onDelete: KeyAction.setNull)();
  DateTimeColumn get updatedAt => dateTime().withDefault(currentDateAndTime)();
}

Each getter is a column. The builder chain ends with an extra (): that call finishes the column definition. By default Drift names the row class after the table in the singular (Task). TaskFlow already has a Task entity from lesson 9.6, so @DataClassName('TaskRow') keeps the database row separate from the domain model. A mapper turns one into the other, exactly as you did with DTOs.

From each table the generator creates a row class (TaskRow, immutable, with copyWith and ==) and a companion (TasksCompanion). A companion wraps each field in Value, so “not given” (Value.absent()) is different from “set to null” (Value(null)). That is how inserts can skip auto-increment ids and defaults, and how updates can change one column only.

The database class and DAOs

@DriftAccessor(tables: [Projects, Tasks])
class TaskDao extends DatabaseAccessor<AppDatabase> with _$TaskDaoMixin {
  TaskDao(super.attachedDatabase);

  Future<int> addTask(String title, {int? projectId}) =>
      into(tasks).insert(TasksCompanion.insert(
          title: title, projectId: Value(projectId)));

  Future<List<TaskRow>> openTasks() => (select(tasks)
        ..where((t) => t.done.equals(false))
        ..orderBy([(t) => OrderingTerm.desc(t.updatedAt)]))
      .get();

  Future<void> toggleDone(TaskRow task) =>
      (update(tasks)..where((t) => t.id.equals(task.id))).write(
          TasksCompanion(done: Value(!task.done), updatedAt: Value(DateTime.now())));

  Future<int> deleteDone() =>
      (delete(tasks)..where((t) => t.done.equals(true))).go();
}

@DriftDatabase(tables: [Projects, Tasks], daos: [TaskDao])
class AppDatabase extends _$AppDatabase {
  AppDatabase([QueryExecutor? executor])
      : super(executor ?? driftDatabase(name: 'taskflow'));

  @override
  int get schemaVersion => 1;
}

A DAO (data access object) groups the queries of one feature, so AppDatabase does not become a 2,000-line file. The generator adds a taskDao getter to the database. The optional executor parameter is for tests: AppDatabase(NativeDatabase.memory()) gives each test a fresh in-memory database.

Read the query style carefully. select(tasks) starts a statement, the cascade ..where and ..orderBy configure it, and get() runs it once. t.done.equals(false) is not a Dart comparison: it builds the SQL expression done = 0. You can combine expressions with & and |, and use helpers such as like, isIn, isNull and isBiggerThanValue.

Joins

To show each task with its project name, you join the tables. select(tasks).join([...]) returns rows that hold both tables, and you read each side with readTable or, for the optional side of a left outer join, readTableOrNull. Mapping each row into a Dart 3 record such as (task: ..., project: ...) keeps the UI code tidy. The second mock shows this query and the screen it feeds.

Screen 2: A join: tasks with their project lib/task_tile.dart

// In TaskDao:
Stream<List<TaskWithProject>> watchTasks() {
  final query = select(tasks).join([
    leftOuterJoin(projects, projects.id.equalsExp(tasks.projectId)),
  ])
    ..orderBy([OrderingTerm.asc(tasks.done), OrderingTerm.desc(tasks.updatedAt)]);
  return query.watch().map((rows) => [
        for (final row in rows)
          (task: row.readTable(tasks), project: row.readTableOrNull(projects)),
      ]);
}

// In the UI:
class TaskTile extends StatelessWidget {
  const TaskTile({super.key, required this.item});
  final TaskWithProject item;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final (:task, :project) = item;
    return ListTile(
      leading: Icon(task.done ? Icons.check_circle : Icons.radio_button_unchecked),
      title: Text(task.title),
      trailing: Chip(label: Text(project?.name ?? 'No project')),
    );
  }
}

One query reads both tables. Tasks without a project still appear because the join is a left outer join, so readTableOrNull returns null and the tile says No project.

watch(): the database as a stream

Swap get() for watch() and the query becomes a Stream. Drift knows which tables the query reads. When any Drift write touches those tables (an insert here, an update in a background sync there), it re-runs the query and emits the new result. The screen simply listens. There is no manual “refresh the list” call after each write, which removes a whole class of stale-screen bugs.

Screen 1: Live task list lib/main.dart

class _TaskListPageState extends State<TaskListPage> {
  // Create the streams once, never inside build().
  late final _tasks = widget.db.taskDao.watchTasks();
  late final _openCount = widget.db.taskDao.watchOpenCount();

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final dao = widget.db.taskDao;
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(
        title: StreamBuilder<int>(
          stream: _openCount,
          builder: (context, snap) {
            final open = snap.data ?? 0;
            return Text('TaskFlow ($open open)');
          },
        ),
      ),
      body: StreamBuilder<List<TaskWithProject>>(
        stream: _tasks,
        builder: (context, snap) {
          if (!snap.hasData) {
            return const Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator());
          }
          final items = snap.data!;
          if (items.isEmpty) {
            return const Center(child: Text('No tasks yet. Tap + to add one.'));
          }
          return ListView.builder(
            itemCount: items.length,
            itemBuilder: (context, i) {
              final (:task, :project) = items[i];
              return CheckboxListTile(
                value: task.done,
                onChanged: (_) => dao.toggleDone(task),
                title: Text(task.title),
                subtitle: Text(project?.name ?? 'No project'),
              );
            },
          );
        },
      ),
      floatingActionButton: FloatingActionButton(
        onPressed: () => dao.addTask('Call the client', projectId: 1),
        child: const Icon(Icons.add),
      ),
    );
  }
}

The screen never calls setState after a write. The StreamBuilder listens to watch(), so adding a task makes Drift re-run the query and push the new list, and the title count updates the same way. States: Empty database → After 3 inserts.

Create the stream once (in initState, a late final field, or a Cubit) and reuse it. Calling watchTasks() inside build() creates a new stream on every rebuild, so StreamBuilder keeps resubscribing and flickers back to its loading state.

Transactions and batches

Future<void> mergeProject({required int fromId, required int intoId}) {
  return transaction(() async {
    await (update(tasks)..where((t) => t.projectId.equals(fromId)))
        .write(TasksCompanion(projectId: Value(intoId)));
    await (delete(projects)..where((p) => p.id.equals(fromId))).go();
  });
}

// Many rows at once, for example after downloading 100 tasks:
Future<void> saveAll(List<TasksCompanion> rows) =>
    batch((b) => b.insertAllOnConflictUpdate(tasks, rows));

Inside transaction, if any statement throws, every change in the block is rolled back. Always await each statement inside the block: a write that is not awaited may run after the transaction has already finished. A batch sends many statements together, which is much faster than a loop of single inserts, and watchers are notified once at the end.

Schema migrations

The first release creates the tables with createAll(). Later you add a priority column. Phones that already have version 1 still have the old file, so the new code must upgrade it:

@override
int get schemaVersion => 2;

@override
MigrationStrategy get migration => MigrationStrategy(
      onCreate: (m) => m.createAll(),
      onUpgrade: (m, from, to) async {
        if (from < 2) {
          await m.addColumn(tasks, tasks.priority);
        }
        // if (from < 3) { ... } comes here in a later release
      },
      beforeOpen: (details) async {
        await customStatement('PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON');
      },
    );

Write each step as if (from < n), never if (from == n - 1): a user may jump from version 1 straight to version 4, and every step in between must run in order. A new non-null column needs a default, or existing rows would break the constraint. beforeOpen runs after migrations on every start; SQLite only enforces foreign keys when you switch them on for each connection, so this is the place.

Screen 3: Migration to version 2 lib/data/app_database.dart

// Version 2 adds a column to Tasks:
//   TextColumn get priority =>
//       textEnum<Priority>().withDefault(Constant(Priority.normal.name))();

@override
int get schemaVersion => 2; // was 1

@override
MigrationStrategy get migration => MigrationStrategy(
      onCreate: (m) => m.createAll(),
      onUpgrade: (m, from, to) async {
        if (from < 2) {
          await m.addColumn(tasks, tasks.priority);
        }
      },
    );

// The tile shows the new column:
ListTile(
  title: Text(task.title),
  subtitle: Text(project?.name ?? 'No project'),
  trailing: Chip(label: Text(switch (task.priority) {
    Priority.low => 'Low',
    Priority.normal => 'Normal',
    Priority.high => 'High',
  })),
)

The same phone before and after the upgrade. onUpgrade added the priority column with a default, so the three old tasks survive and all show Normal. States: Version 1 → After upgrade to 2.

For real projects Drift offers guided migrations: dart run drift_dev make-migrations saves a snapshot of each schema version, generates a stepByStep helper so every step sees the schema as it was at that version, and generates tests that open an old schema, run your migration and verify the result. Use it from your first release: you cannot snapshot a schema you did not save.

Drift vs raw sqflite

QuestionsqfliteDrift
How are queries written?SQL strings, maps in and outTyped Dart API (or checked SQL in .drift files)
Typo in a column nameRuntime errorCompile error
UI updates after a writeYou reload by handwatch() streams update themselves
MigrationsonUpgrade with raw SQL, untested by defaultMigrator helpers, schema snapshots, generated tests
PlatformsAndroid, iOS, macOS (others need extra packages)Mobile, desktop and web
CostNo code generation, tiny APIbuild_runner step, more to learn

sqflite is still fine for one small table. Once you have relations, several screens reading the same data, or a schema that will evolve, Drift pays for itself.

Example: TaskFlow’s AppDatabase

  1. Create lib/data/app_database.dart with Projects and Tasks, the TaskDao and AppDatabase, then run dart run build_runner build -d.
  2. In beforeOpen, switch on foreign keys and, when details.wasCreated is true, insert an “Inbox” project so new tasks have a home.
  3. Create one AppDatabase in main() and pass it down (in module 9 terms: register it as a lazy singleton in get_it, or provide it with RepositoryProvider). One instance per app: two instances on the same file do not see each other’s changes in watch().
  4. The list screen watches watchTasks() and watchOpenCount(). The add button, the checkbox and “delete done” only write; the streams do the rest.
  5. After a release, add priority, bump schemaVersion to 2, add the column in onUpgrade, and confirm old tasks survive.
  6. In lesson 10.3 the repository will fill these tables from the API and the UI will read only from the database.

Common mistakes

  • Editing tables and forgetting build_runner. The generated file is out of date and you get confusing errors about missing members. Rerun the build, or keep watch running.
  • Changing a table without a migration. It works on your emulator because you reinstalled, then crashes for every existing user. Bump schemaVersion and write the step every time.
  • Opening several AppDatabase instances. Streams from one do not see writes from the other, and you can get “database is locked” errors. Create one and inject it.
  • Creating watch() streams in build(). Every rebuild resubscribes. Create them once.
  • Using the database row class everywhere. TaskRow is a storage detail. Map it to the domain Task in the repository so the UI does not depend on Drift.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “How do you keep a list in sync with local data?” Answer with watch() streams into a Cubit or StreamBuilder, and explain why you create the stream once.
  • “How do you handle schema changes after release?” Mention schemaVersion, if (from < n) steps, defaults for new columns, and migration tests with schema snapshots.
  • Know when a transaction is required: any multi-step write where a half-finished state would be wrong.
  • Testing: an in-memory NativeDatabase.memory() per test gives fast, isolated repository tests without a device.

terms.definition: A Dart class extending Table whose getters describe columns, for example IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();
A generated class used for inserts and partial updates. Each field is a Value, so “not set” is different from “set to null”.
Data access object: a class annotated with @DriftAccessor that groups related queries and gets its own generated mixin.
Turns a query into a Stream that re-runs and emits whenever a table it reads is changed through Drift.
The number Drift stores in the database file. Raising it makes Drift call onUpgrade with the old and new versions.
A block of statements that commits together or rolls back together if any of them fails.

lessons.examTip: In interviews, say why: “Drift gives me compile-time checked SQL, reactive streams and tested migrations. With raw sqflite, all three are my job.”

quiz.question: Your task list screen uses a Drift query with watch(). Another screen marks a task as done through the same database. What happens to the list?
options: Nothing until the user pulls to refresh
The stream emits a new list, so the StreamBuilder rebuilds with the change
The app throws because two screens use one table
Only the changed row is updated, the rest of the list is cleared
quiz.explanation: Drift tracks which tables a watched query reads. Any write to those tables through Drift re-runs the query and emits the new result.

quiz.question: You add a priority column to Tasks and run the app on a phone that already has the old database. It crashes with “no such column: priority”. What did you forget?
options: To call m.createAll() in onUpgrade
To delete the .g.dart file
To raise schemaVersion and add the column in onUpgrade
To wrap the insert in a transaction
quiz.explanation: Changing the Dart table does not change an existing file on a device. Raise schemaVersion and add the column in onUpgrade (m.addColumn), so old databases are upgraded.

quiz.question: Why does Drift generate TasksCompanion with Value fields instead of plain nullable fields?
options: To tell apart “leave this column unchanged” (absent) from “set it to null”
Because Dart cannot have nullable fields
So that inserts run on a background isolate
Because SQLite has no NULL
quiz.explanation: Value.absent() means the column is not part of the insert or update. Value(null) writes NULL. A plain null could not express both.

quiz.question: Moving tasks to another project and then deleting the old project must never leave tasks pointing at a deleted project. What should you use?
options: Two separate awaits in the UI
A batch of watch() streams
A bigger schemaVersion
One transaction around both statements
quiz.explanation: A transaction commits both statements together or rolls both back, so the database is never left half-changed.

lessons.title: Choosing local storage
lessons.summaryHtml: Flutter apps have several places to keep data on the device, and each fits a different job. shared_preferences holds a few small settings. flutter_secure_storage holds secrets such as tokens in the platform Keychain or Keystore. sqflite and Drift hold relational data you query. Hive CE is a fast key-value store for Dart objects, and ObjectBox is an object database. You choose by data shape, queries, encryption needs, size and platforms. In this lesson you also learn Hive CE basics (boxes and type adapters) and build a response cache for TaskFlow that shows saved data instantly and refreshes from the network.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A house has different places for different things. Keys go on a hook by the door, documents go in a filing cabinet, valuables go in a safe, and groceries go in the fridge. You could put everything in one big box, but finding things would be slow and your passport would sit next to the milk.

Apps are the same. Flutter gives you several ways to store data on the device, and each one is built for a different kind of data: a few settings, a secret token, thousands of related rows, or a pile of cached objects. Picking the right one is a design decision you will make in every professional app, and interviewers like to ask about it.

Why it matters

The wrong choice causes real problems. A token in shared_preferences sits in a plain file that anyone with a rooted phone or a device backup can read. A list of 5,000 tasks stored as one JSON string must be loaded and parsed in full just to show ten of them. A relational database used for one dark mode flag is extra setup for nothing. And some packages do not run on the web at all, which you discover late if you did not check.

TaskFlow now has four kinds of local data: user settings, auth tokens, the task database from lesson 10.1, and cached API responses. This lesson gives you a way to place each one.

How it works

The options

  • shared_preferences: small key-value pairs (bool, int, double, String, List of String). Use the newer SharedPreferencesAsync or SharedPreferencesWithCache APIs. Not for secrets, not for large data.
  • flutter_secure_storage: small string secrets, encrypted with keys held by the platform (Keychain on iOS and macOS, Keystore-backed encryption on Android). Lesson 11.1 goes deeper. It is slower than preferences, so keep it for secrets.
  • sqflite: SQLite with raw SQL strings. Fine for simple tables.
  • Drift: SQLite with typed queries, streams and migrations (lesson 10.1). The default for structured app data.
  • Hive CE: a key-value store written in pure Dart. You open boxes and put Dart objects in them. It is quick to set up and good for caches and simple object storage. There are no joins or query language: you look up by key or loop over values.
  • ObjectBox: a fast object database with queries and relations, driven by code generation, with its own sync product. Check its documentation for platform support before choosing it for a web app.

A note on Hive: the original hive package is no longer maintained. Hive CE (hive_ce and hive_ce_flutter) is the community edition that continues it with the same style of API. Use it for new code, and plan a migration if you inherit an app on the old package.

A decision table

StoreData shapeQueriesEncryptionSizeWeb
shared_preferencesFew primitive valuesBy key onlyNoTinyYes
flutter_secure_storageFew string secretsBy key onlyYes, platform keysTinyYes, with weaker guarantees than mobile
sqfliteTables and rowsFull SQL, as stringsNot built inLargeNot by itself
DriftTables and relationsTyped SQL, joins, streamsPossible with an encrypted SQLite buildLargeYes, with extra setup
Hive CEKey to objectBy key, or scan valuesYes, per box (AES)Small to mediumYes
ObjectBoxObjects and relationsQuery builderCheck current docsLargeCheck current docs

A quick rule: secret means secure storage; a setting means shared_preferences; data you filter, sort or join means Drift; a cache or simple object list read by key means Hive CE or a Drift table. Sometimes both are fine; then pick the one your team already uses, because one fewer dependency is worth a lot.

Screen 1: Settings backed by three stores lib/settings_page.dart

class SettingsPage extends StatelessWidget {
  const SettingsPage({super.key, required this.dark, required this.onDark,
      required this.signedIn, required this.cache, required this.onClear});
  final bool dark;                    // shared_preferences
  final ValueChanged<bool> onDark;
  final bool signedIn;                // token found in flutter_secure_storage
  final CacheStore cache;             // Hive CE box
  final VoidCallback onClear;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final count = cache.length;
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Settings')),
      body: ListView(children: [
        SwitchListTile(
          secondary: const Icon(Icons.dark_mode),
          title: const Text('Dark mode'),
          subtitle: const Text('shared_preferences'),
          value: dark,
          onChanged: onDark,
        ),
        ListTile(
          leading: const Icon(Icons.lock),
          title: Text(signedIn ? 'Signed in' : 'Signed out'),
          subtitle: const Text('Token in secure storage'),
        ),
        ListTile(
          leading: const Icon(Icons.storage),
          title: const Text('Cached responses'),
          subtitle: const Text('Hive CE box api_cache'),
          trailing: Text('$count'),
        ),
        Padding(
          padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
          child: OutlinedButton(onPressed: onClear, child: const Text('Clear cache')),
        ),
      ]),
    );
  }
}

One screen, three stores: the switch is a shared_preferences bool, the account line reads whether a token exists in secure storage, and the cache line counts entries in a Hive box.

Hive CE basics: boxes

import 'package:hive_ce/hive_ce.dart';
import 'package:hive_ce_flutter/hive_ce_flutter.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  await Hive.initFlutter();                 // choose an app folder for box files
  final recent = await Hive.openBox<String>('recent_searches');

  await recent.put('last', 'invoice');      // write (async: saved to disk)
  final last = recent.get('last');          // read (sync: from memory)
  await recent.delete('last');
  print(recent.length);                     // 0
  runApp(const MyApp());
}

You open a box once, usually at start-up, and then reads are synchronous because the box keeps its data in memory. That is why Hive feels fast, and also why a huge box costs memory. A typed box such as Box<String> only accepts that type. box.watch() gives a stream of changes, and hive_ce_flutter adds box.listenable() for use with ValueListenableBuilder.

Type adapters

Hive stores primitives, lists and maps on its own. For your own classes it needs a TypeAdapter: code that writes the fields to bytes and reads them back. You can write one by hand:

class CachedResponseAdapter extends TypeAdapter<CachedResponse> {
  @override
  final int typeId = 1; // unique in the app, never reused

  @override
  CachedResponse read(BinaryReader reader) {
    final body = reader.readString();
    final millis = reader.readInt();
    return CachedResponse(
        body: body, savedAt: DateTime.fromMillisecondsSinceEpoch(millis));
  }

  @override
  void write(BinaryWriter writer, CachedResponse obj) {
    writer.writeString(obj.body);
    writer.writeInt(obj.savedAt.millisecondsSinceEpoch);
  }
}

// Once, before opening boxes that use it:
Hive.registerAdapter(CachedResponseAdapter());

Read fields in exactly the order you wrote them. For larger models, let the generator do it. Add hive_ce_generator and build_runner as dev dependencies, then list your classes in one file:

// lib/hive/hive_adapters.dart
import 'package:hive_ce/hive_ce.dart';
import '../models/task_draft.dart';

@GenerateAdapters([AdapterSpec<TaskDraft>()])
part 'hive_adapters.g.dart';

// dart run build_runner build -d, then at start-up:
// Hive.registerAdapters();  (from the generated hive_registrar.g.dart)

The generator also writes a schema file (hive_adapters.g.yaml) that tracks field indexes over time. Commit it to git, because it is what keeps old data readable when you add fields later.

Encrypted boxes

const secure = FlutterSecureStorage();
var keyText = await secure.read(key: 'hive_key');
if (keyText == null) {
  keyText = base64UrlEncode(Hive.generateSecureKey());
  await secure.write(key: 'hive_key', value: keyText);
}
final vault = await Hive.openBox<String>('vault',
    encryptionCipher: HiveAesCipher(base64Url.decode(keyText)));

The box contents are encrypted with AES, and the key itself lives in secure storage, not in your code. A key written in the source would ship inside every copy of the app.

Caching API responses

A cache answers “what did the server say last time?”. Four decisions make a cache correct:

  1. Key: include everything that changes the answer, for example the method, path and query (GET /todos?limit=20) and, for per-user data, the user id.
  2. Freshness: a TTL says how long a copy is good enough. Task lists might use minutes; a list of countries might use days.
  3. Strategy: cache-then-network shows the saved copy at once and then refreshes. Network-first tries the server and falls back to the cache on failure.
  4. Invalidation: clear per-user caches on logout, and remove or refresh entries after the user changes the data.
Stream<TodosResult> watchTodos({bool force = false}) async* {
  final cached = _cache.read(_key);
  if (cached != null) {
    yield TodosResult(_parse(cached.body), fromCache: true, savedAt: cached.savedAt);
    if (!force && cached.age < ttl) return;     // fresh: skip the network
  }
  try {
    final res = await _dio.get<String>('/todos',
        queryParameters: {'limit': 20},
        options: Options(responseType: ResponseType.plain));
    final body = res.data!;
    final todos = _parse(body);               // never cache a body you cannot parse
    await _cache.write(_key, jsonDecode(body));
    yield TodosResult(todos, fromCache: false, savedAt: DateTime.now());
  } on DioException {
    if (cached == null) rethrow;               // nothing saved: show the error
    yield TodosResult(_parse(cached.body), fromCache: true,
        savedAt: cached.savedAt, warning: 'Offline: showing saved data');
  }
}

An async* generator fits this nicely: it can yield the cached result, wait for the network, and yield again. The UI simply listens.

Screen 2: Cache-then-network lib/todos_page.dart

StreamBuilder<TodosResult>(
  stream: _todos, // widget.repo.watchTodos(), created once
  builder: (context, snap) {
    if (snap.hasError) {
      return Center(
        child: FilledButton(onPressed: _refresh, child: const Text('Retry')),
      );
    }
    if (!snap.hasData) return const Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator());
    final result = snap.data!;
    final age = _ageText(result.savedAt);
    final source = result.fromCache
        ? 'From cache, saved $age'
        : 'Fresh from the network';
    final colors = Theme.of(context).colorScheme;
    return Column(children: [
      Container(
        width: double.infinity,
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12),
        color: result.warning != null
            ? colors.errorContainer
            : colors.secondaryContainer,
        child: Text(result.warning ?? source),
      ),
      Expanded(
        child: ListView.builder(
          itemCount: result.todos.length,
          itemBuilder: (context, i) => ListTile(
            leading: Icon(result.todos[i].done
                ? Icons.check_circle
                : Icons.radio_button_unchecked),
            title: Text(result.todos[i].title),
          ),
        ),
      ),
    ]);
  },
)

The repository yields twice: the saved copy at once, then the fresh one. When the network fails it yields the saved copy again with a warning, so the list never disappears. States: Instant: cached copy → Network arrives → Offline refresh.

Example: placing TaskFlow’s data

DataStoreWhy
Dark mode, last selected projectshared_preferencesSmall, not secret, read at start-up
Access and refresh tokens (TokenStorage)flutter_secure_storageSecrets; platform-protected storage
Tasks and projectsDrift (AppDatabase)Relations, filters, live queries, migrations
Raw API responses for the todo screenHive CE box with a TTLKey-value by URL, quick to read, safe to clear
Recent search termsHive CE Box<String> or preferencesA short list read by key

On logout, TaskFlow deletes the tokens, clears the response cache box and deletes the user’s rows from the Drift database, so the next person to sign in on that phone sees nothing of the previous user’s data.

Common mistakes

  • Tokens in shared_preferences. It is a plain file (an XML file on Android, a plist on iOS). Use secure storage.
  • Using the cache as the only copy of user edits. A cache can be cleared at any moment. Edits the user made offline belong in the database and an outbox (lesson 10.3).
  • Changing an adapter’s format without a plan. Old bytes on devices no longer match. Add fields at the end with defaults, use the generator’s schema file, or clear the box if it is only a cache.
  • Caching without a key that includes the user. One user sees another user’s data after switching accounts.
  • Starting new work on the original hive package. It is unmaintained; use Hive CE.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “Where do you store tokens?” Secure storage, and explain why preferences are not safe.
  • “SQL or NoSQL on mobile?” Talk about the data: relations and queries point to SQLite and Drift; simple key lookups and caches point to a key-value store.
  • Explain the TTL and the invalidation rules of any cache you built; “it caches” is not an answer.
  • Always check web and desktop support in each package’s platform list before committing to it.

options: shared_preferences, because it is a single string
flutter_secure_storage, which uses the Keychain on iOS and the Keystore on Android

shared_preferences
flutter_secure_storage

quiz.question: The cached todo list is 2 minutes old and the TTL is 5 minutes. The user opens the screen. What does a cache-then-network repository do?
options: Deletes the cache and shows a spinner
Shows nothing until the network answers
Shows the cached list and skips the network call because the copy is still fresh
Always calls the network twice
quiz.explanation: Within the TTL the cached copy is fresh enough, so it is shown at once and no request is sent. After the TTL, or on a forced refresh, the network call follows.

quiz.question: You change the fields that a custom Hive TypeAdapter writes, and some users crash on start with read errors. What is the most likely cause?
options: Hive boxes cannot store strings
The typeId was too small
Hive only works on the web
Old data on the device was written in the old format and the new read() cannot parse it
quiz.explanation: A box keeps the bytes written by the old adapter. Changing the format needs a new typeId or a read() that handles both versions, or clearing the box if it is only a cache.

lessons.title: Offline-first and sync
lessons.summaryHtml: An offline-first app treats the local database as the source of truth. The UI reads only from the database; the network’s job is to keep that database in step with the server. Reads use cache-then-network: show local data at once, refresh in the background. Writes go to the database and to an outbox queue in one transaction, and a sync service sends the queue when the server is reachable, retrying with backoff. connectivity_plus tells you which network is connected, not whether the internet works, so it is only a hint. When the same task changes in two places you need a conflict strategy: last-write-wins, server wins, or a field-level merge. TaskFlow gets all of this, plus an offline banner and per-task sync icons.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Most apps you have built so far are online-first: the screen asks the server, waits, and shows the answer. No signal means a spinner and then an error.

An offline-first app flips this. The screen only ever reads from the phone’s own database. The network runs in the background, like a courier: it brings new data from the server into the database, and it carries the user’s changes from the database to the server. When the courier is stuck in traffic, the app still works. The user can read, tick tasks and add new ones, and everything is delivered later.

Think of writing letters. You do not stand at the post box waiting for a reply before you write the next letter. You drop them in an outbox and the postman takes them when he comes. That outbox is exactly the pattern you build today.

Why it matters

Mobile networks are unreliable: lifts, trains, basements, crowded events, cheap data plans that run out. Field staff, delivery drivers and warehouse teams often work where the signal is worst. For them an app that loses a change, or freezes on a spinner, is an app they stop trusting.

Offline-first also makes the app feel faster when online. Every tap updates the local database and the screen at once; the network round trip happens afterwards. The code is harder than “call the API and show the result”, which is exactly why it is a professional skill worth learning properly.

How it works

1. The local database is the source of truth

The UI watches Drift queries (lesson 10.1) and nothing else. The repository has two jobs: refresh (download from the API and write into the database) and write (change the database and queue the change). Because the UI listens to watch() streams, it updates no matter which job changed the data.

StepOnline-firstOffline-first
Open screenSpinner, then API resultLocal rows at once, then a background refresh
User ticks a taskWait for the API, then updateUpdate the database and outbox, send later
No networkError screenEverything works; a banner says changes are waiting

2. Sync columns and the outbox table

enum SyncState { synced, pending, failed }
enum OutboxOp { create, update, delete }

@DataClassName('TaskRow')
class Tasks extends Table {
  TextColumn get id => text()();                    // made on the device
  TextColumn get title => text()();
  BoolColumn get done => boolean().withDefault(const Constant(false))();
  DateTimeColumn get updatedAt => dateTime()();
  TextColumn get syncState =>
      textEnum<SyncState>().withDefault(Constant(SyncState.synced.name))();

  @override
  Set<Column> get primaryKey => {id};
}

@DataClassName('OutboxEntry')
class Outbox extends Table {
  IntColumn get seq => integer().autoIncrement()();   // keeps the order
  TextColumn get taskId => text()();
  TextColumn get op => textEnum<OutboxOp>()();
  TextColumn get payload => text()();                 // JSON to send
  IntColumn get attempts => integer().withDefault(const Constant(0))();
}

Two design choices matter. First, the id is created on the device (a UUID in a real app), so a task created offline has a stable id before the server has ever seen it, and the outbox can refer to it. If your API insists on its own ids, store a separate remoteId column and fill it in when the create succeeds. Second, syncState on each row lets the UI show a small icon per task.

3. Writes: one transaction, then try to send

Future<void> toggleDone(TaskRow task) async {
  final now = DateTime.now();
  await _db.transaction(() async {
    await (_db.update(_db.tasks)..where((t) => t.id.equals(task.id))).write(
      TasksCompanion(
        done: Value(!task.done),
        updatedAt: Value(now),
        syncState: const Value(SyncState.pending),
      ),
    );
    await _db.into(_db.outbox).insert(OutboxCompanion.insert(
      taskId: task.id,
      op: OutboxOp.update,
      payload: jsonEncode({'completed': !task.done, 'updatedAt': now.toIso8601String()}),
    ));
  });
  unawaited(_sync.flush()); // send now if we can; otherwise it waits
}

The transaction guarantees that a change is never saved without being queued, or queued without being saved, even if the app is killed half-way. Deletes follow the same pattern: remove the row (or mark it with a tombstone flag if other devices must learn about it) and queue a delete.

4. Flushing the outbox

Future<int> flush() async {
  if (_flushing) return 0;               // one flush at a time keeps the order
  _flushing = true;
  var sent = 0;
  try {
    while (true) {
      final entry = await _store.nextInOutbox();   // oldest first
      if (entry == null) break;
      try {
        await _api.send(entry.op, entry.task);
        await _store.removeFromOutbox(entry.seq);
        sent++;
      } on NetworkException {
        await _store.bumpAttempts(entry.seq);
        _retry = Timer(retryDelay(entry.attempts), flush);
        break;                                        // stop; retry later
      } on RejectedException {
        await _store.removeFromOutbox(entry.seq);    // a 4xx will not change
        await _store.setSyncState(entry.task.id, SyncState.failed);
      }
    }
  } finally {
    _flushing = false;
  }
  return sent;
}

static Duration retryDelay(int attempts) {
  final seconds = min(60, 1 << min(attempts, 6));  // 1, 2, 4 ... 60
  return Duration(seconds: seconds, milliseconds: Random().nextInt(500));
}

Rules hidden in this loop:

  • Order matters. “Create task” must reach the server before “tick task”. Stop at the first network failure instead of skipping ahead.
  • Remove only after success. If the app dies mid-request, the entry is still there and will be sent again. So make requests idempotent: a create with a client id, or an idempotency key header, lets the server recognise a repeat.
  • Classify errors. Timeouts, no route and many 5xx errors are worth retrying. A 4xx such as 400 or 422 is a permanent “no”: mark the row failed and let the user fix it. A 401 is an auth problem for the interceptor from lesson 9.2.
  • Back off with jitter. Doubling delays with a cap protect the server; a little randomness stops thousands of phones retrying at the same second.

5. connectivity_plus: a hint, not proof

_sub = Connectivity().onConnectivityChanged.listen((results) {
  // A List: a phone can be on Wi-Fi and mobile data (and a VPN) at once.
  final none = results.every((r) => r == ConnectivityResult.none);
  setState(() => _deviceOffline = none);
  if (!none) _sync.flush();   // a network appeared: worth trying again
});

The plugin reports which links are up. Its own documentation warns not to use that to decide whether a request will succeed. A hotel Wi-Fi with a login page, a router with no uplink, or a server that is down all look “connected”. So use connectivity changes as a trigger to retry, and use the actual request result to decide whether you are online. In a real app, show the banner when the device has no network or the last request failed with a network error. The lab app uses its “Server reachable” switch to play the second part.

Screen 1: Offline banner and sync states lib/tasks_page.dart

@override
Widget build(BuildContext context) {
  return Scaffold(
    appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('TaskFlow'), actions: [
      IconButton(icon: const Icon(Icons.sync), onPressed: _refresh),
    ]),
    body: StreamBuilder<List<Task>>(
      stream: _tasks, // the local database: the source of truth
      builder: (context, snap) {
        final tasks = snap.data ?? const <Task>[];
        final pending =
            tasks.where((t) => t.syncState == SyncState.pending).length;
        return Column(children: [
          if (_offline)
            MaterialBanner(
              leading: const Icon(Icons.cloud_off),
              content: Text('You are offline. Waiting to sync: $pending'),
              actions: [
                TextButton(onPressed: _refresh, child: const Text('Retry')),
              ],
            ),
          Expanded(
            child: ListView(children: [
              for (final t in tasks)
                ListTile(
                  leading: Checkbox(
                    value: t.done,
                    onChanged: (_) => _write(_sync.toggle(t)),
                  ),
                  title: Text(t.title),
                  trailing: _stateIcon(t.syncState),
                ),
            ]),
          ),
        ]);
      },
    ),
  );
}

Widget _stateIcon(SyncState s) => switch (s) {
      SyncState.synced => const Icon(Icons.cloud_done, color: Colors.green),
      SyncState.pending => const Icon(Icons.cloud_upload, color: Colors.orange),
      SyncState.failed => const Icon(Icons.error, color: Colors.red),
    };

Each tile shows its row’s syncState: green cloud when synced, orange upload while queued. The banner appears when the device reports no network or the server cannot be reached, and the pending count comes from the same local data. States: Online, all synced → Offline, 2 queued → Back online.

6. Pulling and conflicts

When refreshing, push first (flush), then download and merge. A conflict happens when the same record changed locally and on the server since the last sync. Pick a strategy per kind of data:

StrategyHow it decidesGood forCost
Last-write-winsLatest updatedAt winsSimple fields such as done or titleThe older edit is lost silently; clock differences matter (prefer server timestamps)
Server winsThe server copy always replaces localData owned by the back office, such as pricesLocal edits can vanish
Client winsLocal pending changes always overwritePersonal data only one user editsOverwrites other devices
MergeCombine per field, or show both to the userNotes, documents, shared recordsMuch more code and UI

The lab uses last-write-wins: a local row that is still pending and not older than the server copy is kept (its outbox entry will push it); otherwise the server copy replaces it and any queued entry for that task is dropped. Rows the server no longer has are removed, unless they are unsent local creations.

Screen 2: Rejected change and a conflict lib/sync/sync_service.dart

// Inside SyncService.flush(), for each outbox entry:
try {
  await _api.send(entry.op, entry.task);
  await _store.removeFromOutbox(entry.seq);
} on NetworkException {
  await _store.bumpAttempts(entry.seq);
  _retry = Timer(retryDelay(entry.attempts), flush);
  break; // keep the order: nothing later may overtake this entry
} on RejectedException {
  await _store.removeFromOutbox(entry.seq); // retrying cannot help
  await _store.setSyncState(entry.task.id, SyncState.failed);
}

// Inside SyncService.refresh(), for each task from the server:
final mine = local.remove(r.id);
final keepMine = mine != null &&
    mine.syncState != SyncState.synced &&
    !r.updatedAt.isAfter(mine.updatedAt);
if (!keepMine) {
  await _store.dropOutboxFor(r.id); // the server copy is newer
  await _store.putTask(r);
}

// On screen, after a failed send:
ScaffoldMessenger.of(context).showSnackBar(
  const SnackBar(content: Text('1 change was rejected by the server')),
);

Left: the server refused a title that is too long, so the task is marked failed instead of being retried forever. Right: after Sync now, a newer rename from another device replaced the older local edit (last write wins). States: Rejected by server → Newer remote edit wins.

7. Background sync

Flushing while the app is open covers most cases. To sync when the app is closed, the workmanager plugin schedules Dart code through Android’s WorkManager and iOS background tasks. The operating system decides when that code runs (it may batch, delay or skip it to save battery, and iOS is especially strict), so treat it as a bonus that shortens the queue, never as a guarantee. Because the outbox is in the database, a background run and the foreground app use the same queue; keep flush safe to run more than once.

Example: TaskFlow goes offline-first

  1. Add syncState to Tasks, add the Outbox table, bump schemaVersion and write the migration.
  2. TaskRepository.watchTasks() maps Drift rows to Task entities; the Cubit only listens to it.
  3. TaskRepository.refresh() calls flush(), downloads /todos through ApiClient, and merges inside one transaction.
  4. Every write goes through writeWithOutbox, then calls flush() without awaiting it, so the UI never waits for the network.
  5. A SyncService listens to connectivity changes and to app resume, and flushes; failures schedule a backoff retry.
  6. The task list shows per-row icons and an offline banner with the pending count, and a failed task opens an edit screen with the server’s message.

Common mistakes

  • Reading from the API response in the UI “just for this screen”. Now two sources of truth disagree. Write the response into the database and read from there.
  • Trusting connectivity_plus as “online”. Always handle timeouts and errors; use connectivity only to trigger retries.
  • Retrying everything forever. Validation errors never succeed and block the queue. Classify errors and fail fast on 4xx responses such as 400 and 422 (408 and 429 are the exceptions that mean “try again later”).
  • Sending queue entries in parallel. Updates can overtake their create. Process the outbox in order, one flush at a time.
  • Using device clocks for conflicts without thought. Phone clocks can be wrong; prefer timestamps set by the server, or version numbers.
  • Removing an outbox entry before the server confirms. A crash then loses the change for good.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Be ready to draw the loop: UI → database → outbox → sync service → API → database → UI.
  • Explain idempotency and why client-generated ids make offline creates safe to retry.
  • Name a conflict strategy and its cost. “Last write wins, and here is what we lose” is a strong answer.
  • Mention testing: a fake API with a “reachable” switch lets you unit-test queueing, backoff and conflicts without a device.
  • Know the limits of background work on each platform before promising “always in sync” to a client.

terms.definition: The one place the UI reads from. Offline-first apps make it the local database, never a network response.
A local table of changes waiting to be sent, processed in order and removed only after the server accepts each one.
Waiting longer after each failed retry (1 s, 2 s, 4 s ...) with a cap and some random jitter, so clients do not hammer a struggling server.
A request that has the same effect if it is sent twice, which makes retrying safe.
A conflict rule that keeps whichever version has the latest timestamp and discards the other.
A marker that records a delete, so the delete can be synced instead of the row simply vanishing.

lessons.examTip: Interview gold: “connectivity_plus says Wi-Fi is connected, not that the internet works. I treat it as a hint to retry; the real test is whether the request succeeds.”

quiz.question: connectivity_plus reports ConnectivityResult.wifi, yet every request times out at a hotel. What is the right conclusion?
options: The plugin has a bug
Being connected to a network does not mean the internet is reachable (for example, a captive portal), so rely on request results
Wi-Fi always means online, so the server must be down
You should disable timeouts
quiz.explanation: The plugin reports the type of network link. Captive portals, broken routers and firewalls all give a connection without internet. Treat it as a hint and handle request failures.

quiz.question: Why is a task write saved to the tasks table and the outbox inside one transaction?
options: Transactions make network calls faster
Drift cannot insert into two tables otherwise
So the UI refreshes twice
So the app can never end up with a local change that is not queued, or a queued change that is not saved
quiz.explanation: If the app is killed between two separate writes, one could exist without the other. A transaction makes both happen or neither.

quiz.question: The server answers a queued update with 422 (invalid data). What should the sync service do?
options: Remove it from the outbox and mark the task as failed so the user can fix it
Retry forever with backoff
Retry immediately in a tight loop
Delete the whole outbox
quiz.explanation: A validation error such as 400 or 422 means the server understood and refused; the same request will fail again. Retries are for network errors, timeouts, some 5xx responses and the few 4xx codes that mean “try later”, such as 408 and 429.

quiz.question: Two phones edit the same task offline. With last-write-wins by updatedAt, what happens when both sync?
options: Both edits are merged field by field
The server rejects both edits
The edit with the later timestamp is kept and the other is silently lost
The first phone to sync always wins
quiz.explanation: Last-write-wins is simple and predictable, but it discards the older edit. For data where that is unacceptable, use a field-level merge or ask the user.
