lessons.title: Secure storage and secrets
lessons.summaryHtml:
Everything you ship inside an app can be read by someone who downloads it. An attacker can unzip an APK or IPA, pull out strings and assets, watch its network traffic and even change its code while it runs. So TaskFlow stores tokens in flutter_secure_storage (Keychain on iOS, Keystore-backed encryption on Android), never plain files or shared_preferences.

Values from --dart-define and --dart-define-from-file are handy for configuration, but they are not secret. Third-party API keys belong on a backend proxy that your app calls with the user's token. --obfuscate --split-debug-info only slows reverse engineering down, and logs must never print passwords or tokens.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

When you publish TaskFlow, you hand a copy of the whole app to every person who installs it. That includes people who want to attack it. Think of it like selling a locked box together with the key taped to its side. If a secret is in the box, anyone patient enough will find it.

This lesson is about being honest about that. Some things the app has to hold, such as the signed-in user’s own tokens, and we store them in the safest place the phone offers. Other things, such as a paid API key for a third-party service, must never be in the app at all. They live on a server you control.

Why it matters

Leaked keys cost real money and real data. A maps or AI API key pulled out of an app can be used by anyone until you notice the bill. A refresh token copied from a plain file on a rooted phone lets someone act as that user for weeks. A log line with a Bearer token that ends up in a crash report can be read by everyone who has access to that dashboard.

Employers expect a professional Flutter developer to know the difference between configuration and secrets, where tokens go, and what obfuscation does and does not do. These are also some of the first questions a security review or a client’s penetration test asks.

How it works

What an attacker can do with your APK or IPA

An APK is a zip file. Your compiled Dart code sits in lib/<abi>/libapp.so, next to your assets and the Android manifest. An IPA is also a zip once it is decrypted. With free tools and some patience, an attacker can:

  • Read strings. URLs, config values and any key you hardcoded are stored as plain text in the compiled snapshot.
  • Read assets. JSON files, .env files you bundled as assets and certificates are all just files in the package.
  • Watch traffic. On a device they control they can install their own trusted certificate and proxy your HTTPS traffic, unless you pin certificates (lesson 11.2).
  • Change behaviour at runtime. Dynamic instrumentation tools can hook functions on a rooted or jailbroken device, for example to make a "has premium" check return true.
  • Read app files. On a rooted device, or through some backups, files in your app’s private folder can be copied out. That includes the shared_preferences file and SQLite databases.
Remember: the app is not a safe place for secrets. It is a safe-enough place for the user’s own data, when you use the platform’s protected storage. Real authorisation checks always happen on the server.

flutter_secure_storage: where tokens belong

flutter_secure_storage gives you a simple key-value API. On iOS it writes to the Keychain. On Android it encrypts the values with a key that lives in the Android Keystore, so the key material itself is protected by the system (often by hardware) and never sits in your app’s files. Install it with flutter pub add flutter_secure_storage. Here is TaskFlow’s TokenStorage, now backed by secure storage. The rest of the app keeps using the same class:

import 'package:flutter_secure_storage/flutter_secure_storage.dart';

class TokenStorage {
  TokenStorage([FlutterSecureStorage? storage])
      : _storage = storage ?? FlutterSecureStorage(iOptions: _iosOptions);

  // Readable after the first unlock since reboot, and never
  // migrated to another device through an iCloud or iTunes backup.
  static const _iosOptions = IOSOptions(
    accessibility: KeychainAccessibility.first_unlock_this_device,
  );

  final FlutterSecureStorage _storage;
  static const _accessKey = 'access_token';
  static const _refreshKey = 'refresh_token';

  Future<void> saveTokens({required String access, required String refresh}) async {
    await _storage.write(key: _accessKey, value: access);
    await _storage.write(key: _refreshKey, value: refresh);
  }

  Future<String?> readAccessToken() => _storage.read(key: _accessKey);
  Future<String?> readRefreshToken() => _storage.read(key: _refreshKey);

  Future<void> clear() async {
    await _storage.delete(key: _accessKey);
    await _storage.delete(key: _refreshKey);
  }
}

The optional constructor parameter lets tests pass a fake, exactly like the dependency injection you did in lesson 9.5. A few practical notes:

  • Android backups. The Keystore key never leaves the device, so encrypted data restored from a backup onto a new phone cannot be decrypted. The package docs recommend android:allowBackup="false" in the manifest, or excluding its storage from backups.
  • Uninstall on iOS. Keychain items can survive an uninstall and reinstall. If a stale token appearing on first launch is a problem, clear storage when your app detects its first run.
  • It is not a database. Store small strings: tokens, a user id, an encryption key for your Drift or Hive CE database. Not lists of tasks.
  • Web. On the web it uses WebCrypto with keys in browser storage and only works over HTTPS or localhost. Treat the web as a weaker environment.
DataWhere it goesWhy
Access and refresh tokensflutter_secure_storageThey prove who the user is; stealing them means acting as the user.
Theme, onboarding seen, last tabshared_preferencesHarmless if read; speed and simplicity matter more.
Cached tasksDrift database (optionally encrypted, key in secure storage)Structured, queryable data.
Third-party API secret, service account, signing keyYour server onlyNothing in the app can stay secret.

Configuration is not a secret

--dart-define puts values into your app at compile time, and --dart-define-from-file reads many of them from a JSON file. You read them with String.fromEnvironment, bool.fromEnvironment or int.fromEnvironment in a const context:

// config/staging.json
// { "API_BASE_URL": "https://staging.example.com", "ENV": "staging" }

class AppConfig {
  static const apiBaseUrl = String.fromEnvironment('API_BASE_URL',
      defaultValue: 'https://dummyjson.com');
  static const environment =
      String.fromEnvironment('ENV', defaultValue: 'dev');
}

// flutter run --dart-define-from-file=config/staging.json
// flutter build appbundle --dart-define-from-file=config/prod.json

This is the right tool for base URLs, feature flags and environment names. It keeps them out of your source code and lets CI build dev, staging and prod from the same commit. But the values end up as constants in the compiled app, so they are exactly as readable as a hardcoded string. Keeping the JSON file out of Git protects it from people browsing your repository, not from people installing your app.

Backend proxy for third-party keys

Suppose TaskFlow wants AI-generated task summaries from a paid API. The key must not be in the app. Instead, the app calls your own endpoint with the user’s token, and your server adds the secret key:

StepWhoHolds
1. POST /summaries with Bearer user tokenTaskFlow appOnly the user’s session token
2. Check the token, rate-limit this user, validate inputYour backend (or a Supabase Edge Function, lesson 12.4)The third-party API key, in server environment variables
3. Call the third-party API and return only what the app needsYour backendSame key, never sent to the app

The proxy also gives you control: you can block abusive users, cap spending per user and swap providers without shipping a new app version. Some providers also offer restricted keys (limited by app signature, bundle id or referrer). Those reduce abuse, but they are a second layer, not a replacement for the proxy when the key is truly secret.

Obfuscation and debug info

Release builds of Flutter apps are compiled ahead of time to machine code, which is already harder to read than source. Adding obfuscation renames your classes, methods and fields to meaningless symbols:

flutter build appbundle --release --obfuscate --split-debug-info=build/debug-info

# later, turn an obfuscated stack trace back into readable names:
flutter symbolize -i crash.txt -d build/debug-info/app.android-arm64.symbols

Keep the debug-info folder for every release you ship (CI should archive it), or crash reports become unreadable. Understand the limits: string literals are not encrypted, and the logic still runs on the attacker’s device. Obfuscation makes their job slower. It never makes a secret safe.

Logging hygiene

Logs leak more secrets than attackers do. Device logs can be read over USB, crash reporters upload breadcrumbs, and screenshots of a debug console get pasted into chat groups. Three rules for TaskFlow:

  • Add network logging only when kDebugMode is true.
  • Redact Authorization, passwords and token fields even in debug. The screen mock below shows the output.
  • Never log whole user objects or response bodies to a crash reporter. Log ids and error types instead.

Screen 2: Redacted debug log lib/network/redacting_log_interceptor.dart

class RedactingLogInterceptor extends Interceptor {
  static const _hidden = {
    'authorization', 'password', 'accesstoken', 'refreshtoken',
  };

  Map<String, dynamic> _redact(Map<String, dynamic> map) => {
        for (final e in map.entries)
          e.key: _hidden.contains(e.key.toLowerCase()) ? '***' : e.value,
      };

  @override
  void onRequest(RequestOptions options, RequestInterceptorHandler handler) {
    final data = options.data;
    final body = data is Map<String, dynamic> ? _redact(data) : data;
    final headers = _redact(options.headers);
    debugPrint('--> ' + options.method + ' ' + options.uri.toString());
    debugPrint('    headers: $headers');
    debugPrint('    body: $body');
    handler.next(options);
  }

  @override
  void onResponse(Response response, ResponseInterceptorHandler handler) {
    final data = response.data;
    final body = data is Map<String, dynamic> ? _redact(data) : '(not a map)';
    final code = response.statusCode;
    debugPrint('<-- $code ' + response.requestOptions.uri.path);
    debugPrint('    body: $body');
    handler.next(response);
  }
}

// In ApiClient:
// if (kDebugMode) dio.interceptors.add(RedactingLogInterceptor());

What the debug console prints for a sign-in and a /auth/me call. The password, both tokens and the Authorization header are replaced with *** before printing, and release builds print nothing.

Example: TaskFlow secure session

In the lab you wire these ideas together into one screen that signs in to DummyJSON as the demo user.

  1. AppConfig reads the base URL and environment name from config/dev.json via --dart-define-from-file.
  2. AuthRepository.login posts to /auth/login and hands accessToken and refreshToken to TokenStorage, which writes them to secure storage.
  3. ApiClient has an interceptor that reads the access token and sets Authorization: Bearer ... on each request. The redacting logger is added only in debug builds.
  4. The screen shows the token through a mask() helper: the first six characters and the length, never the whole value.
  5. Sign out calls TokenStorage.clear(), so nothing is left behind for the next person who picks up the phone.

Screen 1: Secure session screen lib/main.dart

class _SessionPageState extends State<SessionPage> {
  String _access = 'none';
  String _user = '-';
  bool _busy = false;
  // _run(...) calls the repository, then re-reads the token.

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final env = AppConfig.environment + ' | ' + AppConfig.apiBaseUrl;
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('TaskFlow session')),
      body: ListView(padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16), children: [
        ListTile(leading: const Icon(Icons.key),
            title: const Text('Access token'), subtitle: Text(_access)),
        ListTile(leading: const Icon(Icons.person),
            title: const Text('Signed-in user'), subtitle: Text(_user)),
        ListTile(leading: const Icon(Icons.dns),
            title: const Text('Environment'), subtitle: Text(env)),
        const SizedBox(height: 16),
        FilledButton.icon(
          onPressed: _busy ? null
              : () => _run(() => widget.auth.login('emilys', 'emilyspass')),
          icon: const Icon(Icons.login),
          label: const Text('Sign in as emilys'),
        ),
        OutlinedButton(
          onPressed: _busy ? null
              : () => _run(() async => _user = await widget.auth.me()),
          child: const Text('Who am I?'),
        ),
        TextButton(onPressed: _busy ? null : () => _run(_signOut),
            child: const Text('Sign out')),
      ]),
    );
  }
}

The token survives an app restart because it lives in the Keychain or Keystore, and the screen only ever shows a masked version of it. States: Signed out → Signed in.

A small build info page, reachable from a hidden settings entry in staging builds, helps testers report which backend they were using. It also reminds the whole team that every value on it is public.

Screen 3: Build info screen lib/build_info_page.dart

class AppConfig {
  static const apiBaseUrl = String.fromEnvironment('API_BASE_URL',
      defaultValue: 'https://dummyjson.com');
  static const environment =
      String.fromEnvironment('ENV', defaultValue: 'dev');
}

class BuildInfoPage extends StatelessWidget {
  const BuildInfoPage({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Build info')),
      body: ListView(children: [
        const ListTile(leading: Icon(Icons.flag),
            title: Text('Environment'), subtitle: Text(AppConfig.environment)),
        const ListTile(leading: Icon(Icons.dns),
            title: Text('API base URL'), subtitle: Text(AppConfig.apiBaseUrl)),
        const ListTile(leading: Icon(Icons.shield),
            title: Text('Secrets in this build'),
            subtitle: Text('None. Third-party keys live on the server.')),
        Card(
          margin: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
          color: Theme.of(context).colorScheme.secondaryContainer,
          child: const Padding(
            padding: EdgeInsets.all(16),
            child: Text('Anyone who unpacks the app can read these values.'),
          ),
        ),
      ]),
    );
  }
}
// flutter run --dart-define-from-file=config/staging.json

A build info page shows which environment a tester is on. Everything on it came from --dart-define-from-file, and anyone who unpacks the app can read the same values, so none of them is a secret.

Common mistakes

  • "It is in a .env file, so it is hidden." A .env file bundled as an asset or passed through dart-define is inside the app. Git-ignoring it only keeps it off GitHub.
  • Tokens in shared_preferences. It is a plain file. Fine for settings, wrong for credentials.
  • Believing obfuscation is encryption. Strings and logic are still there. It buys time, nothing more.
  • Printing responses in release builds. A leftover print(response.data) can put tokens and personal data into device logs. Gate logging behind kDebugMode and redact.
  • Forgetting to clear on sign out. Deleting only the access token leaves a refresh token that can mint new ones.
  • Losing the debug-info folder. Without it, obfuscated crash reports from production cannot be symbolized.

Interview and real-world notes

  • "Where do you store the auth token?" Answer: flutter_secure_storage, backed by Keychain and Keystore, behind a TokenStorage interface so it can be faked in tests. Mention clearing it on sign out and the Android backup setting.
  • "How do you hide an API key in Flutter?" The strong answer is that you do not: you move the call behind your own backend or an edge function, authenticate the user there and rate-limit. Dart-define is for configuration.
  • "What does --obfuscate do?" It renames symbols to slow reverse engineering, needs --split-debug-info, and does not protect strings.
  • For a structured checklist, the OWASP Mobile Application Security Verification Standard (MASVS) and its testing guide (MASTG) cover storage, cryptography, network and code quality. The MASVS-STORAGE group is exactly this lesson; lesson 11.2 covers the rest.

terms.definition: Plugin that stores key-value strings in the iOS Keychain or in Android storage encrypted with a key held by the Android Keystore.
Build flag that reads compile-time constants from a JSON file. The values are compiled into the app, so they are configuration, not secrets.
Your own server endpoint that holds a third-party API key and calls that API for the app, after checking the user.
Renaming classes and functions in the compiled Dart code (--obfuscate) so it is harder to understand. It does not hide string values.
Folder where the build writes the symbol files you need to turn an obfuscated crash stack trace back into readable names.
Replacing sensitive values such as passwords and tokens with a placeholder before anything is printed or sent to a logging service.

lessons.examTip: Interview line: “A mobile app cannot keep a secret. Keys that must stay private live on the server; the app only holds the user’s own session tokens, in the Keychain or Keystore.”

quiz.question: TaskFlow needs to call a paid translation API that uses a secret API key. Where should the key live?
options: In a const in lib/config.dart
In a JSON file passed with --dart-define-from-file
On a backend endpoint that TaskFlow calls with the user’s token

quiz.question: What does flutter build apk --obfuscate --split-debug-info=build/debug-info protect against?

quiz.question: Why is flutter_secure_storage a better place for a refresh token than shared_preferences?
options: It is faster for large values
It syncs tokens to the cloud automatically

Its values are encrypted with keys protected by the Keychain or Keystore instead of sitting in a plain app file
quiz.explanation: shared_preferences keeps values in a plain, unencrypted app file. On a rooted device or through some backups it can be read directly. Secure storage keeps the value encrypted under a platform-protected key.

quiz.question: Your Dio log interceptor prints full request headers in every build. What is the main risk?
options: Release builds will crash when logging headers
Bearer tokens end up in device logs and crash reports, where other people or tools can read them
Dio refuses to send requests that were logged
Logging headers disables HTTPS
quiz.explanation: Logs are collected by crash reporters and support tools and can be read over USB. Log only in debug builds, and redact Authorization, passwords and tokens even there.

lessons.title: Network and app security
lessons.summaryHtml:
TaskFlow must only talk to its server over HTTPS. Dart’s own HttpClient (used by Dio and http) does not follow Android’s cleartext setting or iOS App Transport Security, so you enforce HTTPS in your own code and still set the platform options for WebViews and native SDKs. Certificate pinning with Dio stops interception by a rogue certificate, at the cost of careful rotation.

Every input is untrusted, including deep links. Biometric unlock with local_auth proves someone who can unlock the phone is present, not who they are to the server. Root and jailbreak checks can be bypassed, so treat them as signals. Before release, walk through the OWASP MASVS checklist.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Lesson 11.1 protected what TaskFlow keeps on the phone. This lesson protects the doors: the connection to the server, the links that open the app, and the moment someone picks up an unlocked phone. Think of a shop. HTTPS is the armoured van that carries the money. Pinning is checking the van driver’s badge against a list you printed yourself. Validating links is not letting anyone into the back room just because they say they work there. Biometric unlock is the lock on the office door, which keeps out passers-by but is not the bank’s vault.

Why it matters

Mobile apps run on networks you do not control: café Wi-Fi, hotel portals, corporate proxies. They receive links from emails and chat messages that anyone can write. And phones get lent, lost and stolen. A security review or penetration test of a client app will check each of these, usually against the OWASP MASVS. Knowing what each defence really achieves, and what it does not, is what separates a professional answer from a checklist copied off a blog.

How it works

HTTPS only, and who enforces it

Both platforms push apps towards HTTPS. Android blocks cleartext by default for apps targeting Android 9 (API 28) or newer, and iOS App Transport Security blocks insecure loads unless Info.plist adds exceptions. Here is the catch that surprises many developers: these policies apply to platform networking, not to Dart’s own sockets. Flutter’s documentation states that when a socket is owned by Dart, no policy is enforced, and you are responsible for securing the connection. Dio and the http package use dart:io on mobile, so an http:// URL will simply work.

So TaskFlow does two things. It keeps the platform settings strict for WebViews and native SDKs (no NSAllowsArbitraryLoads, usesCleartextTraffic="false" or a network security config with cleartext disabled), and it guards its own client:

class HttpsOnlyInterceptor extends Interceptor {
  @override
  void onRequest(RequestOptions options, RequestInterceptorHandler handler) {
    if (options.uri.scheme != 'https') {
      final url = options.uri.toString();
      handler.reject(DioException(
          requestOptions: options, message: 'Blocked insecure URL: $url'));
      return;
    }
    handler.next(options);
  }
}

final dio = Dio(BaseOptions(baseUrl: AppConfig.apiBaseUrl))
  ..interceptors.add(HttpsOnlyInterceptor());

An HTTPS URL that the server later redirects to HTTP is also a problem. Keep the server config tidy, and treat any HTTP URL that arrives in API data (an avatar or an attachment link) with the same rule before you load it.

Certificate pinning with Dio

Normal HTTPS trusts any certificate signed by any authority in the device’s trust store. On a device the attacker controls, they can add their own authority and read your traffic through a proxy. Pinning narrows trust to certificates you chose. With Dio on mobile you configure the IOHttpClientAdapter from package:dio/io.dart. The version below trusts only the authorities bundled as assets, and ships a backup:

import 'dart:io';
import 'package:dio/dio.dart';
import 'package:dio/io.dart';
import 'package:flutter/services.dart';

/// Trust ONLY the CA certificates bundled with the app.
/// Ship the current CA and a backup so a rotation does not lock users out.
Future<Dio> createPinnedDio(String baseUrl) async {
  final context = SecurityContext(withTrustedRoots: false);
  for (final path in ['assets/certs/current_ca.pem', 'assets/certs/backup_ca.pem']) {
    final data = await rootBundle.load(path);
    context.setTrustedCertificatesBytes(data.buffer.asUint8List());
  }
  final dio = Dio(BaseOptions(baseUrl: baseUrl));
  dio.httpClientAdapter = IOHttpClientAdapter(
    createHttpClient: () => HttpClient(context: context),
  );
  dio.interceptors.add(HttpsOnlyInterceptor());
  return dio;
}

The adapter also has a validateCertificate callback that receives the server’s leaf certificate, host and port after the handshake. Dio’s documentation uses it to compare the certificate’s SHA-256 fingerprint with a stored value (you need a hashing library for that). A failed pin shows up as a DioException of type badCertificate, or as a HandshakeException in error when the TLS handshake itself fails. Pinning uses dart:io, so it does not apply on the web, where the browser owns TLS.

What you pinSurvives certificate renewal?Trade-off
Leaf certificate fingerprintNo: breaks at every renewalTightest, but short-lived certificates make it fragile
Server public key (keep the key when renewing)Yes, if the key is reusedNeeds coordination with whoever manages the server
Your CA or intermediateYes, while that CA issues your certificatesLooser, but much easier to operate
Watch out: a pin that no longer matches turns TaskFlow into a brick until users install an update, and some never will. Always ship a backup pin, write down the rotation date, and test a release against a staging server with the new certificate before the old one expires. Pinning also blocks corporate TLS-inspecting proxies and your own debugging proxy, so allow a debug-only bypass that is compiled out of release builds.

Screen 2: Pinning failure with Retry lib/tasks/secure_error_view.dart

bool isTrustFailure(DioException e) =>
    e.type == DioExceptionType.badCertificate ||
    e.error is HandshakeException; // from dart:io

class SecureErrorView extends StatelessWidget {
  const SecureErrorView({super.key, required this.onRetry});
  final VoidCallback onRetry;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final scheme = Theme.of(context).colorScheme;
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Tasks')),
      body: Center(
        child: Padding(
          padding: const EdgeInsets.all(24),
          child: Column(mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min, spacing: 12, children: [
            Icon(Icons.gpp_bad, size: 56, color: scheme.error),
            Text('Secure connection failed',
                style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleMedium),
            const Text(
              'We could not verify the TaskFlow server. '
              'Check your network and try again.',
              textAlign: TextAlign.center,
            ),
            FilledButton.icon(onPressed: onRetry,
                icon: const Icon(Icons.refresh), label: const Text('Retry')),
          ]),
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

When a pinned connection fails, TaskFlow shows a calm message instead of a stack trace, and never offers a “connect anyway” button. The same screen covers a hotel Wi-Fi portal or a proxy that intercepts TLS.

Input validation

Validate in the app for a good experience, and on the server for security, because an attacker can skip your app and call the API directly. In the app: trim and length-limit text fields, use allow-lists (an enum of statuses, not any string), parse numbers with int.tryParse, and never build SQL by string concatenation (Drift and sqflite take parameters). Never render server HTML or Markdown you did not sanitise in a WebView with JavaScript enabled.

Deep link validation

A deep link is input from anyone who can send your user a message. Custom schemes such as taskflow:// can be registered by other apps too. Verified Android App Links and iOS Universal Links tie the link to a domain you prove you own, so prefer them for anything sensitive. Whatever the link type, parse it defensively:

  • Check scheme, host and path shape, and turn the result into a typed value (the LinkTarget in the lab) instead of passing raw strings around.
  • With go_router, validate path parameters in a redirect and send bad ones to a not-found page. The auth redirect from module 9 still runs first, so a link never skips sign-in.
  • Never let a link perform an action by itself (delete, pay, accept an invite) without a confirmation screen.
  • Only accept "return to" parameters that are internal paths, to avoid open redirects.

Screen 3: Validating incoming links lib/links/parse_task_link.dart

sealed class LinkTarget {}

class OpenTask extends LinkTarget {
  OpenTask(this.id);
  final int id;
}

class RejectedLink extends LinkTarget {
  RejectedLink(this.reason);
  final String reason;
}

const _allowedHosts = {'taskflow.example.com'};
final _taskPath = RegExp(r'^/tasks/(\d{1,9})$');

LinkTarget parseTaskLink(Uri uri) {
  if (uri.scheme != 'https' || !_allowedHosts.contains(uri.host)) {
    return RejectedLink('Unknown link source');
  }
  final match = _taskPath.firstMatch(uri.path);
  if (match == null) return RejectedLink('Unknown page');
  return OpenTask(int.parse(match.group(1)!));
}

String describe(LinkTarget target) => switch (target) {
      OpenTask(:final id) => 'Open task $id',
      RejectedLink(:final reason) => 'Rejected: $reason',
    };

// In the list:
// ListTile(leading: const Icon(Icons.link),
//     title: Text(link.host + link.path),
//     subtitle: Text(describe(parseTaskLink(link))))

The same three links before and after validation. The starter trusts any host and any path, so a link from another domain or to an admin path still “opens a task”. States: Starter (no checks) → Validated.

Biometric unlock with local_auth

local_auth shows the system prompt (fingerprint, face or device PIN) and returns a bool. Failures such as a cancel or a lockout arrive as a LocalAuthException with a code. On Android your MainActivity must extend FlutterFragmentActivity; on iOS you add NSFaceIDUsageDescription to Info.plist.

Be precise about what it proves. A true means someone who can unlock this device is present. The server learns nothing. That makes it right for an app lock over tokens already stored in secure storage, and wrong as a replacement for signing in. If a client wants biometrics to protect a secret, the stronger pattern is to keep the token in Keychain or Keystore storage that itself requires user authentication to read, so the operating system enforces the check rather than a boolean in your Dart code, which could be patched on a rooted device.

Screen 1: Biometric app lock lib/app_lock_gate.dart

Future<void> _unlock() async {
  String? message;
  var ok = false;
  try {
    if (!await _auth.isDeviceSupported()) {
      message = 'Set up a screen lock on this device first.';
    } else {
      ok = await _auth.authenticate(
          localizedReason: 'Unlock TaskFlow to see your tasks');
    }
  } on LocalAuthException catch (e) {
    message = switch (e.code) {
      LocalAuthExceptionCode.userCanceled ||
      LocalAuthExceptionCode.systemCanceled => 'Unlock cancelled.',
      LocalAuthExceptionCode.temporaryLockout ||
      LocalAuthExceptionCode.biometricLockout =>
        'Too many attempts. Try again later.',
      _ => 'Could not unlock: ' + e.code.name,
    };
  }
  if (!mounted) return;
  setState(() {
    _locked = !ok;
    _message = message;
  });
}

@override
Widget build(BuildContext context) {
  if (!_locked) return widget.child;
  return Scaffold(
    body: Center(
      child: Column(mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min, spacing: 16, children: [
        const Icon(Icons.lock, size: 64),
        Text('TaskFlow is locked',
            style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleLarge),
        if (_message != null) Text(_message!),
        FilledButton.icon(onPressed: _unlock,
            icon: const Icon(Icons.fingerprint), label: const Text('Unlock')),
      ]),
    ),
  );
}

The lock screen is TaskFlow’s own widget; the prompt in the middle frame is drawn by the operating system, not by Flutter. Success only changes local state: the tasks still load with the access token. States: Locked → System prompt → Cancelled → Unlocked.

Root and jailbreak detection, and screenshots

Community packages can spot common signs of a rooted or jailbroken device. Treat the result as a signal: an attacker who controls the device can hide those signs. Use it to warn the user or disable a high-risk feature. For decisions that matter, the server should ask the platform for attestation (Google’s Play Integrity API, Apple’s App Attest) and judge the result itself.

For screens with sensitive data, Android offers FLAG_SECURE on the window, set through a small platform channel or a plugin, which blocks screenshots and blanks the app in the recent-apps view. iOS has no equivalent flag. A common approach is to cover the content when the app becomes inactive, so the app-switcher snapshot shows a neutral screen.

OWASP MASVS: the release checklist

MASVS groupTaskFlow check before release
STORAGETokens only in secure storage; nothing sensitive in logs, backups or shared_preferences
CRYPTONo home-made crypto; keys come from the platform keystore
AUTHServer checks every request; refresh tokens revoked on sign-out; biometrics only as a local lock
NETWORKHTTPS everywhere, enforced in Dart; pinning decision documented with a rotation plan
PLATFORMDeep links validated; WebViews locked down; permissions minimal
CODEDependencies up to date; inputs validated; release build obfuscated with debug info kept
RESILIENCERoot or jailbreak signals and attestation where the risk justifies them
PRIVACYCollect only the data you need, and explain it to the user

Example: hardening TaskFlow

  1. Add HttpsOnlyInterceptor to ApiClient and keep API_BASE_URL values in every config file on https.
  2. Set usesCleartextTraffic="false" on Android and remove any ATS exceptions on iOS.
  3. Decide on pinning with the backend owner. If yes, pin the CA, bundle a backup, and put the rotation date in the team calendar.
  4. Route every link through parseTaskLink before go_router sees it.
  5. Wrap the app in AppLockGate, which asks local_auth on launch and locks again when the app is hidden.
  6. Walk the MASVS table above and record the result in the release notes.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming platform settings protect Dart code. ATS and Android cleartext rules do not apply to dart:io sockets.
  • Pinning a leaf certificate with no backup. The next renewal breaks every installed copy of the app.
  • Treating biometrics as login. A boolean from local_auth proves nothing to the server.
  • Trusting a link because it has your scheme. Other apps and websites can create it too.
  • Blocking the app on root detection alone. It frustrates honest power users and barely slows attackers.

Interview and real-world notes

  • "How do you secure network calls in Flutter?" HTTPS enforced in the client, tokens attached by an interceptor, optional pinning with a rotation plan, and server-side authorisation on every endpoint.
  • "Would you pin certificates?" A good answer weighs it: yes for high-risk apps such as banking or health, with public key or CA pins and a backup; often no for ordinary apps where an outage from a bad pin costs more than it protects.
  • "What does Face ID give you?" Local user presence. Pair it with Keychain or Keystore access control if a secret must be gated by it.
  • Name the OWASP MASVS and MASTG when asked how you review an app’s security. Clients and auditors use them.

terms.definition: Unencrypted HTTP. Anyone on the same network path can read or change it.
iOS policy that blocks insecure connections made through Apple’s networking APIs unless the app adds exceptions in Info.plist.
Accepting only specific certificates or public keys for your server, instead of any certificate a trusted authority signed.
Plugin that shows the system biometric or device-credential prompt and returns whether the user passed it on this device.
A URL that opens a specific screen in the app. Its path and parameters come from outside, so they are untrusted input.
Mobile Application Security Verification Standard: a list of security requirements for mobile apps, with the MASTG guide describing how to test them.

lessons.examTip: In an interview, say it plainly: “Biometrics unlock something on the device; the server still decides access from the token.”

quiz.question: TaskFlow’s AndroidManifest sets android:usesCleartextTraffic="false", yet a Dio call to an http:// URL still succeeds. Why?
options: Dio automatically upgrades HTTP to HTTPS
The setting only applies to release builds
Dart owns its sockets, so Android’s cleartext policy does not apply to dart:io HttpClient; the app must enforce HTTPS itself
Cleartext is only blocked on Wi-Fi
quiz.explanation: The platform policy covers platform networking (WebViews, native SDKs). Flutter’s docs state that no policy is enforced on Dart-owned sockets, so use https URLs and a guard such as an HTTPS-only interceptor.

quiz.question: What is the main operational risk of certificate pinning?
options: When the server certificate or key changes and the app has no matching backup pin, the app stops connecting until users update
It makes every request noticeably slower
It disables HTTP/2
It exposes the private key in the app
quiz.explanation: Pinning hardcodes trust. Pin a CA or public key rather than a short-lived leaf certificate, ship a backup pin, and plan rotation before it is needed.

quiz.question: After a successful local_auth prompt, what has TaskFlow actually learned?
options: The user’s identity has been verified by the TaskFlow server
The device is not rooted
The user’s access token is valid
Someone who can unlock this device (by biometric or device credential) is holding it now
quiz.explanation: The result is a local true or false. It proves presence of an enrolled user on this device. The server still authorises every request with a token.

quiz.question: A link https://taskflow.example.com/login?next=//evil.example.net arrives. What should the app do with the next parameter?
options: Navigate to it after sign-in, because it came from our domain
Allow only internal paths that start with a single / and match known routes, and ignore anything else
Open it in a WebView to be safe
Strip the // and go to evil.example.net
quiz.explanation: Link parameters are untrusted input. Validate them against an allow-list of internal routes to avoid open redirects and unexpected actions.

domains.name: Supabase
domains.blurb: Supabase auth, Postgres with Row Level Security, realtime, storage and Edge Functions.

lessons.title: Supabase setup and authentication
lessons.summaryHtml:
Supabase is an open-source backend platform built around a real Postgres database, with Auth, Realtime, Storage and Edge Functions on top. You create a project, copy its URL and publishable key (formerly the anon key), and call Supabase.initialize before runApp.

The supabase_flutter auth client supports email and password, magic links and one-time codes, and OAuth providers that return to the app through a deep link. It persists and refreshes the session for you. TaskFlow turns onAuthStateChange into an AuthCubit and uses a go_router redirect so that only signed-in users reach their tasks.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Until now TaskFlow borrowed a practice API. Module 12 gives it a real backend. Supabase is a backend platform built around a Postgres database, the same SQL database many large companies run. Around the database it adds the services an app usually needs: sign-in, live updates, file storage and small server functions. It is open source, so you can use the hosted service or run it yourself.

If Firebase (lesson 7.4) felt like a set of smart folders, Supabase feels like a proper database with a helpful front desk. You write tables and rules in SQL, and the Flutter client turns your Dart calls into requests to that database, checked against those rules.

Why it matters

Many client projects need relational data: projects that have tasks, tasks that have assignees, reports that join them. Postgres handles that naturally, with foreign keys, joins and transactions. Supabase also puts security where it belongs, in the database, through Row Level Security (RLS, lesson 12.2). Knowing both Firebase and Supabase lets you pick the right tool for each client, and Supabase skills transfer directly to any Postgres job.

How it works

The pieces

ProductWhat it isTaskFlow uses it for
DatabaseA full Postgres database with an automatic REST APIprojects and tasks tables (12.2)
AuthUsers, sessions, email, magic links, OTP, OAuth providersSign-in (this lesson)
RealtimePushes database changes to subscribed clientsLive task list (12.3)
StorageFiles in buckets, protected by policiesTask attachments (12.3)
Edge FunctionsServer-side TypeScript functionsSecret keys and third-party calls (12.4)

Project setup and the two kinds of key

In the Supabase dashboard you create a project, choose a region and set a database password. The project’s API settings then show a Project URL and two kinds of key. Supabase renamed them recently, so you will see both names in tutorials:

Current nameOlder nameWhere it goes
Publishable keyanon keyIn the app. Public by design.
Secret keyservice_role keyOnly on servers and Edge Functions. It bypasses RLS.
Remember: lesson 11.1 said an app cannot keep a secret. Supabase is designed around that fact. The publishable key only tells Supabase which project you mean. What a user can do is decided by the user’s session and your RLS policies. If the secret key ever ends up in an app, rotate it immediately.

Install and initialise

Run flutter pub add supabase_flutter. Initialise it once, before runApp. TaskFlow reads the URL and key with --dart-define-from-file, as in lesson 11.1, so dev and prod projects use different files:

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:supabase_flutter/supabase_flutter.dart';

const supabaseUrl = String.fromEnvironment('SUPABASE_URL');
const supabaseKey = String.fromEnvironment('SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY');

Future<void> main() async {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  await Supabase.initialize(url: supabaseUrl, publishableKey: supabaseKey);
  runApp(const TaskFlowApp());
}

// Anywhere later:
final supabase = Supabase.instance.client;

Current versions of supabase_flutter take publishableKey:. The older anonKey: parameter still works but is deprecated, so update it when you meet it in existing code.

Email and password

TaskFlow wraps the auth client in an AuthRepository, the same pattern as module 9, so widgets and tests never call Supabase directly:

const redirectUrl = 'io.supabase.taskflow://login-callback/';

class AuthRepository {
  AuthRepository(this._auth);
  final GoTrueClient _auth; // Supabase.instance.client.auth

  Stream<AuthState> get changes => _auth.onAuthStateChange;

  Future<void> signIn(String email, String password) =>
      _auth.signInWithPassword(email: email, password: password);

  /// false means Supabase sent a confirmation email instead of a session.
  Future<bool> signUp(String email, String password) async {
    final res = await _auth.signUp(
        email: email, password: password, emailRedirectTo: redirectUrl);
    return res.session != null;
  }

  Future<void> sendMagicLink(String email) =>
      _auth.signInWithOtp(email: email, emailRedirectTo: redirectUrl);

  Future<void> signOut() => _auth.signOut();
}

Failures throw an AuthException whose message is safe to show, for example "Invalid login credentials". With "Confirm email" switched on (the default), signUp returns a user with a null session until the address is confirmed.

Screen 1: Sign-in screen lib/auth/sign_in_page.dart

@override
Widget build(BuildContext context) {
  return Scaffold(
    appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Sign in to TaskFlow')),
    body: ListView(padding: const EdgeInsets.all(24), children: [
      TextField(controller: _email,
          keyboardType: TextInputType.emailAddress,
          decoration: const InputDecoration(
              labelText: 'Email', prefixIcon: Icon(Icons.mail))),
      const SizedBox(height: 12),
      TextField(controller: _password, obscureText: true,
          decoration: InputDecoration(labelText: 'Password',
              prefixIcon: const Icon(Icons.lock), errorText: _error)),
      const SizedBox(height: 24),
      FilledButton(
        onPressed: _busy ? null : () => _run((r) => r
            .signIn(_email.text.trim(), _password.text)
            .then((_) => null)),
        child: const Text('Sign in'),
      ),
      OutlinedButton(
        onPressed: _busy ? null : () => _run((r) async =>
            await r.signUp(_email.text.trim(), _password.text)
                ? null
                : 'Check your email to confirm your account.'),
        child: const Text('Create account'),
      ),
      TextButton(
        onPressed: _busy ? null : () => _run((r) async {
          final email = _email.text.trim();
          await r.sendMagicLink(email);
          return 'Magic link sent to $email';
        }),
        child: const Text('Email me a magic link'),
      ),
    ]),
  );
}

One screen covers password sign-in, account creation and magic links. Supabase’s AuthException message appears as the field’s errorText, and a new account gets a SnackBar because its session is null until the email is confirmed. States: Empty → Wrong password → Account created.

Magic links and one-time codes

signInWithOtp(email: ...) emails the user. Depending on the email template, the email holds a link, a code, or both. The link opens your redirect URL, and supabase_flutter spots it and completes the session by itself. For a code, call verifyOTP(type: OtpType.email, email: ..., token: ...). Codes help when users read email on a laptop but use TaskFlow on their phone.

Screen 2: Email one-time code lib/auth/verify_code_page.dart

class VerifyCodePage extends StatefulWidget {
  const VerifyCodePage({super.key, required this.email});
  final String email;

  @override
  State<VerifyCodePage> createState() => _VerifyCodePageState();
}

class _VerifyCodePageState extends State<VerifyCodePage> {
  final _code = TextEditingController();
  String? _error;

  Future<void> _verify() async {
    try {
      await Supabase.instance.client.auth.verifyOTP(
        type: OtpType.email,
        email: widget.email,
        token: _code.text.trim(),
      );
      // No navigation here: the redirect sends a signed-in user to /tasks.
    } on AuthException catch (e) {
      if (mounted) setState(() => _error = e.message);
    }
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Check your email')),
      body: ListView(padding: const EdgeInsets.all(24), children: [
        Text('We sent a code to ' + widget.email),
        const SizedBox(height: 16),
        TextField(controller: _code, keyboardType: TextInputType.number,
            decoration: InputDecoration(labelText: 'Code',
                prefixIcon: const Icon(Icons.pin), errorText: _error)),
        const SizedBox(height: 24),
        FilledButton(onPressed: _verify, child: const Text('Verify')),
      ]),
    );
  }
}

If the email template includes the code instead of (or as well as) the link, the user types it here. verifyOTP creates the session, and the AuthCubit and router take over from there.

OAuth and deep link redirects

For "Continue with Google" or GitHub, call signInWithOAuth(OAuthProvider.google, redirectTo: redirectUrl). It opens the provider in a browser. When the user finishes, the provider sends them back to Supabase, which redirects to your URL. Three things must line up, or the user is stuck in the browser:

  1. The provider is enabled and configured under Authentication in the dashboard.
  2. The exact redirect URL is in the project’s allowed Redirect URLs.
  3. The OS routes that URL to TaskFlow: an intent filter on Android and a URL type in Info.plist on iOS.

The client uses the PKCE flow by default, which ties the returning link to the device that started the sign-in. For a fully native Google or Apple sheet, Supabase also accepts ID tokens from those SDKs through signInWithIdToken. The idea is the same: a session appears on the auth stream.

onAuthStateChange drives the app

Sessions start and end in many places: a password sign-in, a magic link opened from the mail app, a restored session at startup, a failed refresh. So TaskFlow has one source of truth. An AuthCubit mirrors the stream, and the router listens to the cubit. Note the state name: supabase_flutter already exports a class called AuthState, so ours is SessionState:

sealed class SessionState { const SessionState(); }
class SessionUnknown extends SessionState { const SessionUnknown(); }
class SignedOut extends SessionState { const SignedOut(); }
class SignedIn extends SessionState {
  const SignedIn(this.user);
  final User user;
}

class AuthCubit extends Cubit<SessionState> {
  AuthCubit(this.repo) : super(const SessionUnknown()) {
    // First event: initialSession, with the saved session or null.
    _sub = repo.changes.listen(
      (data) {
        final session = data.session;
        emit(session == null ? const SignedOut() : SignedIn(session.user));
      },
      onError: (Object error) {}, // e.g. offline while refreshing
    );
  }

  final AuthRepository repo;
  late final StreamSubscription<AuthState> _sub;

  Future<void> signOut() => repo.signOut();

  @override
  Future<void> close() async {
    await _sub.cancel();
    return super.close();
  }
}

The go_router redirect from lesson 5.2 then becomes a switch over SessionState, and a small ChangeNotifier that listens to cubit.stream is passed as refreshListenable, so the redirect runs again on every change. Sign-in screens never call context.go('/tasks') themselves. They change the session, and the router follows.

Session persistence and sign-out

supabase_flutter saves the session on the device and refreshes the short-lived access token before it expires, so a restarted app comes back signed in. That is why the cubit starts as SessionUnknown and the router shows a splash until initialSession arrives. By default the session is stored with shared_preferences. If your threat model needs more (lesson 11.1), FlutterAuthClientOptions accepts a custom localStorage, which you can back with flutter_secure_storage. signOut() clears the local session and, by default, signs out only this device. Pass a different SignOutScope to end sessions everywhere.

Screen 3: Restored session lib/main.dart

GoRouter buildRouter(AuthCubit cubit) => GoRouter(
      initialLocation: '/tasks',
      refreshListenable: StreamListenable(cubit.stream),
      redirect: (context, state) {
        final at = state.matchedLocation;
        return switch (cubit.state) {
          SessionUnknown() => at == '/splash' ? null : '/splash',
          SignedOut() => at == '/sign-in' ? null : '/sign-in',
          SignedIn() =>
            (at == '/sign-in' || at == '/splash') ? '/tasks' : null,
        };
      },
      routes: [
        GoRoute(path: '/', redirect: (_, __) => '/tasks'),
        GoRoute(path: '/splash', builder: (_, __) => const Scaffold(
            body: Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator()))),
        GoRoute(path: '/sign-in', builder: (_, __) => const SignInPage()),
        GoRoute(path: '/tasks', builder: (_, __) => const TasksPage()),
      ],
    );

class TasksPage extends StatelessWidget {
  const TasksPage({super.key});
  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final state = context.watch<AuthCubit>().state;
    final email = state is SignedIn ? (state.user.email ?? 'unknown') : '';
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('TaskFlow'), actions: [
        IconButton(onPressed: () => context.read<AuthCubit>().signOut(),
            icon: const Icon(Icons.logout)),
      ]),
      body: Center(child: Text(
          'Signed in as $email\nYour tasks arrive in lesson 12.2.',
          textAlign: TextAlign.center)),
    );
  }
}

On a cold start the cubit is SessionUnknown, so the router shows a splash. The initialSession event arrives with the saved session and the redirect moves straight to the tasks screen, without the sign-in page flashing up. States: Cold start → Session restored.

Example: TaskFlow sign-in

  1. Create the taskflow-dev project, copy the URL and publishable key into config/supabase.json, and add io.supabase.taskflow://login-callback/ to the Redirect URLs.
  2. Register the scheme with an Android intent filter and an iOS URL type.
  3. Initialise Supabase in main, build AuthRepository and AuthCubit, and provide the cubit with BlocProvider.value.
  4. Build the router with the SessionState redirect. Add a / route that redirects to /tasks, because the callback link opens the app at the root path.
  5. Sign up a test user, confirm the email, sign in, restart the app and watch it go straight to the tasks screen. Then sign out.

Common mistakes

  • Shipping the secret (service_role) key "just to get it working". It bypasses every RLS policy. Anyone who unpacks the app owns your database.
  • Navigating manually after sign-in. It fights the router and breaks for magic links and OAuth. Let the auth stream and the redirect do it.
  • Forgetting the Redirect URL or the intent filter. The browser shows an error, or the email link opens a web page instead of the app.
  • Naming your state class AuthState. It clashes with the class supabase_flutter exports. Choose another name or hide the import.
  • Expecting a session right after sign-up. With email confirmation on, it is null until the user clicks the link.

Interview and real-world notes

  • "Supabase or Firebase?" Supabase for relational data, SQL and Postgres skills; Firebase for its document model and its wider mobile tooling. Both have auth, realtime and storage.
  • "Is the anon key a leak?" No. Explain publishable versus secret keys and that RLS enforces access.
  • "How do you keep auth state in Flutter?" One stream (onAuthStateChange) feeds a cubit, and the router redirect reads it. Mention initialSession and the splash state.
  • Use separate Supabase projects for dev and prod, each with its own config file. Lesson 12.4 builds on that.

terms.definition: Open-source backend platform: a Postgres database plus Auth, Realtime, Storage and Edge Functions, available as a hosted service or self-hosted.
The public client key (called the anon key in older projects). It identifies your project; security comes from Row Level Security, not from hiding it.
The server-only key (formerly service_role). It bypasses Row Level Security and must never ship in an app.
A short-lived access token (a JWT) plus a refresh token. supabase_flutter stores it and refreshes the access token automatically.
Stream of AuthState events (initialSession, signedIn, signedOut, tokenRefreshed, and more), each carrying the current Session or null.
Passwordless sign-in: Supabase emails a link or a one-time code, and opening the link or entering the code creates the session.

lessons.title: Supabase database and Row Level Security
lessons.summaryHtml: Every Supabase project is a real Postgres database. You create tables with SQL, and your Flutter app reads and writes them through Supabase.instance.client.from('tasks') with select, insert, update and delete, plus filters such as eq, order and range for pagination. Because the publishable key ships inside the app, anyone can call your database directly. Row Level Security (RLS) is what stops them: policies written in SQL decide, row by row, what each signed-in user may see and change, using auth.uid(). In this lesson TaskFlow gets projects and tasks tables with owner-only policies, and a SupabaseTaskRepository that is swapped in through dependency injection without touching the UI.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

In lesson 12.1 you connected TaskFlow to Supabase and signed users in. Now the tasks themselves move there. Behind every Supabase project sits a full Postgres database, the same open-source database that banks and large companies run. You create tables with ordinary SQL, and your Flutter app talks to them through the supabase_flutter client: client.from('tasks').select() reads rows, insert, update and delete change them.

There is no backend code of yours in between. The client sends an HTTPS request to PostgREST, a service that turns it into SQL. So who stops one user reading another user’s tasks? The database itself, through Row Level Security (RLS). Think of an office building. The street address is public: that is your project URL and publishable key. Every office door has a card reader, and the reader checks your badge against a list before it opens. RLS policies are those card readers, and your badge is the JWT from signing in.

Why it matters

Module 11 taught the hard truth: a mobile app cannot keep a secret. The Supabase URL and publishable key (older projects and docs call it the anon key) sit in your APK or IPA, and anyone can extract them in minutes. With those two values an attacker can skip your app and call the REST API with curl. If a table has RLS switched off, that person can read, change or delete every row. Checks in your Dart code do not help, because the attacker is not running your Dart code.

So RLS is not an optional extra. It is the security layer of a Supabase app. The good news is that it is simple SQL, it runs for every request whether it comes from Flutter, a web app or curl, and you can test it. The service_role or secret key bypasses RLS completely, which is exactly why it must never ship in an app. It belongs only on servers and in Edge Functions (lesson 12.4).

How it works

Creating the TaskFlow tables

Open the SQL editor in the Supabase dashboard and run a script. You can also click tables together in the Table editor, but SQL is repeatable, reviewable and later becomes a migration file.

create table public.projects (
  id uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  owner_id uuid not null default auth.uid() references auth.users (id) on delete cascade,
  name text not null check (char_length(name) between 1 and 80),
  created_at timestamptz not null default now()
);

create table public.tasks (
  id uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  project_id uuid not null references public.projects (id) on delete cascade,
  user_id uuid not null default auth.uid() references auth.users (id) on delete cascade,
  title text not null check (char_length(title) between 1 and 200),
  done boolean not null default false,
  created_at timestamptz not null default now()
);

create index on public.tasks (user_id);
create index on public.tasks (project_id, created_at desc);

Three details matter. default auth.uid() fills in the owner from the caller’s JWT, so the app never has to send it. The check constraints validate input in the database, where nobody can skip them. The indexes cover the columns your policies and queries filter on, which Supabase recommends so policies stay fast as tables grow.

Reading and writing from Flutter

final db = Supabase.instance.client;

// Read: returns List<Map<String, dynamic>>
final rows = await db.from('tasks').select('id, title, done').eq('project_id', projectId);

// Create and get the new row back in the same request
final row = await db.from('tasks').insert({'project_id': projectId, 'title': 'Ship v1'}).select().single();

// Update one row
await db.from('tasks').update({'done': true}).eq('id', taskId);

// Delete one row
await db.from('tasks').delete().eq('id', taskId);
CallSQL it becomesNotes
select('a, b')select a, b from …List only the columns you need; select() means all.
insert(map) / insert([maps])insert into …Add .select().single() to get the row with its generated id.
update(map)update … set …Always add a filter, or you target every row you are allowed to change.
delete()delete from …Same: always filter.
upsert(map)insert … on conflict do updateHandy for sync (lesson 10.3).

Filters come right after the command: eq, neq, gt, lt, ilike, inFilter, isFilter and more. Then come modifiers: order, limit, range and single. Pass ascending: to order explicitly so the direction is obvious to the reader. Errors arrive as a PostgrestException with message, code, details and hint.

Pagination with range

range(from, to) asks for rows by position and both ends are inclusive. Page 0 with a page size of 20 is range(0, 19) and page 1 is range(20, 39). Always combine it with a stable order, or rows can jump between pages. If fewer rows come back than the page size, you have reached the end, which is the same hasMore logic you built with the ScrollController in lesson 9.3.

Joins through foreign keys

Because tasks.project_id references projects, PostgREST can embed the related row in one request. You name the table inside the select string, optionally with an alias:

final rows = await db
    .from('tasks')
    .select('id, title, done, project:projects(name)')
    .eq('done', false)
    .order('created_at', ascending: false)
    .limit(20);

// Each row: {id: ..., title: ..., done: false, project: {name: Inbox}}
final projectName = (rows.first['project'] as Map<String, dynamic>?)?['name'];

Embedded tables obey their own RLS policies. If the user may not see the project, the embedded value is null, not a leak.

Row Level Security: enable, then allow

Turning RLS on flips the table to deny by default. Tables made in the dashboard’s Table editor have RLS on by default, but tables made with SQL may not, so always enable it yourself. Then each policy opens one kind of access for one role.

alter table public.tasks enable row level security;

create policy "Read own tasks" on public.tasks
  for select to authenticated
  using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);

create policy "Create own tasks in own projects" on public.tasks
  for insert to authenticated
  with check (
    (select auth.uid()) = user_id
    and exists (select 1 from public.projects p
                where p.id = project_id and p.owner_id = (select auth.uid()))
  );

create policy "Update own tasks" on public.tasks
  for update to authenticated
  using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id)
  with check ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);

create policy "Delete own tasks" on public.tasks
  for delete to authenticated
  using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);
ClauseChecksUsed byIf it fails
usingExisting rows: may this user see or touch this row?select, update, deleteThe row is silently left out: no error, zero rows.
with checkNew values: may this row be written like this?insert, updateAn error: code 42501, “new row violates row-level security policy”.

Wrapping auth.uid() in (select …) is what the Supabase docs recommend: Postgres then evaluates it once per query instead of once per row. to authenticated means signed-out callers match no policy at all. An update also needs a select policy, because Postgres can only update rows the user can see. If an update policy has no with check, Postgres uses its using expression for the new row too; spelling out both, as above, makes the rule obvious.

Remember: RLS runs inside Postgres for every request. Your Dart code can make things friendlier, but only the policies make them safe.

Testing your policies

Never assume a policy works. Test it three ways:

  • In SQL, pretend to be a user inside a transaction you roll back: 
    begin;
set local role authenticated;
select set_config('request.jwt.claims',
  '{"sub":"PUT-USER-A-UUID-HERE","role":"authenticated"}', true);
select count(*) from public.tasks;   -- only user A's rows
rollback;
  • In the app, with two accounts on two devices: user B must never see, edit or delete user A’s rows.
  • Automatically, with pgTAP tests under supabase/tests that the Supabase CLI runs. This is how teams stop a later migration from quietly opening a hole.

For a real team app you would add a project_members table and write policies such as “a member of the task’s project may read it”. Keep policies on the members table simple, because a policy that queries its own table can recurse; the Supabase docs show a security definer helper function for that case.

Example: TaskFlow’s SupabaseTaskRepository

TaskFlow’s domain layer already has the TaskRepository interface from lesson 9.6. The BLoC depends on that interface, not on Dio or Supabase. So the switch is one new class in the data layer plus one line in the get_it setup. To keep this lesson short, its methods throw a sealed TaskFailure instead of returning the Result<T> (Ok or Err) from lesson 9.3; in the full app, _guard would return Err(...) rather than throw.

class SupabaseTaskRepository implements TaskRepository {
  SupabaseTaskRepository(this._db);
  final SupabaseClient _db;

  static Task _fromRow(Map<String, dynamic> row) => Task(
        id: row['id'] as String,
        projectId: row['project_id'] as String,
        title: row['title'] as String,
        done: row['done'] as bool,
        createdAt: DateTime.parse(row['created_at'] as String),
      );

  // One place turns database errors into domain failures.
  Future<T> _guard<T>(Future<T> Function() body) async {
    try {
      return await body();
    } on PostgrestException catch (e) {
      if (e.code == '42501') throw const NotAllowed();
      throw ServerFailure(e.message);
    }
  }

  @override
  Future<Task> add(String projectId, String title) => _guard(() async {
        final row = await _db
            .from('tasks')
            .insert({'project_id': projectId, 'title': title})
            .select('id, project_id, title, done, created_at')
            .single();
        return _fromRow(row);
      });

  @override
  Future<void> setDone(String id, bool done) => _guard(() async {
        final rows = await _db.from('tasks').update({'done': done}).eq('id', id).select('id');
        if (rows.isEmpty) throw const NotAllowed(); // RLS hid the row
      });
}

Notice what is missing: no user_id in the insert (the column default fills it) and no eq('user_id', …) in reads (the policy adds it). The .select('id') after the update turns the silent “zero rows changed” into a clear failure the BLoC can show.

Screen 1: TaskFlow on Supabase lib/main.dart

@override
Widget build(BuildContext context) {
  return Scaffold(
    appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Inbox'), actions: [
      IconButton(
        icon: const Icon(Icons.logout),
        onPressed: () => Supabase.instance.client.auth.signOut(),
      ),
    ]),
    body: Column(crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.stretch, children: [
      Padding(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.fromLTRB(12, 8, 12, 4),
        child: Row(spacing: 8, children: [
          Expanded(
            child: TextField(
              controller: _title,
              decoration: const InputDecoration(hintText: 'New task'),
            ),
          ),
          IconButton.filled(icon: const Icon(Icons.add), onPressed: _add),
        ]),
      ),
      Expanded(
        child: _tasks.isEmpty && _loading
            ? const Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator())
            : ListView.separated(
                itemCount: _tasks.length + 1,
                separatorBuilder: (context, i) => const Divider(height: 1),
                itemBuilder: (context, i) {
                  if (i == _tasks.length) {
                    return _hasMore
                        ? Center(child: TextButton(onPressed: _loadMore, child: const Text('Load more')))
                        : const SizedBox.shrink();
                  }
                  final task = _tasks[i];
                  return ListTile(
                    leading: Checkbox(value: task.done, onChanged: (v) => _toggle(task, v ?? false)),
                    title: Text(task.title),
                  );
                },
              ),
      ),
    ]),
  );
}

The same screen as before, now backed by Postgres. The last frame shows a blocked insert: the database rejected it with code 42501, and the repository turned that into a friendly message. States: Loading → Page 1 loaded → Blocked by RLS.

The same select, run by two different users, returns two different lists. That is RLS doing its job.

Screen 2: Same query, two users lib/main.dart

// No .eq('user_id', ...) here on purpose.
// RLS decides which rows this user may see.
@override
Future<List<Task>> fetchPage(String projectId,
    {required int page, int pageSize = 20}) {
  return _guard(() async {
    final from = page * pageSize;
    final to = from + pageSize - 1; // range() is inclusive
    final rows = await _db
        .from('tasks')
        .select('id, project_id, title, done, created_at')
        .eq('project_id', projectId)
        .order('created_at', ascending: false)
        .range(from, to);
    return rows.map(_fromRow).toList();
  });
}

// In the widget, an empty list shows a friendly message:
// const Center(child: Text('No tasks yet'))

The repository never filters by user. The identical select returns different rows because RLS adds “auth.uid() = user_id” inside Postgres for every request. States: Signed in as Asha → Signed in as Ben.

And this is why the swap was cheap: only the bottom of the stack changed.

Screen 3: How a query travels lib/injection.dart

final getIt = GetIt.instance;

Future<void> configureDependencies() async {
  await Supabase.initialize(
    url: const String.fromEnvironment('SUPABASE_URL'),
    publishableKey: const String.fromEnvironment('SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY'),
  );
  getIt.registerSingleton<SupabaseClient>(Supabase.instance.client);

  // Before: DummyJsonTaskRepository(getIt<ApiClient>())
  getIt.registerLazySingleton<TaskRepository>(
    () => SupabaseTaskRepository(getIt<SupabaseClient>()),
  );
  getIt.registerFactory<TaskBloc>(() => TaskBloc(getIt<TaskRepository>()));
}

An architecture view, not a real screen. Only the bottom box changed when TaskFlow moved to Supabase: the UI and the BLoC still talk to the TaskRepository interface.

Common mistakes

  • Leaving RLS off “until later”. The table is public the moment it exists in an exposed schema. Enable RLS in the same script that creates the table.
  • Filtering by user in Dart and calling it security. .eq('user_id', me) is a convenience. Anyone with curl can drop it.
  • A loose with check on update. With with check (true), or any check weaker than using, users can rewrite user_id and hand rows to someone else, or break your invariants. (Leaving with check out makes Postgres reuse the using expression, but writing both keeps the intent clear to reviewers.)
  • Insert policy but no select policy. insert(...).select() fails, because returning the row is a read.
  • Putting the service_role or secret key in the app “just to make it work”. It bypasses every policy. If it has ever shipped, rotate it.
  • Treating zero updated rows as success. A blocked update is silent; ask for the rows back and check.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Be ready to explain why the publishable key can be public: it only identifies the project, and RLS plus the user’s JWT decide access.
  • Explain using versus with check with an update example. It is the most common RLS question.
  • Mention testing: impersonation in SQL, two-account manual tests and pgTAP in CI. Reviewers love to hear “policies have tests”.
  • Talk about architecture: the repository interface stayed the same, so the BLoC, the UI and their tests did not change when the backend moved from a REST API to Supabase.
  • Performance: index the columns used in policies and wrap auth.uid() in a select.

terms.definition: The service Supabase runs in front of Postgres that turns HTTP requests from the client library into SQL queries.
A Postgres feature that filters or blocks rows per user, based on policies attached to the table.
A SQL rule for one table and one command (select, insert, update or delete) that says which rows are allowed.
A Supabase SQL function that returns the id of the user whose JWT made the request, or null for anonymous calls.
using filters the existing rows a command can see or touch; with check validates the new row values a command writes.
Limits a query to rows from index from to index to, both inclusive, for offset pagination.
