quiz.question: Your TaskFlow app ships with the Supabase publishable key. A tester extracts it and calls the REST API with curl. What stops them reading every task?
options: Row Level Security policies on the tasks table
The key is encrypted inside the APK
Supabase only accepts requests from your app package name
Code obfuscation with --obfuscate
quiz.explanation: The publishable key is public by design. Only RLS policies, checked inside Postgres for every request, decide which rows a caller may read or change.

quiz.question: An update policy has using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id) with check (true). What can a user still do?
options: Nothing, the policy blocks all updates
Read other users' tasks
Update their own task and change user_id to another user's id
Delete other users' tasks
quiz.explanation: using only checks the row before the update. with check (true) accepts any new values, so a user could hand a row to someone else. Use the same condition in with check. (If you leave with check out entirely, Postgres reuses the using expression for the new row, but writing both makes the intent explicit.)

quiz.question: A user updates a task that belongs to someone else. RLS is enabled with correct owner-only policies. What does the Flutter call return?
options: A PostgrestException with code 42501
An AuthException
A 404 error from Storage
No error and no rows changed, because the row is invisible to that user
quiz.explanation: RLS filters the rows an update can see, so the update simply matches zero rows. Ask for .select() after the update and treat an empty list as “not found or not allowed”.

quiz.question: You enable RLS on the tasks table but have not written any policies yet. What happens to requests made with the publishable key?
options: Every row is still readable until you add a policy
No rows are returned and every write is rejected, because RLS denies by default
Only inserts are allowed
Supabase disables the table API
quiz.explanation: With RLS on and no policy for a command, Postgres allows nothing for that command. Policies then open specific access. Only the service role, which bypasses RLS, still sees everything.

lessons.title: Realtime and Storage
lessons.summaryHtml: Supabase Realtime pushes database changes to your app over a WebSocket, so a teammate’s new task appears on your screen without a refresh. The simplest tool is from('tasks').stream(primaryKey: ['id']), which gives a Dart Stream of the whole current list. For finer control you open a channel and listen to onPostgresChanges events (insert, update, delete), and you remove it with removeChannel when the screen closes. Supabase Storage keeps files in buckets. Public buckets serve files to anyone with the URL; private buckets need a signed URL that expires. Access is controlled by SQL policies on storage.objects, just like RLS on your tables. TaskFlow gets a live task list and photo attachments picked with image_picker.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

In lesson 12.2 TaskFlow learned to read and write tasks in Postgres. But if Ben adds a task on his laptop, Asha’s phone still shows the old list until she reloads. Realtime fixes that. Supabase watches the database for changes and pushes them to every connected app over a WebSocket, a connection that stays open so the server can talk first. Think of a news ticker: you do not keep asking “anything new?”, the headlines just scroll in.

The second half of this lesson is Storage: a place for files such as photos and PDFs. Files live in buckets, which are like labelled lockers. Some lockers are open to the public; others need a key that expires. And just as RLS guards table rows, storage policies decide who may put files in, read them or delete them.

Why it matters

Team apps feel broken without live data. Two people tick the same task, or one person assigns work the other never sees. Pull-to-refresh helps, but users forget to pull. With Realtime, every screen that shows tasks stays current, and you write no polling code.

Files are the other everyday need: a photo of a receipt, a screenshot of a bug, a signed delivery note. Those files are often more sensitive than the rows that point to them. A leaked receipt can show a name, an address and card details, so bucket choice and storage policies matter as much as table RLS.

How it works

Switching on Realtime for a table

Postgres changes are only broadcast for tables in the supabase_realtime publication. You can toggle this in the dashboard, or run SQL:

alter publication supabase_realtime add table public.tasks;

-- Optional: include the full old row in update and delete events
alter table public.tasks replica identity full;

Realtime respects your RLS policies for signed-in users: Ben’s phone only receives changes to rows his select policy lets him see. That is why the policies from lesson 12.2 matter here too.

stream(): the easy way

stream() first loads the matching rows, then keeps listening, and every time something changes it emits the whole updated list. That fits a StreamBuilder perfectly.

late final Stream<List<Map<String, dynamic>>> _tasks;

@override
void initState() {
  super.initState();
  _tasks = Supabase.instance.client
      .from('tasks')
      .stream(primaryKey: ['id'])     // needed to merge changes into the list
      .eq('project_id', widget.projectId)
      .order('created_at', ascending: false)
      .limit(50);
}

Rules of thumb: create the stream once in initState (or in a repository or BLoC), never inside build, or every rebuild opens a new subscription. Keep the filter simple. The Supabase docs note two limits worth knowing: for updates, a filter such as eq is checked against the new row only, so a row that stops matching is not removed; and delete events carry only the primary key by default.

Channels and Postgres changes

When you need to react to a specific event rather than redraw a list, open a channel. A channel is a named topic on the Realtime connection. You add listeners, then call subscribe.

final channel = supabase
    .channel('tasks-$projectId')
    .onPostgresChanges(
      event: PostgresChangeEvent.insert,   // insert, update, delete or all
      schema: 'public',
      table: 'tasks',
      filter: PostgresChangeFilter(
        type: PostgresChangeFilterType.eq,
        column: 'project_id',
        value: projectId,
      ),
      callback: (payload) {
        final title = payload.newRecord['title'];
        debugPrint('New task: $title');
      },
    )
    .subscribe((status, error) {
      debugPrint('Channel status: ' + status.name);
    });

// Later, in dispose():
supabase.removeChannel(channel);

The payload gives you eventType, newRecord and oldRecord. The subscribe callback reports a RealtimeSubscribeStatus: subscribed, channelError, timedOut or closed, which you can turn into a “live” indicator.

NeedUseWhy
Show a list that always matches the databasestream()Initial load plus merging is done for you.
Toast, sound or badge when something specific happensChannel with onPostgresChangesYou get each event with old and new values.
Typing indicators, cursor positions, “Ben is viewing”Channel with Broadcast or PresenceMessages between clients that never touch a table.
Data that changes rarelyPlain select() plus pull-to-refreshNo open connection needed.

Unsubscribing

A StreamBuilder cancels its subscription when the widget goes away, so stream() cleans itself up. A channel does not: it belongs to the shared client, not to your widget. If you forget removeChannel in dispose, the callback keeps firing after the screen is gone, often calling setState on a dead widget, and every open channel counts toward your project’s Realtime limits.

Storage buckets: public or private

Public bucketPrivate bucket
Reading a fileAnyone with the URL, no sign-inOnly through a signed URL or an authenticated download
URLgetPublicUrl(path), stable, CDN-cachedcreateSignedUrl(path, seconds), expires
Good forProduct images, public avatars, marketing assetsReceipts, documents, anything personal
Uploading, updating, deletingAlways controlled by policies on storage.objects, for both kinds

Storage policies

Storage keeps one row per file in the storage.objects table, so you protect files with ordinary RLS policies. The usual pattern is “each user writes into a folder named after their own id”:

insert into storage.buckets (id, name, public)
values ('task-files', 'task-files', false)
on conflict (id) do nothing;

create policy "Upload into own folder" on storage.objects
  for insert to authenticated
  with check (bucket_id = 'task-files'
              and (storage.foldername(name))[1] = (select auth.uid()::text));

create policy "Read own files" on storage.objects
  for select to authenticated
  using (bucket_id = 'task-files'
         and (storage.foldername(name))[1] = (select auth.uid()::text));

Uploading with upsert: true also needs an update policy, and deleting needs a delete policy. Creating a signed URL needs the select policy, which is exactly what stops Ben signing links to Asha’s files.

Uploading with image_picker

Run flutter pub add image_picker. On iOS, add NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription (and NSCameraUsageDescription for the camera) to Info.plist, as lesson 8.2 showed. pickImage returns an XFile, or null if the user cancels. Its maxWidth and imageQuality options shrink photos before upload, which saves the user’s data and your storage.

Read the bytes with readAsBytes() and call uploadBinary. Bytes work on mobile, desktop and web alike, which a dart:io File does not. Then save the path in the task row. The next mock shows the full method.

Example: TaskFlow live board with attachments

The TaskFlow Inbox from lesson 12.2 becomes a LiveTasksPage:

  1. In initState it gets the project id from TaskRepository.inboxProjectId(), then creates the stream() once.
  2. It opens one channel listening to inserts in that project. If the new title is not one this device just added, it shows “Added on another device”.
  3. Adding and ticking tasks still go through the repository. The stream redraws the list, so the page no longer patches its own list.

Screen 1: Live task list lib/live_tasks_page.dart

// Created once in initState, never in build().
_tasks = _db
    .from('tasks')
    .stream(primaryKey: ['id'])
    .eq('project_id', projectId)
    .order('created_at', ascending: false);

// In build():
StreamBuilder<List<Map<String, dynamic>>>(
  stream: _tasks,
  builder: (context, snap) {
    if (snap.hasError) return Center(child: Text('Error: ' + snap.error.toString()));
    if (!snap.hasData) return const Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator());
    final rows = snap.data!;
    return ListView.separated(
      itemCount: rows.length,
      separatorBuilder: (context, i) => const Divider(height: 1),
      itemBuilder: (context, i) => ListTile(
        leading: Checkbox(value: rows[i]['done'] as bool, onChanged: (v) {}),
        title: Text(rows[i]['title'] as String),
        trailing: const Icon(Icons.attach_file),
      ),
    );
  },
)

// The channel callback for inserts made elsewhere:
_show('Added on another device: ' + title);

Ben adds a task on his laptop. On the phone, stream() delivers the new list, and a separate channel listener shows who changed what. No refresh, no polling. States: Before → After Ben adds one.

Each task has an attach button. The photo goes to task-files/<uid>/<taskId>/<timestamp>.jpg, and the path is written to a new attachment_path column. Because that update is itself a database change, the stream delivers it and the thumbnail appears on every device.

Screen 2: Attach a photo lib/live_tasks_page.dart

Future<void> _attach(String taskId) async {
  final file = await ImagePicker().pickImage(
      source: ImageSource.gallery, maxWidth: 1600, imageQuality: 85);
  if (file == null || !mounted) return; // cancelled, or the page closed
  final uid = _db.auth.currentUser!.id;
  final stamp = DateTime.now().millisecondsSinceEpoch;
  final path = '$uid/$taskId/$stamp.jpg';
  setState(() => _uploading.add(taskId));
  try {
    await _db.storage.from('task-files').uploadBinary(
          path,
          await file.readAsBytes(),
          fileOptions: FileOptions(contentType: file.mimeType ?? 'image/jpeg'),
        );
    await _db.from('tasks').update({'attachment_path': path}).eq('id', taskId);
  } on StorageException catch (e) {
    _show('Upload failed: ' + e.message);
  } finally {
    if (mounted) setState(() => _uploading.remove(taskId));
  }
}

// Showing it: a signed URL, cached per path
Future<String> _signedUrl(String path) => _signedUrls.putIfAbsent(
    path, () => _db.storage.from('task-files').createSignedUrl(path, 3600));

The picker returns an XFile. The bytes go to a private bucket under the user’s own folder, the path is saved on the task, and a signed URL that expires in one hour displays it. States: Pick → Uploading → Uploaded.

Finally, the channel’s status drives a small banner, so users know when “live” is not live.

Screen 3: Connection status lib/live_tasks_page.dart

_channel = _db
    .channel('tasks-$projectId')
    .onPostgresChanges(
      event: PostgresChangeEvent.insert,
      schema: 'public',
      table: 'tasks',
      filter: PostgresChangeFilter(
        type: PostgresChangeFilterType.eq,
        column: 'project_id',
        value: projectId,
      ),
      callback: _onInsert,
    )
    .subscribe((status, error) {
      if (!mounted) return;
      setState(() => _live = status == RealtimeSubscribeStatus.subscribed);
    });

// In build(), above the list:
if (!_live)
  Container(
    color: Theme.of(context).colorScheme.errorContainer,
    padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12),
    child: const Text('Reconnecting… live updates paused'),
  ),

The subscribe() callback reports the channel status. When it is not subscribed, a banner warns that live updates are paused; the client reconnects on its own. States: Live → Connection lost.

In the full clean-architecture app, move the stream and upload code into TaskRepository as a Stream<List<Task>> watchTasks(projectId) and an attachPhoto method, and let the BLoC listen with emit.forEach. The page code here keeps them visible so you can see each call.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the publication. The first load works, live updates never come. Add the table to supabase_realtime.
  • Creating stream() in build(). Every rebuild resubscribes, the list flickers and you waste connections.
  • Never calling removeChannel. Callbacks outlive the screen and crash with “setState() called after dispose()”.
  • Storing signed URLs in the database. They expire. Store the path and sign when you display.
  • Making a bucket public “because the signed URL was annoying”. Every receipt becomes readable by anyone who guesses or shares a link.
  • Uploading full-size camera photos. Use maxWidth and imageQuality.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Explain the difference between stream() (a live list) and a channel (individual events), and when polling is simply good enough.
  • Know that Realtime and Storage both follow RLS. “How do you stop user B reading user A’s files?” Private bucket, folder-per-user policy and signed URLs.
  • Mention lifecycle: create streams once, remove channels in dispose, and show a connection indicator.
  • For large lists, combine a paginated select with a channel that patches the loaded pages. stream() is best for small, bounded lists.
  • For offline-first TaskFlow (lesson 10.3), Realtime events are a trigger to sync into Drift, not a replacement for the local database.

terms.definition: The Supabase service that sends database changes, broadcast messages and presence updates to clients over a WebSocket.
A client method that loads the current rows, then keeps emitting the updated full list whenever a matching row changes.
A named Realtime connection topic. You attach listeners such as onPostgresChanges, then call subscribe().
A top-level container in Supabase Storage. It is either public (anyone with the URL can read) or private.
A time-limited link to a private file, created by a user who is allowed to read it.
A Storage SQL helper that splits an object path into folders, used in policies such as “first folder must be my user id”.

lessons.examTip: Real-world habit: store the file path in your table, not the URL. Public URLs can be rebuilt and signed URLs expire, but the path stays valid.

quiz.question: You added stream(primaryKey: ['id']) for the tasks table, but the list never updates live, even though the first load works. What is the most likely cause?
options: The tasks table is not in the supabase_realtime publication
image_picker is not installed
stream() only works on web
The bucket is private
quiz.explanation: stream() does an initial select (which works) and then relies on Postgres changes. A table must be added to the supabase_realtime publication before its changes are broadcast.

quiz.question: Where should you remove a Realtime channel that a screen opened in initState?
options: In build()
In dispose(), with removeChannel
Nowhere, channels close by themselves when the widget is gone
In main() after runApp
quiz.explanation: The channel lives on the shared client, not in the widget. If you do not call removeChannel in dispose, it keeps running and firing callbacks after the screen is gone.

quiz.question: TaskFlow stores receipt photos in a private bucket. How should the app show a photo?
options: Use getPublicUrl, because every bucket has public URLs
Download it with the service_role key
Ask the server for a signed URL with a short expiry and load that in Image.network
Store the image bytes in the tasks table instead
quiz.explanation: Private files need a signed URL, which the user can only create if a storage policy lets them read the object. It stops working after the expiry.

quiz.question: Your storage insert policy is: bucket_id = 'task-files' and (storage.foldername(name))[1] = (select auth.uid()::text). Which upload path works for user u1?
options: task-files/u1/photo.jpg
u2/t9/photo.jpg
photo.jpg
u1/t9/photo.jpg
quiz.explanation: The path inside the bucket must start with the user’s own id as the first folder. The bucket name is not part of the object path.

lessons.title: Edge Functions and going to production
lessons.summaryHtml: Some work must never run in the app: anything that needs a secret key, talks to a paid third-party API, receives webhooks or must be trusted. Supabase Edge Functions are small TypeScript functions that run on Deno on Supabase’s servers. Your Flutter app calls one with supabase.functions.invoke('name', body: {...}), and supabase_flutter sends the signed-in user’s JWT with it, so the function knows who is asking and can query the database as that user, still under RLS. Secrets live in the function’s environment via supabase secrets set. To go live you separate dev and prod projects, pick one with --dart-define-from-file, change the schema only through CLI migrations, know your backups and plan limits, and work through a production checklist for TaskFlow.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

So far TaskFlow has no server code of its own. The app talks straight to Postgres, and RLS keeps it safe. That covers most screens, but not everything. Some jobs need a secret, such as a payment key or a Slack webhook URL. Some need to receive calls from other services, such as a payment provider saying “this invoice was paid”. Some must be trusted, such as working out a price the user cannot tamper with.

For those jobs Supabase gives you Edge Functions: small TypeScript functions that run on Deno on Supabase’s servers. Think of a bank. The lobby is self-service (your app plus RLS), but some things only happen behind the glass, where the teller can open the safe. The teller checks your ID first, and you never get the safe’s key.

The second half of this lesson is about going live: separate dev and prod projects, schema changes through migrations, backups and limits, and a final checklist.

Why it matters

Module 11 showed that anything inside an APK or IPA can be extracted, including values passed with --dart-define. A third-party API key in the app is a key you have given to everyone. The fix is always the same: move the call to a server you control and let the app call that server. Edge Functions are that server, with no machines for you to manage.

Production brings its own risks. Real users’ data lives in prod, so you cannot experiment there. A schema change made by hand in the dashboard is easy to forget and impossible to review. Knowing how to separate environments and ship changes safely is what separates a hobby project from a job-ready one.

How it works

Do you need server code?

TaskApp + RLS enough?Why
Read and write the user’s own tasksYesPolicies express “own rows only”.
Call an API that needs a secret key (email, SMS, AI, Slack)No: Edge FunctionThe key must stay on the server.
Receive a webhook from a payment providerNo: Edge FunctionSomething must listen at a URL and verify a signature.
Grant a paid plan after paymentNo: Edge FunctionUsers must not be able to write their own plan.
Validate a title lengthYesA check constraint does it inside Postgres.

Anatomy of an Edge Function

Install the Supabase CLI (the docs list installers for each OS), then from your project folder:

supabase login
supabase init                          # creates the supabase/ folder
supabase link --project-ref YOUR_DEV_REF
supabase functions new project-report  # creates supabase/functions/project-report/index.ts
supabase functions serve project-report   # optional local run (needs Docker)
supabase functions deploy project-report

A function is a Deno web handler. This one checks the caller, then queries as that user by forwarding their JWT:

import { createClient } from 'npm:@supabase/supabase-js';

Deno.serve(async (req: Request) => {
  const authHeader = req.headers.get('Authorization');
  if (!authHeader) return json({ error: 'Not signed in' }, 401);

  const supabase = createClient(
    Deno.env.get('SUPABASE_URL') ?? '',
    Deno.env.get('SUPABASE_ANON_KEY') ?? '',
    { global: { headers: { Authorization: authHeader } } },
  );
  const { data: userData, error } = await supabase.auth.getUser(authHeader.replace('Bearer ', ''));
  if (error || !userData.user) return json({ error: 'Invalid session' }, 401);

  const { projectId } = await req.json();
  const { data: tasks } = await supabase.from('tasks').select('done').eq('project_id', projectId);
  // ...count, call Slack with a secret, return JSON
});

By default verify_jwt is on: the platform rejects requests without a valid Supabase JWT before your code even runs. Supabase’s docs also show a newer withSupabase helper and newer key names (SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEYS, SUPABASE_SECRET_KEYS); the legacy SUPABASE_ANON_KEY and SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY variables are still provided. The idea is the same either way, so copy the exact import and helper from the current Edge Functions auth guide when you start.

Watch out: a client built with the secret or service_role key bypasses RLS. Use it only for work the user genuinely cannot do, and only after your code has checked who the caller is and what they may do.

Secrets

supabase secrets set SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL=https://hooks.slack.com/services/...
supabase secrets list
# Local development: put the same keys in supabase/functions/.env (git-ignored)

Inside the function, read it with Deno.env.get('SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL'). Dev and prod projects each have their own secrets, so a test run never posts to the real team channel.

Calling a function from Flutter

try {
  final res = await Supabase.instance.client.functions.invoke(
    'project-report',
    body: {'projectId': projectId},
  );
  final data = res.data; // decoded JSON, here a Map
} on FunctionException catch (e) {
  debugPrint('Failed with status ' + e.status.toString());
}

supabase_flutter attaches the signed-in user’s access token for you, and refreshes it as the session changes. Any non-2xx response becomes a FunctionException with status and details. Map the status codes to messages the same way you mapped DioException types in lesson 9.1: 401 means “sign in again”, 4xx means “fix the input”, 5xx means “try later”.

Webhooks

A payment provider cannot send a Supabase JWT. For that one function, deploy with supabase functions deploy stripe-webhook --no-verify-jwt (or set verify_jwt = false for it in supabase/config.toml) and verify the provider’s signature inside the function using its signing secret. A webhook function without signature checks is an open door.

Environments: dev and prod

Use two Supabase projects, taskflow-dev and taskflow-prod. Each has its own URL, keys, users, secrets and data. The app picks one at build time:

// env/dev.json  {"APP_ENV":"dev","SUPABASE_URL":"https://DEV.supabase.co","SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY":"..."}
// env/prod.json {"APP_ENV":"prod","SUPABASE_URL":"https://PROD.supabase.co","SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY":"..."}

flutter run --dart-define-from-file=env/dev.json
flutter build appbundle --release --dart-define-from-file=env/prod.json \
  --obfuscate --split-debug-info=build/symbols

Remember from lesson 11.1: these values are configuration, not secrets. The publishable key is public by design, and RLS protects the data. Combine this with the flavors from lesson 8.5 if you want dev and prod installed side by side.

Screen 2: One app, two projects lib/env.dart

// flutter run --dart-define-from-file=env/dev.json
// flutter build appbundle --dart-define-from-file=env/prod.json
abstract final class Env {
  static const name = String.fromEnvironment('APP_ENV', defaultValue: 'dev');
  static const supabaseUrl = String.fromEnvironment('SUPABASE_URL');
  static const supabaseKey = String.fromEnvironment('SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY');
  static bool get isProd => name == 'prod';
}

class EnvBanner extends StatelessWidget {
  const EnvBanner({super.key, required this.child});
  final Widget child;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    if (Env.isProd) return child;
    return Column(children: [
      Container(
        width: double.infinity,
        color: Colors.orange,
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(4),
        child: const SafeArea(
          bottom: false,
          child: Text('DEV · taskflow-dev', textAlign: TextAlign.center),
        ),
      ),
      Expanded(child: child),
    ]);
  }
}

The same code runs against the dev or prod Supabase project, chosen at build time with --dart-define-from-file. A banner makes dev builds impossible to mistake for production. States: Dev build → Prod build.

Migrations with the Supabase CLI

The SQL you ran by hand in lessons 12.2 and 12.3 should become migration files in supabase/migrations, committed to git and reviewed like code:

supabase migration new add_attachment_path   # empty timestamped .sql file to fill in
supabase start                               # local stack in Docker
supabase db reset                            # rebuild local DB from all migrations
supabase test db                             # run pgTAP policy tests
supabase link --project-ref YOUR_DEV_REF && supabase db push    # apply to dev
supabase link --project-ref YOUR_PROD_REF && supabase db push   # then prod

supabase db diff can generate a migration from changes you made locally, and supabase db pull captures an existing remote schema to start from. The rule is simple: prod changes only through migrations that already ran in dev. In a team, a CI job runs db push and functions deploy when the main branch changes.

Backups, limits and monitoring

  • Backups: what you get depends on your plan; point-in-time recovery is an add-on. Read your plan’s current backup terms and practise a restore into a dev project before you need it.
  • Limits: database size, storage, bandwidth, Realtime connections and function calls all have plan limits, and free projects can be paused when inactive. Check the current pricing page rather than trusting old blog posts.
  • Auth email: the built-in email sender is meant for testing. Set up your own SMTP provider before launch.
  • Monitoring: the dashboard has logs for the API, Auth, Storage and each function, plus Security and Performance Advisors that flag tables without RLS and missing indexes.

Example: shipping TaskFlow

The project-report function counts the user’s tasks in a project (as that user, so RLS applies) and, if a SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL secret is set, posts a summary. The Flutter card calls it and handles success and failure.

Screen 1: Project report lib/project_report_card.dart

Future<void> _send() async {
  setState(() {
    _loading = true;
    _error = null;
  });
  try {
    // supabase_flutter adds the user's JWT for you.
    final res = await Supabase.instance.client.functions
        .invoke('project-report', body: {'projectId': widget.projectId});
    if (!mounted) return;
    if (res.data case {'total': int total, 'done': int done, 'open': int open,
        'posted': bool posted, 'slackConfigured': bool slackConfigured}) {
      setState(() => _report = (total: total, done: done, open: open,
          posted: posted, slackConfigured: slackConfigured));
    } else {
      setState(() => _error = 'Unexpected response');
    }
  } on FunctionException catch (e) {
    if (!mounted) return;
    final status = e.status;
    setState(() => _error = status == 401
        ? 'Please sign in again.'
        : 'Report failed (' + status.toString() + ').');
  } finally {
    if (mounted) setState(() => _loading = false);
  }
}

// build(): a Card with the numbers, a FilledButton 'Send report',
// a LinearProgressIndicator while _loading, and _error in red.

The button calls an Edge Function. The function counts tasks as the signed-in user (RLS applies) and posts to Slack with a secret the app never sees. The last frame shows a FunctionException with status 401 turned into a friendly message. States: Idle → Loading → Report → Error 401.

The secret never leaves the server; the app only ever holds public values.

Screen 3: Where the secret lives supabase/functions/project-report/index.ts

// TypeScript (Deno), runs on Supabase, never in the app
Deno.serve(async (req: Request) => {
  const authHeader = req.headers.get('Authorization');
  if (!authHeader) return json({ error: 'Not signed in' }, 401);

  // Acts AS the caller: every query obeys RLS.
  const supabase = createClient(
    Deno.env.get('SUPABASE_URL') ?? '',
    Deno.env.get('SUPABASE_ANON_KEY') ?? '',
    { global: { headers: { Authorization: authHeader } } },
  );

  const webhook = Deno.env.get('SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL'); // secret
  // ...count tasks, post to Slack, return JSON
});

An architecture view, not a real screen. The app holds only public values. The function holds the secret and talks to the database as the user, so RLS still applies.

Before the first store release, walk through this checklist with a teammate:

AreaCheck
KeysOnly the URL and publishable key are in the app. Secret and service_role keys exist only as function secrets. Any key that ever leaked has been rotated.
RLSRLS is on for every table in exposed schemas, every command has a policy, policies have with check where needed, and pgTAP tests pass. The Security Advisor shows no warnings.
StoragePersonal files are in private buckets with folder-per-user policies, shown through signed URLs.
AuthEmail confirmation on, production redirect URLs and deep links set, custom SMTP configured, session tokens stored as lesson 11.1 recommends.
FunctionsEvery function checks the caller; webhook functions verify signatures; errors return clear status codes without leaking internals.
EnvironmentsSeparate dev and prod projects; prod built with env/prod.json; schema changes only through migrations.
Data safetyBackup terms known, a restore practised, plan limits reviewed.
AppRelease build obfuscated with symbols kept for crash reports, no secrets or tokens in logs, OWASP MASVS items from lesson 11.2 reviewed.

Common mistakes

  • Using the service_role key in a function for everything. Every bug becomes a data leak. Query as the user by default.
  • Turning off verify_jwt “because the call failed”. Find out why the token was missing instead. Turn it off only for webhooks that verify a signature.
  • Testing against prod. Test users and junk rows end up in real reports, and one wrong delete is real data loss.
  • Editing the prod schema in the dashboard. The migrations no longer describe reality, and the next db push surprises you.
  • Returning raw error messages from functions. Log details on the server; return a short message and a status code.
  • Assuming backups exist. Check the plan and test a restore.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Explain why a mobile app needs a backend function for secrets, and why --dart-define does not solve it.
  • Describe how the function knows the user (JWT from functions.invoke) and why querying as the user keeps RLS in force.
  • Talk about environments and migrations as a workflow: local, dev, then prod, with CI running pushes and deploys.
  • Mention webhooks with signature verification: it shows you have handled real payments or integrations.
  • Close with the checklist mindset: security, data safety and observability are part of “done”.

terms.definition: A TypeScript function that runs on Deno on Supabase’s servers and is called over HTTPS, usually from your app or a webhook.
The supabase_flutter method that calls an Edge Function with a JSON body and the current user’s access token.
A value set with supabase secrets set and read with Deno.env.get inside the function. It never ships in the app.
The default Edge Function setting that rejects requests without a valid Supabase JWT before your code runs.
A timestamped SQL file in supabase/migrations that changes the schema; the CLI applies migrations in order to each environment.
The Dart exception thrown when a function call fails, with an HTTP status and details.

quiz.question: TaskFlow must post a summary to the team’s Slack webhook. Where should the webhook URL live?
options: In a const in lib/config.dart
In env/prod.json passed with --dart-define-from-file
In an Edge Function secret, used only by server code the app calls
In a hidden Supabase table the app reads at startup
quiz.explanation: Anything in the app, including dart-define values, can be extracted. A function secret stays on the server; the app only asks the function to do the work.

quiz.question: Inside an Edge Function you create the Supabase client with the caller’s Authorization header and the publishable or anon key. What does that give you?
options: Queries run as that user, so RLS still decides which rows they can touch
Queries bypass RLS because they run on the server
The function can read every user’s rows
It removes the need for verify_jwt
quiz.explanation: Forwarding the user’s JWT makes the function act as the caller. Only a client built with the secret or service_role key bypasses RLS, and then your code must do all the checks.

quiz.question: A teammate edited a column in the production dashboard to fix a bug. What is the main risk?
options: Dashboard edits are slower than SQL
Prod no longer matches the migration files, so the next deploy or a fresh environment can break or undo the change
The column becomes public
Edge Functions stop working
quiz.explanation: Migrations are the record of the schema. Hand edits in prod drift from them. Make the change as a migration, test it in dev, then push it to prod.

quiz.question: A Stripe webhook must reach an Edge Function. Stripe cannot send a Supabase JWT. What is the correct setup?
options: Put the service_role key in Stripe’s dashboard
Make the tasks table public
Call the function from the app instead
Deploy that function with JWT verification off and verify Stripe’s signature with a secret inside the function
quiz.explanation: Webhooks use their own authentication. Turn off verify_jwt for that one function only and check the provider’s signature with the signing secret stored as a function secret.
